name: Andhra Pradesh
tagline: Andhra Pradesh stretches along the coast where two big rivers meet the sea, and it is dotted with old temple towns. It is also home to a long-standing Deccani Muslim community, so its culture blends Hindu temple traditions with Muslim history from the Deccan region.

festivals.name: Ugadi
festivals.reach: People celebrate Ugadi widely across the state.
festivals.what: Ugadi is the Telugu New Year. Families clean their houses and decorate their doorways before the day begins. The day starts with everyone tasting a special dish called Ugadi pachadi, which mixes six different tastes together at once.
festivals.who: Telugu-speaking families across Andhra Pradesh and Telangana celebrate Ugadi, as do Telugu communities living in other parts of India and around the world. Kannada and Konkani communities also celebrate the same day, but they call it by different names.
festivals.when: Ugadi falls on the first day of the month of Chaitra in the lunisolar calendar. This usually lands in late March or early April, shortly after the spring equinox.
festivals.origin: The date of Ugadi comes from the lunisolar calendar used across the Deccan region, a calendar that follows both the moon and the sun. The way people celebrate it today developed slowly over many centuries, and no one knows for sure exactly when or how the festival first began.
festivals.signifies: Ugadi is a fresh start for the new year. People show this idea through a special dish called Ugadi pachadi. It mixes six different tastes together at the same time: sweet, sour, salty, spicy, bitter, and tangy. Eating all these flavors together, instead of one at a time, reminds people that a whole year brings many different kinds of days, good and hard, often mixed together, and that this is completely normal.
festivals.beliefs: Many families believe that clues about the coming year can be read on this day. So they gather to listen to the panchangam, a yearly almanac reading that predicts what the next twelve months might bring.
festivals.celebrate: Families string mango leaves across their doorways and draw rice-flour patterns called muggu on the ground at their entrance. People wear new clothes for the day. They make Ugadi pachadi using raw mango, neem flower, jaggery, tamarind, salt, and chilli. Temples hold panchanga sravanam, the public reading of the yearly almanac. In the afternoon, people also hold poetry and music gatherings called kavi sammelanam.
festivals.local: The neem flower in the pachadi is not just there for show, it is meant to be truly tasted. Families often argue about exactly how much of each ingredient to use, and if a family's pachadi turns out too sweet, people jokingly see it as a small sign that they lost their nerve.
festivals.image: Ugadi pachadi being mixed at a home kitchen counter, morning light

festivals.name: Sankranti
festivals.reach: People celebrate Sankranti widely across the state, and it is celebrated most strongly in rural districts.
festivals.what: Sankranti is the biggest harvest festival in the state, and people celebrate it over three or four days. During this time, cities in coastal Andhra empty out because families travel back to their home villages.
festivals.who: Farming families celebrate Sankranti the most, but really the whole state takes part. In Andhra, people call it Pedda Panduga, which means 'the big festival.'
festivals.when: Sankranti falls in mid-January, on the day the sun moves into the zodiac sign of Makara. Unlike most Indian festivals, it follows the solar calendar instead of the lunar one, so it falls on roughly the same date every year.
festivals.origin: People across South Asia have marked this solar, farming-based festival in various forms for many centuries. In Andhra, its timing is tied to the rice-growing calendar of the Krishna and Godavari river deltas.
festivals.signifies: Sankranti marks the end of the harvest season and the moment the sun begins moving north again. People use this time to settle any debts they owe, and they honor the cattle that worked hard through the farming season.
festivals.beliefs: The first day, called Bhogi, is for burning old and unwanted things. The last day, called Kanuma, is for honoring the cattle, because people believe the harvest could not have happened without them.
festivals.celebrate: People light Bhogi bonfires at dawn. They draw rangoli patterns in their courtyards and decorate them with gobbemmalu, small mounds made of cow dung and flowers. Families make ariselu and other sweets using jaggery. People also fly kites and lead decorated bulls through the villages. In parts of coastal Andhra, some people also practice cockfighting during Sankranti, though this tradition is controversial and disputed.
festivals.local: In the Godavari districts, singers called Haridasu walk through the village lanes at first light, balancing a brass pot on their heads and singing devotional songs. If a household does not give them rice, neighbors quietly take notice.
festivals.image: Bhogi bonfire at dawn in a village courtyard, decorated bulls nearby

festivals.name: Tirumala Brahmotsavam
festivals.reach: It draws pilgrims from across South India and beyond.
festivals.what: Tirumala Brahmotsavam is the nine-day annual festival of the Venkateswara temple at Tirumala. During the festival, the temple's processional deity is carried through the streets each morning and evening, riding a different vahana, or vehicle, every time.
festivals.who: Pilgrims from many different language groups attend, including people who speak Telugu, Tamil, Kannada, and Marathi, along with a large number of Indians living abroad. It is one of the most heavily attended temple festivals anywhere in the world.
festivals.when: The festival lasts nine days during the month of Ashwayuja, usually in late September or October. Its exact timing is set to coincide with the star Shravana.
festivals.origin: Temple records and stone inscriptions show that people have been funding festival processions here for many centuries. The Vijayanagara period, in particular, greatly expanded the temple's festival calendar.
festivals.signifies: The festival is about the deity leaving the inner sanctum so that everyone can see him, including people who will never be allowed inside the inner temple itself. Being seen by everyone is the whole point of the celebration.
festivals.beliefs: According to tradition, the god Brahma himself performed this ritual first, which is why it is called Brahmotsavam. Devotees believe that getting darshan, meaning a sacred glimpse of the deity, during these nine days is especially powerful.
festivals.celebrate: The fifth day, called Garuda Seva, draws the largest crowds of the whole festival. On other days, the deity is carried in processions on mounts shaped like a swan, an elephant, a horse, and a chariot. The festival opens on day one with a flag-raising ceremony called Dhwajarohanam, and it closes with Chakrasnanam, a ceremony where the sacred discus is bathed. Lines of waiting pilgrims can stretch for kilometers along the streets.
festivals.local: Regular pilgrims treat each vahana as completely different from the others, not interchangeable at all. Many can tell you exactly which day it is just by seeing which mount is being used, and they plan their whole year's travel around being present for Garuda Seva.
festivals.image: Processional deity on the Garuda vahana, Tirumala street, dense crowd

festivals.name: Dasara
festivals.reach: People celebrate it widely across the state, with especially strong celebrations at the temple centers of Vijayawada and Simhachalam.
festivals.what: Dasara is ten nights devoted to the goddess, and it ends on a day called Vijayadashami. In Andhra Pradesh, the main center of the celebration is the Kanaka Durga temple at Vijayawada, where the goddess is dressed as a different form of herself each day.
festivals.who: Hindu households across the state celebrate Dasara. It is also a holiday season for schools and workplaces, and it is traditionally seen as the right time for children to begin formal learning.
festivals.when: Dasara takes place during the bright half of the month of Ashwayuja, in September or October.
festivals.origin: The wider Navaratri festival is an old tradition observed all across India. The Andhra version of it centers on worshipping the goddess Durga and on the Alankarams, the daily costume changes given to the deity at major temples.
festivals.signifies: The story says the goddess Durga fought and defeated a demon named Mahishasura. People see this as a story about good winning against evil, especially against a kind of evil that cannot be talked out of doing harm.
festivals.beliefs: On the ninth day, people set aside their tools, instruments, and books and worship them instead of using them. The tenth day is believed to be a lucky time to begin anything new.
festivals.celebrate: The Kanaka Durga temple holds a different Alankaram costume for the goddess every day. People perform Ayudha Puja, a ceremony to worship their tools, instruments, and vehicles. On Vijayadashami, people exchange Jammi leaves with each other. In districts near the Telangana border, people also build Bathukamma, stacked arrangements of flowers. Many people choose the tenth day to start new business ventures or begin new schooling.
festivals.local: In Vijayawada, instead of a street procession, the goddess is carried out on a swan-shaped boat during a ceremony called Theppotsavam, which takes place on the Krishna river.
festivals.image: Kanaka Durga temple at Vijayawada during Alankaram, lamps and marigold

festivals.name: Ramzan & Eid al-Fitr
festivals.season: Ninth month of the Hijri calendar
festivals.reach: It is especially significant for Muslim communities, but the culture of iftar, the evening meal that breaks the fast, is shared far beyond them.
festivals.what: Ramzan is a month of fasting from dawn to dusk, and it ends with the celebration of Eid al-Fitr. Andhra Pradesh's Muslim population is mostly concentrated in the old Deccan towns of Kurnool, Kadapa, Nellore, Guntur, and Vijayawada.
festivals.who: Muslim communities across Andhra Pradesh observe Ramzan. Many of them speak Dakhni Urdu, a version of Urdu specific to the Deccan region that is distinct from the Urdu spoken in northern India.
festivals.when: Ramzan falls in the ninth month of the Hijri calendar. Because this calendar is based purely on the moon, Ramzan moves about eleven days earlier each year compared to the regular Gregorian calendar.
festivals.origin: The fast of Ramzan is commanded in the Qur'an. The way it is practiced in the Deccan region developed under the Bahmani and Qutb Shahi kingdoms, and later under Hyderabad state, and this history shaped both the special foods and the mosque calendar of this region.
festivals.signifies: Ramzan represents self-control, required charity toward others, and the deliberate idea that everyone, rich or poor, shares the same table at sunset when the fast breaks.
festivals.beliefs: People believe the last ten nights of Ramzan carry special spiritual importance, and among them they search for Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power, believed to be the holiest night of the year.
festivals.celebrate: Before dawn, families eat a meal called sehri, which is often announced by drummers walking through the lanes to wake people up. At sunset, they break the fast with iftar, eating dates, haleem, and a Deccan sweet called double ka meetha. At night, people perform special Taraweeh prayers. Before Eid arrives, they give Zakat and Fitra, forms of charity. On Eid morning, everyone gathers for a congregational prayer, and afterward, families open their homes to visitors.
festivals.local: Haleem stalls pop up outside mosques in Kurnool and Guntur only during the month of Ramzan, and then they disappear completely once it ends. This is part of why the whole city notices Ramzan happening, even among people who are not fasting.
festivals.image: Iftar table at sunset outside a mosque, dates and haleem, Dakhni town

festivals.name: Peerla Panduga
festivals.season: First month of the Hijri calendar
festivals.reach: It is especially significant in rural coastal villages and in the Rayalaseema region, where people of different religious communities take part together.
festivals.what: Peerla Panduga is how rural Andhra observes Muharram, and its name locally means 'the festival of the peers.' Villagers set up tall metal poles called alams. Each alam stands for one of the people who died fighting in the battle of Karbala long ago. People carry the alams through the village in a procession, and at the end they cool the poles down by pouring water over them.
festivals.who: Muslim families are the traditional caretakers of this festival, but in many villages, Hindu households also make vows to the alams, help carry them, or host them in their own homes. Researchers have documented this kind of shared practice across the wider Deccan region.
festivals.when: Peerla Panduga takes place during the first ten days of the month of Muharram, and its dates shift each year because they follow the lunar calendar.
festivals.origin: The tradition of remembering Husain's death at Karbala came into the Deccan region through Shi'a rulers, first under the Qutb Shahi state and later under Hyderabad state. Over time, village communities added their own local traditions of making vows on top of this original commemoration.
festivals.signifies: The festival represents mourning for what happened at Karbala. Locally, it also represents an agreement between a village and its 'peers,' protector figures that villagers turn to for help during illness or drought.
festivals.beliefs: People make vows to the alams, for example asking for a sick child to recover or for a good farming season. If their wish comes true, they repay the vow by carrying the alam in the procession or by walking across a fire pit.
festivals.celebrate: Special buildings called ashurkhanas are opened, and the alams are set up inside them. At night, people play drums and sing marsiya, songs of mourning. In some villages, people walk across fire pits as part of the observance. People also hand out malida and sweet rice to those gathered. On the tenth day, the alams are carried down to a body of water.
festivals.local: Anthropologists have long noted that in some Deccan villages, a Hindu family holds the inherited right to carry a specific alam, a right passed down through generations. Locally, nobody finds this unusual at all.
festivals.image: Alam standards installed in a village ashurkhana, night, drums

festivals.name: Christmas
festivals.aliases: Pedda Panduga (among some Christian families), Bada Din
festivals.reach: It is especially significant for Andhra's Protestant and Catholic communities, who are concentrated in the coastal districts.
festivals.what: Christmas in coastal Andhra is a large, long-standing community festival built around church-centered village life, especially in the districts of Krishna, Guntur, West Godavari, and Prakasam.
festivals.who: Protestant churches take part, including Lutheran, Baptist, and Church of South India congregations, along with Catholic parishes. Telugu Christian hymn music forms its own large and distinct body of songs.
festivals.when: Christmas falls on December 25th. Weeks of carol singing lead up to it, and new year church services follow afterward.
festivals.origin: In the nineteenth century, Lutheran, Baptist, and Anglican missionaries built large numbers of congregations in the delta districts. The Telugu style of Christmas grew naturally out of those village churches, rather than being copied directly from anywhere else.
festivals.signifies: Christmas represents the birth of Jesus, and in the delta villages, it also represents the yearly reunion of families whose members have moved away for work.
festivals.beliefs: Many churches hold watch-night services on December 31st, so that people cross into the new year while inside the church rather than out celebrating elsewhere.
festivals.celebrate: Carol teams walk from house to house throughout December. Churches hold a midnight service on Christmas Eve. Families hang paper stars over their doorways and wear new clothes. At midday, they often eat biryani or mutton curry. People sing Telugu Christian keertanas, devotional songs, accompanied by harmonium and dholak drums instead of an organ.
festivals.local: Telugu carols are often set to tunes influenced by Carnatic classical music and sung with dholak drums and cymbals. Because of this, a carol round in a delta village sounds completely different from a European one.
festivals.image: Carol singers with dholak walking a delta village lane at night, paper star

festivals.name: Prabhala Teertham
festivals.reach: This festival is concentrated in the Konaseema region, in Dr. B. R. Ambedkar Konaseema district.
festivals.what: During Prabhala Teertham, eleven village deities are carried on tall, decorated palanquins called prabhalu across flooded paddy fields. They are brought to a shared meeting ground at Jagganna Thota, where all eleven meet together once a year.
festivals.who: The eleven villages of the Konaseema cluster take part, and each village is responsible for building its own prabha and providing its own bearers to carry it.
festivals.when: The festival happens the day after Kanuma, which is immediately after Sankranti, so it falls in mid-January.
festivals.origin: This is a local tradition of the villages in the Godavari delta, kept alive through village custom rather than run by any large temple institution. Its history has mostly been passed down through spoken stories rather than written records.
festivals.signifies: The festival represents kinship between villages. The deities visit one another, and because of this, the villages themselves are obligated to meet each year too.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that when the prabhalu meet, it renews the bond between the eleven villages for the year ahead.
festivals.celebrate: Villagers build the prabhalu out of bamboo and cloth, and some of them stand several stories tall. Bearers wade waist-deep through flooded fields and canals while carrying these tall structures. Drums, brass bands, and crowds line the raised paths along the fields. The deities are set down together for a few hours, and then carried back home again on the very same day.
festivals.local: The prabhalu are carried straight through the water rather than around it. The photos that circulate every January, showing men standing shoulder-deep in a canal while holding up a tall bamboo tower, capture exactly what makes this festival special.
festivals.image: Tall bamboo prabhalu carried through flooded paddy fields, Konaseema

name: Kerala
tagline: Kerala is a narrow strip of land along the coast. For a very long time, Hindu, Muslim, Christian, and Jewish communities have all lived here side by side.

festivals.name: Onam
festivals.reach: People across the state celebrate Onam, no matter which community they belong to.
festivals.what: Onam is Kerala's harvest festival and its official state festival, and people celebrate it over ten days. It is one of the rare Indian festivals that is widely celebrated across different religions within a single language community.
festivals.who: Malayalis in general celebrate Onam. Hindu, Christian, and Muslim families all keep some form of the festival, and so does the large community of Malayalis living in the Gulf countries.
festivals.when: Onam falls on the Onam star, or asterism, during the month of Chingam, which is in August or September.
festivals.origin: Onam combines an old farming harvest cycle with the legend of King Mahabali. It is hard to separate these two parts historically, and scholars still disagree about which one came first.
festivals.signifies: Onam represents the yearly return of King Mahabali to visit his people, and the idea that everyone should appear prosperous and equal while he is watching.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that Mahabali visits Kerala for these ten days. This story is unusual among Indian myths because it treats a defeated king as the beloved, celebrated figure, rather than the god who defeated him.
festivals.celebrate: Families create pookalam, flower carpets that grow bigger each day of the festival. They share the Onasadya, a vegetarian feast of twenty or more dishes eaten off a banana leaf. Kerala also holds Vallam Kali, snake-boat races, and in Thrissur, performers dress up as tigers for the Pulikali dance. Households give everyone new clothes, called Onakkodi, including the people who work for them.
festivals.local: The sadya is served in a fixed order along the banana leaf, and a Malayali can often tell where a cook was trained just by looking at which pickle is placed at the top left corner.
festivals.image: Onasadya on a banana leaf, twenty items, overhead

festivals.name: Vishu
festivals.reach: People celebrate Vishu widely across the state.
festivals.what: Vishu is the astronomical new year, and it begins with Vishukkani, the very first thing a person sees when they wake up. The night before, families arrange this sight carefully, using a lamp, a mirror, gold, rice, and the yellow konna flower.
festivals.who: Hindu households across Kerala celebrate Vishu, along with Malayali families living elsewhere.
festivals.when: Vishu happens when the sun enters the zodiac sign of Medam, around April 14th. This is the same solar moment that other parts of India mark as Baisakhi, Puthandu, and Bihu.
festivals.origin: Vishu is a solar new year celebration shared across South and Southeast Asia. The specific practice of arranging the kani, though, is unique to Kerala, and nobody knows exactly how old it is.
festivals.signifies: Vishu represents the idea that the quality of your whole year is set by the very first thing you look at.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that what you see right after waking up shapes how your whole year will go. Because of this, families arrange the Vishukkani with great care, and they lead children to it with their eyes covered until it is time to look.
festivals.celebrate: Families lay out the Vishukkani in front of a mirror. Elders give coins to children in a custom called Vishukkaineettam. People eat a mixed sweet-and-bitter dish called Vishu katta, along with a full feast called sadya. The konna flower blooms right on time for the festival every year. In some districts, people also set off firecrackers at dawn.
festivals.local: If the konna tree blooms early or late, people read it as a comment on the weather that year. A Vishu without konna flowers is considered a small, real disappointment locally.
festivals.image: Vishukkani arrangement before a mirror, lamp and konna flowers, pre-dawn

festivals.name: Thrissur Pooram
festivals.reach: It is a city festival of Thrissur that draws visitors from across Kerala.
festivals.what: Thrissur Pooram is a day-long temple festival in which two rival groups of temples face off against each other across the Thekkinkad ground. They compete using panchavadyam and melam percussion ensembles, colorful parasol exchanges, and, at night, competitive fireworks displays.
festivals.who: The whole city of Thrissur takes part, organized around the two rival temples of Paramekkavu and Thiruvambady. The festival even has dedicated percussion fans who follow individual drummers the way some people follow sports stars.
festivals.when: Thrissur Pooram takes place on the Pooram star, or asterism, during the month of Medam, in April or May.
festivals.origin: People generally credit Sakthan Thampuran of Kochi with organizing the festival in the late eighteenth century. He is said to have combined several scattered local poorams into one single city-wide festival.
festivals.signifies: The festival represents a city's rivalry expressed as art. The competition between the two temple groups is completely real, but it plays out through percussion music and color rather than through conflict.
festivals.beliefs: The festival has a devotional purpose, but it is also honestly about beauty and performance. Many people in the audience openly admit they come mainly for the Ilanjithara Melam, the big percussion performance.
festivals.celebrate: Musicians perform Ilanjithara Melam, a percussion performance that lasts several hours under a tree. During Kudamattam, people standing on elephant-back rapidly exchange colorful decorated parasols. Panchavadyam percussion ensembles also perform. At night, the two temple groups compete in a fireworks exchange that runs on into the early morning.
festivals.local: Each year, the Kudamattam parasols are designed in complete secrecy and only revealed during the exchange itself. Because of this, the crowd's reaction the moment a new parasol is lifted becomes part of how people judge the competition.
festivals.image: Kudamattam parasol exchange at Thrissur Pooram, Thekkinkad maidan, afternoon

festivals.name: Attukal Pongala
festivals.reach: It is concentrated in Thiruvananthapuram, though participants travel there from across Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
festivals.what: Attukal Pongala is an offering cooked outdoors by women. For a single morning, they fill the streets of Thiruvananthapuram around the Attukal temple with brick hearths and earthen cooking pots.
festivals.who: Only women take part, and they come from many different communities and social classes. The number of women who attend is so large that it has drawn official record-keeping attention.
festivals.when: It falls on the ninth day of the larger Attukal festival, during the month of Kumbham, in February or March.
festivals.origin: The Attukal temple is connected to the story of Kannaki, which links it to the Tamil epic tradition called Silappadikaram. However, the Pongala event reaching its current massive scale is a more recent development.
festivals.signifies: The festival represents a ritual performed by women in public space, on streets that are given over entirely to them for as long as the festival lasts.
festivals.beliefs: People believe the offering is accepted once the temple priest sprinkles holy water over the cooking pots. Many families keep this as an annual vow, returning to take part every year.
festivals.celebrate: The night before, women build brick hearths along kilometers of road. On the day itself, they cook rice, jaggery, and coconut together in new earthen pots. The temple priest makes rounds to bless the offerings. The city reroutes its traffic to make room for the event, and residents along the route give out free food and water to everyone taking part.
festivals.local: Households along the route let strangers use their front steps, water taps, and shade for the day without being asked twice. Nobody organizes this formally, but somehow it always works smoothly.
festivals.image: Streets filled with earthen pots on brick hearths at dawn, Attukal

festivals.name: Eid al-Fitr
festivals.reach: It is especially significant for Kerala's Mappila Muslim communities, and it is strongest in the Malabar region.
festivals.what: Eid al-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan, and locally people call it Cheriya Perunnal, meaning 'the small feast.' Kerala's Muslim community is among the oldest in India, with trade connections across the Arabian Sea that go back even before medieval times.
festivals.who: Mappila Muslims of the Malabar region celebrate it the most, especially in Malappuram, Kozhikode, and Kannur, along with Muslim communities across the rest of the state.
festivals.when: Eid al-Fitr falls on the first day of the month of Shawwal, and its date shifts every year because it follows the Hijri lunar calendar.
festivals.origin: Islam arrived on the Malabar coast by sea trade rather than through conquest. Because of this, the Mappila culture that grew from it, including its own way of speaking, its food, and its songs, developed together with the rest of Kerala's culture rather than separately from it.
festivals.signifies: Eid al-Fitr represents the end of the fast, and it is a day for visiting others, where people feel obligated to visit their neighbors no matter what religion those neighbors follow.
festivals.beliefs: People give Zakat al-Fitr, a form of charity, before the Eid prayer, so that the feast afterward can be shared with everyone rather than kept private.
festivals.celebrate: People gather for Eid prayer at the mosque or at an open prayer ground called the Eidgah. They eat Mappila dishes such as pathiri, thalassery biryani, chatti pathiri, and a layered sweet called mutta mala. People wear new clothes and perfume called attar. In the wedding season that follows, people sing Oppana and Mappilappattu songs. Throughout the day, families keep their homes open to visitors.
festivals.local: Thalassery biryani is made with short-grained kaima rice instead of basmati rice. Malabar cooks will tell you this is not a substitute ingredient at all, it is simply what the real dish is supposed to use.
festivals.image: Mappila Eid table, pathiri and biryani, Malabar household

festivals.name: Christmas & Carols
festivals.reach: It is especially significant for Kerala's Syrian Christian, Latin Catholic, and Protestant communities.
festivals.what: Christmas in Kerala is celebrated by one of the oldest continuously existing Christian communities in the world, and both its church services and its food have taken on a distinctly local Kerala shape.
festivals.who: Many groups celebrate it, including Syro-Malabar and Syro-Malankara Catholics, Orthodox and Jacobite churches, the Marthoma church, Latin Catholics along the coast, and various Protestant denominations.
festivals.when: Christmas falls on December 25th. Before it, many observe a period of Advent fasting, and church feasts continue on into January afterward.
festivals.origin: Kerala's Christian community traces its beginnings back to the apostle Thomas in the first century. Historians agree the tradition is genuinely very old, though written records only begin later, and they can confirm links to the Persian church starting from the early medieval period.
festivals.signifies: Christmas represents the birth of Jesus, and for these churches, it is also a way of asserting that their traditions are as ancient as any in the whole Christian world.
festivals.beliefs: Many families observe a twenty-five day Advent fast leading up to Christmas, and they break this fast at the midnight church service.
festivals.celebrate: Churches hold a midnight qurbana, a service using a liturgy descended from the ancient Syriac language. Families hang star-shaped lanterns at their gates. Carol groups go house to house, often with someone in costume leading them. Families make plum cake and wine at home weeks in advance. After the midnight service, they eat appam with stew, or sometimes duck roast.
festivals.local: Syrian Christian Christmas food is simply Kerala food, appam, stew, and duck roast, and it gets served after a church service partly sung in the ancient Syriac language. Neither the food nor the liturgy is treated as a compromise to the other, both are fully kept as they are.
festivals.image: Star lantern at a Kerala house gate at night, midnight service crowd behind

festivals.name: Maramon Convention
festivals.season: Dry season, on the Pamba riverbed
festivals.reach: It is especially significant for the Marthoma church and other reformed Christian communities of central Travancore.
festivals.what: The Maramon Convention is a week-long Christian gathering held right on the dry, sandy bed of the Pamba river at Maramon. Organizers build a temporary pandal, or pavilion, that seats tens of thousands of people.
festivals.who: The Marthoma Syrian Church organizes it mainly, but people from other Christian denominations across central Kerala attend as well.
festivals.when: The convention happens in February, during the dry weeks of the year when the riverbed is dry enough to support the huge temporary structure.
festivals.origin: The convention began in 1895, growing out of a reform movement within the Malankara church, and it has been held every year since then, except for a few interruptions.
festivals.signifies: The convention represents preaching and teaching done on a huge scale, out in the open air, on ground that is actually underwater for most of the rest of the year.
festivals.beliefs: The convention is meant for teaching rather than for religious rituals or sacraments. Attending it is a habit that many families pass down from one generation to the next.
festivals.celebrate: Workers raise a huge pandal made of bamboo and palm leaves on the sand. The convention holds sessions both morning and evening, with congregational singing in Malayalam. Families travel in from far away and camp nearby for the week. Afterward, the entire structure is taken apart completely.
festivals.local: The venue only exists during February. By the time the monsoon arrives, the Pamba river has taken the ground back completely, and the convention's own literature likes to point this fact out.
festivals.image: Bamboo pandal on the dry Pamba riverbed, crowd seated, Maramon

name: West Bengal
tagline: In West Bengal, the yearly calendar of festivals is built around the worship of the goddess, the rhythms of the river, and a deep love of the printed word.

festivals.name: Durga Puja
festivals.reach: People celebrate it across the state, and the culture of public pandals involves Bengalis from every community.
festivals.what: Durga Puja is five days during which Kolkata and the surrounding districts fill up with temporary pavilions called pandals. Each pandal is specially commissioned from artists and designers, and each one houses a clay image of the goddess Durga made in the Kumartuli workshops.
festivals.who: Bengali Hindu households celebrate Durga Puja, and through the public pandals, effectively the whole state takes part. UNESCO added Kolkata's Durga Puja to its list of intangible cultural heritage in 2021.
festivals.when: It takes place during the bright half of the month of Ashwin, in September or October, running from the day called Shashthi through to the day called Dashami.
festivals.origin: Records show that autumn worship of Durga in Bengal goes back to the late medieval period. The large public celebrations, known as sarbojanin pujas, are a twentieth-century development connected to urban neighborhood associations.
festivals.signifies: The festival represents the goddess's yearly visit to her parents' home, and then her return afterward. In Bengal, people see the festival as much as a daughter coming home as they see it as a story of victory.
festivals.beliefs: At the end of the festival, people immerse the clay images in the river, returning the material back to the water. The idea is that the image is not meant to last forever.
festivals.celebrate: Before dawn on Mahalaya day, people listen to a famous radio recitation. Through the nights of the festival, people go pandal-hopping, visiting one pandal after another. Drummers play the dhaak, and people perform the dhunuchi dance holding burning incense pots. Sandhi Puja is held at the exact junction between the eighth and ninth days. On the tenth day, married women take part in Sindoor Khela, smearing each other with red vermilion powder, and people exchange Bijoya greetings. Throughout all five days, people eat street food continuously.
festivals.local: Designing pandals has become a competitive, contemporary art industry in its own right. Past themes have covered subjects like migrant labor, climate change, and cinema, and crowds will queue for hours just to see a structure that will be taken apart again within the week.
festivals.image: Pandal interior with Durga idol and contemporary art installation, night crowd

festivals.name: Kali Puja
festivals.reach: People celebrate it widely across the state, with major centers of celebration at Kalighat, Dakshineswar, and Tarapith.
festivals.what: Kali Puja is a night festival for the goddess Kali, held on the same new moon night that is celebrated as Diwali in the rest of India. Bengal still lights lamps like everywhere else, but it dedicates the night itself to the goddess Kali.
festivals.who: Bengali Hindu households and neighborhood associations celebrate Kali Puja. It is also central to the state's Shakta and tantric religious traditions.
festivals.when: It falls on Kartik Amavasya, the darkest, moonless night of the month of Kartik, in October or November.
festivals.origin: The worship of Kali in Bengal grew starting in the eighteenth century, supported both by temple patrons and by tantric religious lineages. The Ramakrishna tradition of the nineteenth century then helped spread it much more widely.
festivals.signifies: Kali Puja represents a goddess who is not softened or made gentler for the occasion. Her imagery is deliberately meant to be intense and confronting.
festivals.beliefs: The main worship takes place at midnight. On the evening before, many households also light lamps in memory of their ancestors, which is a separate practice from the Kali Puja itself.
festivals.celebrate: People perform a midnight puja using hibiscus flowers and red cloth. They line their rooftops and parapets with lamps and set off fireworks. Devotees hold an all-night vigil at the temples of Kalighat and Dakshineswar. At Tarapith, there is a tradition of tantric religious practice that draws practitioners from far outside Bengal.
festivals.local: In Bengal, the new moon night of Diwali belongs to Kali. So the same night that is simply lit with lamps in the rest of India is, here, also a night of drumming and long midnight queues at the temples.
festivals.image: Midnight Kali Puja, hibiscus garlands and lamps, Kolkata neighbourhood

festivals.name: Poila Boishakh
festivals.reach: Bengalis of every community celebrate it across the state.
festivals.what: Poila Boishakh is the Bengali new year. Shops open fresh account books called the Haal Khata, and people mark the day mostly with music, processions, and food rather than with religious ritual.
festivals.who: Bengalis of all religions celebrate it. It is also the national new year of Bangladesh, where the Mangal Shobhajatra procession is recognized on UNESCO's heritage list.
festivals.when: It falls in mid-April, around the 14th or 15th, based on the solar Bengali calendar.
festivals.origin: People usually connect the reform of the Bengali calendar to the Mughal period and to the practical needs of collecting agricultural taxes on a yearly cycle. The exact details of how the calendar was formed are still debated.
festivals.signifies: Poila Boishakh represents more of a civic and business reset than a religious one, which is part of why people from every community can celebrate it so easily together.
festivals.beliefs: Starting the year's account book with a small prayer and a sweet is a trade custom that even businesses who follow very few other traditions still keep.
festivals.celebrate: Shops hold Haal Khata ceremonies and give out sweets to customers. People hold Rabindrasangeet concerts, songs written by Rabindranath Tagore, at dawn. There are processions and cultural programs throughout the day. People wear new clothes, and at midday, families eat a meal of fish and rice, using ilish fish if the household can find it.
festivals.local: The Haal Khata is a real, working account book. Shop owners open it with vermilion powder and either a swastika symbol or a Bismillah blessing, depending on the shop's religion. Old Kolkata businesses even keep a specific budget line just for the sweets they give out on this day.
festivals.image: Haal Khata ceremony at an old Kolkata shop, ledger and sweets

festivals.name: Saraswati Puja
festivals.season: Fifth day of the bright fortnight of Magh
festivals.reach: People celebrate it widely, and across the state it works out to be, in effect, a student festival.
festivals.what: Saraswati Puja is a day dedicated to the goddess of learning, and students run most of the celebration themselves. Schools, colleges, and neighborhood clubs called para clubs hold their own pujas, and people place their books in front of the goddess's image.
festivals.who: Students celebrate it above everyone else. It works as Bengal's festival for teenagers, complete with its own unwritten rules about what to wear and what freedoms are allowed on this day.
festivals.when: It falls on the fifth day of the bright half of the month of Magh, in late January or February.
festivals.origin: The wider festival of Basant Panchami is observed across much of India. The way it became a student-organized event in Bengal is tied to the expansion of schooling across the province during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.
festivals.signifies: The festival treats learning as something you must ask for, rather than something you can simply assume you will have.
festivals.beliefs: Students place their books in front of the goddess's image the night before, and they are not supposed to read them again until the puja is finished. Students enforce this rule on each other cheerfully.
festivals.celebrate: People wear yellow saris and panjabis for the occasion. Young children take part in Hatekhori, a ceremony where they write their very first letter while a priest guides their hand. People eat khichuri and labra, a mixed vegetable dish, served on leaf plates. They offer anjali, prayers, using palash flowers. The next day, the images of the goddess are immersed in water.
festivals.local: It is Bengal's unofficial day for teenagers to be seen together in public, with the puja itself acting as the only real chaperone. Generations of Bengali novels and stories have used the day exactly this way in their plots.
festivals.image: College courtyard Saraswati Puja, yellow saris, books at the idol

festivals.name: Eid al-Fitr
festivals.reach: It is especially significant for Bengali Muslim communities, who make up around a quarter of the state's population.
festivals.what: Eid al-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan, and it is kept by a Bengali Muslim population concentrated in Murshidabad, Malda, Uttar Dinajpur, and central Kolkata.
festivals.who: Bengali-speaking Muslim communities across the districts celebrate it, along with Kolkata's Urdu-speaking neighborhoods around Nakhoda Masjid and Zakaria Street.
festivals.when: It falls on the first day of the month of Shawwal, and its date shifts each year because it follows the Hijri lunar calendar.
festivals.origin: Islam has been present in Bengal since the Delhi Sultanate expanded eastward. Over the centuries that followed, Bengali Muslim religious culture developed its own distinct literature, architecture, and food.
festivals.signifies: Eid al-Fitr represents the end of the fast, and in Kolkata, it also brings a night market economy that the whole city ends up using, not just Muslim residents.
festivals.beliefs: People give Zakat, a form of charity, before the Eid prayer. Everyone follows the moon sighting closely, and the actual date of Eid is only confirmed the night before it happens.
festivals.celebrate: People gather for Eid prayer at Nakhoda Masjid and at Red Road. At home, families eat sewai, a sweet vermicelli dish, and shahi tukda. Along Zakaria Street, vendors sell haleem and kebabs throughout the nights of Ramzan. People wear new clothes and spend the afternoon visiting family and friends.
festivals.local: During Ramzan, Zakaria Street becomes a food destination for the whole of Kolkata, whether people are fasting or not. It is one of the clearest examples of how a religious calendar can shape habits that the entire city shares.
festivals.image: Zakaria Street food stalls at night during Ramzan, Kolkata

festivals.name: Bara Din
festivals.reach: It is especially significant for Kolkata's Christian, Anglo-Indian, and Armenian communities, though the Park Street holiday season is enjoyed citywide.
festivals.what: Bara Din means 'the big day.' Kolkata's Christmas is both a church festival for its Christian communities and a secular citywide season centered on Park Street and Bow Barracks.
festivals.who: Catholic and Protestant congregations celebrate it, along with the Anglo-Indian community of Bow Barracks and Armenian and Greek Orthodox congregations whose churches are older than the colonial city's own expansion. The general public of Kolkata also joins in the wider season.
festivals.when: Christmas falls on December 25th, and the Park Street light displays run for weeks on either side of the day.
festivals.origin: Kolkata's Christian institutions date back to the early colonial period, and Armenian and Portuguese communities were actually present even before British expansion into the city. The city's Bara Din culture grew out of this whole mix of communities, rather than out of any single church.
festivals.signifies: Bara Din represents an inheritance from the colonial era that the city kept and made its own, and it has now become largely detached from where it originally came from.
festivals.beliefs: Midnight mass at St Paul's Cathedral and the city's older parish churches remains central for Christian families.
festivals.celebrate: Park Street is lit up from one end to the other, and enormous crowds walk along it. At Nahoum's cake shop in New Market, queues stretch down the aisle. Bow Barracks is decorated and opened up to visitors. Churches hold midnight mass, and many families start baking rum-soaked fruit cake at home as early as November.
festivals.local: Nahoum's, a Jewish-owned bakery in New Market, is where much of Kolkata buys its Christmas cake. The city's Christmas celebration has never really been organized around just one single community.
festivals.image: Park Street illuminations at night, crowds, Kolkata

festivals.name: Poush Mela
festivals.reach: It is concentrated at Santiniketan in Birbhum district, and Baul performers travel there from across Birbhum and from Bangladesh.
festivals.what: Poush Mela is a winter fair at Santiniketan, founded within the Tagore tradition. It features Baul singers, craft stalls from the surrounding districts, and open-air performances that run over several days.
festivals.who: Visva-Bharati University and the town of Santiniketan organize it, along with the Baul and Fakir singers of Birbhum and craftspeople from the Bolpur region.
festivals.when: It falls on the seventh day of the month of Poush, in late December.
festivals.origin: The fair began in the nineteenth century, connected to the Brahmo religious observance at Santiniketan. Rabindranath Tagore then developed it further into a fair that joined the institution together with the countryside surrounding it.
festivals.signifies: The fair represents a deliberate effort to keep an educational institution open and connected to the rural culture that surrounds it, rather than closed off from it.
festivals.beliefs: The Baul tradition featured at the fair is itself a blended devotional practice that draws on Vaishnav, Sufi, and tantric religious strands together, and it resists being neatly classified into any single religion.
festivals.celebrate: Baul singers perform their songs, called Baul gaan, through the day and night. People hold Brahmo prayer services, called upasana, at the Chhatimtala. Craft stalls sell kantha embroidery, dokra metalwork, and leather goods. People eat Poush sweets made from date palm jaggery. The whole fair is surrounded by the winter picnic culture of the Bolpur region.
festivals.local: Nolen gur, fresh date-palm jaggery that is only available for a few weeks each winter, is the reason many Bengalis plan their trip to Santiniketan specifically around Poush Mela.
festivals.image: Baul singer performing at Poush Mela, Santiniketan, winter afternoon

name: Punjab
tagline: Punjab is a wheat farming region built around the gurdwara, the harvest, and long memories of Partition, when India and Pakistan split apart in 1947. Life here still follows the rhythm of the fields and the faith side by side.

festivals.name: Baisakhi
festivals.reach: People celebrate this festival across the whole state, in both rural and urban areas alike.
festivals.what: Baisakhi is the wheat harvest festival. For Sikhs it is also the day the Khalsa, the community of initiated Sikhs, was founded. These two events fall on the same day and are celebrated together, so on the same morning you might see a village fair in the fields and a big gathering at the gurdwara.
festivals.who: Farming families across the state celebrate Baisakhi as a harvest festival. Sikh communities in Punjab and around the world also celebrate it, and for them the day carries extra weight.
festivals.when: Baisakhi falls on April 13 or 14 every year because it is set by the solar calendar rather than the moon. The exact same astronomical moment is celebrated as Vishu in Kerala and as Bihu in Assam.
festivals.origin: As a harvest festival, Baisakhi is very old and existed before Sikhism began. Its second meaning comes from 1699, when Guru Gobind Singh started the Khalsa by initiating its first members at a place called Anandpur Sahib.
festivals.signifies: Baisakhi stands for two things happening on the same day, a crop that has been finished and a community that has just begun. People treat it as two versions of the same idea, something ending and something starting.
festivals.beliefs: Sikhs believe the Khalsa initiation of 1699 was the moment their faith took the form it still has today. Soon after that event, the five articles of faith, special items every initiated Sikh wears or carries, and the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sikh holy book, were established as the eternal Guru, meaning the book itself is treated as a living teacher.
festivals.celebrate: People hold nagar kirtan processions, parades through the streets with religious singing, led by five people called the Panj Pyare, the Five Beloved Ones. There are gatka displays, which are Sikh martial arts performances with swords and sticks, and Akhand Path readings, an unbroken continuous reading of the holy book, at gurdwaras. In village fairgrounds people dance bhangra and giddha, two lively Punjabi folk dances. Wheat stalks are cut and threshed, meaning separated from their husks, with special ceremony on this day. Fairs called melas run into the evening with wrestling matches and folk singing.
festivals.local: In rural Punjab the day still starts in the fields before people move on to the gurdwara. The harvest comes first, and the memory of the Khalsa comes after, and neither one is treated as less important than the other.
festivals.image: Nagar kirtan procession with Panj Pyare, Amritsar street, morning crowd

festivals.name: Lohri
festivals.reach: Households from every community across the state celebrate this festival.
festivals.what: Lohri is a bonfire festival that marks the coldest point of winter and the end of the sugarcane harvest. It is celebrated the evening before another festival called Maghi. Neighbors and extended families gather together around one shared fire.
festivals.who: Punjabi households in general celebrate Lohri, but it is treated as an especially important occasion for a couple who just got married or a family with a newborn baby, since their first Lohri is celebrated in a bigger way.
festivals.when: Lohri happens every year on January 13, the night before Makar Sankranti, and its date is fixed by the solar calendar.
festivals.origin: Lohri has been celebrated on the plains of Punjab for many generations as a way to mark the winter solstice and the end of the sugarcane season. The songs sung at Lohri, including the story of a folk hero named Dulla Bhatti, come from Punjabi oral tradition, meaning they were passed down by word of mouth rather than written down by any single author.
festivals.signifies: Lohri stands for warmth being won back at the coldest turn of the year. It also marks the end of the sugarcane season, and its products, jaggery, a raw sugar called gur, and sesame seeds, called til, are thrown right into the fire that celebrates the festival.
festivals.beliefs: People throw sesame seeds, popcorn, peanuts, and a sweet called gachak into the flames as an offering before eating some themselves. Walking around the fire is meant to be done together with other people, not alone.
festivals.celebrate: A bonfire is lit at dusk in the street or in a courtyard. Sesame seeds, jaggery, and popcorn are offered to the fire and then handed out to eat. Children go door to door singing the ballad of Dulla Bhatti and collecting sweets and money. People dance bhangra and giddha around the flames late into the night.
festivals.local: A household that just had a new baby or a new bride is expected to host a bigger Lohri celebration than usual, and neighbors notice if they are not invited to join in.
festivals.image: Family and neighbours around a Lohri bonfire at night, throwing sesame and popcorn

festivals.name: Hola Mohalla
festivals.reach: This festival is centered on Anandpur Sahib, and it draws Sikhs from across Punjab and from other countries as well.
festivals.what: Hola Mohalla is a three day gathering at Anandpur Sahib built around mock battles, meaning pretend fights staged for show, horseback riding skills, and displays of martial arts. It takes place the day after the festival of Holi.
festivals.who: Nihang Sikhs, who belong to a traditional order of Sikh warriors, are the main performers at Hola Mohalla. Large numbers of Sikhs from the wider community also attend.
festivals.when: Hola Mohalla takes place the day after Holi, usually in March, at Anandpur Sahib in the foothills of the Shivalik mountains.
festivals.origin: Guru Gobind Singh started this gathering in 1701 at Anandpur Sahib. He turned the usual spring festival into a chance for military practice and to review his soldiers along the banks of a river called the Charan Ganga.
festivals.signifies: Hola Mohalla takes the color and fun of Holi and points it toward discipline instead. Where Holi is about play, Hola Mohalla uses that same time of year to keep an army's skills sharp.
festivals.beliefs: People hold this gathering to keep going exactly what the Guru himself used to do, without any break in the tradition. The Nihang orders see their part in it as a duty passed down to them, not as a show performed for onlookers.
festivals.celebrate: There are mock battles and horseback sword fighting displays on the riverbed of the Charan Ganga. People also perform gatka, hold turban tying and tent pegging competitions, a horseback skill, and serve langar, free community meals, to the crowds throughout. A procession of armed Nihangs rides through on decorated horses and elephants.
festivals.local: Nihang riders still stage their mock cavalry charges, on foot and on horseback, on the very same stretch of riverbed where the Guru's soldiers once trained. That is why the crowd gathers close by instead of watching from a distance.
festivals.image: Nihang Sikh horsemen in blue robes performing mock swordplay, Anandpur Sahib

festivals.name: Guru Nanak Gurpurab
festivals.reach: People celebrate this festival across the state and among Sikh communities around the world.
festivals.what: This festival celebrates the birthday of Guru Nanak, who founded the Sikh religion. It is marked with a forty eight hour continuous reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sikh holy book, timed to finish exactly on the day of the festival.
festivals.who: Sikh households across Punjab observe this day closely, and the wider community joins in too, through nagar kirtan processions that pass through neighborhoods where people of many different backgrounds live.
festivals.when: The festival falls on the full moon day of the month of Kartik, usually in November.
festivals.origin: This festival has been observed since organized Sikh institutions grew during the 1700s and 1800s. Its modern form, including the nagar kirtan procession, developed alongside gurdwara reform movements in the early 1900s.
festivals.signifies: The festival marks Sikhism's founding teaching, that there is one God and that caste and empty ritual should be rejected. The holy book is read aloud without stopping for two days as an act of devotion, not simply as a lesson.
festivals.beliefs: The Akhand Path, meaning the unbroken reading, must be read by a continuous chain of readers with no gaps. The reading is timed so it finishes right at dawn on the day of Gurpurab itself.
festivals.celebrate: The Akhand Path begins two days ahead of time. The day before the festival there is a nagar kirtan procession led by the Panj Pyare, with hymn singing and gatka displays. The gurdwara is lit up and decorated, and langar is served to everyone along the entire procession route without exception. In the evening there are kirtan gatherings called darbars.
festivals.local: On Gurpurab the langar is cooked for anyone who shows up, in numbers nobody even tries to estimate ahead of time. Arriving hungry and unannounced is the normal way to take part, not something that would be seen as rude.
festivals.image: Nagar kirtan procession at dusk, Panj Pyare leading, Golden Temple in the distance

festivals.name: Bandi Chhor Divas
festivals.reach: People celebrate this festival across the state, and the observance at the Golden Temple draws pilgrims from all over India.
festivals.what: This festival marks the Sikh meaning behind Diwali, the day Guru Hargobind, the sixth Sikh Guru, was released from being held prisoner by the Mughal rulers at Gwalior fort. He then returned to Amritsar, where the Golden Temple was lit up to welcome him home.
festivals.who: Sikh households across Punjab celebrate this day for its specific history, even though it falls on the very same date that Hindu neighbors celebrate the more general festival of Diwali.
festivals.when: It falls on the same new moon night as Diwali, in October or November.
festivals.origin: This festival remembers the year 1619, when Guru Hargobind was released. According to belief, he made sure fifty two other imprisoned princes were freed along with him, by having a cloak made with fifty two tassels, each prince holding one tassel as they all walked out of prison together.
festivals.signifies: This story turns one Guru's freedom into freedom for a whole group of people. It is read as an example of using one's own standing or power on behalf of others, not just for oneself.
festivals.beliefs: Sikhs believe that Guru Hargobind's arrival in Amritsar on the night of Diwali, and the lighting of the Golden Temple that followed, is the real reason the site is lit up on this date, not simply because it happens to be Diwali.
festivals.celebrate: The Golden Temple is lit with lamps and fireworks that reflect in the sarovar, the pool of water around it. There are Akhand Path readings, and people set off fireworks and eat sweets at home just as they would for the general Diwali. Kirtan singing retells the story of the fifty two freed princes, and gurdwaras across Punjab are lit up for the night.
festivals.local: According to the Sikh version of events, the Golden Temple's Diwali lights are actually older than the Hindu festival's connection to this same night in this particular region. People in Amritsar will point this out if the two stories get mixed up.
festivals.image: Golden Temple illuminated at night, lamps reflected in the sarovar, Diwali

festivals.name: Teeyan
festivals.reach: People celebrate this festival across both rural and urban Punjab, especially among women.
festivals.what: Teeyan is a monsoon season festival celebrated mainly by women and girls. It centers on swings hung from trees, a folk dance called giddha, and married daughters visiting their parents' homes.
festivals.who: Women and girls across Punjab celebrate Teeyan. A central part of the tradition is that married women return to their maika, meaning their parents' house, for the season.
festivals.when: It falls on the third day of the bright half of the lunar month of Sawan, during the monsoon rains, usually in August.
festivals.origin: This is an old monsoon and fertility festival from the Punjab plains. Its swing songs and the legends told about giddha dancing have been passed down through spoken tradition rather than coming from one written source.
festivals.signifies: The monsoon rains bring both relief and a kind of freedom. They create a break from farm work that people use for singing, swinging, and visiting family, rather than for formal religious ritual.
festivals.beliefs: People believe swinging on this day brings good luck to women. The giddha dance performed at Teeyan is thought of as a dance specifically for women, unlike some other Punjabi dances which are not tied to one gender.
festivals.celebrate: Swings are hung from trees in courtyards and orchards. Women perform giddha in circles, clapping their hands to keep rhythm instead of using instruments. They wear new clothes, often bright red or green, along with bangles and henna designs called mehndi. Married daughters visit their birth families, bringing gifts that are sent back home with them.
festivals.local: The giddha danced at Teeyan is looser and more playful than the version performed at weddings or on stage. Women take turns making up verses, often teasing their in-laws in ways that would never survive being sung if the in-laws were actually listening.
festivals.image: Women in bright dupattas on rope swings under trees, giddha circle nearby

festivals.name: Eid al-Fitr
festivals.reach: This festival is celebrated most visibly in Malerkotla, the state's only town with a Muslim majority population.
festivals.what: Eid al-Fitr marks the end of the fasting month of Ramadan. It is celebrated with special visibility in Malerkotla, a town whose Muslim population and old Nawabi era institutions, from a local Muslim ruling family, survived Partition mostly intact, even though most other Muslim communities in Punjab left the region or were forced to move.
festivals.who: The Muslim community of Malerkotla celebrates this festival, along with smaller Muslim communities elsewhere in the state.
festivals.when: It falls on the first day of the Islamic month of Shawwal, which moves earlier each year because it follows the Hijri lunar calendar.
festivals.origin: Malerkotla's Muslim population traces back to a princely state from the Sufi era. Locals often explain that the town's community survived largely undisturbed through 1947, when almost every other Muslim community in Indian Punjab was displaced, because of a historical act of protection that an earlier Nawab, a local ruler, showed toward the Sikh Gurus.
festivals.signifies: For everyone this day marks the end of the fast. For Malerkotla specifically it also represents a sense of continuity that the town treats as part of its own identity.
festivals.beliefs: Before the Eid prayer, people give zakat al-Fitr, a required charitable donation. The town's mosques coordinate their moon sighting, which decides the exact date, together with the wider Muslim community of Punjab and Haryana.
festivals.celebrate: People attend Eid prayers at the town's Jama Masjid, its main mosque, and its Eidgah, an open prayer ground. Families eat sewaiyan, a sweet vermicelli dish, and other sweets at home, wear new clothes, and visit each other. The town's markets close for the morning prayer and then get busy again through the afternoon.
festivals.local: People in Punjab often describe Malerkotla as the exception that proves the rule about 1947, a single town where daily Muslim life was never interrupted.
festivals.image: Eid morning prayer crowd outside Malerkotla's Jama Masjid

name: Haryana
tagline: Haryana is a land of wheat fields and wrestling arenas called akhadas. It also turned an ancient battlefield into a festival built around philosophy and ideas.

festivals.name: Baisakhi
festivals.reach: People celebrate this festival across rural Haryana.
festivals.what: Baisakhi is the wheat harvest festival. It is celebrated across Haryana's grain growing region, but here it does not carry the specific Sikh religious weight it has in neighboring Punjab, even though the two states share the same day and much of the same customs.
festivals.who: Farming families across the state celebrate Baisakhi, both Hindu and Sikh alike.
festivals.when: Baisakhi falls on April 13 or 14 every year, fixed by the solar calendar.
festivals.origin: This is an old solar harvest festival celebrated across the northern plains of India. It shares its date with Vishu in Kerala and Bihu in Assam. Haryana's version of the festival borrows heavily from the shared customs of the Punjab plains.
festivals.signifies: Baisakhi marks the wheat crop being brought in, and it treats the hardest labor of the farming year as officially finished.
festivals.beliefs: People consider this day lucky for starting new things, so many families plan weddings and new business openings around it.
festivals.celebrate: Wheat is harvested and threshed with special ceremony. People sing folk songs and dance in the fields and courtyards. Market towns hold fairs with wrestling matches, a specialty of Haryana. Sweets are shared among neighbors.
festivals.local: A Baisakhi fair in a Haryana town is just as likely to be built around a wrestling match at the local akhada as around any temple. That shows where the state's competitive spirit really lies.
festivals.image: Wheat harvest festival, threshing floor and folk dancers, rural Haryana

festivals.name: Teej
festivals.reach: People celebrate this festival across the state, especially among women.
festivals.what: Teej is a monsoon season festival for women. It is celebrated with swings, folk songs, and a custom in which a married daughter visits her parents' home during the rainy season.
festivals.who: Women and girls across Haryana celebrate Teej. There is a specific named custom called Sinjara, in which the visiting daughter stays away from her husband's home for the days of the festival.
festivals.when: It falls on the third day of the bright half of the lunar month of Sawan.
festivals.origin: This is a monsoon fertility festival for women, shared across the northern plains of India. Haryana's version has its own set of folk songs that are different from those sung in Punjab or Rajasthan.
festivals.signifies: Teej marks the relief that comes with the monsoon rains after a hot summer. It is celebrated through a custom meant specifically for women, rather than as a festival the whole household observes together.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that swinging and singing on this day brings good fortune to a marriage. In some households married women keep a partial fast for their husbands' wellbeing.
festivals.celebrate: Swings are hung from trees. Groups of women sing Haryanvi folk songs called teej geet. Henna is applied to hands. A married daughter's parents send sinjara ahead of her visit, a gift of clothes and sweets. Towns such as Sonipat and Panipat hold fairs.
festivals.local: Sinjara is a specific duty, not just a nice gesture. If a family fails to send it to a married daughter, people see that as failing an obligation, not simply forgetting a small courtesy.
festivals.image: Women on swings singing teej geet under a tree, Haryana village

festivals.name: Gugga Naumi
festivals.reach: People celebrate this festival across rural Haryana, and it is also shared with Punjab, Rajasthan, and western Uttar Pradesh.
festivals.what: Gugga Naumi is a folk festival honoring Gugga Pir, a warrior figure believed to protect people from snakebite. Both Hindu and Muslim villagers worship him, though they call him by different names.
festivals.who: Rural households across Haryana celebrate this festival, especially families who keep livestock, since snakebite is a real seasonal danger for them.
festivals.when: It falls on the ninth day of the dark half of the lunar month of Bhadrapada, in August or September.
festivals.origin: Gugga is usually identified as a medieval warrior from the Chauhan clan. Over the centuries his story picked up both Hindu and Muslim religious elements. Village worship of him as a snake deity and protector is very old and is not based on any single written text.
festivals.signifies: Gugga is a figure that people ask specifically for protection. Different communities call him by different names in their own languages, but nobody disputes his protective powers.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that keeping this vow makes snakebite less likely in the coming year. Gugga's shrines, called maris, are visited at other times of year too, whenever people feel the need.
festivals.celebrate: Villagers hold processions carrying a decorated bamboo pole that represents Gugga's banner. There is drumming and folk singing that tells his story. People make offerings of milk and grain at village shrines called maris. In some areas people walk over fire or perform symbolic snake worship at the shrine.
festivals.local: In many Haryana villages the very same shrine is looked after by both Hindu and Muslim families, taking turns. Locals see this as perfectly ordinary rather than as proof of anything special.
festivals.image: Village procession carrying a decorated Gugga standard, drummers alongside

festivals.name: International Gita Mahotsav
festivals.reach: This festival is centered at Kurukshetra, and it draws pilgrims and scholars from across India and from other countries.
festivals.what: This festival marks the day the Bhagavad Gita, a Hindu scripture, is believed to have been spoken by the god Krishna to the warrior Arjuna at Kurukshetra. Since 2016 the state government has expanded it into a multi week fair featuring talks, crafts, and performances.
festivals.who: Pilgrims and scholars who study the Gita attend for its religious meaning, alongside the larger general festival crowd that the state fair draws to Kurukshetra.
festivals.when: Gita Jayanti, the specific day the Gita was spoken, falls on a day called Mokshada Ekadashi in the month of Margashirsha, usually late November or December. The larger state Mahotsav, meaning festival, runs for several weeks around that date.
festivals.origin: The Haryana government has run a Gita Mahotsav at Kurukshetra together with the Kurukshetra Development Board since 1989. In 2016 it was renamed and expanded into the International Gita Mahotsav.
festivals.signifies: This festival takes a single set of philosophical teachings and gives it a fairground and a yearly calendar slot, held on the very ground where the story says the conversation took place.
festivals.beliefs: On Gita Jayanti itself, people mark the day by reciting or reading the text, especially its eighteenth chapter. Some believe the recitation should be finished within that single day rather than spread across several.
festivals.celebrate: People perform havan, a fire ritual, and recite the Gita at the Jyotisar tree, believed to be the actual spot of the original conversation. There are scholarly seminars and discussion sessions, a craft fair with stalls from all over India, light and sound shows at the Brahma Sarovar, a sacred pool, and in recent years attempts at a mass Gita recitation aiming for record numbers of participants.
festivals.local: The festival's growth from a small state event into an international one happened recently and on purpose. It is a clear example of a state government building tourism around one specific religious claim about one specific piece of land.
festivals.image: Mass Gita recitation at Jyotisar, Kurukshetra, crowd seated with texts

festivals.name: Holi
festivals.reach: People celebrate this festival across the state.
festivals.what: Holi is the festival of colors. Haryana celebrates it with the same basic customs as the rest of the northern plains, but some districts add their own distinct traditions of wrestling and folk theater around it.
festivals.who: Hindu households across the state celebrate Holi, and neighbors from other communities often join in the general play with colored powder.
festivals.when: It falls on the full moon day of the month of Phalguna and the day after, usually in March.
festivals.origin: Holi's core stories, the burning of a demoness named Holika and the playful antics of Krishna with the gopis, the cowherd women, are shared across North India. Haryana's rural wrestling culture has attached its own contests to this time of year.
festivals.signifies: Holi is a day when normal social distance is set aside. People throw colored powder at each other without regard for who is throwing it or receiving it.
festivals.beliefs: People believe the Holika bonfire lit the night before represents the destruction of arrogance and cruelty, and the colorful play the next day is a kind of release that follows it.
festivals.celebrate: People light Holika Dahan bonfires at dusk the night before. From the morning onward they throw colored powder and water at each other. Some Haryana villages hold folk singing and a folk theater form called swang. Wrestling matches take place at akhadas around this time of year, and people share sweets through the day, especially a pastry called gujiya.
festivals.local: A Holi crowd in Haryana is just as likely to spend the afternoon watching a wrestling match at the village akhada as visiting anyone's house. The colors and the wrestling contest are treated as part of the same day, not as separate events.
festivals.image: Holi colour play in a Haryana village square, wrestling akhada nearby

festivals.name: Diwali
festivals.reach: People celebrate this festival across the state.
festivals.what: Diwali is the festival of lights. Haryana celebrates it across its towns and villages with the household lamp lighting, sweets, and firecrackers common throughout North India.
festivals.who: Hindu households across the state celebrate Diwali, and in practice nearly everyone takes part through shared lights, sweets, and gift giving.
festivals.when: It falls on the new moon night of the month of Kartik, in October or November.
festivals.origin: Diwali's core story, about the god Rama returning to the city of Ayodhya after fourteen years of exile, is shared across North India. Its combination with worship of the goddess Lakshmi for prosperity is old and widespread, not specific to Haryana.
festivals.signifies: Diwali sets light against the darkest night of the year. Many trading families also treat it as the start of a new financial year.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that the goddess Lakshmi visits homes that are lit up and clean on this night, which is why cleaning starts days in advance.
festivals.celebrate: Homes are cleaned and whitewashed ahead of time. Earthen oil lamps called diyas and electric lights are lit at dusk. People perform Lakshmi puja, meaning worship, at home and in shops, set off firecrackers through the evening, and exchange sweets with family, neighbors, and business contacts.
festivals.local: In Haryana's market towns, traders open new account ledgers on Diwali night with the same seriousness seen anywhere else in North India. The festival's fresh financial start is treated as just as real as its religious meaning.
festivals.image: Diyas lit along a Haryana shopfront at dusk, Diwali evening

festivals.name: Eid al-Fitr
festivals.reach: This festival is centered in Nuh and the wider Mewat region, home to the state's largest Muslim population.
festivals.what: Eid al-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan. It is celebrated by the Meo Muslim community of Nuh district, a farming population whose homeland once stretched across the wider Mewat region before Partition era and later district borders cut through it.
festivals.who: The Meo community of Nuh celebrates this festival, and Muslims form the large majority of the district's population there. Smaller Muslim communities elsewhere in Haryana also celebrate it.
festivals.when: It falls on the first day of the Islamic month of Shawwal, which moves each year according to the Hijri lunar calendar.
festivals.origin: The Meo people have lived in the Mewat region since before most of the borders now drawn around it existed. Historians understand their conversion to Islam as something that happened gradually over time, blending with earlier Rajput customs rather than happening all at once.
festivals.signifies: This day marks the end of the fast. It is kept by a community whose religious practice has long existed alongside farming customs shared across the wider Mewat region, regardless of people's faith.
festivals.beliefs: People give zakat al-Fitr, a required charitable donation, before the Eid prayer. The moon sighting that sets the exact date is confirmed only the evening before.
festivals.celebrate: People attend Eid prayers at Nuh's mosques and Eidgahs, open prayer grounds. They eat sewaiyan, sweet vermicelli, and meat dishes at home, wear new clothes, and visit extended family across Mewat's villages.
festivals.local: Meo villages in Nuh have long kept certain Rajput clan customs, such as surname and family lineage traditions, alongside their Islamic practice. This blending existed before the district even had its current name and borders.
festivals.image: Eid prayer gathering at an Eidgah, Nuh district, Mewat

name: Delhi
tagline: Delhi is the country's capital, and it feels like a city built out of other people's festivals. Each community that settled here kept celebrating its festivals the same way it always had back home.

festivals.name: Diwali
festivals.reach: People across the city celebrate this festival, regardless of their background.
festivals.what: Diwali is the festival of lights. Delhi celebrates it the way most of North India does, but the city's crowded density makes it feel even bigger, because markets, apartment buildings, and government offices are all lit up at once.
festivals.who: Hindu households across the city celebrate Diwali, and in practice almost the entire capital takes part, through shared lights, gift giving, and the city's firecracker culture, which is now heavily restricted by rules.
festivals.when: It falls on the new moon night of the month of Kartik, in October or November.
festivals.origin: Diwali's core story, about Rama returning to the city of Ayodhya, is shared across North India. Delhi's celebration does not have its own separate local origin story different from the wider North Indian festival.
festivals.signifies: Diwali sets light against the darkest night of the year. In Delhi specifically it also marks a shopping season that markets from Chandni Chowk to Sarojini Nagar are built around.
festivals.beliefs: People believe the goddess Lakshmi visits homes that are lit and clean, so many business owners perform puja, or worship, at their shop or office as well as at home.
festivals.celebrate: Markets get crowded for weeks beforehand. Homes are lit with diyas, oil lamps, and string lights. People perform Lakshmi puja at home and in offices, exchange boxes of sweets and dried fruit with neighbors and coworkers, and set off firecrackers, though these are now restricted by court order because of the city's poor winter air quality.
festivals.local: Delhi's ban on fireworks, renewed and argued about almost every year because of the city's smog, has become just as much a part of the season as the lights themselves. It is a genuinely local complication that no other state's Diwali has in quite the same way.
festivals.image: Diyas and string lights along a Delhi market street at dusk, Diwali shopping crowd

festivals.name: Holi
festivals.reach: People celebrate this festival widely across the city.
