festivals.what: Holi is the festival of colors. In Delhi people play it in neighborhoods, parks, and open grounds, and in recent decades large organized events have grown up alongside the older, more traditional household version.
festivals.who: Hindu households across the city celebrate Holi, many people from other communities join in the general color play, and tourists often attend the organized events.
festivals.when: It falls on the full moon day of the month of Phalguna and the day after, usually in March.
festivals.origin: Holi's mythology, the burning of Holika and Krishna's playful antics with the gopis, the cowherd women, is shared across North India. Delhi's large scale, ticketed Holi events are a recent addition driven by commercial interest, layered on top of the older, more private household festival.
festivals.signifies: Holi is a day when the city's usual formality gets set aside, and colored powder is thrown at people regardless of who is throwing it.
festivals.beliefs: People believe the Holika bonfire lit the night before marks the defeat of cruelty and pride, and the color play the next day is a kind of release that follows it.
festivals.celebrate: People light Holika Dahan bonfires in neighborhood parks and housing colonies the night before. From the morning onward they throw colored powder and water at each other. Some households drink bhang thandai, a traditional drink. Large ticketed Holi events with live music are held at grounds across the city, and people share gujiya and other sweets from house to house.
festivals.local: The older neighborhoods of Old Delhi still play a version closer to the original household style, thick with colored powder and without big music systems. This is an increasing contrast to the ticketed events that now dominate south Delhi's Holi weekend.
festivals.image: Holi colour crowd in a Delhi park, powder in the air, midday

festivals.name: Eid al-Fitr
festivals.reach: This festival is especially significant in Old Delhi and across the city's Muslim neighborhoods.
festivals.what: Eid al-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan. In Delhi it centers on Old Delhi's Jama Masjid, a major mosque, and the surrounding lanes, which fill up through the fasting month with food stalls that stay open until the meal eaten just before dawn.
festivals.who: Delhi's Muslim communities celebrate this festival, historically concentrated in Old Delhi, Nizamuddin, and other older neighborhoods, though the food culture of the fasting month draws people from across the whole city.
festivals.when: It falls on the first day of the Islamic month of Shawwal, which moves each year according to the Hijri lunar calendar.
festivals.origin: Delhi's Muslim population and its Mughal era institutions, especially the Jama Masjid built by the emperor Shah Jahan, existed long before the modern city took shape. The neighborhood's Ramadan food culture grew over many generations of continuous settlement there.
festivals.signifies: This day marks the end of the fast. In Old Delhi specifically it also marks the close of a specific food season that ends just as suddenly as it began.
festivals.beliefs: People give zakat al-Fitr, a required charitable donation, before the Eid prayer. So many people pray at Jama Masjid that the surrounding streets close to traffic.
festivals.celebrate: People attend Eid prayers at Jama Masjid and at Eidgahs, open prayer grounds, across the city. They eat sewaiyan, sweet vermicelli, and biryani at home. Old Delhi's lanes, especially around Matia Mahal, are packed every night through Ramadan with kebabs and a dish called haleem. People wear new clothes and visit each other on Eid day.
festivals.local: The Ramadan food stalls around Jama Masjid are a Delhi institution that reaches far beyond the Muslim community. Many people come there only to eat, and the lanes empty out again the moment the month ends.
festivals.image: Matia Mahal lane at night during Ramadan, food stalls lit, Jama Masjid behind

festivals.name: Durga Puja
festivals.reach: This festival is centered in Chittaranjan Park and other Bengali neighborhoods, and it draws visitors from across the city.
festivals.what: Durga Puja is five days of worship centered on decorated temporary structures called pandals. In Delhi it is centered on Chittaranjan Park, the Bengali neighborhood in south Delhi built by refugees from East Bengal after Partition, with dozens of community pujas, or worship events, across its blocks.
festivals.who: Delhi's Bengali community celebrates this festival, settled mainly in CR Park, Chittaranjan Park, and scattered across other neighborhoods. The wider city joins in too, visiting the pandals and eating the food.
festivals.when: It falls during the bright half of the month of Ashwin, in September or October, running from a day called Shashthi through a day called Dashami.
festivals.origin: CR Park was developed starting in the 1960s to resettle Bengali refugee families who had fled from East Pakistan. Its Durga Puja tradition grew directly out of that displaced community rebuilding a home festival far away from Bengal.
festivals.signifies: For CR Park specifically, this is a transplanted festival that became the neighborhood's whole identity. The pandal stands in for a Bengal that many residents' families had already lost once before.
festivals.beliefs: As in Bengal, the clay images of the goddess are immersed in water at the end of the festival. On the final day married women take part in a ritual called Sindoor Khela, done in the same form as it is in Kolkata.
festivals.celebrate: Pandals are built across CR Park's blocks, each one run by a separate community association. Bengali food stalls sell fish, sweets called mishti, and street snacks. There is dhaak drumming and a dhunuchi dance performed with smoking incense pots. On the final days there is a special ritual called Sandhi Puja, followed by Sindoor Khela and Bijoya greetings, when people wish each other well.
festivals.local: Many people who attend CR Park's pujas are not Bengali at all. They simply come for the food stalls, which by the third day of the festival are doing more business than the actual worship side of things.
festivals.image: Pandal in CR Park at night, food stalls and crowds along the block

festivals.name: Guru Nanak Gurpurab
festivals.reach: This festival is especially significant for Delhi's Sikh community, which is concentrated in Punjabi Bagh, Rajouri Garden, and other neighborhoods.
festivals.what: This festival celebrates the birthday of Guru Nanak, the founder of Sikhism. In Delhi it is marked with a nagar kirtan procession and a continuous reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sikh holy book, at gurdwaras across the city, especially at Bangla Sahib and Sis Ganj.
festivals.who: Delhi's Sikh community celebrates this festival. They have lived in large numbers across the city since Partition. The wider public also takes part, through the free community meal called langar and the processions.
festivals.when: It falls on the full moon day of the month of Kartik, usually in November.
festivals.origin: Delhi's Sikh population grew substantially when many people migrated from West Punjab during Partition in 1947. The city's major Gurpurab celebrations, at gurdwaras such as Bangla Sahib and Sis Ganj Sahib, existed before that migration but grew larger because of it.
festivals.signifies: This festival marks the founding teaching of Sikhism. It is celebrated in a city where the Sikh community had to rebuild itself after 1947, rather than one where it had always lived at its current size.
festivals.beliefs: People believe the Akhand Path, the unbroken reading of the holy book, must be read by a continuous chain of readers, finishing at dawn on the day of the festival itself.
festivals.celebrate: The Akhand Path begins two days ahead of time. The day before the festival there is a nagar kirtan procession led by the Panj Pyare. Gurdwara Bangla Sahib is lit up and its kitchen runs around the clock. Langar is served to any visitor regardless of their faith, and there is kirtan singing in the evening.
festivals.local: Bangla Sahib's langar hall feeds thousands of people on an ordinary evening, and even more on Gurpurab. The volunteers who work there come from across the whole city, not only from the Sikh community.
festivals.image: Bangla Sahib gurdwara illuminated at night, Gurpurab crowd at the sarovar

festivals.name: Phool Walon Ki Sair
festivals.reach: This festival is centered in Mehrauli, and it has been revived as an occasion the whole city can take part in.
festivals.what: This is a procession of flower sellers who carry large decorated fans made of flowers, called pankhas, from the shrine, or dargah, of the Sufi saint Khwaja Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki to the nearby Yogmaya temple in Mehrauli.
festivals.who: Delhi's flower sellers take part, along with the Anjuman Sair-e-Gul Faroshan, the committee that organizes the event. Both the dargah, a Muslim shrine, and the temple, a Hindu temple, are fixed stops on the very same route.
festivals.when: It takes place over a few days in September or October, just after the monsoon rains end, with the exact dates set each year by the organizing committee.
festivals.origin: The festival began in 1812, when a Mughal noblewoman named Mumtaz Mahal Begum, wife of the emperor Akbar Shah II, fulfilled a promise to make floral offerings at the dargah after her exiled son returned home safely. The emperor himself extended the day's offerings to include the temple as well. The festival was later revived in 1962 by Jawaharlal Nehru, India's first prime minister, after it had been stopped during the colonial period.
festivals.signifies: A single vow made in the Mughal royal court turned into a lasting local habit of visiting both a dargah and a temple on the same afternoon. People in Delhi see this as proof the city has managed this kind of thing before.
festivals.beliefs: People consider the flower fans, called pankhas, to be offerings at both religious sites in turn. What matters most is thought to be the procession's route itself, not either single destination alone.
festivals.celebrate: Flower sellers spend the preceding weeks building large decorated fans. There is a procession from the dargah to the Yogmaya temple and on to a building called Jahaz Mahal. There is qawwali singing, a form of devotional Sufi music, and cultural programs at Jahaz Mahal, along with wrestling matches and kite flying, older traditions that go along with the day.
festivals.local: The procession's stop at both the dargah and the temple on the same afternoon is not treated in Mehrauli as some special gesture of tolerance that needs to be pointed out. It is simply the route the fans have always taken.
festivals.image: Flower sellers carrying decorated floral pankhas through Mehrauli lanes

festivals.name: Christmas
festivals.reach: This festival is especially significant for Delhi's Christian communities, and it also involves citywide markets and church visits from the wider public.
festivals.what: Christmas in Delhi is a church festival for the city's Catholic and Protestant congregations. It is also a wider seasonal event for the whole city, centered around churches such as Sacred Heart Cathedral and markets like Khan Market and Connaught Place, which get decorated throughout December.
festivals.who: Delhi's Catholic and Protestant congregations celebrate Christmas as a religious festival. These communities are historically smaller and more recently established than in South India or the northeast. A wider general public also treats the season as a time for shopping and decorating.
festivals.when: Christmas Day is December 25, with carol services and holiday markets running through the weeks before it.
festivals.origin: Delhi's Christian institutions mostly date to the colonial period and afterward, making them newer and smaller than the older Christian communities of Kerala or Goa. They were built around churches that served both the old colonial government and later migrant congregations from across India.
festivals.signifies: Christmas celebrates the birth of Jesus, kept by a fairly small and diverse city congregation whose members come from many different regional Christian traditions rather than from one single local tradition.
festivals.beliefs: Midnight mass, the late night church service on Christmas Eve, is widely attended even by families who do not regularly go to church the rest of the year.
festivals.celebrate: People attend midnight mass at Sacred Heart Cathedral and other churches, along with carol services throughout Advent, the weeks leading up to Christmas. Markets are decorated with lights, cakes and plum cake are sold at Delhi's older bakeries, and families gather and exchange gifts on Christmas Day itself.
festivals.local: Delhi's Christian congregations are unusually mixed for a single city. Malayali, Tamil, Northeastern, and Anglo-Indian families all attend the same parish, so a single midnight mass can end up being sung partly in more than one language.
festivals.image: Sacred Heart Cathedral lit for Christmas, midnight mass crowd outside

name: Chandigarh
tagline: Chandigarh is a carefully planned city sitting between Punjab and Haryana, and it borrowed its festival traditions from both of the states that surround it.

festivals.name: Baisakhi
festivals.reach: People celebrate this festival across the city, and it is strongest in its older sectors and villages.
festivals.what: Baisakhi is the harvest and Khalsa founding festival, celebrated here just as it is across the Punjab plains. In Chandigarh it is marked in the city's sector gurdwaras and in the villages that were absorbed into the city's boundaries when it was built.
festivals.who: Chandigarh's Sikh and Hindu Punjabi population, who make up a majority of the city's residents, celebrate this festival. Many of them still have family land being farmed in the surrounding districts of Punjab and Haryana.
festivals.when: Baisakhi falls on April 13 or 14 every year, fixed by the solar calendar.
festivals.origin: As elsewhere in Punjab, the harvest celebration existed before Sikhism began. Its Khalsa founding meaning comes from Guru Gobind Singh's 1699 initiation ceremony at Anandpur Sahib, a town within a day's travel of Chandigarh.
festivals.signifies: This is a harvest festival kept by a city that was itself built on farmland only decades ago. Most residents still have a village they can go back to for the occasion.
festivals.beliefs: People believe the founding of the Khalsa gave Sikhism the form it still has today, so the day is treated with religious importance separate from its harvest meaning.
festivals.celebrate: There are nagar kirtan processions through the city's sectors, gatka displays, and Akhand Path readings at Gurdwara Sector 34 and other major gurdwaras. Families visit their ancestral villages nearby for the harvest side of the celebration, and there are fairs with folk music.
festivals.local: Many Chandigarh families spend Baisakhi entirely outside the city, in whichever Punjab or Haryana village their grandparents came from when the city's sectors were first allotted to residents. This makes the city noticeably quieter on the day itself.
festivals.image: Nagar kirtan procession through a Chandigarh sector road, Panj Pyare leading

festivals.name: Lohri
festivals.reach: People celebrate this festival across the city.
festivals.what: Lohri is a bonfire festival celebrated in Chandigarh's sector parks and courtyards, following the same customs as the wider Punjab region the city was built out of.
festivals.who: Households across the city celebrate Lohri, especially Punjabi Hindu and Sikh families, for whom it remains an important occasion at home.
festivals.when: It falls on January 13 every year, the night before Makar Sankranti.
festivals.origin: This is a winter solstice and harvest festival shared across the Punjab plains. It arrived in Chandigarh with the families who settled the city after Partition and during its construction, which began in 1952.
festivals.signifies: Lohri stands for warmth won back at the coldest point of winter. It is celebrated in this planned city the same way it was once celebrated in the villages that used to stand on this land.
festivals.beliefs: People treat sesame seeds, jaggery, and popcorn thrown into the fire as an offering. This is considered especially important for households marking their first Lohri after a birth or a wedding.
festivals.celebrate: Bonfires are lit in sector parks and residential courtyards. Sesame and jaggery sweets are shared. Children sing the ballad of Dulla Bhatti as they collect treats from house to house, and people dance bhangra and giddha around the fire.
festivals.local: Because of Chandigarh's sector layout, Lohri fires now light up planned green belts and roundabouts, rather than the fields and lanes of the villages that stood there before 1952. It is the same fire, just kept in a very different kind of space.
festivals.image: Lohri bonfire in a Chandigarh sector park at night, families gathered

festivals.name: Guru Nanak Gurpurab
festivals.reach: People celebrate this festival across the city, especially at Gurdwara Sector 34.
festivals.what: This festival celebrates the birthday of Guru Nanak. It is marked with a citywide nagar kirtan procession and a continuous reading of scripture at Chandigarh's major gurdwaras.
festivals.who: Chandigarh's large Sikh population celebrates this festival, and the wider city joins in through the langar meal and the procession route.
festivals.when: It falls on the full moon day of the month of Kartik, usually in November.
festivals.origin: This festival has been observed since organized Sikh gurdwara practice developed across Punjab during the 1700s and 1800s. Chandigarh's own gurdwaras, and their Gurpurab celebrations, only date back to the city's founding starting in the 1950s.
festivals.signifies: This festival marks the founding teaching of Sikhism, celebrated in a city whose buildings are recent even though the community's traditions are not.
festivals.beliefs: People believe the Akhand Path, the unbroken reading of scripture, must be timed to finish right at dawn on the day of the festival.
festivals.celebrate: The Akhand Path begins two days ahead of time. The day before, there is a nagar kirtan procession led by the Panj Pyare. Gurdwaras are decorated and lit up, langar is served without any restriction, and there is kirtan singing through the evening.
festivals.local: Gurdwara Sector 34's langar on Gurpurab draws visitors from across the whole tricity area, which includes Chandigarh, Mohali, and Panchkula. People treat it as one shared occasion, even though a boundary otherwise separates these three different local governments.
festivals.image: Gurdwara Sector 34 illuminated for Gurpurab, langar hall crowded

festivals.name: Diwali
festivals.reach: People celebrate this festival across the city.
festivals.what: Diwali is the festival of lights, celebrated across Chandigarh's sectors with household lighting, sweets, and firecrackers. It also carries a separate Sikh meaning as Bandi Chhor Divas, observed on the very same night at the city's gurdwaras.
festivals.who: Hindu households across the city celebrate Diwali, while Sikh households mark Bandi Chhor Divas on the same date.
festivals.when: It falls on the new moon night of the month of Kartik, in October or November.
festivals.origin: Diwali's core story, about Rama's return to Ayodhya, is shared across North India. The Sikh meaning of the same night traces back to Guru Hargobind's release from Mughal imprisonment in 1619 and his arrival in Amritsar.
festivals.signifies: Both festivals set light against the darkest night of the year, but the city's two largest communities mark the same evening for two different, specific reasons.
festivals.beliefs: Hindus believe the goddess Lakshmi visits homes that are clean and lit up, while Sikh households mark the night for Guru Hargobind's release, not for Lakshmi at all.
festivals.celebrate: Homes across the sectors are lit with diyas and lights. Hindu households perform Lakshmi puja, and gurdwaras are lit up for Bandi Chhor Divas. Firecrackers are now restricted in timing by order of the local administration, and sweets are widely exchanged.
festivals.local: On Diwali night a single Chandigarh sector might have Hindu households performing Lakshmi puja while Sikh households head to the gurdwara for Bandi Chhor Divas, all within the same few streets. The two occasions are marked separately even though they fall on the exact same evening.
festivals.image: Sector market lit with diyas and lights, Chandigarh, Diwali evening

festivals.name: Hola Mohalla
festivals.reach: Chandigarh residents travel to nearby Anandpur Sahib to take part in the main gathering.
festivals.what: This is the Sikh martial gathering held at Anandpur Sahib, which is close enough to Chandigarh that a large part of the city's Sikh population travels there for the day instead of celebrating it locally.
festivals.who: Chandigarh's Sikh residents celebrate this festival, especially families connected to the Nihang order of Sikh warriors, along with the wider Sikh public who make the short trip north.
festivals.when: It takes place the day after Holi, usually in March, at Anandpur Sahib.
festivals.origin: Guru Gobind Singh started this gathering in 1701 at Anandpur Sahib, as a martial exercise that replaced the ordinary play of Holi with mock battles and a review of his soldiers.
festivals.signifies: For Chandigarh residents, this has become a short yearly trip north, rather than a festival celebrated inside the city's own sectors.
festivals.beliefs: People believe this gathering keeps going exactly what the Guru himself once did, at the very same location, without any break in the tradition.
festivals.celebrate: There are mock cavalry battles and gatka displays on the riverbed of the Charan Ganga at Anandpur Sahib, along with Nihang processions and langar meals. In the days before and after, there is a steady stream of vehicles traveling from Chandigarh and the tricity area.
festivals.local: The road from Chandigarh to Anandpur Sahib is noticeably busier for several days around Hola Mohalla. This small yearly migration shows up in the city's traffic patterns even though the festival itself happens somewhere else.
festivals.image: Highway traffic toward Anandpur Sahib ahead of Hola Mohalla, Nihang flags visible

festivals.name: Chandigarh Rose Festival
festivals.reach: This is a city event centered on the Zakir Hussain Rose Garden, and it draws visitors from across the tricity area.
festivals.what: This is a three day civic festival held at the Zakir Hussain Rose Garden, one of the larger rose gardens in Asia. It is timed to when the flowers are at their peak bloom and combines the flower display with cultural performances and competitions.
festivals.who: Chandigarh's Municipal Corporation organizes this festival, and it draws residents from across the wider tricity area of Chandigarh, Mohali, and Panchkula.
festivals.when: It usually takes place during the third week of February, timed each year to match the rose bloom.
festivals.origin: The city administration started this festival in the early 1970s to show off the Rose Garden, which had been part of Chandigarh's original modernist city plan. It has been held every year since as one of the city's few festivals created specifically for civic purposes.
festivals.signifies: This festival has no religious content at all. It was created by a carefully planned city to give itself a yearly occasion, the kind of thing older cities usually end up with by accident rather than by design.
festivals.beliefs: There is no religious or devotional meaning to this festival. Its organizers describe it as being about horticulture, meaning gardening, and culture, not religion.
festivals.celebrate: Hundreds of rose varieties bloom across the garden. There are folk dance and music performances on an open stage, along with competitions in flower arranging, rangoli, a form of decorative floor art, painting, and photography. Food and craft stalls are set up throughout the grounds.
festivals.local: In some recent years the festival has run on a low budget funded by the organizers themselves. Residents mention this as proof of how fond the city is of the festival, even when there isn't much money available for it.
festivals.image: Zakir Hussain Rose Garden in bloom during the festival, stage performance in the distance

name: Uttar Pradesh
tagline: Uttar Pradesh is home to temple towns along the Ganges river plain, an old capital city once ruled by Shia Muslim kings, and the largest gathering of pilgrims found anywhere in the country.

festivals.name: Deepotsav
festivals.season: New moon of Kartik, eve of Diwali
festivals.reach: This festival is centered at Ayodhya, and it now draws pilgrims and visitors from across India.
festivals.what: Deepotsav is a festival of oil lamps organized by the state government in the city of Ayodhya, held on the evening before Diwali. It recreates the city's welcome for the god Rama's return from exile by lighting oil lamps called diyas along the banks of the Saryu river, on a scale large enough to set Guinness World Records for the biggest display of oil lamps ever.
festivals.who: Uttar Pradesh Tourism has organized this festival since 2017. Pilgrims and visitors now travel to Ayodhya specifically to see the event.
festivals.when: It takes place the evening before Diwali, in October or November, at a place called Ram Ki Paidi on the Saryu river.
festivals.origin: The state government began this festival in 2017 with 171,000 diyas, a number written in India as 1.71 lakh. It has grown bigger every year since, reaching about 2.5 million diyas, or twenty five lakh, in 2024, the first year the festival was held after the new Ram Mandir temple was formally opened in January of that year.
festivals.signifies: This festival restages Ayodhya's own Diwali story, in which the city lit itself up to welcome Rama home. It is done each year on a scale meant to be seen well beyond Ayodhya itself.
festivals.beliefs: Devotees believe that lighting a lamp on the bank of the Saryu river on this night makes them part of the city's original welcome for Rama, not just something that reminds them of it.
festivals.celebrate: Diyas are laid out and lit along kilometers of the Saryu riverbank. A mass aarti, a worship ritual using lamps, is performed at the same time by a large number of priests. There are laser and light shows depicting the story of the Ramayana, along with processions and cultural performances through the city in the days around the festival.
festivals.local: The number of diyas lit is now tracked and announced each year like a sports record, and Ayodhya residents discuss the previous year's total the way people in another city might discuss a cricket score.
festivals.image: Saryu riverbank covered in lit diyas at dusk, Ayodhya Deepotsav

festivals.name: Lathmar Holi
festivals.reach: This festival is centered in Barsana and Nandgaon, and it draws visitors from across India for the whole week.
festivals.what: This is a week of Holi celebrations in the Braj region around the city of Mathura. It opens with a distinctive event called Lathmar Holi at the town of Barsana, where women beat men with sticks in a ritual mock battle, before the main day of Holi arrives.
festivals.who: The towns of Barsana and Nandgaon take part, connected respectively to the goddess Radha and the god Krishna. The wider network of Krishna temples across the Braj region also takes part through the week.
festivals.when: It takes place in the days leading up to the main Holi full moon, usually about a week before, in the month of Phalguna.
festivals.origin: This tradition is rooted in the devotional culture around Radha and Krishna that grew out of the Bhakti movement, a religious movement of poet saints from the 1400s and 1500s who wove the region's Krishna legends into local Holi customs.
festivals.signifies: This festival reenacts Krishna's playful teasing of Radha and the gopis, the cowherd women, as a kind of theater. The sticks and shields used are part of a performance, not real hostility.
festivals.beliefs: People believe the mock battle reenacts a specific event in the Radha Krishna story, in which Krishna's visits to Barsana were met by Radha's friends chasing him away.
festivals.celebrate: Men travel from Nandgaon to Barsana to be beaten with sticks by women, who wield the sticks while the men raise shields to defend themselves. People sing Braj folk holi songs, and there is color and flower play at the region's Krishna temples throughout the week. Similar events follow afterward at Nandgaon and Vrindavan.
festivals.local: Braj's Holi celebrations last a full week, much longer than the single national holiday most of the rest of India observes. Residents plan around a whole week of events moving from temple to temple.
festivals.image: Women wielding sticks at Barsana's Lathmar Holi, men with shields, colour in the air

festivals.name: Krishna Janmashtami
festivals.reach: This festival is centered in Mathura and Vrindavan, and it draws pilgrims from across India and from other countries.
festivals.what: This festival celebrates the birth of the god Krishna. It is marked with special intensity at Mathura, believed to be his birthplace, and at Vrindavan, the town where he grew up, with temples across both towns holding celebrations that run through the night.
festivals.who: Pilgrims travel specifically to Mathura and Vrindavan for this festival, while Hindu households across the state and the country celebrate it more generally.
festivals.when: It falls on the eighth day of the dark half of the month of Bhadrapada, usually in August or September, with celebrations running past midnight, right up to the moment believed to be Krishna's actual birth.
festivals.origin: Krishna's birth at Mathura is central to the Bhagavata religious tradition. The Krishna Janmabhoomi temple complex there, along with Vrindavan's dense network of Krishna temples, developed over many centuries of continuous pilgrimage.
festivals.signifies: This festival celebrates the birth of a god who is worshipped as much for his mischievous childhood as for his later teachings, which is why the festival's mood leans toward playfulness rather than solemn seriousness.
festivals.beliefs: People believe the fast kept during the day should only be broken at midnight, the moment held to be exactly when Krishna was born.
festivals.celebrate: People keep a day long fast, broken at midnight with the ringing of temple bells. There is jhulan, meaning decorated swings for an image of the infant Krishna, and dahi handi, in which human pyramids break pots of curd, more common in western India but echoed in some Uttar Pradesh towns too. There is also all night devotional singing called bhajan and kirtan at the temples of Mathura and Vrindavan.
festivals.local: Vrindavan's temples run programs through the entire night that a visitor can walk between on foot, one after another, each one with its own crowd and its own version of the midnight celebration.
festivals.image: Krishna Janmabhoomi temple at midnight, bells and lamps, Mathura crowd

festivals.name: Magh Mela and Kumbh Mela
festivals.aliases: Prayagraj Kumbh, Maha Kumbh, Ardh Kumbh
festivals.reach: This is an annual event at Prayagraj that becomes the largest known human gathering in the world during its Kumbh years.
festivals.what: This is an annual month long fair held at the Sangam, the meeting point of the Ganga river, the Yamuna river, and a mythical third river called the Saraswati, at the city of Prayagraj. It is held every year as the Magh Mela, and roughly every twelve years it is expanded into the much larger Maha Kumbh Mela, one of the biggest gatherings of people found anywhere in the world.
festivals.who: Akharas, organized orders of Hindu ascetics, meaning holy people who give up worldly comforts, form the ritual core of this festival. Pilgrims attend in numbers that, during Kumbh years, reach into the tens of millions across the length of the fair.
festivals.when: It takes place during the month of Magh, from January to February. The full Kumbh cycle follows a roughly twelve year pattern, with a smaller Ardh, or half, Kumbh held at the midpoint between two full Kumbhs.
festivals.origin: The Sangam has been considered a sacred spot for a very long time, and the Magh Mela has been documented as an annual event for many centuries. The modern Kumbh cycle, as celebrated today at four different sites including Prayagraj, took its current organized shape during the 1800s and 1900s. Its mythical origin story traces back to the churning of the cosmic ocean and a fight over a pot of nectar.
festivals.signifies: This is a bathing pilgrimage believed to wash away the wrongdoing a person has built up over time. The confluence of rivers is considered so sacred that timing a visit to match specific planetary positions is itself part of how people practice the pilgrimage.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that bathing at the Sangam on the most auspicious days, especially a day called Mauni Amavasya, carries exceptional spiritual merit, which is why the number of visitors spikes sharply on those specific dates within the longer festival.
festivals.celebrate: A temporary tent city is built fresh each year on the exposed riverbed, complete with roads, electricity, and administration. Akharas process to bathe in a fixed order of precedence, called the Shahi Snan, or royal bath. There are religious discourses, akhada camps that visitors can tour, and a whole temporary economy of pilgrimage services that exists only for the length of the fair.
festivals.local: The tent city is completely taken down after the fair ends, and the ground goes back to being farmland or riverbed until the following year. An entire temporary city is built and then unbuilt on a schedule that is ultimately controlled by the Sangam's flood cycle.
festivals.image: Tent city and crowds at the Sangam, Prayagraj, dawn bathing

festivals.name: Eid al-Fitr
festivals.reach: This festival is especially significant across the state's large Muslim population, and it is strongest in western Uttar Pradesh and in Lucknow.
festivals.what: Eid al-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan. It is celebrated across a state with one of India's largest Muslim populations by total numbers, concentrated in the western districts and in old urban centers such as Lucknow and Bareilly.
festivals.who: Muslim communities across the state celebrate this festival, both Sunni and Shia, and different districts have their own distinct local food and mosque traditions.
festivals.when: It falls on the first day of the Islamic month of Shawwal, which moves each year according to the Hijri lunar calendar.
festivals.origin: Muslim settlement in this region dates back through the Delhi Sultanate and Mughal periods, and in the Awadh region specifically, through the Nawabi era centered on Lucknow starting in the 1700s. This history shaped a distinct regional Muslim culture.
festivals.signifies: This day marks the end of the fast, celebrated across a wide range of local traditions found within just this one state.
festivals.beliefs: People give zakat al-Fitr, a required charitable donation, before the Eid prayer. Announcements from state moon sighting committees, which confirm the exact date, are followed closely.
festivals.celebrate: People attend Eid prayers at Eidgahs, open prayer grounds, and major mosques, including Lucknow's Aishbagh Eidgah. They eat sewaiyan, sweet vermicelli, and biryani at home, wear new clothes, and visit family and neighbors throughout the day.
festivals.local: Lucknow's Eid biryani and kebab culture is distinct enough from the rest of the state that residents of other Uttar Pradesh cities will travel there specifically during the season just to eat. This regional food identity is just as strong as the religious occasion itself.
festivals.image: Eid prayer crowd at Aishbagh Eidgah, Lucknow, morning

festivals.name: Muharram
festivals.season: First month of the Hijri calendar
festivals.reach: This festival is especially significant in Lucknow, which was historically the capital of a state ruled by Shia Muslim kings.
festivals.what: Muharram is a period of mourning for the death of Imam Husain at the battle of Karbala. It is observed with particular depth in Lucknow, whose Nawab rulers of Awadh were Shia Muslims. Lucknow's imambaras, buildings meant for religious gatherings, especially the Bara Imambara, were built specifically to hold Muharram mourning assemblies.
festivals.who: Lucknow's Shia Muslim community observes this festival especially closely, though Sunni Muslims across the state observe the month too. The imambaras themselves are considered a heritage belonging to the whole city, not just to one religious community.
festivals.when: It is observed during the first ten days of Muharram, the first month of the Islamic calendar, which moves each year relative to the regular calendar.
festivals.origin: The Bara Imambara was built in 1784 by Asaf-ud-Daula, the Nawab of Awadh. It served two purposes at once, providing paid work during a famine and creating a permanent hall for Muharram mourning. Lucknow's wider Shia culture developed under the Nawabs of Awadh across the 1700s and 1800s.
festivals.signifies: This festival expresses grief for Husain's death at Karbala. At Lucknow's imambaras, that grief is treated as a permanent architectural commitment, something built into the city, rather than something improvised fresh each year.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that majlis gatherings, where the story of Karbala is retold, are themselves an act of mourning, separate from and in addition to the physical processions.
festivals.celebrate: There are majlis gatherings with the recitation of mourning poems called marsiya and noha at imambaras throughout the ten days. People carry metal standards called alams and models called tazias in processions, and perform matam, a ritual form of mourning. The Bara Imambara and Chota Imambara are at the center of the city's observance, and food is distributed in the name of Husain's household.
festivals.local: The Bara Imambara's central hall is said to be the largest vaulted hall of its kind ever built without any supporting beams inside it. It was built using a specific labor arrangement in which wealthy people tore down by night what poor laborers had built by day, so the workers could keep earning wages without it looking like charity. Lucknow still tells this story to explain the sheer scale of the building.
festivals.image: Majlis gathering inside Bara Imambara, Lucknow, lamps lit for Muharram

festivals.name: Chhath Puja
festivals.reach: This festival is especially significant in Purvanchal, the eastern part of Uttar Pradesh, and among migrant communities from that region wherever they have settled.
festivals.what: Chhath Puja is a four day festival of sun worship, celebrated intensely across Purvanchal, the eastern districts around Varanasi, Gorakhpur, and Ballia. People make offerings while standing in river water, once at sunset and again at the next sunrise.
festivals.who: Purvanchali households across the eastern districts celebrate this festival. By extension so do migrant communities from the region who have settled in places like Delhi and Mumbai, either by returning home for it or recreating the celebration wherever they now live.
festivals.when: It falls on the fourth through sixth days after Diwali, in the month of Kartik, so roughly a week after the main Diwali date.
festivals.origin: Chhath has very old roots as a sun worship festival, with references going back to Vedic era sun worship and folk connections to the epics Ramayana and Mahabharata. Its strict discipline, an unbroken fast lasting more than a day for the person observing it, is treated as ancient practice rather than something added recently.
festivals.signifies: This festival gives direct thanks to the sun. Offerings are made by standing in a river, rather than going through a temple or a priest as a go-between, and thanks are given both when the sun sets and when it rises.
festivals.beliefs: The fast, called kharna, is kept without drinking any water for more than a full day. Its difficulty is seen as part of what makes the offering valuable, not just something to be endured.
festivals.celebrate: On the first day people take a ritual bath and eat a single meal, called nahay khay. On the second day they keep the day long fast called kharna. On the third day they make an evening offering called sandhya arghya to the setting sun while standing in a river or pond. On the fourth day at dawn they make a similar offering called usha arghya to the rising sun. Folk songs in the Bhojpuri language are sung throughout.
festivals.local: At dusk, the riverbank ghats along the Ganges at Varanasi and Ballia fill with women standing waist deep in the water, holding bamboo baskets of fruit and sugarcane up toward the setting sun. The same scene repeats the next dawn facing the opposite direction. The songs sung during both moments are specifically in Bhojpuri, rather than the more formal Sanskrit hymns used in other festivals.
festivals.image: Women standing in the Ganga at sunset with offering baskets, Chhath Puja, Varanasi ghat

name: Himachal Pradesh
tagline: Himachal Pradesh is a state of apple orchards on mountain terraces and towns full of old temples. Each autumn, gods from villages all over the region are carried out to visit a king, even though that king does not actually rule anymore.

festivals.name: Kullu Dussehra
festivals.season: Begins on Vijayadashami, when Dussehra ends elsewhere
festivals.reach: This is the central festival of the valley. It draws gods and devotees from all across Kullu district.
festivals.what: This is a festival that lasts a whole week and takes place at a big open field called Dhalpur maidan. It begins on the very day that Dussehra ends in the rest of India. On that day, people carry out Raghunathji, the main god of the valley, so that he can receive visits from all the other local gods.
festivals.who: The whole of Kullu district takes part. About two hundred local gods come to attend, and each one has its own temple, its own priest, and its own team of people who carry its palanquin. Some of these gods travel from villages that are several days' walk away.
festivals.when: The festival lasts seven days and starts on Vijayadashami, which is the tenth day of Sharad Navaratri. This means it opens in early or mid October, right when Dussehra is ending in the rest of India.
festivals.origin: In the seventeenth century, a king named Raja Jagat Singh of Kullu did something as an act of penance for something he had done wrong. He placed a statue of Raghunath, a form of the god Rama that was brought from the city of Ayodhya, on his own royal throne. He then declared that all the local gods of the valley were now subjects of Raghunath, meaning they had to come and pay him a visit once every year.
festivals.signifies: What started as one king's personal way of making up for a mistake turned into a yearly tradition that has lasted long after his kingdom disappeared. The gathering shows that Raghunath is considered more important than the other gods, and it also shows that each village is still loyal to that order.
festivals.beliefs: The people who carry each god's palanquin believe that the god itself controls how the palanquin moves. When it tips or sways, they believe the god is showing its own wishes, not that the carriers are doing it on purpose.
festivals.celebrate: On the first evening, people pull Raghunathji's chariot through Dhalpur maidan. The visiting gods set up camp in rows of tents, and people go around visiting them one by one. Folk dancing and music continue all week long. On the very last night, the festival ends with the ritual burning of a big pile of grass that stands for the city of Lanka.
festivals.local: Experienced bearers say they can tell which god is being carried just by the special rhythm of its palanquin's swaying, without even looking. Arguments over which god should go first in the procession line are taken just as seriously as any other temple matter.
festivals.image: Raghunathji's chariot pulled through Dhalpur maidan, palanquins of visiting deities in rows behind

festivals.name: Mandi Shivratri
festivals.reach: This festival draws devotees from across Himachal Pradesh and even from outside the state. After Kullu Dussehra, it is the largest gathering of local deities in the region.
festivals.what: This is a week-long fair centered on the Bhootnath temple in Mandi town. During the week, about two hundred local gods are carried in from villages across the district so that they can pay their respects to Shiva.
festivals.who: The people who take part are Mandi district's temple communities and the gods they look after, along with pilgrims and traders who fill the town for the whole week.
festivals.when: The fair lasts seven days and begins on Maha Shivratri, which falls in February or March.
festivals.origin: A king named Raja Ajber Sen founded Mandi town in 1526 and built the Bhootnath temple right at its center. According to the story, he invited all the district's gods to the founding ceremony, and the fair repeats that same invitation every single year since then.
festivals.signifies: The fair renews the town's founding every year, and the gods that attend stand in for all the villages that make up the district.
festivals.beliefs: People believe the gathering confirms that the local gods are still loyal to Bhootnath, the form of Shiva who presides over the town, in the same way that subjects once renewed their loyalty to a king.
festivals.celebrate: On the opening day, the palanquins of the visiting gods are paraded into town. For the rest of the week there is folk dancing, trade fairs, and other cultural programs. At the end, a final procession carries the gods back out to their home villages.
festivals.local: Mandi calls itself the temple town of Himachal because it has about eighty shrines packed into a small grid of streets along the river. Shivratri is the one week when the town's huge number of gods all becomes visible at the same time.
festivals.image: Palanquins of local deities arriving at Bhootnath temple, Mandi, crowds along the street

festivals.name: Minjar Mela
festivals.season: A week around the maize harvest, Shravan
festivals.reach: This is the main fair of Chamba town, and it draws people from the wider district as well.
festivals.what: This is a week-long harvest fair held in Chamba town. It is named after the minjar, a small tassel made of silk thread and paddy grain that people wear during the week. The fair closes with a procession that carries the deity Raghuvira down to the Ravi river.
festivals.who: The town and district of Chamba take part, and the whole event is organized around the temple of Raghuvira, who is a form of the god Rama.
festivals.when: The fair lasts a week in the month of Shravan, which falls in July or August. It is timed to match the maize harvest, and the exact dates are fixed each year by the district administration.
festivals.origin: According to the story, the fair marks the time a king of Chamba returned home after winning a battle against the ruler of Trigarta, which is now called Kangra, back in the tenth century. When he came home, people welcomed him with bundles of paddy and maize. Chamba has kept up this custom ever since.
festivals.signifies: The fair combines a harvest celebration and a homecoming celebration into one single occasion. The tassel worn by every household stands for both of these things at once.
festivals.beliefs: People treat the minjar itself as a small offering. They wear it all week long, and then instead of keeping it, they give it up to the river when the fair ends.
festivals.celebrate: People wear minjar tassels made of silk thread and paddy pinned to their clothing all week long. On the closing day, there is a procession of the god Raghuvira through the town. Fruit, coconut, and the minjar tassels themselves are thrown into the Ravi river. Cultural programs and a trade fair run alongside all of this.
festivals.local: At the start of the week, anyone who has a spare minjar hands it out for free to others. Because of this, even a stranger visiting Chamba during the fair rarely goes without one for long.
festivals.image: Raghuvira procession reaching the banks of the Ravi river, Chamba, minjar tassels being cast in

festivals.name: Renuka Fair
festivals.reach: This fair is centered at Renuka Lake in Sirmaur district, and it draws pilgrims from Himachal, Punjab, and beyond.
festivals.what: This is a five-day fair at Renuka Lake. People believe the lake's curved shoreline is actually the shape taken by the goddess Renuka, who was the mother of the sage Parashurama. The fair centers on the one day each year when the two of them are said to meet.
festivals.who: Pilgrims from Sirmaur district and neighboring states gather around the temple complex by the lake.
festivals.when: The fair lasts five days and ends on Kartik Purnima, the full moon day in November.
festivals.origin: According to the story, Parashurama beheaded his own mother Renuka because his father ordered him to. As a reward for obeying, he was granted one wish, so he asked for her life to be given back. Local tradition says that when she came back to life, she took the form of the lake itself. The fair is held on the day that her husband Jamadagni's palanquin is said to travel from a nearby hill to meet her.
festivals.signifies: The fair acts out a reunion that happens once a year between a mother, who takes the shape of the lake, and her son, who is worshipped as a temple god somewhere else.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that bathing in the lake during the fair washes away impurities. The moment when the two palanquins meet is watched by everyone as the emotional heart of the whole event, not just as a formal ritual.
festivals.celebrate: Parashurama's palanquin is carried down from Jamu Koti hill to the shore of the lake. There is a ceremonial meeting between the two gods, boat processions on the lake, folk dancing, and a large trade fair. The week closes with everyone bathing in the lake on Kartik Purnima.
festivals.local: Families in Sirmaur plan their visits to relatives around this fair, the same way people in other districts plan visits around wedding season. This is because the road to the lake is otherwise a long journey to make.
festivals.image: Palanquin procession arriving at Renuka Lake, crowds along the shoreline, November light

festivals.name: Losar
festivals.season: New year of the Tibetan lunar calendar
festivals.reach: This new year is kept in Lahaul-Spiti and upper Kinnaur, which are Himachal's Buddhist districts.
festivals.what: Losar is the Buddhist new year. In Himachal's high districts of Lahaul-Spiti and upper Kinnaur, it is kept with monastery rituals, visits between houses, and archery contests. It is a much smaller, quieter celebration than the big market-town festivals like Kullu Dussehra or Mandi Shivratri.
festivals.who: The Buddhist communities of Spiti, Lahaul, and upper Kinnaur take part. Their religious calendar and their connections to monasteries follow Ladakh and Tibet, rather than the Hindu hill towns further south in Himachal.
festivals.when: The date follows the Tibetan lunar calendar, so it shifts around compared to our regular Gregorian calendar. Monasteries in this region often celebrate it on a date fixed locally, rather than on the same date observed in Lhasa, Tibet.
festivals.origin: Losar existed even before Buddhism came to Tibet, as a new year festival meant to celebrate the harvest and calm down spirits. Later, it became part of the Buddhist calendar as monasteries spread along the trade routes across the Himalayas, routes that also reached Spiti and Lahaul.
festivals.signifies: Losar marks a kind of settling up with the spirit world before the year changes, along with the usual new year hope for good fortune.
festivals.beliefs: Families believe that in the days before Losar, the house must be swept clean of the past year's bad luck. They believe this bad luck needs to be physically carried out of the house, not just cleaned away like ordinary dirt.
festivals.celebrate: At monasteries, people light butter lamps and chant prayers. In Kinnaur, villages hold archery contests against each other. Families share chang, a local barley beer, from house to house. People wear new clothes and pay visits to each other in a strict order based on age and seniority.
festivals.local: In Spiti, the order in which households visit each other during Losar still roughly follows old rankings based on how much land families used to own. Younger residents will point this out, but more with a shrug than a complaint.
festivals.image: Monks with butter lamps at a Spiti monastery courtyard, Losar morning, snow outside

festivals.name: Phulaich
festivals.season: Flowering season in the high meadows of Kinnaur
festivals.reach: This festival is kept across all of Kinnaur district.
festivals.what: Phulaich is a Kinnauri festival built around a day-long climb up to high alpine meadows to gather wildflowers. People carry the flowers back down and offer them to the village god and in memory of family members who have died.
festivals.who: The villages of Kinnaur district take part. Their Kinnauri identity and their local style of worship are quite different from the Hindu calendar followed in the plains.
festivals.when: The festival falls on a fixed day in the local calendar, during the Hindu month of Bhadrapada, which corresponds to September or October. This timing matches when wildflowers bloom high up in the mountains.
festivals.origin: Phulaich is a Kinnauri custom, not something taken from classical Hindu texts. It has long been recorded locally as a regular part of the region's farming and ancestor-honoring calendar, and there is no single date when it was first started.
festivals.signifies: The festival is a yearly way of recognizing both the mountain's flowering season and the memory of family members who have died, done through the same single act of gathering flowers.
festivals.beliefs: People believe the flowers keep away bad luck. Villagers also believe that the climb, which is done by chosen men from the village, must be finished before it gets dark.
festivals.celebrate: At dawn, men climb up to the high meadows to gather flowers. The village god's palanquin is carried out to meet them when they return. The flowers are offered at the temple and to the goddess Kali. In the evening, the festival closes with singing and dancing in the village santhang, which is the temple courtyard.
festivals.local: Each village keeps its own exact Phulaich date within the same general time window. Because of this, a road trip through Kinnaur in early autumn can pass through two or three different village festivals in a single day's drive.
festivals.image: Villagers descending from alpine meadows with armfuls of wildflowers, Kinnaur, late afternoon

festivals.name: Christmas in Shimla
festivals.reach: This is centered among Shimla's old church community and the Christian settlements in the apple-growing belt that were founded by Christian missions.
festivals.what: Christmas in Shimla still looks much like it did in colonial times, when Shimla was a hill station. The Ridge, a well-known open area in town, is lit up. There is a midnight service at Christ Church, and carol singing that first spread out from nineteenth-century mission schools and orchard settlements.
festivals.who: Shimla's small but long-established Christian community takes part, along with Christian families from mission-founded settlements such as Kotgarh in the apple belt.
festivals.when: Christmas falls on December 25th, but the town's season of lights and carol events runs through the weeks leading up to it.
festivals.origin: Christ Church on the Ridge was consecrated in 1857. It was built for the British colonial government, which used Shimla as its summer capital. The wider Christian presence in the hills grew out of nineteenth-century Christian missions, which also introduced the apple varieties that the region is now famous for.
festivals.signifies: This Christmas tradition is something inherited from the town's founding as a colonial hill station. It has been kept alive by the community that stayed on even after the British administration left.
festivals.beliefs: The midnight service at Christ Church is treated as an event for the whole town, not just a private religious service. Many people who are not themselves Christian attend it too.
festivals.celebrate: Christ Church is lit up and decorated on the Ridge, and there is a midnight service. Carol singers walk through Shimla's Mall Road. Families bake fruit cake at home. In Kotgarh and nearby orchard villages, there is a smaller church-centered gathering that is tied to the same mission history that first brought apple growing to the region.
festivals.local: Locally, Kotgarh's Christian settlement is remembered just as much for the American missionary who introduced grafted apple trees there as it is for its church. People tell the two stories, the church and the apples, as one single history.
festivals.image: Christ Church lit for Christmas on the Shimla Ridge, evening crowd

name: Uttarakhand
tagline: Uttarakhand is home to four shrines located where major rivers begin high in the mountains, and to Haridwar, a town where pilgrims bathe in the Ganga. Its farming calendar is built around whatever the monsoon rains leave behind.

festivals.name: Kumbh Mela
festivals.month: Varies, roughly every twelve years, with an Ardh Kumbh at the six-year midpoint
festivals.season: Weeks around bathing dates set by planetary position
festivals.reach: This is one of the largest gatherings of human beings that happens anywhere in the world on a regular basis. It draws pilgrims from across India and from Indian communities living abroad.
festivals.what: The Kumbh Mela is a gathering of organized groups of Hindu ascetics, along with ordinary pilgrims, at Haridwar, the place where the Ganga river leaves the Himalayas and flows out onto the plains. The gathering is built around bathing in the river on a series of dates that are fixed according to the positions of the planets.
festivals.who: Akharas, which are organized orders of Hindu ascetics, take part, along with tens of millions of ordinary pilgrims over the whole length of the mela.
festivals.when: The Kumbh Mela is held at Haridwar roughly every twelve years, with a smaller Ardh Kumbh, meaning half Kumbh, held at the six-year midpoint. The exact bathing dates are set by the position of the sun and the planet Jupiter, and they fall somewhere between January and April of the mela year.
festivals.origin: The Kumbh Mela is traced back to an old myth about the churning of the ocean, in which drops of a nectar of immortality fell at four riverbank places, including Haridwar. Records show that gatherings at Haridwar have happened since at least the early seventeenth century. The modern pattern, in which the Kumbh rotates every twelve years between four sites, Haridwar, Prayagraj, Nashik and Ujjain, developed gradually over the centuries that followed.
festivals.signifies: The Kumbh Mela treats the spot where the Ganga comes down to the plains as a special place where the ordinary rules about the river relax. It is also one of the rare times the ascetic orders appear in public.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that bathing at the exact fixed hour can free a person from the cycle of rebirth in a way that ordinary bathing cannot.
festivals.celebrate: The most important event is the Shahi Snan, or royal bath, in which the akharas march to the river in a fixed order and bathe first. Ordinary pilgrims follow over the days and weeks after that. There are also sermons, akhara camps, and a huge temporary town of tents set up along the riverbank.
festivals.local: Over many generations, the akharas have argued over and eventually settled the order in which they bathe. This means the order used today is actually the result of old disputes, not an unbroken tradition that nobody ever questioned.
festivals.image: Akhara procession to the Ganga at Har Ki Pauri, Haridwar, dawn bathing crowd

festivals.name: Char Dham Yatra
festivals.season: The Himalayan pilgrimage season, between snowmelt and the first heavy snow
festivals.reach: This pilgrimage circuit organizes much of the religious life of the state, and it draws devotees from across India.
festivals.what: The Char Dham Yatra is a circuit of four shrines: Yamunotri, Gangotri, Kedarnath, and Badrinath. Each shrine opens and closes for the year on fixed dates, and all of them are completely shut during the winter snow.
festivals.who: Hindu pilgrims from across India take part, along with the Garhwal communities whose priests, guides, and mule and porter businesses depend on the pilgrimage season for their livelihood.
festivals.when: The shrines open in April, usually on or near the day of Akshaya Tritiya for Yamunotri and Gangotri, and a few days later for Kedarnath and Badrinath. They close again around Diwali, as winter begins to set in.
festivals.origin: Each of the four shrines has its own older history. Badrinath's history, for example, is connected to the philosopher Adi Shankaracharya, who helped revive the site in earlier centuries. However, it was only in more modern times, as roads and pilgrimage facilities improved, that the four shrines were formally grouped together into one named circuit.
festivals.signifies: The Char Dham Yatra treats the four rivers and shrines of Garhwal as one single journey that pilgrims are expected to complete, rather than as four separate destinations to visit independently.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that visiting all four shrines brings more religious merit than visiting just one on its own. Pilgrims often speak of the whole circuit as unfinished business until they have completed every part of it.
festivals.celebrate: Each shrine has an elaborate kapat, or door-opening, ceremony. Pilgrims travel to Kedarnath and Yamunotri either on foot or by pony, and helicopter services now also run alongside the traditional trek. In autumn, there is a kapat closing ceremony at which each god's winter image is moved down to a shrine at a lower altitude.
festivals.local: The deity of Badrinath is moved down to the Narsingh temple in Joshimath for the winter, and then moved back up again each spring. This means the god itself makes the same seasonal journey up and down the mountain that the pilgrims do.
festivals.image: Pilgrims on the trail to Kedarnath temple against a snow-lined valley, early morning

festivals.name: Nanda Devi Raj Jat
festivals.reach: This pilgrimage involves the whole of Garhwal, but it only happens once during a person's working memory, since it comes around just once every twelve years.
festivals.what: This is a pilgrimage on foot, covering about 280 kilometers through Chamoli district. Pilgrims follow a four-horned ram that is believed to carry the goddess Nanda Devi back to her home high in the Himalayas. It only happens once every twelve years.
festivals.who: Villages across Garhwal take part, and the event has been organized for generations by the Kunwar family of Kansuwa, who inherited the job of overseeing it. Thousands of pilgrims also join for the big twelve-year edition.
festivals.when: The full Raj Jat happens on a twelve-year cycle, and the most recent one was in 2014. In the years in between, smaller local jats, or pilgrimages, are held for Nanda Devi instead.
festivals.origin: Local tradition traces this pilgrimage back to a seventh-century Garhwal ruler named Shalipal, and says it was later expanded by King Kanakpal. The Kunwar family took over organizing it around the year 1730. Because the pilgrimage covers such a long history and happens so rarely, it is hard for outsiders to check the earliest dates, so much of its timeline relies on local records and memory rather than outside proof.
festivals.signifies: The pilgrimage represents a goddess's journey back to the high mountain home where she was born, and it is also the moment when Garhwal's villages walk out together to see her off.
festivals.beliefs: The four-horned ram used in the pilgrimage must have been born without human help, and it is raised specially for this journey. People believe it carries the spirit of Nanda Devi inside it. At the end of the pilgrimage, the ram is set free to walk alone into the high mountains, and it is never seen again.
festivals.celebrate: A procession of palanquins, flags, and the ram moves from village to village over three weeks. Each night, the procession stays over in a different named village, taking turns in a strict rotation. There are ritual farewells at each stage of the journey, and it ends with a final climb up to Homkund lake, from which the ram walks off alone.
festivals.local: The moment the ram walks alone into the mountains at the very end, watched by everyone in the procession but followed by no one, is treated locally as the single most important moment that the entire three-week walk has been building up to.
festivals.image: Procession with the four-horned ram approaching Homkund lake, Chamoli district, high altitude

festivals.name: Harela
festivals.reach: Harela is kept across the Kumaon region, and a related version of it is also marked in Garhwal.
festivals.what: Harela is a Kumaoni festival built around seedlings that are grown indoors in the dark for nine days. On the tenth day, people cut the seedlings and wear them as a blessing. The timing matches the start of the sowing season.
festivals.who: Kumaoni households take part, and more and more schools and offices have also started marking Harela because of its connection with planting trees, treating it as a kind of environmental observance.
festivals.when: The festival begins on the first day of the dark half of the month of Shravan and ends nine days later, sometime in July or August.
festivals.origin: Harela is an old Kumaoni farming custom tied to the sowing calendar of the month of Shravan. It is also connected to the marriage of the gods Shiva and Parvati, which is celebrated locally around the same time. These two strands, one about farming and one about the gods' marriage, are woven together so closely that people today do not clearly separate them when talking about the festival.
festivals.signifies: Harela is like a household's own small harvest forecast. Instead of looking at a real field, families grow seedlings in a tray and read them for clues about how healthy the year's crop will be, even before the actual crop has been sown.
festivals.beliefs: On the tenth day, people look at the color and thickness of the harela shoots and read them as a sign of what the coming harvest will be like. If the shoots are thin and pale, that is taken as a bad sign.
festivals.celebrate: People sow seven or nine kinds of grain in a basket, keep it in the dark for nine days, and water it every day. Small clay images of Shiva, Parvati, and Ganesha are worshipped alongside the basket. On the tenth day, the yellow shoots are cut and worn behind the ear or tucked into a cap. Tree saplings are also planted in the festival's name.
festivals.local: Older Kumaoni women insist that the harela shoots must be grown in complete darkness, not just indoors, and they treat this as a rule that cannot be broken. They say that if the shoots get direct light, it ruins the reading of the omen.
festivals.image: Harela shoots grown in a woven basket, being cut and distributed, Kumaon household

festivals.name: Uttarayani
festivals.reach: Uttarayani is kept across both Kumaon and Garhwal, and the fair held at Bageshwar is the largest annual gathering in that district.
festivals.what: Uttarayani is Uttarakhand's version of the festival Makar Sankranti. In Kumaon it is best known as Ghughutia, a day when children wear garlands made of sweet dough shaped like birds, and call crows down from the rooftops to feed them.
festivals.who: Households across Kumaon and Garhwal take part. At Bageshwar, the wider district is drawn in by a week-long fair held on the grounds of the Bagnath temple.
festivals.when: The main day is Makar Sankranti in mid-January, and the Bageshwar fair runs for about a week around that date.
festivals.origin: The custom of making Ghughutia sweets and calling crows is a Kumaoni folk practice, and nobody knows for sure exactly how or when it began. It is kept alongside the same Makar Sankranti festival observed all across India based on the sun's position. The Bageshwar fair at the Bagnath temple has its own separate and older history, going back to when it was a trading gathering on the banks of the Saryu river.
festivals.signifies: Uttarayani marks the sun's turn toward the north, but here it is marked through a children's ritual rather than through a ceremony led by adults.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that feeding the ghughutia sweets to crows is an offering that brings good fortune for the year ahead, with the crow acting as a kind of messenger.
festivals.celebrate: Sweet dough is shaped into birds, drums, and other small figures, then deep-fried and strung into garlands for children to wear. Children call crows to the rooftop with a special rhyme and feed them pieces of the garland. Many households eat kicheri, a dish made of rice and lentils. At Bageshwar, there are folk dance troupes, traders, and a large fair on the grounds of the Bagnath temple.
festivals.local: Children in Kumaon still learn the specific crow-calling rhyme by heart before they learn much else about the festival. Reciting it correctly is treated as the real point of the whole morning.
festivals.image: Children with ghughutia dough-bird garlands calling crows from a rooftop, Kumaon morning

festivals.name: Phool Dei
festivals.reach: Phool Dei is kept across villages in both Kumaon and Garhwal.
festivals.what: Phool Dei is a spring custom that lasts a whole month. Young children go from door to door at dawn, scattering fresh flowers on doorsteps, and in return they receive sweets and small gifts.
festivals.who: Village children, mostly girls, take part. They organize themselves informally by neighborhood, rather than through any temple or official institution.
festivals.when: It begins on the first day of the month of Chaitra, in March, and continues through the whole month as the hill orchards come into flower.
festivals.origin: Phool Dei is a Kumaoni and Garhwali folk custom, and there is no record of any single founding moment. It is tied to the spring flowering of peach, plum, apricot, and rhododendron trees, rather than to any religious text's festival calendar.
festivals.signifies: Phool Dei is a welcome to spring given by the youngest members of a household rather than by its elders. It is also a small act of neighborliness that gets repeated every day for a month.
festivals.beliefs: People believe the flowers laid at each doorstep bring good fortune to that household for the whole year. If a family turns the children away, it is thought that they have also turned away the year's good luck along with them.
festivals.celebrate: Children get up before dawn to gather rhododendron, peach blossoms, and other spring flowers. They scatter the flowers on doorsteps and thresholds, sometimes arranging them into small patterns. At each house, they sing a short verse. On the last day of the month, called Sankranti, the households that were visited all month give the children sweets, coins, and food.
festivals.local: The flower patterns the children leave on doorsteps get walked over and disappear within the same day, but nobody minds this, since the real point was the visit itself, not how the pattern looked.
festivals.image: Children scattering rhododendron petals on a village doorstep at dawn, Garhwal

festivals.name: Urs at Piran Kaliyar
festivals.season: Rabi al-Awwal, the third month of the Hijri calendar
festivals.reach: This gathering draws pilgrims of several different faiths from across North India and beyond, and it is centered at Kaliyar, near Roorkee.
festivals.what: This is the yearly gathering held on the death anniversary of Alauddin Sabir Kaliyari, a Sufi saint from the thirteenth century. It takes place at his dargah, or shrine, near Roorkee, which is one of the most visited Chishti Sufi shrines in North India.
festivals.who: Muslim pilgrims travel to the shrine, along with a large number of Hindu and Sikh visitors. These Hindu and Sikh visitors do not follow any other part of the Islamic calendar, but they still come specifically for this event.
festivals.when: The Urs falls on the thirteenth to fifteenth days of Rabi al-Awwal, a month in the Islamic calendar. Because that calendar is lunar, the date moves each year compared to our regular Gregorian calendar.
festivals.origin: Sabir Kaliyari was a nephew and student of the Chishti saint Baba Farid. He settled at Kaliyar and died there around the year 1291. The Urs marking his death has been kept at the shrine for generations, and over time it grew into the large regional gathering it draws today.
festivals.signifies: In Sufi tradition, a saint's death is treated as a kind of wedding with God rather than as a loss. This is why the day is marked with music and celebration instead of mourning.
festivals.beliefs: Visitors from several different faiths widely believe that the shrine can heal illness and free troubled people from evil spirits. Many pilgrims travel there specifically for this reason, not only because it is the date of the Urs.
festivals.celebrate: Qawwali music is performed throughout the days of the Urs. Pilgrims and official delegations lay chadars, which are ceremonial cloths, over the saint's grave. A large temporary market springs up around the shrine, and langar, meaning free communal food, is served to all visitors no matter what faith they follow.
festivals.local: Because the shrine has a reputation for healing, it draws a steady stream of visitors even outside the days of the Urs itself. This means Kaliyar actually functions as a pilgrimage town on more days of the year than not.
festivals.image: Chadar offering procession at the Kaliyar Sharif dargah, Roorkee, Urs crowd

name: Jammu and Kashmir
tagline: Jammu and Kashmir is a valley full of shrines and fruit orchards. For government purposes, it is paired with the plains city of Jammu, and the two cities take turns being the capital twice a year.

festivals.name: Eid al-Fitr
festivals.reach: This is the central festival of the Muslim majority in the Kashmir valley. It is also kept by Muslim communities in Poonch, Rajouri, and Doda, which are in Jammu division.
festivals.what: Eid al-Fitr marks the end of the fasting month of Ramadan. It is kept at mosques and shrines across the Kashmir valley, and in the Muslim-majority areas of Jammu division. Some of the largest gatherings happen at Srinagar's Jama Masjid and at Hazratbal.
festivals.who: The Muslim majority of the Kashmir valley takes part above all, along with Muslim communities in Poonch, Rajouri, and Doda in Jammu division. Many of these people are Gujjar and Bakarwal herders who are returning home from grazing their animals in the high pastures over summer.
festivals.when: Eid al-Fitr falls on the first day of the month of Shawwal, and because it follows the lunar Hijri calendar, the date moves each year.
festivals.origin: The fast and its ending are prescribed in the Qur'an. Islam reached Kashmir mainly starting in the fourteenth century, brought by Sufi missionaries and through contact with Central Asia and Persia. This shaped a Kashmiri Muslim culture that is distinct both from the Arab world and from the rest of India's Muslim community.
festivals.signifies: Eid al-Fitr marks the end of the fast. In Kashmir, it is also a homecoming for Gujjar and Bakarwal families, whose herds have spent the summer grazing in the high mountain pastures.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that Zakat al-Fitr, a charitable payment, must be given before the Eid prayer, so that no household is left out of the feast.
festivals.celebrate: People offer Eid prayers at the Jama Masjid in Srinagar and at neighborhood mosques. They wear new clothes, called Eid ded. Wealthier households prepare wazwan dishes, while other households make simpler meat dishes. People visit each other throughout the day, and in the mountain districts, herding families time their return from the highlands so they can be home for the day.
festivals.local: Kashmiri wazwan is a mutton feast with many courses, usually served at weddings and other major occasions. For an ordinary Eid table, families make a smaller version of it, but people still notice if a household skips it altogether.
festivals.image: Eid morning prayers at Srinagar's Jama Masjid, courtyard filled with worshippers

festivals.name: Eid al-Adha
festivals.reach: Eid al-Adha is kept across the Kashmir valley and in the Muslim-majority districts of Jammu division.
festivals.what: Eid al-Adha is the festival of sacrifice. It is marked by the ritual slaughter of a sheep or goat, and most of the meat is given away to poor people and to neighbors.
festivals.who: Muslim households across Kashmir and in the Muslim-majority districts of Jammu division take part.
festivals.when: It falls on the tenth day of Dhu al-Hijjah, the last month of the Hijri calendar, and because that calendar is lunar, the date moves each year compared to the Gregorian calendar.
festivals.origin: Eid al-Adha commemorates the moment when the prophet Ibrahim was willing to sacrifice his own son because God commanded it, and God then provided a ram to sacrifice instead. In the weeks before the festival, livestock markets across Srinagar and other towns grow much busier, as families come to buy an animal ahead of the date.
festivals.signifies: The festival represents submission to God being tested and then answered with mercy. Families re-enact this idea through an act that actually costs them something real, since sacrificing an animal is not free.
festivals.beliefs: People believe the meat is only properly distributed if some of it goes to people who could not otherwise afford meat. Keeping all the meat just for one's own household is considered to miss the whole point of the festival.
festivals.celebrate: People offer Eid prayer at mosques and at open prayer grounds called Eidgahs. The sacrifice is performed either at home or by a hired butcher. The meat is divided into roughly three equal parts, one for the family, one for relatives, and one for the poor. Visiting between families continues over the following days.
festivals.local: In the days before Eid al-Adha, sheep markets on the outskirts of Srinagar become a small annual event of their own, with buyers sometimes bargaining over a single animal for hours.
festivals.image: Sheep market on the outskirts of Srinagar ahead of Eid al-Adha, buyers inspecting animals

festivals.name: Moi-e-Muqaddas Display
festivals.month: Varies, tied to the Islamic calendar
festivals.season: Major Islamic anniversaries through the year
festivals.reach: This event is centered on the Hazratbal shrine in Srinagar, and it is one of the most attended religious occasions in the valley.
