festivals.what: This is the public showing of a relic that is believed to be a hair of the Prophet Muhammad. It is kept at the Hazratbal shrine on the shore of Dal Lake, and it is shown to worshippers on only a small number of major anniversaries each year.
festivals.who: Kashmiri Muslims from Srinagar and the surrounding valley form the shrine's regular congregation, and visitors from farther away also come specifically on display days.
festivals.when: The relic is displayed on occasions such as Milad-un-Nabi, the Prophet's birthday, and on the anniversaries of his close companions. The shrine also draws a very large crowd on Jumat-ul-Vida, the last Friday of Ramadan, although the relic itself is not always displayed on that particular day.
festivals.origin: According to the story, the relic reached Kashmir in the seventeenth century, and it was installed at Hazratbal after a period during which people disputed who should have custody of it. In 1963, the relic was stolen and later recovered, an event that is well documented and that drew huge crowds and political attention across the valley at the time.
festivals.signifies: The relic represents a direct, physical link to the Prophet, kept right inside the valley itself. This is part of the reason Hazratbal carries more weight in Kashmiri religious life than an ordinary shrine would.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that viewing the relic on a display day brings a special blessing. Even worshippers who cannot get close enough to actually see it often still feel the visit was worthwhile.
festivals.celebrate: After prayers, the relic is brought out and shown to the crowd from a raised position. There is recitation and prayer around the display. On Jumat-ul-Vida, the congregational Friday prayer draws one of the largest single gatherings anywhere in the valley.
festivals.local: People in Srinagar still talk about the 1963 theft of the relic as a moment when the whole city came out onto the streets. Older residents describe it from their own memory rather than from anything they read in a book.
festivals.image: Crowd gathered at Hazratbal shrine on Dal Lake for a relic display, Srinagar

festivals.name: Urs at Charar-e-Sharief
festivals.season: Death anniversary of Sheikh Noor-ud-din Noorani
festivals.reach: This Urs is centered at Charar-e-Sharief in Budgam district, and it is one of the most widely attended Sufi observances in the valley.
festivals.what: This is the yearly gathering at the shrine of Sheikh Noor-ud-din Noorani, also known as Nund Rishi. He lived in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, founded Kashmir's Rishi religious order, and is one of the most widely honored figures in the valley.
festivals.who: Kashmiri Muslims across the valley take part, and they consider Nund Rishi a shared spiritual founder rather than someone belonging to any one particular sect. Kashmiri Pandits have historically honored him too.
festivals.when: The Urs is held on the saint's death anniversary according to the Islamic calendar, and it generally falls in April or May.
festivals.origin: Nund Rishi was born around 1377 near Kulgam. He founded the Rishi order, a Sufi tradition unique to Kashmir that drew on both Islamic teachings and older ascetic practices already present in the valley. His shrine at Charar-e-Sharief was rebuilt after the original wooden building burned down during an armed standoff in 1995.
festivals.signifies: This Urs honors a form of Islam that is specifically Kashmiri, shaped by the valley's own older ascetic traditions. It is celebrated at the grave of the man credited with founding that tradition.
festivals.beliefs: Nund Rishi's verses are still recited and sung today, and locally people consider them the plainest and most trusted religious guidance available in the Kashmiri language.
festivals.celebrate: People recite Nund Rishi's shrukhs, his mystical verses written in Kashmiri. There is a procession and a chadar offering at the rebuilt shrine, along with qawwali music and devotional singing. A large trade fair also runs around the town for the whole event.
festivals.local: The 1995 fire that destroyed the original shrine is remembered locally as a loss for the whole valley, not just for one community. This is part of why rebuilding it was treated as a shared civic matter rather than the concern of only one group.
festivals.image: Chadar offering at the rebuilt Charar-e-Sharief shrine, Budgam, Urs crowd

festivals.name: Herath
festivals.season: Thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Phalguna
festivals.reach: Herath is the central festival of the Kashmiri Pandit community. It is kept both in the valley and among the community members who left after being displaced in the early 1990s and now live elsewhere.
festivals.what: Herath is a fifteen-day observance among Kashmiri Pandits marking the marriage of the gods Shiva and Parvati. It is built around worship at home of a water vessel called the vatuk, rather than around a ritual performed at a temple.
festivals.who: Kashmiri Pandit households take part. Most of this community was displaced from the valley starting in the early 1990s, and they are now mostly concentrated in Jammu, Delhi, and other places further away, along with a much smaller number who stayed behind in the valley.
festivals.when: The main worship falls on the thirteenth day of the dark half of the month of Phalguna, which is one day before the Maha Shivratri celebrated across the rest of India, in February or March.
festivals.origin: Herath has been recorded as the central social and religious festival of the Kashmiri Pandit community for centuries. Its rituals and even its vocabulary are specific to Kashmiri Shaivism, a particular tradition of worshipping Shiva, and are different from how Shivratri is observed elsewhere in India.
festivals.signifies: Herath shows how a community has kept its calendar intact even through displacement. The same vatuk ritual is observed whether it is performed in Srinagar or in an apartment in Jammu.
festivals.beliefs: Many households believe that Herath brings rain to the valley. This belief is tied so closely to the festival that people still notice when the expected rain does not come.
festivals.celebrate: A steel vessel filled with water and walnuts, which represents the Vedas, is worshipped over several days. The day after the main worship is called Salam, on which Muslim neighbors would traditionally visit Pandit households. This day is remembered as a sign of how close the two communities used to be. On the festival's final day, called Dooni Mavas, walnuts are shared among family members.
festivals.local: Older Kashmiri Pandits describe Salam, the neighborly visiting day, with a particular sadness and longing. This is because it depended on living close to Muslim neighbors, something that has become rare since the community's displacement.
festivals.image: Vatuk pooja vessel with walnuts set out for Herath, Kashmiri Pandit household

festivals.name: Navratra at Vaishno Devi
festivals.month: March to April and September to October
festivals.reach: This is one of the most visited pilgrimage sites in India, and it is a defining occasion for the whole of Jammu division.
festivals.what: This pilgrimage is a thirteen-kilometer uphill walk to a cave shrine in the Trikuta hills. It is at its most crowded during the nine nights of Navratra, when the goddess is believed to be especially present.
festivals.who: Hindu pilgrims come from across India. The Dogra Hindu population of Jammu division plays a prominent role too, since they act as the shrine's local caretakers and their local economy runs largely on the pilgrimage.
festivals.when: It is kept twice a year, once during Chaitra Navratri around March to April, and again during Sharad Navratri around September to October. Both of these are peak pilgrimage seasons at the shrine.
festivals.origin: The cave and its worship are old, but the way the shrine is managed today, along with the modern pilgrim route, was mostly organized in the twentieth century as more and more visitors began coming. At this shrine, the goddess is worshipped in the form of three natural rock shapes, rather than as a carved statue.
festivals.signifies: The pilgrimage treats the climb itself as part of the devotion. Pilgrims deliberately take on this physical challenge rather than trying to avoid it.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that reaching the cave helps fulfill vows and resolve hardships. Many pilgrims make the climb specifically to keep a promise they made in an earlier year.
festivals.celebrate: Pilgrims climb up from the town of Katra on foot, by pony, by palanquin, or by helicopter. At the cave shrine, queues are managed in timed batches, and aarti is performed at fixed hours. During Navratra specifically, the shrine stays open longer, and there is a noticeable increase in both the number of pilgrims and the number of temporary stalls along the route.
festivals.local: The economy of Katra town runs almost entirely on this pilgrimage. Its shops, which sell everything from bangles to trekking poles, are stocked mainly for pilgrims first, and only secondly for local residents.
festivals.image: Pilgrims ascending the Trikuta hills path to Vaishno Devi cave, Navratra crowd

festivals.name: Amarnath Yatra
festivals.season: Shravan, from Skanda Shashthi to Shravan Purnima
festivals.reach: This is a major Hindu pilgrimage that draws people from across India, and it takes place through the Kashmir valley.
festivals.what: This is a high-altitude trek to a cave that sits at 3,888 meters in the Kashmir Himalaya. Inside the cave, an ice formation on the floor is seen as a lingam, and it is believed to be a natural manifestation of the god Shiva.
festivals.who: Hindu pilgrims come from across India. On the ground, Kashmir valley's Muslim pony operators, porters, and shopkeepers help run the pilgrimage, a role they have played for a very long time. In ordinary years, this involvement is widely accepted by local people.
festivals.when: The pilgrimage runs through the month of Shravan, from around Skanda Shashthi to Shravan Purnima, roughly from July into August.
festivals.origin: The cave's connection to Shiva comes from older Hindu myth. The pilgrimage to it was largely revived in the nineteenth century with support from the Dogra state, after going through a period when it was little known. The modern version of the pilgrimage, with fixed routes, base camps, and registration, involving very large numbers of pilgrims, is a more recent development set up by the administration.
festivals.signifies: The pilgrimage centers on an image of the divine that forms and melts away with the seasons. Devotees treat this natural cycle as a deliberate image of Shiva, not as something accidental.
festivals.beliefs: Devotees believe that the size of the ice lingam in any given year carries a meaning, and local accounts say it grows and shrinks along with the phases of the moon. In reality, though, its shape is actually controlled by temperature and how much it melts.
festivals.celebrate: Before departure, pilgrims must register and pass medical checks. They trek along either the Pahalgam route or the Baltal route, staying in overnight camps along the way. At the cave itself, they have darshan, meaning a sacred viewing. Volunteer committees run langar, or free food, all along both routes.
festivals.local: The pilgrimage's langar network, run mostly by volunteer groups from outside Kashmir, is itself a small logistical achievement. It feeds tens of thousands of pilgrims a day, using makeshift kitchens set up all along a mountain trail.
festivals.image: Pilgrims trekking the Amarnath route through the Kashmir Himalaya, tents at a base camp

festivals.name: Lohri
festivals.reach: Lohri is kept across Dogra Hindu and Sikh households in Jammu division.
festivals.what: Lohri is a bonfire festival marking the winter solstice and the rabi crop cycle. It is kept in Jammu division much the same way it is kept across Punjab and Himachal, with people throwing sesame seeds, jaggery, and popcorn into the fire.
festivals.who: Dogra Hindu and Sikh households of Jammu division take part, especially households that had a birth or a wedding in the previous year.
festivals.when: Lohri falls on the night before Makar Sankranti, in mid-January.
festivals.origin: Lohri is a winter solstice custom from the Punjab plains, shared across Jammu, Himachal, and Punjab. It is tied to the rabi sowing season and to the shortest days of the year. Its exact origin comes from folk tradition rather than religious texts, and its songs and legends differ from district to district.
festivals.signifies: Lohri marks the turning point of the year's darkest stretch of days. It is marked with fire, and by sharing foods that store well through the winter.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that a family's first Lohri after a new baby is born, or after a couple gets married, is especially significant. It is marked with extra visitors and extra gifts.
festivals.celebrate: A bonfire is lit at dusk. People throw sesame seeds, gajak, and popcorn into the flames, and also eat them. Folk songs are sung around the fire. Gifts are given to households celebrating their first Lohri. The next morning, Makar Sankranti is kept, and in some Jammu neighborhoods people fly kites.
festivals.local: In Jammu city, a first Lohri celebrating a new baby can draw every household on an entire street to one shared bonfire. Neighbors take this obligation seriously, even in years when they might otherwise skip celebrating the festival themselves.
festivals.image: Bonfire gathering with sesame and jaggery offerings, Jammu neighbourhood, winter night

name: Ladakh
tagline: Ladakh is a high mountain desert. Part of it is made up of Buddhist monastery towns, and just one mountain pass away lies a valley where most people are Shia Muslim.

festivals.name: Hemis Tsechu
festivals.season: Tenth day of the fifth Tibetan month
festivals.reach: This is Ladakh's best known monastery festival, and it draws visitors from across India and from abroad to Hemis monastery.
festivals.what: This is a two-day festival of masked dancing at Hemis monastery. It marks the birth of Guru Padmasambhava, an eighth-century Buddhist master who is credited with spreading Buddhism across the Himalayas.
festivals.who: The Drukpa Kagyu monks of Hemis monastery take part. Hemis is the largest and wealthiest monastery in Ladakh. The wider Buddhist population of Leh district also joins in.
festivals.when: It falls on the tenth day of the fifth month of the Tibetan lunar calendar, which is usually in June or July.
festivals.origin: According to reports, this festival has been held without a single break since around 1730, during the time of the monastery's patron Gyalsras Rinpoche. It commemorates events from the traditional life story of Padmasambhava himself, rather than marking any historical founding date of its own.
festivals.signifies: The festival represents the eight different forms that Padmasambhava is said to have taken, each one overcoming a different obstacle to the spread of Buddhism. These stories are acted out during the festival, rather than simply told out loud.
festivals.beliefs: People believe the cham dances carry real spiritual power, not just that they illustrate a story. This is why the exact choreography and the order of the masks are preserved so carefully.
festivals.celebrate: Masked monks perform the cham dance to the sound of horns and cymbals in the monastery courtyard over the two days. Once every twelve years, during the Tibetan Monkey Year, an enormous embroidered thangka, a religious cloth painting of Padmasambhava, is unrolled and displayed. The rest of the time, it is kept rolled up and stored away.
festivals.local: Locally, people treat the twelve-year unrolling of the thangka as a completely different kind of event from the regular annual festival. Ladakhis will describe which year's Hemis festival they attended by mentioning whether or not they got to see the thangka unrolled.
festivals.image: Masked cham dancers in the Hemis monastery courtyard, mountain light, drums and horns

festivals.name: Losar
festivals.season: New year of the Tibetan calendar, kept early in Ladakh
festivals.reach: This new year is kept across Ladakh's Buddhist villages and monasteries.
festivals.what: This is Ladakh's new year, and it is kept roughly two months earlier than the Losar observed in Tibet itself and in Sikkim. Local tradition explains this difference by telling the story of a king who moved the date forward before going on a military campaign.
festivals.who: Ladakh's Buddhist population takes part, concentrated mainly in Leh district and in parts of Kargil district, such as Zanskar.
festivals.when: Ladakh's main new year observance is called Galdan Namchot, and it falls on the twenty-fifth day of the tenth Tibetan month, in December. This is different from the Losar celebrated in February elsewhere in the Tibetan Buddhist world.
festivals.origin: According to Ladakhi tradition, a sixteenth-century king named Jamyang Namgyal was planning a military campaign against Baltistan. An oracle advised him to wait until after Losar before marching out. Rather than delaying his campaign or ignoring the oracle's advice, he decided to simply move the new year forward by two months instead. Ladakh has kept this earlier date ever since.
festivals.signifies: This new year is deliberately kept out of step with the rest of the Tibetan Buddhist calendar. Ladakhis point to this as evidence that their region has its own distinct history, rather than simply being a smaller copy of Tibet.
festivals.beliefs: Households believe that before the new year begins, all debts must be settled and the house must be thoroughly cleaned. They believe this groundwork must be laid before the new year's good fortune can properly begin.
festivals.celebrate: Butter lamps are lit at monasteries and in home shrines. Chang, the local beer, is shared from house to house. Some villages hold archery and polo matches. Families visit each other in order of seniority, and on the night of Galdan Namchot specifically, houses light rows of lamps on their rooftops.
festivals.local: The gap between Ladakh's Losar date and the February date kept elsewhere is a source of quiet local pride. People point to it as proof that Ladakh's Buddhism has always followed its own calendar, rather than simply copying the calendar from Lhasa.
festivals.image: Rooftop butter lamps lit for Galdan Namchot, Leh village, winter night

festivals.name: Dosmoche
festivals.season: Last days of the Tibetan year
festivals.reach: Dosmoche is kept at the monasteries of Leh, Likir, and Diskit.
festivals.what: Dosmoche is a year-end purification festival. People build effigies that represent the past year's misfortune, parade them through the village, and then destroy them, clearing the way for the new year.
festivals.who: The monastic communities at Leh, Likir, and Diskit take part, along with the ordinary villages attached to each monastery.
festivals.when: It falls on the twenty-eighth and twenty-ninth days of the twelfth Tibetan month, which is generally in February.
festivals.origin: Dosmoche belongs to a wider group of Tibetan Buddhist year-end rituals found across the Tibetan plateau, in which a symbolic scapegoat carries away the year's bad luck. Each Ladakhi monastery has adapted the ritual to its own local calendar and imagery. Most people accept that the practice is old, but exactly when it started in Ladakh is not closely documented.
festivals.signifies: Dosmoche gives a whole year's worth of bad luck a physical form, so that it can be carried away and destroyed, instead of being left to linger unaddressed.
festivals.beliefs: People believe the effigies actually absorb the community's misfortune over the course of the ritual. This is why the effigies are burned or thrown away outside the settlement, rather than kept.
festivals.celebrate: Monks perform the cham dance in the monastery courtyards. Large thread-cross structures and effigies made of dough, wood, and paper are built and carried in procession through the village. They are eventually burned or left far away from the settlement, which formally closes out the year.
festivals.local: Villagers say that the effigy's journey out of town matters more than the dance itself, since that is the moment when the year's bad luck is physically carried away.
festivals.image: Thread-cross effigy carried out of a Ladakhi village at dusk during Dosmoche

festivals.name: Saka Dawa
festivals.season: Fourth month of the Tibetan calendar
festivals.reach: Saka Dawa is observed at monasteries across Ladakh, notably at Hemis, Thiksey, and Spituk.
festivals.what: Saka Dawa is a whole month that marks the Buddha's birth, enlightenment, and death together, all on its full moon day. In Ladakh it is treated as a period of increased religious practice, rather than just a single day of celebration.
festivals.who: Ladakh's Buddhist monasteries and the ordinary Buddhist population take part.
festivals.when: It falls in the fourth month of the Tibetan lunar calendar, corresponding to May or June, and its main focus is the fifteenth day, the day of the full moon.
festivals.origin: The tradition of marking all three major events of the Buddha's life on one single day is old and is found widely across Tibetan Buddhism, not just in Ladakh. Ladakh observes it within the same monastic calendar shared with Tibet, Sikkim, and the wider Himalayan Buddhist world.
festivals.signifies: Saka Dawa lets a single day stand in for the Buddha's whole life. It is also a month during which ordinary religious merit is believed to count for much more than usual.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that good deeds done during Saka Dawa, and especially on the full moon day itself, carry far greater merit than the exact same good deeds would at any other time of year.
festivals.celebrate: Monastery attendance and prayer increase throughout the month. People make offerings of butter lamps, and some release captive animals as an act of merit. Some lay devotees fast, and special assemblies are held at Hemis, Thiksey, and Spituk monasteries on the full moon day.
festivals.local: Meat is widely avoided in Leh's markets and restaurants throughout the month. This is a voluntary shift in the town's everyday food supply, rather than a rule forced by any single authority.
festivals.image: Butter lamp offerings at Thiksey monastery during Saka Dawa, Ladakh

festivals.name: Sindhu Darshan
festivals.reach: This is a modern civic festival held at Shey, near Leh, and it is promoted as a symbol of national unity.
festivals.what: Sindhu Darshan is a fairly recent festival, promoted by the government, held on the banks of the Indus river at Shey. Visitors from across India bring water from their home rivers and pour it into the Sindhu, another name for the Indus.
festivals.who: Visitors and official delegations come from across India, along with Leh's own residents and monastic representatives, who take part in the rituals.
festivals.when: The festival lasts three days, centered on Guru Purnima, the full moon in June.
festivals.origin: The festival was started in 1997, after a visit by the politician L. K. Advani and journalist Tarun Vijay. It was designed from the start as a modern civic occasion celebrating the Indus as a symbol that unites the whole nation, rather than as the revival of any older local ritual.
festivals.signifies: The festival presents the Indus river as something the whole country shares and inherits together. This matters especially in a region whose politics have often been shaped by feeling far away and disconnected from the rest of the country.
festivals.beliefs: Organizers and participants treat the act of pouring river water from other Indian states into the Sindhu as a genuine act of symbolic unity, not just an empty ceremonial gesture.
festivals.celebrate: Water brought from rivers all across India is poured into the Indus at Shey. Ladakhi monks offer prayers on the riverbank. There are cultural performances from Ladakh and from visiting states, and a sightseeing program around Leh for the delegations who attend.
festivals.local: Because the festival is recent and was openly created for civic reasons, Ladakhis themselves say plainly that it feels different from festivals like Hemis or Losar. They see it as useful for tourism and visibility, rather than as something carrying the weight of an inherited religious tradition.
festivals.image: Delegations pouring river water into the Indus at Shey, prayer flags along the bank

festivals.name: Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha
festivals.season: Close of Ramadan; tenth of Dhu al-Hijjah
festivals.reach: These are the central festivals of Kargil district, where Shia Muslims make up the majority, and of the smaller Muslim population of Leh town.
festivals.what: Kargil district, which makes up Ladakh's other half alongside Leh, is majority Shia Muslim. Its towns mark both Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha with congregational prayer, sacrifice, and visiting between families. This religious calendar is entirely separate from the Buddhist festivals of Leh district.
festivals.who: The Balti and Purigi Shia Muslim communities of Kargil take part, along with a smaller Sunni and Shia Muslim population in Leh town itself.
festivals.when: Both Eids move each year with the lunar Hijri calendar. Eid al-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan, and Eid al-Adha falls on the tenth day of Dhu al-Hijjah.
festivals.origin: Islam reached Baltistan and the Kargil region mainly through contact with Central Asia and Kashmir, starting around the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, and Shia religious scholarship took particularly strong hold there. The region's religious identity developed through ongoing contact with both Kashmir and Baltistan, rather than growing up in isolation.
festivals.signifies: These festivals show that there is a Muslim Ladakh existing alongside the region's better known Buddhist monastery culture, even though it is often overlooked next to it.
festivals.beliefs: Both festivals carry the same standard obligations found in the wider Muslim calendar: charity before Eid al-Fitr, and the animal sacrifice at Eid al-Adha. These are observed in Kargil with the same seriousness as anywhere else in the Muslim world.
festivals.celebrate: People offer congregational prayer at Kargil's mosques and imambaras. At Eid al-Adha, there is sacrifice and meat distribution, and at Eid al-Fitr, people wear new clothes and visit each other. Community meals draw on Balti food traditions, which are distinct from both Kashmiri cooking and plains Indian Muslim cooking.
festivals.local: Visitors who come to Ladakh expecting to see only monasteries frequently miss Kargil's own food and religious calendar. This is because the town sits only a few hours from Leh, yet it runs on an entirely different religious year.
festivals.image: Eid prayer at a Kargil mosque, Balti architecture, mountain backdrop

festivals.name: Muharram
festivals.season: First month of the Hijri calendar
festivals.reach: Muharram is centered on Kargil town and district, where Shia mourning processions are a major annual observance.
festivals.what: Muharram is ten days of mourning for the death of Imam Hussain at the battle of Karbala. In Kargil, it is observed with a seriousness and a scale that make it one of the district's defining annual events.
festivals.who: Kargil's Shia Muslim majority takes part, organized through local religious bodies and mourning committees.
festivals.when: It takes place during the first ten days of the Islamic month of Muharram, and because the Islamic calendar is lunar, the dates move each year against the Gregorian calendar.
festivals.origin: Commemorating the battle of Karbala is central to Shia religious practice everywhere it is observed. Kargil's Shia population has strong historical and religious ties to Iran that developed over the twentieth century, and given the size of the community, it keeps this observance with particular intensity.
festivals.signifies: Muharram treats grief over an old injustice as a living moral lesson for today, rather than as something that happened in a distant, disconnected past.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that taking part in the mourning processions, including chest-beating and reciting elegies, is a genuine act of solidarity with Hussain's suffering, not just a symbolic performance.
festivals.celebrate: Azadari processions carry alam standards, which are tall metal poles that represent the martyrs of Karbala, through Kargil's streets. People recite noha, which are mourning laments, and hold majalis, gatherings where sermons about the story of Karbala are given, throughout the ten days. On the tenth day, there is a climactic procession called Ashura.
festivals.local: Kargil's local administration arranges road closures and security for the Ashura procession every year as a matter of routine. This shows how central the observance is to the town's civic calendar, rather than being a minor religious event.
festivals.image: Ashura procession with alam standards through Kargil's main street

name: Sikkim
tagline: Sikkim was once a small Himalayan kingdom, and it still keeps its old ritual calendar today. However, the state is now mostly made up of Nepali-speaking people.

festivals.name: Losoong
festivals.season: First day of the eleventh Tibetan month
festivals.reach: This is the new year celebrated by the Sikkimese Bhutia and Lepcha communities, and it is kept across the whole state.
festivals.what: This is the Sikkimese new year and harvest festival. The Bhutia community calls it Losoong, and the Lepcha community calls it Namsoong. It marks both the end of the farming year and the turning of the calendar.
festivals.who: Sikkim's Bhutia and Lepcha communities take part, and for them this is the main new year celebration. It is different from the Losar kept by Tibetan and other Buddhist communities in February.
festivals.when: It falls on the first day of the eleventh month of the Tibetan lunar calendar, which is in December, roughly two months before the Tibetan Losar.
festivals.origin: Losoong developed as a farming new year. Sonam means agriculture, and the festival was originally a way of giving thanks for the completed harvest. Over time it absorbed the wider new year customs of the Tibetan Buddhist calendar that it now sits within.
festivals.signifies: Losoong closes out one farming year and begins a new one in the very same gesture. The harvest and the calendar turn are treated as one single occasion rather than two separate ones.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that the Black Hat cham dance, performed in the days leading up to Losoong, drives out the old year's negative forces before the new year properly begins.
festivals.celebrate: Monasteries perform chaam mask dances in the days leading up to Losoong. There are archery competitions, and families gather to share chhaang, a local beer made from millet. People wear new clothes, and in some areas, monks perform a mock battle between the forces of good and evil.
festivals.local: Because the Lepcha and Bhutia communities keep the same day under two different names, Losoong and Namsoong are treated locally as one shared festival, not two separate ones. The two communities celebrate it together rather than side by side.
festivals.image: Black Hat cham dance at a Sikkim monastery ahead of Losoong, December

festivals.name: Pang Lhabsol
festivals.season: Fifteenth day of the seventh Tibetan month
festivals.reach: This festival is unique to Sikkim, and it is kept at monasteries across the state.
festivals.what: Pang Lhabsol is a festival found only in Sikkim. It consecrates Mount Khangchendzonga as the state's guardian deity, and this is done through a warrior dance performed by monks dressed in full battle costume.
festivals.who: Sikkim's Buddhist monasteries take part. The festival's origin is historically tied to a treaty made between the Lepcha and Bhutia peoples.
festivals.when: It falls on the fifteenth day of the seventh month of the Tibetan calendar, usually in August or September.
festivals.origin: According to the story, the festival commemorates a blood-brotherhood treaty between the Lepcha and Bhutia peoples. It was later made into an official state ritual by Chogyal Chagdor Namgyal, Sikkim's third ruler, who introduced the Pang Toed warrior dance to it.
festivals.signifies: Pang Lhabsol installs a mountain, rather than a god in human form, as the kingdom's protector. It also keeps an old treaty between communities alive through ritual, not just through written records.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that Mount Khangchendzonga actively protects Sikkim. The warrior dance is understood as a way of renewing that protection each year, not just as a performance to commemorate the past.
festivals.celebrate: The Pang Toed dance is performed by monks trained in swordsmanship, dressed in full battle costume. Mount Khangchendzonga is represented by a red mask crowned with skulls. There are ritual offerings at monasteries, and processions at major monasteries including Tsuklakhang and Pemayangtse.
festivals.local: Dancers for the Pang Toed are chosen based on actual physical fitness and skill with a sword, not just on seniority. This is because the dance was originally designed as a martial exercise, and it is still performed with that same expectation today.
festivals.image: Pangtoed Chaam warrior dance, red skull-crowned mask, Sikkim monastery courtyard

festivals.name: Bumchu
festivals.season: Fourteenth and fifteenth days of the first Tibetan lunar month
festivals.reach: This festival is centered at Tashiding monastery in West Sikkim, and it draws pilgrims from Sikkim, Bhutan, and Nepal.
festivals.what: Bumchu is a festival built around the yearly opening of a sealed vase of water kept at Tashiding monastery. The water level inside is read as an omen for the year ahead.
festivals.who: Only the monks of Tashiding monastery are allowed to handle the vase. Pilgrims come from across Sikkim and from neighboring Buddhist regions to witness it.
festivals.when: It falls on the fourteenth and fifteenth days of the first month of the Tibetan lunar calendar, usually in February or March.
festivals.origin: According to local tradition, a deity once directed a lama to collect water from a hidden spring using a vase that never ran empty, no matter how much water was drawn from it. The vase was then brought to Tashiding and kept as a relic. This story works as an origin legend rather than as documented history.
festivals.signifies: Bumchu reads a whole year's fortune in advance from something as simple as a water level, rather than through a more elaborate ritual.
festivals.beliefs: People believe the amount of water in the vase when it is opened forecasts the coming year. A full vessel is read as a good sign, and a low one is read as a warning.
festivals.celebrate: Monks open the sealed vase in front of an assembled crowd. They examine the water level and top it up from the same hidden spring before resealing it. Small amounts of the water are then given out to pilgrims, who believe it carries healing power. Prayers and ceremonies continue at Tashiding monastery through both days.
festivals.local: Pilgrims who receive even just a few drops of the Bumchu water treat it as worth the whole journey from Bhutan or Nepal on its own, no matter what the water level that year is said to predict.
festivals.image: Monks opening the sealed Bumchu vase before pilgrims, Tashiding monastery

festivals.name: Saga Dawa
festivals.season: Fourth month of the Tibetan calendar
festivals.reach: Saga Dawa is observed at monasteries across Sikkim, notably at Tsuklakhang in Gangtok.
festivals.what: Saga Dawa is a month that marks the Buddha's birth, enlightenment, and death together. In Sikkim, it is observed with a procession of monks and lay devotees around Gangtok on its full moon day, the day the month builds up to.
festivals.who: Sikkim's Buddhist population takes part, both monks and ordinary people, including the Bhutia, the Lepcha, and the Buddhist minority within the state's Nepali population.
festivals.when: It falls in the fourth month of the Tibetan lunar calendar, corresponding to May or June, and builds up to its climax on the full moon day.
festivals.origin: As across the wider Tibetan Buddhist world, the tradition of marking the Buddha's birth, enlightenment, and death on one shared day is old, and it is not unique to Sikkim. It is observed within the same monastic calendar kept in Ladakh, Tibet, and Bhutan.
festivals.signifies: Saga Dawa compresses the Buddha's whole life into a single day of heightened observance, and this same day is marked across the Himalayan Buddhist world all at once.
festivals.beliefs: As elsewhere in Tibetan Buddhism, people believe that religious merit earned during Saga Dawa, and especially on the full moon day, is multiplied far beyond its ordinary value.
festivals.celebrate: A procession carrying holy scriptures moves through Gangtok, led by monks from Tsuklakhang monastery. People release captive animals as an act of merit, make offerings of butter lamps, and increase their prayer and fasting throughout the month.
festivals.local: Meat shops in Gangtok visibly quiet down on the day of the procession. It is a small but consistent seasonal shift in the capital's food trade.
festivals.image: Scripture procession through Gangtok during Saga Dawa, monks leading, full moon day

festivals.name: Dashain
festivals.reach: This is the main festival of Sikkim's Nepali-speaking Hindu population, which is the largest linguistic community in the state.
festivals.what: Dashain is Sikkim's version of the Durga Puja and Dussehra cycle observed elsewhere in India. The state's Nepali-speaking Hindu majority keeps it over ten days, closing with Bijaya Dashami.
festivals.who: Sikkim's Nepali-speaking Hindu community takes part. Nepali is the most widely spoken language in the state.
festivals.when: It falls during the bright half of the month of Ashwin, in September or October, starting with Ghatasthapana on the first day and ending with Bijaya Dashami on the tenth day.
festivals.origin: Dashain follows the same Durga Puja and Navaratri tradition kept across much of Hindu India. It was brought into Sikkim's hills through Nepali migration starting in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, and it has been kept in its own distinctly Nepali form ever since.
festivals.signifies: Dashain marks the goddess's victory over evil. In its Nepali form, this is shown through a tika, a mark applied to the forehead, and a blessing given by elders to younger family members, rather than through public processions carrying the deity.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that the tika made of rice, yoghurt, and vermilion, given by an elder on Bijaya Dashami, carries the elder's blessing physically, not just as a symbol, for the year ahead.
festivals.celebrate: Barley seedlings called jamara are grown in the dark starting on the first day and are cut on the tenth. Families gather, and elders give tika and jamara to younger family members in strict order of age. Goat and duck meat are prepared for the closing days. People fly kites, and in villages, bamboo swings are built for children.
festivals.local: The bamboo swings, called linge ping, are put up specially for Dashain in Sikkim's villages. They come down again once the festival ends and are not kept up for the rest of the year, which is part of what makes this season feel distinct.
festivals.image: Family Bijaya Dashami tika ceremony, elder blessing a younger relative, Sikkim household

festivals.name: Tihar
festivals.reach: Tihar is kept across Sikkim's Nepali-speaking Hindu households.
festivals.what: Tihar is a five-day festival of lights, the Nepali equivalent of Diwali. Each day in turn is dedicated to a different theme: crows, dogs, cows, oxen, and finally the bond between brothers and sisters.
festivals.who: Sikkim's Nepali-speaking Hindu community takes part, along with similar communities in Darjeeling and across Nepal.
festivals.when: It lasts five days around Kartik Amavasya, the same new moon that is marked as Diwali elsewhere in India, falling in October or November.
festivals.origin: Tihar falls on the same lunar calendar occasion as Diwali, but it developed its own distinct five-day structure, honoring specific animals on separate days. This structure grew within Nepali Hindu practice, rather than within the North Indian tradition that most Diwali celebrations draw on.
festivals.signifies: Tihar extends a household's sense of obligation outward, day by day, starting with crows and dogs, moving to livestock, and finally arriving at the closest human bond of all, that between brothers and sisters.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that Bhai Tika, the closing day, protects a brother from harm for the coming year through the ritual his sister performs over him.
festivals.celebrate: Crows and dogs are garlanded and fed on the festival's opening days. Cows and oxen are worshipped on the following two days. Oil lamps are lit around homes throughout the festival. On the fifth day, called Bhai Tika, sisters apply a seven-colored tika to their brothers' foreheads and tie a garland of makhamali flowers around their necks, and in exchange the brothers give gifts and promise to protect their sisters.
festivals.local: The makhamali flower used in the Bhai Tika garland is specifically chosen because it does not wilt. Nepali families in Sikkim see this as a deliberate part of the ritual's meaning, not just a coincidence of plant biology.
festivals.image: Bhai Tika ceremony, sister applying tika to brother's forehead, makhamali garland, Sikkim

festivals.name: Christmas
festivals.reach: Christmas is kept by Sikkim's small Christian community, which is concentrated in Gangtok and among sections of the Lepcha and Nepali population that were reached by Christian mission activity.
festivals.what: Christmas in Sikkim is kept by a small but well-established Christian community. This community grew out of nineteenth-century mission work among the Lepcha and, later, the Nepali population, and it is centered on Gangtok's churches.
festivals.who: Sikkim's Christian minority takes part, made up of Lepcha, Nepali, and Bhutia converts and their descendants.
festivals.when: Christmas falls on December 25th, with carol services held through the weeks leading up to it.
festivals.origin: Christian missions, mostly Scottish and other Protestant groups, worked in Sikkim and the Darjeeling hills starting in the nineteenth century. They translated scripture into Lepcha and Nepali and set up schools alongside churches. This legacy is still visible today in Gangtok's older mission institutions.
festivals.signifies: Christmas keeps a minority faith's own calendar visible in a state whose public year otherwise runs on Buddhist and Nepali Hindu observances.
festivals.beliefs: The midnight service is treated as the most important observance, drawing wider attendance than any other point in the Christian calendar year.
festivals.celebrate: Churches are decorated and carol singing happens throughout Advent. There is a midnight service on Christmas Eve, and families share meals on the day itself. Gangtok's markets and its main street, MG Marg, are decorated for the season, drawing visitors well beyond the Christian community itself.
festivals.local: Gangtok's MG Marg is lit up for Christmas and New Year together, treated as one continuous festive season. Because of this, the town's own festive period runs a good two weeks beyond Christmas Day itself.
festivals.image: MG Marg decorated for Christmas, Gangtok, evening crowds

name: Rajasthan
tagline: Rajasthan is a desert state that was once home to royal courts and busy camel trade routes. It is also home to a famous Sufi shrine in Ajmer that draws pilgrims from many different faiths, not just Muslims.

festivals.name: Gangaur
festivals.season: Chaitra, beginning the day after Holi
festivals.reach: People celebrate Gangaur across the whole state, but the biggest and most elaborate celebrations happen in Jaipur, Udaipur and Jodhpur.
festivals.what: For sixteen to eighteen days, people worship the goddess Gauri, who is a form of the goddess Parvati. Every day during this time, people dress a statue of the goddess in new clothes. At the end, they carry the statue out in a big procession through the old cities.
festivals.who: Mostly women and girls take part, whether they are married or not. But when the big processions happen in Jaipur and Udaipur, many more people from the public come out to watch.
festivals.when: Gangaur begins the day right after the festival of Holi, and it ends on a day called Chaitra Shukla Tritiya, which falls in March or April.
festivals.origin: Nobody knows exactly how old this festival is, but it started as a simple farming and marriage tradition. Later, the royal families who ruled Mewar and Jaipur turned it into a much bigger, more formal event with large processions, and for a long time the royal households themselves led these public celebrations.
festivals.signifies: The festival celebrates a wife's devotion to her husband and tells the story of Gauri being reunited with the god Shiva after they were apart for a while. Local people see this story as an example of how a marriage should stay strong and loyal over time.
festivals.beliefs: Unmarried women pray to the goddess Gauri hoping she will help them find a good husband. Married women pray to her for their husband's long life and for their family's overall wellbeing.
festivals.celebrate: People dress and decorate clay or wood statues of Gauri every day. In Jaipur, they carry the statue in a procession starting from the City Palace, with elephants and folk musicians joining in. In Udaipur, they carry the statue by boat across Lake Pichola. In the final days of the festival, girls carry small clay pots called Ghudlas through the streets. These pots have holes poked in them and lamps lit inside, so they glow as the girls carry them.
festivals.local: Even today, Jaipur's Gangaur procession still starts at the gates of the City Palace, and the royal family's own ceremonial elephants lead the way. This shows how the festival used to be a private event just for the royal court, before it became something the whole public celebrates.
festivals.image: Gangaur procession with the Gauri idol passing Jaipur's City Palace gate, women in traditional dress

festivals.name: Teej
festivals.reach: People celebrate Teej widely all across the state, and Jaipur holds a large public procession for it.
festivals.what: Teej is a monsoon festival that honors the goddess Parvati. People mark it by wearing green bangles and green clothing, decorating their hands with henna, and hanging swings from trees. In Jaipur, there is also a formal procession where a statue of the goddess is carried through the old city.
festivals.who: Mostly women take part, whether married or unmarried, and this happens in both villages and cities across Rajasthan.
festivals.when: Teej falls on the third day of the bright half of the month of Shravan, which is in July or August.
festivals.origin: At the household level, this is a very old monsoon tradition connected to the story of how Parvati did a long, difficult penance in order to win Shiva as her husband. Jaipur's grand public procession took its current large-scale form later, under the royal patronage of the Kachhwaha rulers of the city.
festivals.signifies: Teej celebrates the return of the rains after a hot summer, and it celebrates devotion being rewarded, which people connect to Parvati's own long wait to marry Shiva.
festivals.beliefs: Married women fast on this day, and some do not even drink water, all for the sake of their husband's wellbeing. Unmarried women keep a lighter version of the fast while hoping for a good husband in the future.
festivals.celebrate: People wear green bangles, green clothing and henna designs. They hang swings from trees and from the beams of courtyards. They sing special folk songs made just for this season, called Teej ke geet. In Jaipur, people carry a silver palanquin holding the goddess through the old city, accompanied by elephants, camels and dancers.
festivals.local: Jaipur holds both Teej and Gangaur as separate royal-style processions within a few months of each other. People who live in the old city can easily tell the two crowds and the two goddesses apart, even though visitors from outside sometimes get them confused.
festivals.image: Teej procession with a silver palanquin moving through Jaipur's old city, elephants alongside

festivals.name: Pushkar Fair
festivals.reach: The fair draws herding and trading communities from all over Rajasthan, as well as visitors from farther away.
festivals.what: This is a fair where people buy, sell and trade camels, horses and cattle. It takes place on the sand dunes just outside the town of Pushkar. At the same time, pilgrims come to bathe at the steps beside Pushkar Lake and to visit one of the very few temples in India dedicated specifically to the god Brahma.
festivals.who: Herding and trading communities attend, especially camel herders from the Raika and Rebari groups. Pilgrims come too, and more and more tourists visit each year.
festivals.when: The fair runs for the days leading up to and including Kartik Purnima, which is the full moon day of the month of Kartik, in October or November.
festivals.origin: Nobody has written down exactly how the fair began. It seems to have grown up over a long time alongside Pushkar's reputation as a place of pilgrimage. The livestock trading part of the fair does not have its own separately recorded origin either.
festivals.signifies: People believe that bathing in the lake on the full moon day of Kartik brings special spiritual merit. At the same time, these same days serve a very practical purpose, because they let herders trade their livestock before winter arrives.
festivals.beliefs: Local belief holds that bathing at Pushkar's ghats, which are the steps leading down to the lake, on the full moon day brings great merit, similar to bathing at other major holy pilgrimage sites.
festivals.celebrate: People trade camels and cattle on the fairgrounds. There are camel races and competitions for the best-decorated camel. Pilgrims bathe at the lake's fifty two ghats and attend an evening prayer ceremony called aarti. For visitors, there is folk music, and even contests for the best moustache and the best turban-tying.
festivals.local: Traders who have been coming for many years say that the livestock trading side of the fair has shrunk as the tourist side has grown bigger. This complaint about the fair becoming too popular has itself become something visitors are told about when they come.
festivals.image: Camel fair grounds at Pushkar, dust and dawn light, ghats visible beyond

festivals.name: Urs Ajmer Sharif
festivals.season: Rajab, seventh month of the Hijri calendar
festivals.reach: The event draws pilgrims of every faith from across South Asia.
festivals.what: This is a six-day observance marking the anniversary of the death of the Sufi saint Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti. It takes place at his shrine, called a dargah, in Ajmer. The event is called an urs, which means a wedding, because it is treated as a joyful celebration rather than a time of mourning.
festivals.who: Followers of the Chishti Sufi order take part, along with a wide range of both Muslims and non-Muslims who visit the dargah throughout the year, but come in much greater numbers during the urs.
festivals.when: It runs from the first to the sixth day of the Islamic month of Rajab. Because it follows the lunar Hijri calendar, the date shifts earlier each year compared to the regular calendar we use.
festivals.origin: The dargah grew up around the saint's tomb after he died in the early thirteenth century. Over time, the urs observance received support from a series of rulers, including Mughal emperors who visited the shrine themselves.
festivals.signifies: The festival marks the saint becoming united with the divine at the moment of his death. It is treated as a wedding rather than a loss, which is exactly why the event is called an urs at all.
festivals.beliefs: Pilgrims believe that wishes made at the dargah, especially inside its innermost chamber, will come true. They also believe that food handed out from the shrine's kitchens carries a special blessing.
festivals.celebrate: Every night there is qawwali, which is a kind of devotional singing. People carry cloth coverings called chadars in a procession to drape over the saint's tomb. Food called langar is cooked in two large historic iron cauldrons and given out to everyone. A flag-hoisting ceremony marks the opening of the six days.
festivals.local: The dargah still uses its two huge cooking pots, called degs, which were gifts from the emperors Akbar and Jahangir centuries ago. Every year, certain men who specialize in reaching into the boiling sugar syrup inside these pots to pull out cooked rice by hand, for a small fee, are a familiar sight in the crowd.
festivals.image: Chadar procession approaching the Ajmer Sharif dargah gate at night, qawwali crowd

festivals.name: Paryushana Parva
festivals.reach: This is an important festival among Rajasthan's Jain communities, especially in Jaipur, Bikaner and the towns of the Shekhawati region.
festivals.what: This is the most important observance of the Jain year. It lasts eight days for Shwetambar Jains and ten days for Digambar Jains, and it is a time devoted to fasting, reading scripture, and formally looking back at one's behavior over the past year.
festivals.who: Jain households from both of the major Jain groups take part. Rajasthan's Jain merchant families have historically paid for much of the state's temple architecture.
festivals.when: It happens during the month of Bhadrapada, in August or September. The exact dates are set by each sect's own calendar, and these calendars run close to each other but not exactly the same.
festivals.origin: This practice comes from ascetic traditions that go all the way back to the earliest Jain religious texts. Its current form, as something practiced by whole households and communities, developed slowly over a very long period that was never fully written down.
festivals.signifies: The festival represents non-violence and self-control taken to their most serious yearly expression. It ends with people formally making things right with anyone they may have wronged during the year.
festivals.beliefs: The observance closes with a day called Samvatsari for Shwetambar Jains, or Kshamavani for Digambar Jains. This is a day of universal forgiveness, when people exchange the greeting 'Micchami Dukkadam,' meaning 'may all my faults be forgiven,' no matter who was actually at fault.
festivals.celebrate: People take part in extended fasting, including a multi-day fast called Attham, and a smaller number of very devoted people even take on a fast that lasts a whole year, called Varshi Tap. There are public readings from a scripture called the Kalpa Sutra. People visit temples dressed in white. On Samvatsari, they make calls and send letters asking forgiveness from family, neighbors and business partners.
festivals.local: In the old Jain neighborhoods of Jaipur and Bikaner, Samvatsari is the day when old disputes, whether about business or family, are expected to be formally settled, whether or not they actually get resolved.
festivals.image: Jain temple courtyard during Paryushana, scripture reading, white-clad worshippers

festivals.name: Marwar Festival
festivals.reach: This is a Jodhpur city festival, and it mostly draws visitors from within Rajasthan.
festivals.what: This is a two-day festival organized by the state tourism department to showcase the folk music and dance of the Marwar region. It is timed to the autumn full moon and takes place around Jodhpur's forts, in memory of the region's Rajput history.
festivals.who: The performers are the Manganiyar and Langa communities, families of musicians who have passed down their skills for generations, along with folk dancers. The tourism department organizes and runs the whole event.
festivals.when: It happens on Sharad Purnima, a full moon day in the month of Ashwin, which falls in September or October.
festivals.origin: This is a modern festival created by Rajasthan Tourism, not an ancient religious ritual. It is built around the older tradition of Sharad Purnima, the full moon observance, and around Marwar's long history of court-supported folk music.
festivals.signifies: This is a civic festival that presents an older regional music tradition to the public and to visitors. It is not a religious ritual with its own independent spiritual meaning.
festivals.beliefs: Separately from the festival itself, people believe that Sharad Purnima has the clearest, brightest moonlight of the whole year. On this night, people traditionally set out a sweet rice pudding called kheer overnight so it can soak up the moonlight.
festivals.celebrate: The Manganiyar and Langa musicians perform at Mehrangarh Fort and on the grounds of Umaid Bhawan Palace. There are camel tattoo shows, and contests for turban-tying and moustaches aimed at visitors. The festival closes with a polo match or a tent-pegging competition.
festivals.local: The festival depends on hereditary musicians whose families have sung for the royal courts of Marwar for generations. For local people, a well-known Manganiyar or Langa performer is actually a bigger draw than the fort where the show takes place.
festivals.image: Manganiyar musicians performing at Mehrangarh Fort at dusk, Marwar Festival

festivals.name: Karva Chauth
festivals.season: Kartik, fourth day of the dark fortnight
festivals.reach: Karva Chauth is widely celebrated across Rajasthan, and it is especially strong among urban Marwari and Rajput households.
festivals.what: This is a day-long fast that married women keep for the sake of their husbands' long lives. They do not eat or drink anything until they see the moon at night through a sieve, and only then do they break the fast.
festivals.who: Mostly married women take part, and in some families, women who are newly engaged are also starting to join in.
festivals.when: It falls on the fourth day of the dark half of the month of Kartik, which is nine days before Diwali.
festivals.origin: Nobody knows exactly how old this North Indian and Rajasthani custom is. Local memory connects it to military families, whose men were often away fighting, but this connection is based on folk memory rather than any written historical record.
festivals.signifies: The fast represents a wife's promise and devotion, made even though her husband may be far away or in danger. She keeps this promise by going without food or water until the moon appears.
festivals.beliefs: People believe the fast does not count if it is broken before the moonrise ritual is finished. Husbands are expected to be present when their wives finally look at the moon.
festivals.celebrate: The day before, women apply henna to their hands. Before dawn, a mother-in-law sends a special meal called sargi for her daughter-in-law to eat. Then the woman goes the whole day without food or water. In the evening, she performs a prayer ceremony called puja and listens to the story of Karva Chauth being told. Finally, she breaks her fast by looking at the moon through a sieve, then looking at her husband's face, and then drinking water that he offers her.
festivals.local: In the old marketplaces of Jaipur and Jodhpur, shops selling sieves and prayer plates called puja-thalis do a whole season's worth of business in the two weeks before the festival. Even the popular design of the sieve changes from year to year, just like anything else made to sell for one special occasion.
festivals.image: Woman viewing the moon through a decorated sieve, Karva Chauth evening, Jaipur rooftop

name: Gujarat
tagline: Gujarat grew up around busy trading ports and important temple towns. The state also carries a long Jain merchant history, one that has literally been recorded in its own account books.

festivals.name: Navratri
festivals.reach: This is the state's biggest public festival, celebrated in every city and in most villages too.
festivals.what: For nine nights, people dance Garba and Dandiya Raas in large circles around a central lamp or an image of the goddess. In Gujarat, this is less of a quiet household ritual and more of a huge nightly public event.
festivals.who: Gujaratis everywhere take part, both across the state and among Gujarati communities living abroad, where these Navratri garba gatherings are often the biggest Indian cultural event of the whole year.
festivals.when: It happens over the nine nights of the bright half of the month of Ashwin, in September or October.
festivals.origin: Garba began as a devotional dance performed around a lit clay lantern called a garbo or garbi, which represents the goddess. This part of the tradition is old and specifically Gujarati. However, the large, carefully choreographed public events we see today are much newer, developing from the middle to late twentieth century.
festivals.signifies: The nine nights honor the goddess in her many different forms, and here people express that devotion through dance rather than just quiet observation.
festivals.beliefs: People understand the garbo lamp as representing both the goddess and the human body, which is seen as a vessel holding life. Dancing in a circle around the lamp is itself considered an act of worship, not just something people do before worshipping.
festivals.celebrate: People dance in circles called garba around a garbo lamp or an image of the goddess Durga. In dandiya raas, dancers use sticks in a kind of playful mock battle. Clubs and community groups hold competitions judged on choreography and costumes. On the ninth day, people perform kanya puja, which means worshipping young girls.
festivals.local: In Ahmedabad and Vadodara, neighborhood groups book grounds, sound systems and choreographers many months in advance. Running a well-organized garba group is genuinely something that brings respect and status in the local community.
festivals.image: Garba circle at night under string lights, Ahmedabad society ground

festivals.name: Uttarayan
festivals.reach: It is celebrated across the whole state, and especially intensely in Ahmedabad and Surat.
festivals.what: This is Gujarat's version of the festival Makar Sankranti. It is marked less by religious rituals and more by two entire days spent almost completely on flying kites from every rooftop available.
festivals.who: Basically the whole state takes part, people of all ages, and in Ahmedabad the rooftops fill up with kite flyers even before dawn.
festivals.when: It falls on 14 and 15 January every year, fixed dates based on the solar calendar's Makar Sankranti.
festivals.origin: Makar Sankranti itself is an old festival tied to the sun and to farming, celebrated all across India. Kite flying became attached to it in Gujarat over a long period of time that isn't clearly documented. In the 1980s, the state turned it into an official tourism event called the International Kite Festival.
festivals.signifies: The festival marks the sun beginning to move northward and winter starting to shorten. Here, people mark this change by looking up at the sky rather than by going to a temple.
festivals.beliefs: Some families treat the day as a good time for giving charity, especially sweets made with sesame seeds, called til, and warm clothing for those in need. However, the kite flying itself does not carry any fixed religious meaning.
festivals.celebrate: People fly kites from dawn until dusk, using a special glass-coated string called manja to try to cut down other people's kites in duels. They eat undhiyu, a mixed vegetable dish, and sweets made with sesame and jaggery. Loudspeakers play music through the night before the festival. The state also runs the official International Kite Festival, which brings kite flyers from other countries to Ahmedabad.
festivals.local: Every January, the city argues about the manja string, because its glass coating is dangerous. It can injure birds, and in some years, it has even hurt motorcyclists riding on the roads below.
festivals.image: Ahmedabad rooftops crowded with kite flyers at dawn, Uttarayan

festivals.name: Rann Utsav
festivals.reach: The festival is centered at Dhordo and the white salt desert of Kutch, and it draws visitors from across India and from abroad.
festivals.what: This is a tented festival that runs for months on the white salt desert of the Rann of Kutch. The state government organizes it around the region's older craft and music traditions.
festivals.who: Artisan and herding communities from Kutch take part, and for many of them, Rann Utsav has become an important way to make a living. Most visitors come from outside the region.
festivals.when: It runs roughly from November through February, and the nights with a full moon are considered the high point of the festival.
festivals.origin: Gujarat Tourism started this festival in the 2000s. It is built around older Kutchi traditions, such as Bandhani tie-dye fabric, Rogan painting, Ajrakh block printing, and the craftwork of the Rabari and Meghwal herding communities. The festival itself is not an old tradition, but the traditions it showcases are.
festivals.signifies: This festival mainly works as a way to display and support Kutch's craft economy, rather than as a ritual with its own independent religious meaning.
festivals.beliefs: There is no fixed religious belief tied to the festival itself. However, local people separately consider the white Rann to be a striking landscape that deserves attention on its own, especially when lit by the full moon.
festivals.celebrate: Visitors can stay in a tent city set up at the edge of the Rann. There are craft markets selling Bandhani fabric, mirror work and leather goods. Kutchi musicians perform folk music and dance. Visitors can also go on camel and jeep safaris and walk out onto the salt flat itself under the full moon.
festivals.local: Before the festival began, Dhordo, the main base village, was just a small, quiet border settlement. Today its households run homestays and craft stalls that did not exist a generation ago, a change that local families describe with mixed feelings.
festivals.image: White salt desert of the Rann of Kutch under full moon, tent city lights

festivals.name: Paryushana Parva
festivals.reach: This festival is especially important in Ahmedabad, Surat and the pilgrim town of Palitana.
festivals.what: This is the most important observance of the Jain year. It lasts eight days for Shwetambar Jains and ten days for Digambar Jains, and it is a time for fasting, studying scripture, and formally reflecting on one's conduct over the year.
festivals.who: Jain households from both of the major sects take part. Gujarat's Jain merchant families have paid for a large share of the state's temple building for centuries.
festivals.when: It takes place during the month of Bhadrapada, in August or September. The exact dates are set by each sect's own calendar, and these calendars are close together but not exactly the same.
festivals.origin: This tradition comes from an ascetic practice that goes back to the earliest Jain religious texts. Its current form, observed by whole households and communities, developed slowly over a very long, undocumented period of time.
festivals.signifies: This festival represents non-violence and self-control at their most serious yearly expression. It also marks a yearly settling of accounts with everyone the observer may have wronged.
festivals.beliefs: The observance closes with a day called Samvatsari for Shwetambar Jains, or Kshamavani for Digambar Jains, the day of universal forgiveness. On this day, people exchange the greeting 'Micchami Dukkadam,' meaning 'may all my faults be forgiven,' regardless of who was actually at fault.
festivals.celebrate: People take part in extended fasting, including a multi-day fast called Attham, and for some, a fast lasting a full year called Varshi Tap. There are public readings from the Kalpa Sutra scripture. People visit temples dressed in white, and on Samvatsari they make calls and send letters asking forgiveness from family, neighbors and business partners.
festivals.local: In Ahmedabad's Jain neighborhoods, people make Samvatsari calls even to people they barely know, on the idea that even an accidental offense is still worth clearing up. The pilgrim hill at Palitana, which people climb before dawn to reach its marble temple city, is traditionally at its busiest with Jain pilgrims during these weeks.
festivals.image: White-clad worshippers reading scripture in a Jain temple hall, Ahmedabad, Paryushana

festivals.name: Eid al-Fitr
festivals.reach: This festival is especially significant in Ahmedabad's old city, in Surat, and in the Kathiawar coast towns of Junagadh and Bhavnagar.
festivals.what: This festival marks the end of a month-long fast. It is kept by Gujarati Muslim communities, who are concentrated in Ahmedabad's walled old city and in Surat, where the Dawoodi Bohra community follows its own related but distinct festival calendar.
festivals.who: Gujarati-speaking Muslim communities in general take part, along with the Dawoodi Bohra community specifically, whose clothing, dates and greetings differ in detail from the wider Sunni Muslim majority.
festivals.when: It falls on the first day of the month of Shawwal. Because it follows the lunar Hijri calendar, the date moves earlier each year compared to our regular calendar.
festivals.origin: Trade across the Arabian Sea brought Islam to Gujarat's ports very early on. Ahmedabad's growth under the Gujarat Sultanate starting in the fifteenth century gave the old city its mosque architecture and shaped how Ramzan is observed there.
festivals.signifies: The festival marks the end of the fast, and it brings a leveling of the table at Eid, since everyone shares a feast after charity has already been given beforehand.
festivals.beliefs: A form of charity called Zakat al-Fitr is paid before the Eid prayer, so that the feast itself is something shared with others rather than kept private. The Bohra community sets its own calendar independently through its own religious authority, rather than relying on local moon sighting like others do.
festivals.celebrate: People attend Eid prayers at the Jama Masjid and at neighborhood mosques across the old city. They eat a sweet dish called sheer khurma and other festive foods, and wear new clothes. In Surat's Bohra neighborhoods, women wear a distinct garment called the rida and men wear a cap called the topi during the greeting visits that follow.
festivals.local: For weeks before Eid, Ahmedabad's Manek Chowk market and the lanes around the Jama Masjid fill up with night markets selling Ramzan food. This food economy is used by the whole city, not just by the people who are fasting.
festivals.image: Eid prayer crowd outside Ahmedabad's Jama Masjid, old city, morning

festivals.name: Tarnetar Fair
festivals.reach: This fair is centered at Tarnetar village in Surendranagar district, and it specifically draws tribal and pastoral communities from the Saurashtra region.
festivals.what: This is a three-day fair held around the Trinetreshwar Mahadev temple. It also serves as the best-known open matchmaking ground for Saurashtra's tribal communities.
festivals.who: The Koli, Bharwad and other pastoral and tribal communities of the Panchal region of Saurashtra take part.
festivals.when: It happens during the month of Bhadrapada, in August or September, timed to fit the temple's own festival calendar.
festivals.origin: The temple itself dates back to the Solanki era. Local tradition, which is hard to independently confirm, connects this site to the story from the Mahabharata where the hero Arjuna wins the hand of Draupadi. Over an uncertain span of time, the fair's matchmaking custom seems to have grown up around that story.
festivals.signifies: This is a sacred bathing site that has also become, through long-standing local custom rather than any official religious rule, a place where marriages begin in public rather than through private arrangement.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that bathing in the temple's Papanshu Kund pool carries the same spiritual merit as bathing in the Ganges river. If a young woman stops to talk with a young man during the fair, this is understood as her own personal choice, made openly, and it is respected by the watching families rather than questioned.
festivals.celebrate: Young men spend months embroidering decorative umbrellas that they carry through the fairground while dancing and singing to attract attention. Alongside the matchmaking tradition, there are craft stalls, folk music and tribal dancing, and people bathe in the temple's tank at dawn.
festivals.local: The embroidered umbrella is the main tool of courtship at this fair. People pay close attention to its stitching and colors, as well as to the dancing performed under it, reading these details as carefully as anything actually spoken.
festivals.image: Young man dancing under an embroidered umbrella at Tarnetar Fair, crowd gathered around

festivals.name: Rath Yatra
festivals.season: Ashadha, second day of the bright fortnight
festivals.reach: This is a citywide Ahmedabad festival, and it is one of the largest Rath Yatra processions in India, after the ones held in Puri and Kolkata.
festivals.what: Three large chariots carrying the deities Jagannath, Balabhadra and Subhadra are pulled from the centuries-old Jagannath Mandir temple in Jamalpur through the old city. For the whole day, the route is lined with crowds, elephants and trucks carrying decorated scenes.
festivals.who: Ahmedabad's Vaishnav community organizes the procession, though the whole city treats it as an event for everyone, well beyond just that community.
festivals.when: It happens on Ashadha Sud Bij, the second day of the bright half of the month of Ashadha, in June or July, the very same day the processions happen in Puri and Kolkata.
festivals.origin: The tradition began in 1878. According to tradition, it started after the temple's head priest, Narsinhji Maharaj, had a dream instructing him to take the deity through the city. The procession has continued every year since then.
festivals.signifies: The festival represents Jagannath's yearly visit across the city and back, made visible all along the route rather than staying hidden inside the temple grounds.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that pulling the ropes of the chariot, even just for a moment, brings religious merit. Because of this, crowds along the route compete for the chance to pull.
festivals.celebrate: Elephants march ahead of the chariots, and trucks carrying scenes from mythology follow behind. The chariots stop many times along the route so people can make offerings, before finally returning to Jamalpur by evening.
festivals.local: For this one day, Ahmedabad's city administration essentially shuts down the old city, closing roads and running the procession almost like a piece of city planning as much as a religious event, which is unusual for a festival like this.
festivals.image: Jagannath chariot pulled through Ahmedabad's old city streets, crowd and elephants

name: Goa
tagline: Goa sits along the Konkan coast, where a Catholic parish calendar and a Hindu village calendar run side by side. Sometimes their festivals even happen on the very same night.

festivals.name: Shigmo
festivals.reach: It is celebrated across the whole state, with large organized parades in Panaji and Margao.
festivals.what: This is Goa's spring festival, and it works like the Konkan region's version of Holi. At the village level, it is built around folk dance. Since the middle of the twentieth century, it has also grown into large organized parades, called Shigmotsav, that move through Panaji and Margao with lit-up floats showing scenes from mythology.
festivals.who: Goa's farming and fishing Hindu communities keep the festival at the village level. The state tourism department organizes the city parades, which draw a much bigger audience.
festivals.when: It takes place during Phalgun, the last month of the Hindu calendar, in February or March, building up to the full moon.
festivals.origin: The village form of Shigmo, built around folk dances like Perni Jagor and Ghode Modni performed by hereditary local troupes, is old and deeply rooted in the local area. The large lit-up parade format is a twentieth-century addition organized by the state, added on top of that older village tradition.
festivals.signifies: The festival marks the turning point of the farming year and a release of energy after the hard work of the winter fields, expressed through dance and color rather than temple ritual.
festivals.beliefs: The folk dances performed during Shigmo, especially Perni Jagor with its tradition of ancestral masks, are locally understood as a way of calling on and honoring ancestral and local spirits, rather than one single specific god.
festivals.celebrate: Village troupes perform Ghode Modni, which is a mock cavalry dance, along with Perni Jagor and Romat processions with drums and cymbals in the days leading up to the full moon. People throw colored powder similar to Holi. In the cities, there are parades with lit-up floats, dance troupes and folk music competitions.
festivals.local: The Perni Jagor mask dancers train within specific families, passing the tradition down through generations. A troupe's masks, some of which are genuinely very old, are treated as inherited family property rather than costumes bought new each year.
festivals.image: Illuminated Shigmo parade float and folk dancers, Panaji street at night

festivals.name: Ganesh Chaturthi
festivals.reach: This is Goa's largest Hindu festival, kept in nearly every Hindu household.
festivals.what: Known locally as Chavath, Goa's version of Ganesh Chaturthi is much more centered on the home and village than Mumbai's version, which is famous for its huge public displays. Goa's version is built around a distinctive local custom called the matoli, which is a wooden canopy hung above the statue of Ganesh and packed full of produce gathered from the surrounding forests and gardens.
festivals.who: Goan Hindu households take part, with entire extended families returning to their ancestral village homes for the days of the festival.
festivals.when: It falls on Bhadrapada Shukla Chaturthi, the same date observed across all of India, in August or September. Depending on family custom, it is kept for one and a half days, five days, or eleven days.
festivals.origin: Household worship of Ganesh in Goa is an old tradition. Unlike in Maharashtra, it was never reshaped by the nationalist public festivals organized under the leader Tilak. Instead, it developed along its own separate path in Goa's villages.
festivals.signifies: The festival represents a household's welcome of the god Ganesh for the days he stays with them. Through the matoli canopy, it also represents a yearly accounting of everything the land and forest around the village currently have to offer.
