festivals.beliefs: The produce used to build the matoli, which can include more than a hundred different kinds of fruit, seeds, leaves and roots gathered from the forest rather than bought at a store, is treated as an offering. People believe this offering must be genuinely local and in season, not just a symbolic stand-in.
festivals.celebrate: Families install clay statues of Ganesh at home beneath the matoli canopy. They perform daily prayer ceremonies called aarti and offer sweets called modak. Family members who have moved away to Mumbai, the Gulf countries and elsewhere return home specifically for these days. At the end of the observance, the statue is carried out and immersed in a local river, water tank, or the sea.
festivals.local: Building the matoli properly means that someone in the family still needs to know which forest plants are in season and exactly where to find them. Some village families now say that holding onto this specific, fading knowledge is actually the hardest part of keeping Chavath the right way.
festivals.image: Ganesh idol beneath a matoli canopy of forest produce, Goan village home

festivals.name: Feast of St. Francis Xavier
festivals.reach: This feast draws pilgrims of every faith from across Goa, from the rest of India, and from Goans living abroad. It is the largest annual Christian gathering in the state.
festivals.what: This feast honors Goa's patron saint, whose body is kept in a silver casket inside the Basilica of Bom Jesus in Old Goa. The church and its devotees believe that his body has remained largely uncorrupted long after his death in 1552.
festivals.who: Goan Catholics are the main participants, but large numbers of Goan Hindus also attend the feast, along with pilgrims who travel from across India.
festivals.when: It falls on 3 December, closing a nine-day period of prayer called a novena. The body itself is put on public display for veneration in a major exposition only about once every ten years, not every single year.
festivals.origin: Francis Xavier was a Jesuit missionary who died in 1552 off the coast of China. His remains were brought to Goa in 1554 and placed inside the Basilica of Bom Jesus, which was built over the following decades. The annual feast has continued ever since.
festivals.signifies: The feast honors Goa's patron saint on behalf of the whole territory. This devotion has historically crossed the line between the state's Catholic and Hindu communities, rather than staying limited to just one group.
festivals.beliefs: Devotees pray to the saint for healing and for general protection. The devout consider the preserved state of his body to be evidence of his holiness, though this is a matter of religious faith that cannot be independently verified.
festivals.celebrate: There is a nine-day novena held at the basilica, and the feast day mass draws enormous crowds to Old Goa. A fair with many stalls sets up around the church. In the years when the body is put on public display, weeks of viewing take place, with lines of people waiting for hours.
festivals.local: Families from well outside Goa's Catholic areas, including many Hindu households, keep a personal promise called a mannat to Saint Xavier and walk to Old Goa for the feast. This custom existed long before anyone framed it as an example of different faiths coming together. It is simply how the feast has always been kept locally.
festivals.image: Basilica of Bom Jesus at night, feast day crowd, Old Goa

festivals.name: Christmas
festivals.reach: Christmas is celebrated across Goa's Catholic communities, and it also fills Panaji and Margao with a citywide festive season that reaches far beyond just Catholic households.
festivals.what: Christmas in Goa carries the specific legacy of nearly four and a half centuries of Portuguese rule. It is kept through parish church life, home baking, and a festive street season in Panaji that the wider state, which is mostly Hindu, also turns out to enjoy.
festivals.who: Goa's Catholic population, which makes up close to a quarter of the state, celebrates through its parish churches. A much wider public also joins in through the season's lights, markets and music.
festivals.when: It falls on 25 December, with a festive season that runs from Advent all the way through to early January.
festivals.origin: Goa's Christian community and its church calendar date back to Portuguese colonization, which began in 1510. Parish churches were built across the territory over the following centuries, first under Portuguese clergy and later under Goan clergy.
festivals.signifies: Christmas celebrates the birth of Jesus, and in Goa it is marked with a distinct musical and religious inheritance, including carols sung in the Konkani language and local church choirs, which sets it apart from how Christmas is practiced elsewhere in India.
festivals.beliefs: Midnight mass is the most important part of the celebration for practicing families, and even many people who do not regularly attend church throughout the year come to this service.
festivals.celebrate: Families spend weeks baking elaborate sweets at home, including bebinca, a dessert made of many coconut layers, along with kulkuls and other treats. People set up star-shaped lanterns and nativity scenes called cribs at home and at churches. Carols are sung in both Konkani and English. Families attend midnight mass, and Panaji is lit up throughout the season.
festivals.local: A Goan Catholic family's Christmas sweet box, which includes bebinca, kulkuls, dodol and neuris, is put together over several weeks by the women of the family working together in shifts. The exact recipe proportions are treated as a family inheritance, sometimes even argued over between sisters-in-law.
festivals.image: Bebinca and kulkuls laid out on a table, star lantern above, Goan Catholic home

festivals.name: Carnival
festivals.reach: This festival is centered on Panaji, Margao and Vasco, and the parade route draws crowds from across the state.
festivals.what: This is a three-day street festival held just before Lent, first introduced under Portuguese rule. It is led by a costumed figure called King Momo, who opens the festival by declaring a call to eat, drink and enjoy life. This is followed by float parades, music and colored powder thrown through the streets of Goa's main towns.
festivals.who: The state tourism department organizes Carnival in its current form. People of every religion take part, unlike the church-specific feasts, which mostly draw Catholic communities.
festivals.when: It happens during the three days right before Ash Wednesday, in February or March, timed to the start of Lent in the Christian church calendar.
festivals.origin: Carnival was introduced during Portuguese colonial rule as a European pre-Lent tradition. After Goa became part of India in 1961, it was revived and expanded as an official state tourism event.
festivals.signifies: The festival represents one last, deliberately excessive celebration before the forty days of restraint during Lent. However, for much of today's audience, it now works more as a fun, non-religious street festival rather than as specifically religious preparation.
festivals.beliefs: There is no fixed religious belief attached to Carnival itself. What gives it meaning within the Catholic calendar is simply its timing, right before Lent begins.
festivals.celebrate: King Momo leads an opening parade. Over the following days, float processions move through Panaji, Margao and Vasco, with performing troupes in costume doing choreographed routines. Colored powder and foam are thrown at bystanders, and street food and music fill the towns for the whole event.
festivals.local: Being chosen as King Momo each year is treated as a small local celebrity honor, and Goan newspapers cover who gets picked the same way other cities might cover who leads a big city parade.
festivals.image: King Momo float leading the Carnival parade, Panaji street, crowd and colour

festivals.name: Sao Joao
festivals.aliases: Feast of St. John the Baptist
festivals.reach: This feast is kept across Goa's Catholic villages, and Siolim and other towns in the Bardez region are especially known for it.
festivals.what: This is a monsoon feast that takes a form unique to Goa. Groups of young men, often wearing a flower crown called a kopel, jump into wells, ponds and other bodies of water that have filled up with the new monsoon rains.
festivals.who: Goan Catholic villages in general take part, and young men are the main participants in the actual well-jumping.
festivals.when: It falls on 24 June, the birthday of St. John the Baptist, which is timed to land just as the monsoon rains have arrived.
festivals.origin: This feast is observed on this date across the whole Catholic world, but the specific practice of jumping into wells is unique to Goa, and its own origin was never written down. Locally, people read it as acting out the moment when the infant John leapt inside his mother Elizabeth's womb when Mary came to visit her.
festivals.signifies: The festival expresses joy through the physical act of jumping, tied directly to the Bible story of John leaping before he was even born, and also tied to the arrival of the year's first full water supply after the dry season.
festivals.beliefs: People understand the jump as a joyful reenactment rather than as a baptism ritual itself. Goa is the only place where this feast takes on this particular physical form.
festivals.celebrate: People wear kopel flower crowns and move in groups between villages, singing and jumping into one well or pond after another along the way. Some coastal areas hold boat processions, and families gather for feasts afterward.
festivals.local: Newly married sons-in-law are traditionally expected to jump into a well at their in-laws' house, after which they are sent home with gifts of fruit and vegetables. This is a very specific part of the tradition that families still hold each other to.
festivals.image: Young men jumping into a flower-decorated well, Sao Joao, Goan village

festivals.name: Zagor
festivals.reach: This tradition is specific to Siolim and a small number of other villages in the Bardez region.
festivals.what: This is an all-night folk drama that includes singing, dancing and acting. It is staged jointly by Siolim's Hindu and Catholic residents together, with certain performing roles passed down within particular families from both communities.
festivals.who: Hindu and Catholic villagers of Siolim work together on this, which is an unusual case in Goa of a single festival organized and performed jointly, rather than one community celebrating while the other just watches as a guest.
festivals.when: It takes place on a single night in December or January. The exact date is set by village custom rather than any fixed calendar.
festivals.origin: This practice was banned for a period under Portuguese rule, which treated it as a pagan tradition. It was revived in 1865 after villagers petitioned for it with the support of the church. Its origin before that ban is undocumented local custom.
festivals.signifies: The festival represents a night-long watch kept for the village's protection. It is performed as much through storytelling and satire about everyday village life as it is through religious devotion.
festivals.beliefs: The word Zagor roughly means to keep watch through the night for the protection of the village. People believe the entire vigil itself, not any single scene within the drama, is what actually protects the village.
festivals.celebrate: The night opens with a torch-lit procession called the suari. Devotional songs are sung before the drama itself begins, mixing mythological stories with tales of everyday village life, acted out until dawn.
festivals.local: The performing roles in Zagor are passed down within specific Siolim families, both Hindu and Catholic. Having a hereditary part in the Zagor is a specific mark of standing in the local community, not something just anyone can decide to take on.
festivals.image: Torch-lit suari procession opening Zagor, Siolim village, night

name: Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu
st_nm: Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu
tagline: This territory combines two old Portuguese port towns with a tribal inland area. They were joined together administratively, but they still keep their own separate festival calendars.

festivals.name: Tarpa Festival
festivals.reach: It is kept among the Varli, Kokna and Dhodia communities across Dadra and Nagar Haveli.
festivals.what: This is a dance festival held after the harvest by the Varli, Kokna and Dhodia tribal communities. It is built around an instrument called the tarpa, a wind instrument made from a dried bottle gourd and bamboo pipes. Someone plays this instrument to lead a circling line dance that can go on for hours.
festivals.who: The Varli, Kokna and Dhodia communities of Dadra and Nagar Haveli take part, along with nearby tribal areas of Gujarat and Maharashtra, where the same instrument and dance are also kept alive.
festivals.when: It happens in December or January, once the harvest is finished and the granaries are full of grain.
festivals.origin: This is an old farming tradition among tribal communities, and nobody has recorded exactly how old it is. Practically speaking, it is tied to the season when fieldwork ends and people finally have both free time and extra grain to celebrate with.
festivals.signifies: The festival expresses gratitude for a finished harvest, shown through people moving together in dance rather than through an offering made to a god.
festivals.beliefs: People understand the tarpa player as actually leading the dance, not just accompanying it. Dancers follow the changing rhythm of the instrument without any fixed steps planned out in advance.
festivals.celebrate: A single tarpa player stands in the center while dancers, both men and women together, form a moving spiral or circle around him. They hold hands or hold each other's waists, continuing for hours as the player turns to face different parts of the circle one after another.
festivals.local: Each year, people usually make a brand new tarpa instrument from a gourd grown specifically for that purpose, instead of reusing the same one. Locals say this is part of why the sound is never quite exactly the same from one year to the next.
festivals.image: Circle of Varli dancers around a tarpa player, winter evening, Dadra and Nagar Haveli

festivals.name: Holi
festivals.reach: It is kept across the tribal villages of Dadra and Nagar Haveli.
festivals.what: This is Holi as celebrated by the region's Varli and Kokna communities. It includes a distinct dance form called Bhawada, performed by traveling troupes who move between villages during the days around the bonfire and the throwing of colored powder.
festivals.who: The Varli and Kokna tribal communities of Dadra and Nagar Haveli take part.
festivals.when: It falls on Phalgun Purnima, the same full moon that is marked elsewhere in India as Holi, in the month of March.
festivals.origin: The core of Holi, the bonfire and the throwing of color, is an old tradition shared across all of India. The Bhawada dance form attached to it here is a local tribal addition of unknown age, and what makes this celebration different from the wider Holi tradition is how it is performed, not when it happens.
festivals.signifies: This festival marks the same change of season that Holi celebrates everywhere else, but here that change is expressed through a specific local dance form rather than just throwing colored powder.
festivals.beliefs: The bonfire, called Holika, carries the same meaning here as it does everywhere else in India, the idea of burning away whatever should not survive into the new season. Here, that meaning is layered on top of the community's own dance tradition rather than being replaced by it.
festivals.celebrate: Bonfires are lit the night before. Bhawada troupes travel from village to village performing over the following days. People throw colored powder among each other, and communities gather for shared feasts.
festivals.local: A Bhawada troupe plans its route between villages days ahead of time for Holi. If a village gets skipped one year, its residents will make sure to mention it pointedly to the troupe's organizers the following year.
festivals.image: Bhawada dance troupe performing in a Dadra and Nagar Haveli village, Holi colours

festivals.name: Nariyal Purnima
festivals.reach: It is kept by Daman's fishing community along the Damanganga waterfront.
festivals.what: Daman's fishing families mark the end of the monsoon fishing ban by decorating their boats and offering coconuts to the sea, right before they go back out to work.
festivals.who: Daman's Koli and other fishing communities take part. Their boats line the Damanganga river between the areas of Moti Daman and Nani Daman.
festivals.when: It falls on Shravan Purnima, the same full moon that is celebrated elsewhere as Raksha Bandhan, in the month of August.
festivals.origin: This is a coastal community custom whose exact origin was never written down. Practically speaking, it is tied to the end of the monsoon's rough seas and the reopening of the fishing season.
festivals.signifies: The festival represents a formal request made to the sea for a safe fishing season, made before the boats head back out to earn a living from it.
festivals.beliefs: People believe the coconut they offer helps to calm and please the sea. In this ritual, the sea is treated less like scenery and more like a partner that people must deal with directly before going back to work on it.
festivals.celebrate: In the days before the festival, boats are cleaned, repainted and decorated with flags. On the day itself, a coconut is thrown into the water from each boat. The fishing community performs the Machhi dance, in which men act out rowing and casting nets while women dance carrying baskets. The day closes with a community feast.
festivals.local: According to local accounts, the days when decorated boats line the Damanganga bridge are the one time each year the working fishing fleet is dressed up for anything other than actual work.
festivals.image: Decorated fishing boats along the Damanganga waterfront, Daman, Nariyal Purnima

festivals.name: Christmas
festivals.reach: It is kept by the small Catholic communities of Diu and Daman, both of which were once Portuguese territories.
festivals.what: Christmas is kept within the small, historically Portuguese Catholic communities of Diu and Daman. It is centered on churches built during nearly four centuries of Portuguese rule, including Diu's St. Paul's Church. This church is dedicated to Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception, and it is one of the more elaborately carved Portuguese-era churches anywhere on India's west coast.
festivals.who: The Catholic communities of Diu and Daman take part. Today they number only a few hundred families between them, since most residents of Portuguese descent left after the territories joined India in 1961.
festivals.when: It falls on 25 December, following the period of Advent.
festivals.origin: Portugal controlled Diu and Daman from the sixteenth century until 1961. The churches built there, including St. Paul's in Diu, one of the most prominent, mostly date back to the early seventeenth century, built under Portuguese rule.
festivals.signifies: Christmas celebrates the birth of Jesus. It is kept by communities whose numbers have shrunk sharply since 1961, but whose church life has continued without any interruption.
festivals.beliefs: Midnight mass remains the central part of the celebration for the remaining Catholic families, held in churches that were originally built for congregations many times larger than they are today.
festivals.celebrate: Families attend midnight mass at St. Paul's Church in Diu and at Daman's parish churches. Homes are decorated with lights and small nativity scenes called cribs. A festive meal is shared among the extended community, which now often includes non-Catholic neighbors invited to join in.
festivals.local: St. Paul's Church in Diu was built for a Portuguese-era town of thousands of people. Today it serves a Catholic population so small that the church's caretakers can name most of the families who still attend, a fact they mention to visitors more with resignation than with pride.
festivals.image: St. Paul's Church interior lit for midnight mass, Diu, small congregation

name: Maharashtra
tagline: Maharashtra sits on the Deccan plateau, and its festival life centers on a saint's pilgrimage road to Pandharpur and on a merchant god who is welcomed into every street. Mumbai, in turn, takes in everyone's festival and makes it its own.

festivals.name: Ganesh Chaturthi
festivals.reach: This is the state's largest public festival. It is overwhelming in scale in Mumbai and Pune, and it is kept in some form almost everywhere else too.
festivals.what: For ten days, clay statues of the god Ganesh are set up in homes and in enormous neighborhood tents called pandals. People worship them daily, and then carry them in a procession to be immersed in the sea, a river, or a water tank.
festivals.who: Maharashtrian Hindu households broadly take part, and through the public pandals, effectively all of Mumbai and Pune joins in regardless of background. These public, or sarvajanik, pandals are run by neighborhood committees rather than by any single organization.
festivals.when: It runs from Bhadrapada Shukla Chaturthi through a day called Anant Chaturdashi, a total of ten days, in August or September.
festivals.origin: Household worship of Ganesh has long been practiced in Maharashtra. Its transformation into a huge public festival is credited to the leader Lokmanya Tilak, who starting in 1893 organized public installations to gather large crowds for the nationalist movement, using religious gatherings as cover at a time when the British colonial government restricted openly political meetings.
festivals.signifies: The festival represents Ganesh living among his devotees for the length of the celebration. Since Tilak's time, it has also come to represent a demonstration of people organizing together, not just a private act of devotion.
festivals.beliefs: People believe the clay statue holds the god's actual presence only for the length of the festival. The final immersion, called visarjan, is understood not as throwing the statue away, but as sending the god back home. People invite him to return the following year with the call 'Ganpati Bappa Morya, pudhchya varshi lavkar ya,' which means 'come again next year.'
festivals.celebrate: Elaborate pandals compete with each other on scale and theme, especially Mumbai's famous Lalbaugcha Raja, which draws lines of people that last for many hours. There are daily aarti prayer ceremonies, and modak sweets are offered because they are believed to be Ganesh's favorite. On the final day, there is a big procession to the sea or a river with drumming and dancing. In recent years, there has also been an organized push toward eco-friendly, quick-dissolving statues, in order to limit the effect all this immersion has on water bodies.
festivals.local: The line to see Mumbai's Lalbaugcha Raja statue is a well-known institution in its own right, sometimes running through the entire night. Devotees who finally reach the statue are usually given just a few seconds in front of it, not minutes, before volunteers move them along.
festivals.image: Ganesh idol procession toward the sea for visarjan, Mumbai crowd, drums

festivals.name: Gudi Padwa
festivals.reach: It is celebrated across Maharashtra, and Konkani communities celebrate it on the same day under different names.
festivals.what: This is the Marathi New Year. People mark it by raising a gudi, which is a bright piece of cloth tied over an upside-down copper or silver pot, mounted on top of a bamboo pole placed outside the main door or window.
festivals.who: Marathi-speaking Hindu households across the state take part, as well as Maharashtrian communities living abroad.
festivals.when: It falls on Chaitra Shukla Pratipada, the same lunisolar new year that is celebrated elsewhere in India as Ugadi, usually in late March or early April.
festivals.origin: This is a lunisolar new year that shares its basic meaning with Ugadi and other regional new year celebrations. The gudi symbol specifically belongs to Maharashtra and the Konkan region, and nobody knows exactly how old it is. Some local tradition connects the day to the military victories of the ruler Chhatrapati Shivaji, but this connection comes from folk memory layered on top of an older calendar festival, rather than being its actual origin.
festivals.signifies: The festival represents a household planting its own marker outside for the year ahead, and it treats a fresh calendar page as a sign of what is to come.
festivals.beliefs: People eat neem leaves on this day, sometimes mixed with jaggery, based on the idea that starting the year with something bitter protects against a bitter year ahead.
festivals.celebrate: The gudi is raised at sunrise and taken down at sunset. Families draw rangoli patterns at their doorstep, wear new clothes, and eat puran poli or shrikhand for their midday meal. Some cities hold processions with traditional dress and music.
festivals.local: A common sight on this day is a Mumbai apartment building where every balcony flies its own gudi on the same morning, a scene quite different from the more private way Ugadi is observed next door in Andhra households.
festivals.image: Gudi raised outside a Maharashtrian home, bright cloth and copper pot, morning

festivals.name: Pandharpur Wari
festivals.season: Ashadha, eleventh day of the bright fortnight
festivals.reach: This is a statewide pilgrimage, with processions called palkhis converging on Pandharpur from all across Maharashtra.
festivals.what: This is a walking pilgrimage that lasts several weeks. Processions called palkhis carry the sandals of Warkari saints, most famously Dnyaneshwar from Alandi and Tukaram from Dehu, and walk roughly two hundred fifty kilometers to the Vitthal temple in Pandharpur, arriving in time for a day called Ashadhi Ekadashi.
festivals.who: The Warkari sect takes part, a centuries-old devotional movement that is meant to be open to people of all castes, though not always perfectly in practice. Hundreds of thousands of people join the walking palkhis every year.
festivals.when: The palkhis set out in June and converge on Pandharpur in time for Ashadhi Ekadashi, the eleventh day of the bright half of the month of Ashadha.
festivals.origin: The Warkari tradition traces back to the medieval Bhakti poet-saints of Maharashtra, including Dnyaneshwar, Namdev and Tukaram, starting from roughly the thirteenth century onward. Later Warkari leaders are credited with organizing the palkhi walk into the form it takes today, building on that older devotional foundation.
festivals.signifies: The pilgrimage represents equality, shown through the act of walking, singing and eating together for weeks, no matter what caste hierarchy the pilgrims return to afterward.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that reaching Pandharpur for Ekadashi and seeing Vitthal, who is shown standing with his hands on his hips atop a brick, is the true devotional goal of a Warkari's whole life, not just one trip among many others.
festivals.celebrate: Pilgrims spend days walking while singing devotional songs called abhang, accompanied by rhythmic instruments called the tal and the mridang. People cook and eat together along the route. Groups called dindis are organized by village and family line. When they finally arrive, there is a crush of people at Pandharpur's temple hoping for a glimpse of Vitthal and his consort Rukmini.
festivals.local: Farming families close their fields for these weeks specifically so they can make the walk. This is an economic sacrifice that a Warkari household makes every single year, no matter what the season otherwise demands of them, something outsiders sometimes find harder to understand than the religious ideas behind it.
festivals.image: Warkari palkhi procession on the road to Pandharpur, white flags, walking crowd

festivals.name: Gokulashtami
festivals.reach: It is kept across Maharashtra, and Dahi Handi in particular is a spectacle specific to the cities of Mumbai and Thane.
festivals.what: This festival celebrates Krishna's birthday. It is kept overnight with fasting and worship at midnight. The following day, in Mumbai's neighborhoods, teams of young men form human pyramids, called govindas, to break open a pot of curd, called a dahi handi, which is strung up high between buildings.
festivals.who: Hindu households take part in the birth observance. For the Dahi Handi competitions, teams of young men called govinda pathaks compete, many of them named and sponsored by businesses or political groups.
festivals.when: Krishna Janmashtami falls on the eighth day of the dark half of the month, with Dahi Handi taking place the next day, in August or September.
festivals.origin: Janmashtami is an old festival celebrated all across India. The human-pyramid form of Dahi Handi as a public street competition developed specifically in the Mumbai region. It reenacts young Krishna's playful mischief of stealing curd from pots that were hung out of his reach, and it has grown considerably in scale and prize money since the late twentieth century.
festivals.signifies: The festival marks Krishna's birth at midnight, and separately, through the human pyramids, it turns his childhood mischief into a public sporting performance.
festivals.beliefs: People believe midnight is the exact moment Krishna was born, and they mark it with devotional songs called bhajans while rocking a cradle holding a baby image of him. The Dahi Handi pot is understood as young Krishna's actual target, being reenacted rather than just symbolized.
festivals.celebrate: People keep a day-long fast, which they break at midnight with a sweet called panjiri. Temples fill up for the midnight prayer ceremony. The next day, govinda teams tour the city in trucks, building human pyramids up to nine levels high to reach pots strung between buildings, all while being doused with water thrown from balconies as they climb.
festivals.local: Political parties and local strongmen sponsor the biggest Dahi Handi events with large amounts of prize money. This has turned the competitive scale of the event, and the injuries that come with taller pyramids, into an ongoing public argument in Mumbai and Thane most years.
festivals.image: Human pyramid reaching for a dahi handi pot strung between buildings, Mumbai street

festivals.name: Narali Purnima
festivals.reach: It is kept along Maharashtra's Konkan coast, and specifically by Mumbai's Koli fishing settlements.
festivals.what: On this day, the Koli fishing community marks the end of the monsoon fishing ban by offering coconuts to the sea, right before the boats go back out to work.
festivals.who: Koli fisherfolk of Mumbai take part, especially in the areas of Worli, Mahim and Colaba, along with fishing communities along the Konkan coast.
festivals.when: It falls on Shravan Purnima, the same full moon that is celebrated elsewhere in India as Raksha Bandhan, in the month of August.
festivals.origin: This is a coastal community observance whose exact age is unknown. Practically speaking, it is tied to the end of the monsoon's rough seas and the reopening of the fishing season, rather than to any documented origin story.
festivals.signifies: The festival represents a direct request made to the sea, asking for calm water and a safe season, before people go back to earning their living from it.
festivals.beliefs: People believe the coconut offered to the sea helps to calm it and thank it. In this ritual, the sea is treated less like a resource to be used and more like an entity that is owed a formal gesture of respect before people work on it again.
festivals.celebrate: Boats are cleaned, repainted, and decorated with flags and flowers. A coconut is thrown into the water from each boat along with a short prayer. Afterward, communities gather for feasts of fish and coconut-based sweets, and Koli song and dance fill the fishing settlements through the evening.
festivals.local: In Worli and Mahim, families decorate their boats days ahead of time, and this has become a point of competitive pride between families, even though these same boats will all be doing exactly the same undecorated job the very next morning.
festivals.image: Decorated fishing boats at a Konkan coast jetty, coconuts offered to the sea

festivals.name: Eid al-Fitr
festivals.reach: This festival is especially significant in Mumbai, Malegaon, Bhiwandi and Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar.
festivals.what: This festival marks the end of Ramadan. It is kept by one of India's larger urban Muslim populations, historically concentrated around Mumbai's older neighborhoods and the Deccan towns that were once part of the Nizam's territory.
festivals.who: Maharashtra's Muslim communities broadly take part, including Konkani, Marathi, Urdu and Deccani speakers, depending on the region.
festivals.when: It falls on the first day of the month of Shawwal, and because it follows the lunar calendar, the date moves earlier each year compared to our regular calendar.
festivals.origin: Islam's presence in Maharashtra dates back to early Arabian Sea trade along the Konkan coast, continuing through the later Deccan sultanates and up to the Nizam's rule from Aurangabad. Each of these historical periods left behind its own architecture, food, and way of observing the calendar.
festivals.signifies: The festival marks the end of the fast, and it brings a leveling of the table at Eid, after a full month of self-restraint.
festivals.beliefs: A form of charity called Zakat al-Fitr is settled before the Eid prayer, and moon sighting is watched closely, confirmed only the night before the festival.
festivals.celebrate: People attend Eid prayers at the Eidgah prayer ground and at neighborhood mosques. They eat a sweet dish called sheer khurma and wear new clothes. In Mumbai, the Mohammed Ali Road area runs a busy food market through the nights of Ramzan that draws visitors well beyond just the fasting community.
festivals.local: The Ramzan food stalls on Mohammed Ali Road, known especially for kebabs and a sweet pancake called malpua, are just as much a Mumbai institution for non-Muslims as they are for the Muslim community that originally built the market for their own evening meal to break the fast.
festivals.image: Mohammed Ali Road food stalls at night during Ramzan, Mumbai crowd

festivals.name: Feast of Mount Mary
festivals.season: Eight days around the Nativity of Mary
festivals.reach: This feast is centered on Bandra, Mumbai, and it draws visitors of all faiths from across the city.
festivals.what: This is an eight-day feast held at the Basilica of Our Lady of the Mount in Bandra. It closes with a large fair, called the Bandra Fair, that spreads through the surrounding streets.
festivals.who: Mumbai's East Indian Catholic community, the city's oldest Christian population, takes part, along with Goan and Mangalorean Catholics who have settled in the city. A wide public of people from every background also attends the fair, regardless of their religion.
festivals.when: The feast closes on or near 8 September, the day marking the Nativity of Mary, following a period of prayer called a novena.
festivals.origin: Devotion at Mount Mary dates back to a Portuguese-era Franciscan presence at the site starting in the sixteenth century. The current basilica was rebuilt in the early twentieth century, after the original was damaged during earlier conflicts in the region's colonial history.
festivals.signifies: The feast represents a wish made and, if it comes true, repaid. This particular church is known specifically as a place to ask for favors, not just for regular worship.
festivals.beliefs: Devotees who receive what they asked for come back with a wax offering shaped like their wish, such as a limb for healing, a baby for fertility, or a house for a new home. These wax shapes are sold outside the church specifically for this purpose.
festivals.celebrate: Novena masses are held all through the week leading up to the feast. A large fair with stalls selling food, toys and devotional wax offerings fills Hill Road and the streets around the basilica. Candlelit processions take place on the closing days of the feast.
festivals.local: The wax offering stalls outside Mount Mary form their own small trade, and the shapes for sale, whether a pair of lungs, a car, or a pass certificate, give a fairly accurate picture of what Mumbai residents are currently worried about.
festivals.image: Wax votive offering stalls outside Mount Mary Basilica, Bandra Fair crowd

name: Madhya Pradesh
tagline: Madhya Pradesh is a plateau state made up of old kingdoms, tribal regions, and towns built along rivers. It does not have one single center that everything revolves around. Instead, many different places and cultures come together to make up the state.

festivals.name: Simhastha
festivals.season: When Jupiter enters Leo (Simha), timed to Vaisakh
festivals.reach: This is one of the four Kumbh Mela sites in India, and it draws pilgrims from all across the country.
festivals.what: Simhastha is the Ujjain version of the Kumbh Mela. It happens on the banks of the Kshipra river once every twelve years. During the festival, groups of ascetics called akharas march in procession down to the riverbank steps called ghats, and millions of people bathe in the river over several weeks.
festivals.who: Naga sadhus, who are Hindu holy men, and akharas, which are organized groups of ascetics, come from all over India. Ordinary pilgrims also arrive in huge numbers, tens of millions of people in total. The people who live in Ujjain end up hosting what feels like a whole temporary city.
festivals.when: The festival happens when the planet Jupiter enters the zodiac sign Leo during the month of Vaisakh, which happens roughly once every twelve years. The last Simhastha was held in 2016, and the next one is expected in 2028.
festivals.origin: There are four Kumbh Mela sites in India: Haridwar, Prayagraj, Ujjain, and Nashik. All four share the same old legend, that drops of amrita, a mythical drink that grants immortality, fell to earth at these places. Ujjain's own fair has a recorded history as a mass bathing event going back several centuries, to the time when the region was ruled by the kings of Malwa.
festivals.signifies: People believe that during this short window of time, the river itself becomes especially powerful at washing away sins. Bathing in it now is believed to matter much more than bathing in it at any other time.
festivals.beliefs: There is a belief that bathing at exactly the right astrological moment, called the shahi snan or royal bath, brings a person spiritual merit that an ordinary bath in the river cannot give.
festivals.celebrate: Groups of ascetics called akharas march in procession into the city. People take the shahi snan, or royal bath, at set ghats and at set times. A huge tent city is built along the banks of the Kshipra river just for the length of the festival. There are also religious talks, camps set up by the akharas, and a bathing schedule that the government plans years in advance.
festivals.local: The city of Ujjain clears its own calendar of other events to make room for the mela. Roads, camps, and steps down to the river are all rebuilt just for these few weeks of use, and then taken apart again afterward. For a short time, the city's population grows to many times its normal size.
festivals.image: Akhara procession of sadhus heading to the Kshipra ghats at dawn, Ujjain

festivals.name: Bhagoria
festivals.season: Seven days before Holi, in Phalgun
festivals.reach: This festival is centered in the districts of Jhabua, Alirajpur, Dhar, and Khargone, an area where the Bhil and Bhilala communities live.
festivals.what: Bhagoria is a week of haats, which are weekly markets, held in about twenty villages between Jhabua and Alirajpur in the days leading up to Holi. At these crowded markets, people come together to trade goods, play music, and look for romantic partners, all in the same place at the same time.
festivals.who: The Bhil, Bhilala, and Pateliya communities of western Madhya Pradesh celebrate this festival.
festivals.when: It takes place during the week before Holi, in the Hindu month of Phalgun, which usually falls in March.
festivals.origin: These haats began as old farming markets held right after the harvest was finished. Their current form, where they also work as a fair for finding a partner, is a long documented custom rather than something new. No one knows exactly how old this custom is.
festivals.signifies: Bhagoria turns the end of the farming year into the biggest social event of the year. Villages that do not normally meet each other come together in one place.
festivals.beliefs: If a couple chooses each other at the haat, this is treated as a real and binding decision. If the couple then elopes, this is seen as an accepted way to get married, not as something shameful or scandalous.
festivals.celebrate: The haat grounds are set up with Ferris wheels and market stalls. People play drums and dance the mandal dance. Young men and women wear new clothes as they meet each other and choose partners, sometimes marking the choice by exchanging gulal, which is colored powder, or tobacco. Food and liquor are sold late into the day.
festivals.local: People from outside the area often describe Bhagoria as just a spring fair. But locally, its reputation comes specifically from the courtship custom. Bhil families see this custom as a real and proper way to arrange a marriage, not as a way to get around the usual rules.
festivals.image: Ferris wheel and crowded haat ground at Bhagoria, Jhabua district, afternoon

festivals.name: Tansen Sangeet Samaroh
festivals.reach: This is a classical music festival of national importance, held in the city of Gwalior.
festivals.what: This is a four day classical music festival held next to the tomb of Tansen, a famous musician who lived in the sixteenth century, in the city of Gwalior. It draws performers from across India who work in the Hindustani classical music tradition.
festivals.who: Singers and instrument players who perform Hindustani classical music take part, along with an audience of serious music lovers who travel specifically to attend.
festivals.when: The festival is held in December and lasts four days.
festivals.origin: The gathering began as an urs, which is an annual remembrance ceremony held at a person's tomb. In the twentieth century, the state government expanded it into a full classical music festival.
festivals.signifies: The festival draws a direct connection between Tansen, who was a musician at the Mughal royal court, and today's Hindustani classical music tradition. This connection is made real by holding the festival right at his own grave.
festivals.beliefs: Many classical musicians see performing at Tansen's tomb as a sign that they have truly arrived in their field. During the festival, a senior honor called the Rashtriya Tansen Samman is given out, and it is considered one of the top awards in classical music.
festivals.celebrate: Evening concerts are held at the tomb complex and other venues around Gwalior over the four nights of the festival. The Tansen Samman award is given to a senior musician, and younger performers get a chance to perform alongside well known, established names.
festivals.local: The concerts run late into the cold Gwalior winter night. Regular attendees wrap themselves in shawls instead of leaving early, treating the cold as simply part of sitting through the performance.
festivals.image: Classical vocalist performing at night near Tansen's tomb, Gwalior, lit courtyard

festivals.name: Khajuraho Dance Festival
festivals.reach: This classical dance festival is held at the temple complex in Khajuraho.
festivals.what: For a week, classical Indian dance is performed with the floodlit temples of Khajuraho, built in the tenth and eleventh centuries, as the backdrop.
festivals.who: Dancers who perform Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Odissi, Kuchipudi, and other classical Indian dance styles are invited from all across the country.
festivals.when: The festival is held in February and lasts about a week.
festivals.origin: The state government started this festival in the 1970s. The idea was to actually bring classical dance to the temple site itself, instead of holding it somewhere else and only using pictures of the temples as scenery.
festivals.signifies: The festival makes the claim that the dance poses carved into the temple walls and today's living dance tradition come from the very same lineage. In other words, it says the connection is real, not just something that looks similar by coincidence.
festivals.beliefs: Dancers and organizers say that performing in front of the temples feels completely different from performing on a normal indoor stage. They feel it is closer to what the temple sculptures were originally made to go along with.
festivals.celebrate: Every night, performances are staged outdoors, facing the lit up Western Group of temples. A different classical dance style is featured each evening. During the day, there are also seminars and craft stalls running alongside the performances.
festivals.local: The floodlights are angled so that the dancers and the centuries old carved figures behind them can both be seen in the same view at once. This is the whole design idea behind the festival.
festivals.image: Odissi dancer performing at night before the floodlit Khajuraho temples

festivals.name: Navratri at Maihar and Salkanpur
festivals.reach: This festival draws pilgrims from across Madhya Pradesh and from neighboring states to the Sharda Devi temple and the Bijasen Devi temple.
festivals.what: This is nine nights of worshipping the goddess, centered on two temples that sit on top of hills, the Sharda Devi temple at Maihar and the Bijasen Devi temple at Salkanpur. Both temples can only be reached by climbing up, and during Navratri that climb turns into a huge mass pilgrimage.
festivals.who: Devotees of the goddess Devi come from across Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, and beyond. Both temples also attract large numbers of pilgrims who are keeping a personal vow and climb the whole way up barefoot.
festivals.when: The festival takes place over the nine nights of Sharad Navratri, during the bright half of the month of Ashwin, which falls in September or October.
festivals.origin: Both temples are old hilltop shrines with pilgrimage traditions that go back a long time locally. They have grown into major Navratri destinations mainly because roads and trains have made them easier to reach, not because of any single event that started it all.
festivals.signifies: For pilgrims, climbing the mountain is itself part of fulfilling a vow. The climb is treated as part of the offering to the goddess, not as an obstacle standing in the way of it.
festivals.beliefs: Many pilgrims climb the temple steps barefoot because they made a vow earlier in the year that they would do this specifically during Navratri.
festivals.celebrate: Steady lines of pilgrims fill the temple steps starting before dawn. The temples are given special Navratri decorations, and darshan, the viewing of the deity, is allowed for longer hours than usual. At the base of both hills, there are Ramlila performances and fair stalls, and the cable car at Maihar runs at full capacity.
festivals.local: At Maihar, many pilgrims still climb the steep final stretch on foot even though they could take the cable car instead. This is because their vow was about making the climb itself, not just about seeing the view from the top.
festivals.image: Pilgrims climbing the temple steps at Maihar during Navratri, early morning queue

festivals.name: Eid al-Fitr
festivals.reach: This festival is especially significant in Bhopal's old city, in Burhanpur, and in other towns across the state with large Muslim populations.
festivals.what: Eid al-Fitr marks the end of a month of fasting from dawn to dusk. It is kept with special depth in Bhopal, whose old city still carries the mark of the Muslim rulers of the former Bhopal state, including a line of women rulers known as Begums.
festivals.who: Muslim communities celebrate this festival, especially in Bhopal, Burhanpur, Ratlam, and Khandwa, along with other towns that have had a Muslim presence since Mughal times or the era of the Bhopal state.
festivals.when: Eid al-Fitr falls on the first day of the Islamic month of Shawwal. Because it follows the lunar calendar, the date moves earlier each year compared to the regular Gregorian calendar.
festivals.origin: Bhopal's Muslim institutions and neighborhoods date back to the founding of the Bhopal state in the eighteenth century. Burhanpur's Muslim history is even older, connected to its role as a staging town for the Mughals on their way into the Deccan region.
festivals.signifies: Eid al-Fitr marks the end of the fast. In Bhopal specifically, it is also a citywide occasion that the old city still organizes itself around each year.
festivals.beliefs: Muslims give zakat al-Fitr, a form of charity, before the Eid prayer, so that people who could not otherwise afford a festive meal are able to share in the feast too.
festivals.celebrate: People gather for Eid prayers at the Taj-ul-Masajid in Bhopal, one of the largest mosques in India, and at open prayer grounds called Eidgahs elsewhere. At home, families eat sheer khurma, a sweet vermicelli dish, and biryani. People wear new clothes and spend the day visiting family and friends.
festivals.local: On Eid morning, the streets leading to the Taj-ul-Masajid fill with a crowd larger than the old city's own streets were built to hold. This happens every year and reminds everyone just how huge the mosque really is.
festivals.image: Crowd gathered for Eid prayer outside Taj-ul-Masajid, Bhopal, morning

festivals.name: Christmas
festivals.reach: Christmas is particularly significant for Jabalpur's older Christian congregations and for smaller Christian communities found across the state.
festivals.what: Christmas in Madhya Pradesh is kept by a fairly small but long established Christian community. It is strongest in Jabalpur, which has had a Church of North India diocese and mission institutions since the colonial period.
festivals.who: Catholic and Protestant congregations celebrate Christmas, including Church of North India parishes. They are concentrated in Jabalpur, Indore, and the cantonment areas of Bhopal.
festivals.when: Christmas falls on December 25, with carol services held throughout the weeks of Advent leading up to it.
festivals.origin: In the nineteenth century, mission schools, hospitals, and churches were built, many of them connected to Jabalpur's cantonment area. These institutions established a Christian presence in the region that has continued ever since as a small but stable minority community.
festivals.signifies: Christmas marks the birth of Jesus, called the nativity. It is kept by a community that is small compared to the rest of the state's population, but whose institutions, like its schools and churches, are quite old.
festivals.beliefs: For most families, midnight mass is the service the whole day is built around.
festivals.celebrate: In the week before Christmas, there are carol services. On Christmas Eve, there is a midnight mass. Churches in Jabalpur's older cantonment neighborhoods are decorated for the season, and on Christmas Day itself, families share meals together and visit one another.
festivals.local: Jabalpur's Christian institutions, including several of its schools and its old cantonment church, are old enough that their networks of former students and members stay strong even though no single congregation is very large.
festivals.image: Candlelit midnight mass at a Jabalpur cantonment era church

name: Chhattisgarh
languages: Hindi (हिन्दी), Chhattisgarhi (छत्तीसगढ़ी), and tribal languages spoken among the state's substantial Gond and other tribal populations
tagline: Chhattisgarh is a state of forested highlands. Here, the customs of the Gond people and the Bastar tribal communities shape the yearly calendar just as much as any Hindu temple does.

festivals.name: Hareli
festivals.reach: Hareli is Chhattisgarh's own festival that opens the farming year, and it is kept all across the state.
festivals.what: Hareli is the very first festival of the farming year in Chhattisgarh. It is kept on the dark moon day of the month of Shravan. On this day, farm tools like ploughs, sickles, and spades are washed, given a rest, and worshipped instead of being used for work.
festivals.who: Farming households across Chhattisgarh celebrate Hareli, and it carries particular importance among the Gond and other farming communities.
festivals.when: Hareli falls on Amavasya, the new moon day, of the month of Shravan, which usually falls in July or August. This is shortly after the rice, or paddy, has been sown in the fields.
festivals.origin: Hareli is a regional farming festival tied to the sowing season during the month of Shravan. Its name in the Chhattisgarhi language comes from the word hariyali, which means greenery, marking the moment when the fields turn green after the first rains.
festivals.signifies: Hareli is a pause built into the middle of the farming season. It is a time to thank the tools and animals that are doing the work, even though the harvest itself is still far off.
festivals.beliefs: People call on Kutki Dai, a local guardian spirit of the crop, and ask for a good growing season. They also hang neem tree branches over their doors, because these are believed to keep illness away from the household.
festivals.celebrate: People wash their ploughs and iron farm tools and smear them with vermilion, a red powder. They hang neem leaves over their doorways and feed their cattle a special mix of grain. Children walk on gedi, which are bamboo stilts, a tradition unique to Hareli in Chhattisgarh. In some villages, there are also wrestling matches.
festivals.local: The gedi stilts are not just a minor sideshow. Boys in Chhattisgarhi villages start practicing weeks ahead of time, and being able to walk well on tall gedi at Hareli earns a person real respect in the village.
festivals.image: Children walking on bamboo gedi stilts through a village lane at Hareli

festivals.name: Pola
festivals.reach: Pola is kept across rural Chhattisgarh, as well as in neighboring Maharashtra and the Vidarbha region.
festivals.what: Pola is a festival held for bullocks, once the fields have been sown. On this day, the animals that did the hard work of ploughing are given a day of rest and decoration instead of work.
festivals.who: Farming households across the plains districts of Chhattisgarh celebrate Pola.
festivals.when: Pola falls on the new moon day of the month of Bhadrapada, usually in August or September, about a month after Hareli.
festivals.origin: Pola is an old farming custom shared with Maharashtra and other parts of central India. It is tied to the quiet pause between finishing the sowing and the long wait for the harvest to come.
festivals.signifies: Pola recognizes that it is the bullock's hard work, not only the farmer's, that will produce the crop still to come.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that a bullock that has worked hard through the sowing season has truly earned this day of rest and decoration. It is seen as something the animal deserves, not as a favor being done for it.
festivals.celebrate: Bullocks are bathed, their horns are painted, and they are dressed in decorated cloth and bells. Children are given clay bullock toys called nandi baila, and they run their own pretend processions with them. A real procession of decorated animals also moves through the village, and in the evening, everyone shares a feast.
festivals.local: Clay bullock toys for children are sold at Pola fairs made specifically for this one day. A village's potters judge how well their whole season of trade has gone based on the sales at this one festival's stalls.
festivals.image: Decorated bullocks led through a Chhattisgarh village at Pola, painted horns

festivals.name: Bastar Dussehra
festivals.season: Seventy five days, from Hareli through Sharad Navratri to Diwali
festivals.reach: This festival is centered on the city of Jagdalpur and draws participants from villages all across the Bastar plateau.
festivals.what: Bastar Dussehra is the longest Dussehra celebration anywhere in India, lasting about seventy five days. Unlike Dussehra elsewhere, which is built around the story of Ram and Ravana, this one is built around the goddess Danteshwari.
festivals.who: The former royal family of Bastar still holds ceremonial responsibility for this festival. The Gond, Halba, Bhatra, and other communities of the Bastar plateau provide the rituals and labor that make it happen.
festivals.when: The festival begins around the time of Hareli in July and runs all the way through Sharad Navratri to a closing rite held near Diwali. Its most important days fall in September and October.
festivals.origin: Tradition says this festival was founded by the Bastar ruler Purushottam Dev, around the thirteenth century. Its present form combines tribal deity worship with royal support, rather than being based on the Ramayana story the way Dussehra is elsewhere.
festivals.signifies: This is a goddess festival organized entirely according to tribal tradition. No effigy of the demon king Ravana is burned here, and the central act of the festival is pulling a chariot, not acting out a battle.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that the goddess Danteshwari gives her approval for each stage of the festival through a young tribal girl chosen to represent her, called the Kanya. Her word is what authorizes the rituals to move forward.
festivals.celebrate: A giant wooden chariot is pulled by hundreds of people through the streets of Jagdalpur, on several separate days. There are also the Kachin Devi and Muria Durbar rites, in which the goddess is symbolically consulted for her opinion. Idols of deities are brought in from surrounding villages, and the festival ends with the Ohadi rite, when the goddess Danteshwari is said to leave the town.
festivals.local: Building and pulling the chariot is the hereditary right of specific village communities. This means the same families show up year after year to do the same job, and no one treats their role as something that could just be given to someone else.
festivals.image: Giant wooden chariot pulled through Jagdalpur streets at Bastar Dussehra, crowd hauling ropes

festivals.name: Rajim Kumbh Mela
festivals.reach: This is Chhattisgarh's largest river fair, and it draws pilgrims from across the state and beyond.
festivals.what: This is a two week long fair held at Rajim, the place where the Mahanadi, Pairi, and Sondur rivers all meet. It centers on bathing at this river meeting point, called a sangam, and on worship at the Rajivlochan and Kuleshwar Mahadev temples.
festivals.who: Pilgrims come from across Chhattisgarh and from neighboring states, along with sadhus, who are Hindu holy men, and akharas, organized groups of ascetics, who set up camp for the whole length of the fair.
festivals.when: The fair lasts two weeks, beginning on Magh Purnima, the full moon day of the month of Magh, which falls in January or February.
festivals.origin: Rajim's temples are old shrines built at this river meeting point. The fair's growth into a Kumbh scale event, with akharas taking part, is a more recent development sponsored by the state government, built on top of a much older local pilgrimage tradition.
festivals.signifies: Locally, people make the claim, without much argument, that Rajim's triveni sangam, the meeting point of three rivers, is Chhattisgarh's own version of the more famous one at Prayagraj.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that bathing at the sangam during this mela carries the same purifying power as bathing at a full Kumbh Mela, just on a smaller scale.
festivals.celebrate: People bathe at the sangam before dawn, and a special puja, or worship ceremony, is held at the Rajivlochan temple. Akharas set up camps and hold processions. Folk music and dance programs run throughout the two weeks, alongside craft and produce stalls from across the state.
festivals.local: Local officials and pilgrims alike often call Rajim the Prayag of Chhattisgarh, comparing it to the famous pilgrimage site of Prayagraj. The fair's own organizers have embraced this comparison rather than playing it down.
festivals.image: Pilgrims bathing at the Triveni Sangam at dawn, Rajim, temple spires behind

festivals.name: Madai
festivals.reach: Madai travels through Bastar, Kanker, Narayanpur, and Bhanupratappur over the course of the winter.
festivals.what: Madai is a traveling series of village fairs across the Bastar plateau. At each one, the guardian deities of different villages, called pen, are brought out and carried in procession to meet each other on shared ground.
festivals.who: Madai is celebrated mainly by Gond communities, along with other groups from the Bastar plateau. Each Madai fair is hosted by a different cluster of villages, taking turns.
festivals.when: Madai fairs happen through the winter, roughly from December to March, moving from village to village rather than falling on one single fixed date.
festivals.origin: Madai is a hereditary village tradition of deities visiting each other and of market trading. It is documented as a long standing local custom rather than something tied to any single founding event.
festivals.signifies: Madai shows that village deities, just like the villages themselves, have obligations to visit their neighbors and show them hospitality.
festivals.beliefs: People believe the deities actually meet each other during the procession. The priest's worship at the fair ground is treated as a real meeting between the deities, not just a symbolic one.
festivals.celebrate: Village deities are carried in procession to the fair ground. A priest performs worship while the crowd stays silent. At the same time, a market runs alongside the ritual, trading in produce, tools, and livestock. Once the worship is finished, people sing and dance folk songs.
festivals.local: The market and the worship happen on the same ground at the same time. This means a Madai is a fair and a religious rite happening together, with no clear line separating the two.
festivals.image: Village deity carried in procession to a Madai fair ground, Bastar, Gond dancers

festivals.name: Eid al-Fitr
festivals.reach: This is a minority observance, concentrated in the older Muslim neighborhoods of Raipur, Bilaspur, and Rajnandgaon.
festivals.what: Eid al-Fitr marks the close of Ramadan. It is kept by a small but long settled Muslim population in Chhattisgarh's older market towns.
festivals.who: Muslim communities celebrate Eid, concentrated in Raipur, Bilaspur, Rajnandgaon, and Ratanpur. Overall, they make up a small share of the state's population.
festivals.when: Eid falls on the first day of the Islamic month of Shawwal, which moves earlier each year compared to the regular Gregorian calendar.
festivals.origin: Muslim trading and craftsman families settled in these towns over several centuries. Their presence is often tied to the region's cloth and metalwork trade routes, rather than to any ruling dynasty of their own.
festivals.signifies: Eid marks the end of the fast. It is celebrated at a fairly modest scale compared to the much bigger Hindu and tribal festival calendar around it.
festivals.beliefs: As elsewhere, people give zakat, a form of charity, before the Eid prayer.
festivals.celebrate: People gather for Eid prayers at neighborhood mosques and at open prayer grounds called Eidgahs in Raipur and Bilaspur. At home, they eat sheer khurma, a sweet vermicelli dish, and biryani. They wear new clothes and spend the day visiting others.
festivals.local: In towns like Ratanpur, the old mosque and temple neighborhoods sit close enough together that Eid and the Hindu festival calendar have shared the very same streets for generations, without this being seen as anything unusual.
festivals.image: Eid morning prayer at a neighbourhood mosque, Raipur old city

festivals.name: Christmas
festivals.reach: Christmas is particularly significant in Jashpur district, where Oraon Christian communities make up a substantial share of the population.
festivals.what: Christmas is kept with particular strength in Jashpur. More than a hundred years of mission work among Oraon tribal families there produced one of Chhattisgarh's largest Christian populations.
festivals.who: Oraon Christian families, concentrated in Jashpur district, celebrate Christmas, along with smaller Catholic and Protestant congregations elsewhere in the state.
festivals.when: Christmas falls on December 25, with church services held throughout Advent.
festivals.origin: Belgian Jesuit missionaries, working out of the neighboring Ranchi diocese, began converting Oraon families in Jashpur starting in the early twentieth century. This came after local rulers had refused to let missionaries in for decades before that.
festivals.signifies: Christmas marks the nativity, the birth of Jesus. Locally, it also stands for how a hundred year old wave of religious conversion reshaped Jashpur's religious makeup, without erasing the tribal identity of the people who converted.
festivals.beliefs: Midnight mass and carol singing through the villages remain the main events that families build their Christmas Day around.
festivals.celebrate: In the days before Christmas, groups walk between villages singing carols. There is a midnight mass at Jashpur's churches. People wear new clothes and share a meal together on the day. Church choirs perform hymns in the Oraon and Sadri languages, alongside hymns in Hindi.
festivals.local: Jashpur's Oraon Christian families generally kept their tribal dress, dance, and earlier Sarna nature-worship customs alongside their new religion. Because of this, a Christmas carol procession in Jashpur can look and sound a lot like a Sarhul procession, just headed to a different destination.
festivals.image: Carol singers walking between Jashpur village houses at dusk, winter

name: Bihar
tagline: Bihar is a state on the Gangetic plain, full of old pilgrimage routes and old trading records. Here, the year's biggest fast, Chhath, ends with worshippers facing the river.

festivals.name: Chhath Puja
festivals.reach: Chhath Puja is Bihar's defining festival, and it is kept by people from Bihar no matter where in the world they have settled.
festivals.what: Chhath Puja is four days of fasting and sun worship in which no idol or statue is used at all. Worshippers stand waist deep in a river or pond to make offerings, first to the setting sun in the evening, and then, the next morning at dawn, to the rising sun.
festivals.who: Bihari households of every background celebrate Chhath Puja, both at home in Bihar and across the large community of Biharis living in Delhi, Mumbai, and other countries. Many of them travel all the way back home just for this festival.
festivals.when: The festival lasts four days, starting on the sixth day of the waxing fortnight of the month of Kartik, which begins six days after Diwali, in October or November. A smaller version of Chhath is also kept in spring, during the month of Chaitra.
festivals.origin: Worshipping the sun in this way is an old practice, recorded in various forms across the Gangetic plain. But it is Bihar's own four day version of Chhath that has come to define the state's festival calendar more than any other celebration.
festivals.signifies: Chhath Puja shows gratitude directly to the sun itself, with no statue or image standing in for it. The fast is so strict that the self-discipline it takes is treated as an offering all on its own.
festivals.beliefs: The vrat, or fast, is often taken on behalf of the wellbeing of a whole family. Once someone begins the fast, it is considered binding, and people avoid breaking it even when it costs them real physical hardship.
festivals.celebrate: On the first main day, people fast for a full day without even drinking water. The following evening, they make sandhya arghya, offerings to the setting sun, while standing in a river. The next dawn, they make usha arghya, offerings to the rising sun. Thekua, a type of fried sweet, and fruit are offered in bamboo baskets called soop. In the days before the festival, whole neighborhoods work together to clean and light up the riverbanks and ghats.
festivals.local: Patna prepares its Ganga riverbank steps for Chhath with a citywide effort, lighting them, cleaning them, and managing the crowds, on a scale that rivals anything the city does even for an election. This is because the ghats simply cannot be allowed to fail the fasting women on the evening of the arghya offering.
festivals.image: Women standing waist deep in the Ganga at sunset, offering arghya, Patna ghat

festivals.name: Sonepur Mela
festivals.aliases: Sonepur Cattle Fair, Harihar Kshetra Mela
festivals.reach: This fair is held at Sonepur, where the Ganga and Gandak rivers meet, and it draws traders from across the region.
festivals.what: Sonepur Mela is a month long fair held where the Ganga and Gandak rivers meet. Historically, it has been one of the largest cattle and livestock markets in all of Asia, and it is held alongside a bathing pilgrimage to the Harihar Nath temple.
festivals.who: Livestock traders from across North India and pilgrims heading to the Harihar Nath temple both attend. In recent decades, a steadily growing crowd of general visitors has also joined in, even as the animal trading part of the fair has shrunk because of new government regulations.
festivals.when: The fair lasts a month, beginning on Kartik Purnima, the full moon day of the month of Kartik, in November.
festivals.origin: The fair's roots are both commercial and religious at the same time, tied both to this ancient river meeting point and to old trade routes that used the rivers. Its huge size as a livestock market grew over many centuries, rather than starting from one single founding date.
festivals.signifies: This place shows a river meeting point doing two jobs at once, working as both a sacred bathing spot and the subcontinent's biggest animal market, without people seeing much contradiction between the two.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that bathing at the meeting point of the Ganga and Gandak rivers on Kartik Purnima carries special spiritual merit, separate from whatever else is happening at the fair around it.
festivals.celebrate: People take a bath at dawn at the river meeting point and worship at the Harihar Nath temple. Livestock, which historically included elephants, horses, and every kind of working animal, is bought and sold in open grounds. Folk performances, circus tents, and handicraft stalls fill out the rest of the month long fair.
festivals.local: Elephant sales, once the fair's most famous feature, are now so heavily regulated by the government that they have almost disappeared. Older visitors will tell you the fair is not what it used to be, even though the crowds attending it keep growing.
festivals.image: Livestock traders and animals at Sonepur Mela grounds, Gandak riverbank

festivals.name: Vivah Panchami
festivals.season: Fifth day of the bright fortnight of Margashirsha
festivals.reach: This festival is centered on Sitamarhi, which is believed to be Sita's birthplace, and it marks the anniversary of her wedding.
festivals.what: Vivah Panchami is a re-enactment of the wedding of Ram and Sita. It is staged with particular importance at Sitamarhi, which local tradition holds to be the birthplace of Sita.
festivals.who: Vaishnav pilgrims, who worship Vishnu and his forms, come from Bihar and neighboring Uttar Pradesh and Nepal. The wedding story also runs through Janakpur, which is just across the modern border in Nepal.
festivals.when: The festival falls on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Margashirsha, usually in late November or December.
festivals.origin: The account of the wedding in the Ramcharitmanas, a famous retelling of the Ramayana, underlies this observance across North India. Sitamarhi's claim to be Sita's birthplace gives its own local version of the festival particular importance, though this identification is based on tradition rather than on settled historical fact.
festivals.signifies: This festival treats the wedding less like a myth and more like a real local event that happened at a real address. It is still marked every year on its own specific calendar date.
festivals.beliefs: Pilgrims believe that visiting Sitamarhi on this day, or attending the linked celebrations in Janakpur across the border, carries the blessing of a marriage made according to dharma, meaning proper moral and religious order.
festivals.celebrate: A procession re-enacts the arrival of the wedding party. The Janaki temple in Sitamarhi is specially decorated, and darshan, the viewing of the deity, is extended for longer hours. Devotional singing continues through the night, and a large fair with stalls sets up around the temple.
festivals.local: The crowd at Sitamarhi's Vivah Panchami includes a steady flow of pilgrims crossing over from Janakpur on the Nepal side. The two towns treat the same wedding story as something they share, rather than as something to compete over.
festivals.image: Wedding procession re-enactment at the Janaki temple, Sitamarhi, night lights

festivals.name: Makar Sankranti
festivals.reach: Makar Sankranti is kept across the whole state, in both cities and villages.
festivals.what: Makar Sankranti is a winter festival marked by eating til, which means sesame, and khichdi, a rice and lentil dish, along with flying kites. It is timed to the moment the sun moves into the zodiac sign Makara, or Capricorn.
festivals.who: Households across Bihar celebrate Makar Sankranti regardless of caste or religious sect. It is one of the most evenly observed festivals in the whole state.
festivals.when: Makar Sankranti falls in mid-January. Because it is fixed to the solar calendar rather than the lunar one, it lands on roughly the same date every year.
festivals.origin: This is a sun-based farming festival recorded across North India under various different names. Bihar's particular combination of sesame sweets and khichdi is a regional version of a festival that is widely shared across the country.
festivals.signifies: Makar Sankranti marks a turning point for the sun, and in practical terms, it is also the point in winter after which the cold is believed to start easing up.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that eating sesame based sweets and khichdi on this day helps protect their health for the rest of the winter.
festivals.celebrate: People make tilkut and til laddu, both sesame based sweets, at home, and these are also sold fresh in markets for weeks around the date. Khichdi is cooked with seasonal vegetables, kites are flown from rooftops, and people take a ritual bath if a river is nearby.
festivals.local: Bihar's tilkut is a hard sesame and jaggery disc that is worked by hand until it hardens. It has its own dedicated markets in Gaya and Patna that only operate for this one season of the year.
festivals.image: Tilkut being hand worked at a market stall, Gaya, winter morning

festivals.name: Eid al-Fitr
festivals.reach: This festival is particularly significant in Kishanganj, Araria, Katihar, and the wider Seemanchal region, as well as across Patna and other cities.
festivals.what: Eid al-Fitr marks the close of Ramadan. It is kept across a state where Muslims make up a substantial share of the population, and in parts of Seemanchal they are actually the majority.
festivals.who: Muslim communities across Bihar celebrate Eid, most densely in the Seemanchal districts of Kishanganj, Katihar, Araria, and Purnia, as well as in the older city neighborhoods of Patna and Gaya.
festivals.when: Eid falls on the first day of the Islamic month of Shawwal, which moves earlier each year compared to the regular Gregorian calendar.
festivals.origin: Muslim settlement in Bihar goes back through the Delhi Sultanate and Mughal periods. Seemanchal's particularly large Muslim population is tied to later migration and to the region's location on the route toward Bengal.
festivals.signifies: Eid marks the end of the fast. In Seemanchal, it is not treated as a minority observance at all, but as a genuinely shared part of the whole region's civic calendar.
festivals.beliefs: Zakat al-Fitr, a form of charity, is given before the Eid prayer. The exact date is only confirmed the evening before, once the new moon has actually been sighted.
festivals.celebrate: People gather for Eid prayers at large open prayer grounds called Eidgahs in Kishanganj and Patna. At home, they eat sheer khurma, a sweet vermicelli dish, and biryani. They wear new clothes, and markets stay open late in the nights before Eid so people can shop.
festivals.local: In Kishanganj town, where Muslims are the clear majority, Eid works less like a minority festival and more like the district's own new year. The rest of the local calendar bends around it for the whole week.
festivals.image: Crowd gathered for Eid prayer at a large Eidgah, Kishanganj, morning

festivals.name: Buddha Purnima
festivals.reach: This festival is centered on Bodh Gaya, and it draws pilgrims from across the entire Buddhist world.
festivals.what: Buddha Purnima marks the anniversary of the Buddha's birth, enlightenment, and death, all of which are believed to have happened on the same full moon day. It is marked with particular importance at Bodh Gaya, where the Buddha is believed to have reached enlightenment under a tree that is a descendant of the original Bodhi tree.
festivals.who: Buddhist pilgrims and monks come from Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Japan, Tibet, and Bhutan, among many other countries, alongside Indian Buddhist communities.
festivals.when: The festival falls on the full moon day of the month of Vaisakh, in April or May.
festivals.origin: The Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya marks a site connected to the Buddha's enlightenment, going back to the earliest period of Buddhist tradition. The temple complex fell into decline for centuries but was restored to active worship in modern times, and it is now a UNESCO World Heritage site.
festivals.signifies: Bodh Gaya marks the point where the Buddha's teaching is believed to have actually begun. It is still treated as a living pilgrimage destination today, not just as a historical marker of something that happened long ago.
festivals.beliefs: Many pilgrims believe that praying and meditating under the Bodhi tree on this day carries special weight, because the tree has a direct lineage back to the very tree under which the Buddha's enlightenment is said to have happened.
festivals.celebrate: People chant and meditate throughout the day and into the night at the Mahabodhi Temple. Monks from different national traditions hold their own separate services at their own monasteries nearby.
