Lamps are lit around the temple compound, and in some years there is also a procession of monks.
festivals.local: Bodh Gaya's monasteries are built and run separately by nationality, with Thai, Japanese, Tibetan, Bhutanese, and other communities each running their own. This means that celebrating Buddha Purnima there involves walking between very different national styles of worship, all within just a few hundred meters of each other.
festivals.image: Monks and pilgrims meditating under lamps at the Mahabodhi Temple, Bodh Gaya, dusk

festivals.name: Christmas
festivals.reach: Christmas in Bihar is a small minority observance, strongest among Patna's older church congregations.
festivals.what: Christmas in Bihar is a modest but long standing celebration kept by the state's small Christian population. It is concentrated around colonial era churches in Patna, along with a scattering of mission institutions elsewhere in the state.
festivals.who: Catholic and Protestant congregations in Patna celebrate Christmas, along with mission schools and hospitals founded during the colonial period. These institutions still anchor small congregations in towns like Bettiah and Muzaffarpur.
festivals.when: Christmas falls on December 25, with church services held throughout Advent.
festivals.origin: Missions and colonial era churches established congregations starting in the nineteenth century. The Christian community here has stayed small compared to the rest of the state's population, but it has kept its institutions running continuously ever since.
festivals.signifies: Christmas marks the nativity, the birth of Jesus. It is kept by a community whose visibility in Bihar comes more from its schools and hospitals than from its actual numbers.
festivals.beliefs: For most families, midnight mass remains the central service of the day.
festivals.celebrate: In the week before Christmas, there are carol services. On Christmas Eve there is a midnight mass at Patna's older churches. Families share a meal together on the day, and churches and mission school buildings are decorated for the season.
festivals.local: Several of Patna's oldest schools can trace their roots back to these mission congregations. Because of this, the city's Christmas is felt more strongly through networks of former students than through any large present day Christian population.
festivals.image: Midnight mass at an old Patna church, candlelight, small congregation

name: Jharkhand
languages: Hindi (हिन्दी), Santali (ᱥᱟᱱᱛᱟᱲᱤ), and other tribal languages spoken among the state's significant Santal, Munda, and Oraon populations
tagline: Jharkhand is a plateau rich in forests and minerals. Here, the old Sarna tribal traditions and the Christianity brought by missionaries sit side by side.

festivals.name: Sarhul
festivals.season: Third day of the bright fortnight of Chaitra
festivals.reach: Sarhul is Jharkhand's main tribal new year festival, kept across the Munda, Oraon, and Ho communities.
festivals.what: Sarhul is a new year and nature festival built around the flowering of the sal tree. Village priests worship the sal tree grove before the year's farming season begins.
festivals.who: Sarhul is celebrated mainly by the Munda, Oraon, and Ho communities across Jharkhand, along with related celebrations among other tribal groups who follow the Sarna faith.
festivals.when: Sarhul falls on the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Chaitra, usually in March or April.
festivals.origin: Sarhul is an observance of the Sarna faith, which is the animist, nature-worshipping tradition of the region's tribal communities. It is tied to the flowering of the sal tree and existed before either the Hindu or Christian calendars arrived in the region.
festivals.signifies: Sarhul reads the renewal of the year directly from the forest itself. The blossoming of the sal tree is treated as the signal that gives permission for farming to begin.
festivals.beliefs: The sacred grove, called the sarna sthal, is believed to be the home of the village's spirits. The pahan, or village priest, is believed to be able to read the year's fortune from the rituals performed on this day.
festivals.celebrate: The pahan performs worship at the sarna sthal grove, offering sal flowers and a sacrificed fowl. Afterward, sal flowers are given out to households. For three days, people dance through the village to drums and flutes, and there is a ceremonial procession that, in Ranchi, has grown into a large public event.
festivals.local: Ranchi's Sarhul procession has grown into a citywide event, with vehicles decorated for days beforehand. But the ritual that gives the whole event its authority still happens first, quietly, when the pahan worships at a single sacred grove.
festivals.image: Pahan priest performing Sarhul rites at a sacred sal grove, Jharkhand village

festivals.name: Karma
festivals.season: Eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Bhadrapada
festivals.reach: Karma is kept across the Munda, Oraon, Ho, and Santal communities.
festivals.what: Karma is a festival centered on a branch of the karam tree. The branch is cut and planted at the center of the village, where it is worshipped as Karam Devta, the god of youth and strength, so that the season's crop will be fertile.
festivals.who: Munda, Oraon, Ho, and Santal communities celebrate Karma. Unmarried girls, who take care of the ritual jawa seedlings, play a particularly important role.
festivals.when: Karma falls on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhadrapada, in August or September.
festivals.origin: Karma is an old farming and tribal fertility observance, recorded across the wider Chota Nagpur plateau and not limited to Jharkhand alone. No one has documented exactly how old it is, only that it has continued for a very long time.
festivals.signifies: Karma asks directly for strength and fertility from a tree, which is treated as a living deity for as long as the festival lasts.
festivals.beliefs: The jawa seedlings, which are grown from nine kinds of grain in the days before the festival, are believed to forecast how good the coming harvest will be, based on how well they sprout.
festivals.celebrate: A karam branch is cut, carried into the village, and planted in ground that has been plastered with cow dung. Jawa seeds are sown in baskets and cared for over the seven to nine days before the festival. People dance the karma naach through the night around the planted branch, and afterward the branch is placed into a river or pond.
festivals.local: The girls tending the jawa baskets watch over them almost anxiously, because a poor sprout is read as a real warning about the coming season, not just a minor disappointment.
festivals.image: Karma naach dancers circling a planted karam branch at night, drums

festivals.name: Sohrai
festivals.season: The dark moon of Kartik, the day after Diwali
festivals.reach: Sohrai is kept across Santal and other tribal communities of Jharkhand.
festivals.what: Sohrai is a cattle and harvest festival. Women paint their houses with Sohrai murals, and cattle are washed, decorated, and worshipped as the animals that carried out the season's hard work.
festivals.who: Sohrai is celebrated mainly by Santal communities, with related observances among other tribal groups of the Chota Nagpur plateau.
festivals.when: Sohrai falls on Kartik Amavasya, the dark moon day that follows Diwali, in October or November.
festivals.origin: Sohrai wall painting is documented as a very old tradition. Some scholars trace the technique of using mineral pigments back to ancient rock art in the region. The festival itself marks the end of the harvest and gives thanks for the work of cattle.
festivals.signifies: Sohrai gives thanks to cattle and to the tools and animals that made the harvest possible. This thanks is expressed through art that is painted fresh on the house wall every single year, rather than being kept as one permanent object.
festivals.beliefs: The murals are believed to welcome the cattle and the harvest into a clean, prepared home. They are repainted each year rather than preserved, because this welcome is meant to be renewed annually.
festivals.celebrate: Houses are cleaned, and their walls are freshly painted with Sohrai murals using natural earth pigments. Cattle are bathed, their horns are painted, and they are given garlands. A procession of decorated animals moves through the village, and in the evening, everyone shares a feast.
festivals.local: In recent decades, Sohrai painting has also moved from house walls onto paper and canvas, made for buyers from outside the region. But the version that matters locally is still the one painted on a mud wall each year, which is then simply left to weather away over time.
festivals.image: Woman painting Sohrai mural on a mud house wall, Jharkhand village, earth pigments

festivals.name: Tusu Parab
festivals.season: Last day of Poush, at Makar Sankranti
festivals.reach: Tusu Parab is concentrated among Kurmi communities in Jharkhand's southeastern belt, around Bundu, Tamar, and Raidih.
festivals.what: Tusu Parab is a month long observance kept mainly by unmarried girls. They tend a small shrine to the goddess Tusu throughout the month of Poush, and on the last day, they place a decorated bamboo structure called the choudal into a river.
festivals.who: Kurmi communities of Jharkhand's southeastern districts celebrate Tusu Parab, and it is also shared with neighboring parts of West Bengal and Odisha.
festivals.when: The observance runs through the month of Poush, closing on its very last day, which falls at the same time as Makar Sankranti in mid-January.
festivals.origin: Tusu Parab is a regional harvest and folk goddess tradition from the Chota Nagpur region and the neighboring borderlands of Bengal and Odisha. It has been kept alive mainly through a spoken and sung collection of Tusu songs, rather than through any written religious text.
festivals.signifies: Tusu Parab is a harvest thanksgiving carried almost entirely by young unmarried women. They compose and sing brand new Tusu songs every year as part of the observance.
festivals.beliefs: Tusu is believed to be a form of the goddess, and her presence throughout the month is believed to bring prosperity. Her departure on the day the choudal is immersed in the river is treated as a real goodbye, and it is sung about with real sadness.
festivals.celebrate: A small clay or symbolic image of Tusu is cared for daily throughout the month of Poush, along with songs composed just for that year. A decorated bamboo and paper structure called the choudal is built for the final day. Processions carry the choudal to a river or pond, and it is immersed there while more singing continues. Afterward, people share gur pitha and other sweets.
festivals.local: The Tusu songs are brand new compositions every year, and they often deal with local complaints and gossip just as much as with devotion. Because of this, someone experienced with the tradition can almost date a village's Tusu season the way they would read a diary.
festivals.image: Girls carrying a decorated choudal structure to the riverbank at Tusu Parab, dusk

festivals.name: Shravani Mela
festivals.reach: This festival is centered on the Baidyanath temple in Deoghar, one of the twelve Jyotirlingas, and it draws pilgrims from Bihar, West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh, and Nepal.
festivals.what: Shravani Mela is a month long pilgrimage in which pilgrims called kanwariyas walk roughly a hundred kilometers, from Sultanganj on the Ganga river to the Baidyanath temple at Deoghar. They carry river water on a shoulder pole the whole way, in order to pour it over the shrine's lingam, a symbol of the god Shiva.
festivals.who: The kanwariyas are mostly young men, though not only men, from Bihar, West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh, and Nepal, and they walk the route in organized groups.
festivals.when: The pilgrimage takes place over the entire month of Shravan, from July to August.
festivals.origin: Baidyanath is one of the twelve Jyotirlingas of Shiva, sacred shrines representing him. The walk from Sultanganj to Deoghar is a long documented regional pilgrimage. Its current scale, with hundreds of thousands of pilgrims and heavy support from the state government, has grown a great deal in recent decades.
festivals.signifies: Shravani Mela offers water to Shiva at a real physical cost to the pilgrims. The long distance they walk is treated as part of the offering itself, not just something incidental along the way.
festivals.beliefs: The jalabhishek, the act of pouring the carried Ganga water over the lingam, is believed to bring more spiritual merit because of the effort of the long walk that came before it.
festivals.celebrate: Kanwariyas walk the route from Sultanganj to Deoghar in decorated groups, chanting Bol Bam. Villages and organizations set up roadside camps and free food stalls along the entire route. The jalabhishek offering is performed at the Baidyanath temple around the clock throughout the month, and the state government runs a heavy security and medical operation for the whole time.
festivals.local: For the whole month, the hundred kilometer route is lined by ordinary households who set up free water and food stops for passing kanwariyas. This informal chain of hospitality is something the pilgrimage could not function without.
festivals.image: Kanwariyas walking the Sultanganj to Deoghar road at dawn, shoulder poles, orange clothing

festivals.name: Eid al-Fitr
festivals.reach: Eid al-Fitr is significant in Ranchi, Jamshedpur, Palamu, and Sahibganj.
festivals.what: Eid al-Fitr marks the close of Ramadan. It is kept by a Muslim population settled across Jharkhand's cities and its northern districts, which border Bihar and West Bengal.
festivals.who: Muslim communities celebrate Eid, concentrated in Ranchi, Jamshedpur, Palamu, Sahibganj, and Pakur.
festivals.when: Eid falls on the first day of the Islamic month of Shawwal, which moves earlier each year compared to the regular Gregorian calendar.
festivals.origin: Muslim settlement in the region grew through trade, and from the colonial period onward, through labor migration into the coal and steel towns that industrialized the Chota Nagpur plateau.
festivals.signifies: Eid marks the end of the fast. In industrial towns like Jamshedpur, it is a shared holiday across a workforce that is genuinely made up of people from many different backgrounds.
festivals.beliefs: As elsewhere, zakat al-Fitr, a form of charity, is given before the Eid prayer.
festivals.celebrate: People gather for Eid prayers at large open prayer grounds called Eidgahs in Ranchi and Jamshedpur. At home, they eat sheer khurma, a sweet vermicelli dish, and biryani. They wear new clothes and spend the day visiting family and friends.
festivals.local: Jamshedpur's Eid crowds are made up heavily of a steel town workforce recruited from far outside Jharkhand. Because of this, the festival there has a distinctly mixed, multi-regional character, shaped by workers who came from many different places.
festivals.image: Eid prayer at a large Eidgah, Jamshedpur, steel town skyline behind

festivals.name: Christmas
festivals.reach: Christmas is particularly significant among Ranchi's Munda and Oraon Christian communities, which form one of India's oldest tribal Christian populations.
festivals.what: This Christmas is kept by one of India's oldest tribal Christian communities. It grew out of German Lutheran mission work, and later Anglican and Catholic mission work, among Munda and Oraon families around Ranchi starting in the mid-nineteenth century.
festivals.who: Munda and Oraon Christian congregations, concentrated around Ranchi, celebrate Christmas, along with Kharia, Ho, and other tribal Christian communities elsewhere in the state.
festivals.when: Christmas falls on December 25, with church services held throughout Advent.
festivals.origin: German Lutheran missionaries arrived in Chota Nagpur in 1845 and baptized their first Oraon and Munda converts within just a few years. Anglican and Catholic missions followed after that, and by the early twentieth century, tribal Christians in the Ranchi area numbered in the tens of thousands.
festivals.signifies: Christmas marks the nativity, the birth of Jesus. Locally, the history of conversion to Christianity is now old enough that people treat it as part of their heritage, rather than as some recent change.
festivals.beliefs: Midnight mass remains central to the day. It is sung partly in the Mundari, Kurukh, or Sadri languages, alongside Hindi and English.
festivals.celebrate: In December, carol groups sing in tribal languages as they move between village houses. There is a midnight mass at Ranchi's older churches, including the Gossner Lutheran and Catholic cathedrals. People wear new clothes and share a feast together on the day.
festivals.local: Congregations that trace their roots back to the 1845 mission still sing some carols in the Mundari and Kurukh languages. Because of this, a Christmas celebration in the Ranchi area can sound just as much like a tribal festival as a church one.
festivals.image: Carol singers in tribal dress outside a church, Ranchi, December evening

name: Odisha
tagline: Odisha is a coastal region that was once home to old kingdoms. Even today, the calendar of one single temple, the Jagannath temple in Puri, still sets the rhythm for festivals across the whole state.

festivals.name: Rath Yatra
festivals.season: Second day of the bright fortnight of Ashadha
festivals.reach: Rath Yatra is Puri's defining festival. It is watched by people everywhere and copied in similar celebrations across the Hindu world.
festivals.what: During Rath Yatra, the deities Jagannath, Balabhadra, and Subhadra are taken out of the Jagannath temple. They are placed on three newly built wooden chariots and pulled roughly three kilometers down Puri's main road, called the Bada Danda, to the Gundicha temple. They stay there for a while before making the return journey.
festivals.who: Puri's temple establishment and its hereditary servitors take part. These servitors number in the thousands, and each one holds a specific job in the festival that has been passed down in their family for generations. Pilgrims also come from across India and from Hindu communities around the world.
festivals.when: Rath Yatra falls on the second day of the bright fortnight of the month of Ashadha, in June or July. The return journey, called Bahuda Yatra, happens about a week later.
festivals.origin: The worship of Jagannath at Puri, and its chariot festival, have been documented since medieval times. The huge scale of the festival, and the fact that the deities' wooden forms look deliberately unfinished, are both treated as central and still not fully explained parts of an old and layered tradition.
festivals.signifies: Rath Yatra shows the god leaving his inner sanctuary so that anyone in the crowd who can reach a rope can help pull his chariot. For the length of the pull, the deity and the devotees share the very same road.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that pulling the ropes of the chariots brings spiritual merit no matter what caste or background a person comes from. This equal treatment of everyone is something the festival is specifically known for.
festivals.celebrate: New chariots are built completely from scratch every single year, following fixed specifications. The Pahandi ceremony carries the deities from the temple to the chariots. Huge crowds then pull the chariots down the Bada Danda road. The deities stay for a while at the Gundicha temple, and about a week later, the chariots are pulled back in the return journey called Bahuda Yatra.
festivals.local: The three chariots, named Nandighosha, Taladhwaja, and Darpadalana, are entirely rebuilt every year from fresh wood by specific families of carpenters whose job has been passed down for generations. Once the festival ends, the chariots are broken up for scrap wood or kept as relics, rather than being saved to use again next year.
festivals.image: Jagannath rath yatra chariots pulled down Puri's Bada Danda, crowd hauling ropes

festivals.name: Durga Puja
festivals.reach: Durga Puja is celebrated across the state, and Cuttack's silver filigree idols are a particular signature of the Odisha celebration.
festivals.what: Durga Puja is five days of worshipping the goddess, kept across Odisha with the same intensity as in neighboring Bengal. In Odisha, it is distinguished by Cuttack's tradition of dressing the idol in fine sterling silver filigree work, called chandi medha.
festivals.who: Odia Hindu households across the state celebrate Durga Puja. In Cuttack specifically, the city's silver filigree artisans are heavily involved, since much of their whole year revolves around this one commission.
festivals.when: Durga Puja is celebrated during the bright fortnight of the month of Ashwin, in September or October, running from the sixth day, Shashthi, to the tenth day, Dashami.
festivals.origin: Worshipping the goddess Durga in autumn is an old and widespread tradition across eastern India. Cuttack's silver filigree idol tradition is a distinct local addition, built on top of the city's long standing tarakasi silverwork craft.
festivals.signifies: Just like in Bengal, the goddess's visit is understood as a homecoming. Cuttack's version of the festival puts particular civic pride in the fine craftsmanship of how the goddess appears.
festivals.beliefs: At the end of the festival, the clay images of the goddess are placed into a river or pond. But the silver ornaments are removed first and kept to be used again, since the metalwork, unlike the clay, is not meant to be given up for good.
festivals.celebrate: People go pandal hopping through the nights, visiting different decorated pandals, or temporary shrines, set up around the city. Cuttack's chandi medha pandals display silver filigree work on both the idol and its backdrop. Sandhi Puja is performed at the exact junction between the eighth and ninth days of the festival, and on the tenth day, Dashami, processions carry the idols to the Mahanadi river and other rivers for immersion.
festivals.local: Cuttack's silver filigree pandals are commissioned a full year ahead of time. The artisans, who work together in a craft community with roots going back generations, treat the Puja deadline as the single biggest test of their trade all year.
festivals.image: Silver filigree Durga idol in a Cuttack pandal, chandi medha work, night lights

festivals.name: Raja Parba
festivals.season: Four days at the start of the month of Mithuna
festivals.reach: Raja Parba is celebrated across the state, especially in rural Odisha.
festivals.what: Raja Parba is a four day festival that honors the fertility of the earth. Locally, it is understood as the earth goddess Bhudevi going through her own menstrual cycle. During these four days, all ploughing, digging, and sowing stops completely.
festivals.who: Odia households across the state celebrate Raja Parba. Young and unmarried women are given a particularly important role in how it is observed.
festivals.when: Raja Parba lasts four days, beginning the day before Mithuna Sankranti in mid-June, timed to the start of the monsoon season.
festivals.origin: The festival's name comes from the Sanskrit word rajas, meaning menstruation. It is an old rural custom tied to the arrival of the monsoon, rather than coming from any single religious text.
festivals.signifies: Raja Parba treats menstruation as a fertility rite for the land itself. The rest that the earth is given during these days is also extended, for the length of the festival, to women themselves.
festivals.beliefs: Farm work is avoided during the festival because the earth is believed to be resting. The grinding stone, which stands in for the earth goddess Bhudevi, is ceremonially bathed on the closing day.
festivals.celebrate: Women and girls dress in new clothes and wear alta, a red dye, on their hands and feet, while resting from household chores. Swings are hung from trees for the days of the festival. Poda pitha, a baked rice cake, is prepared specifically for Raja. On the fourth day, Vasumati Snana takes place, which is the ceremonial bathing of the grinding stone.
festivals.local: Most girls treat the swing hung from a tree during these few days as the real centerpiece of the festival. A village's Raja celebration is judged partly by how many good trees it can offer for swinging.
festivals.image: Girls on a rope swing hung from a tree during Raja Parba, village courtyard

festivals.name: Nuakhai
festivals.season: Fifth day of the bright fortnight of Bhadrapada
festivals.reach: Nuakhai is western Odisha's own new rice festival, strongest in Sambalpur, Bargarh, Bolangir, and Kalahandi.
festivals.what: Nuakhai is a festival specific to western Odisha, celebrating the very first of the new rice crop. The newly harvested rice is offered to the goddess Samaleswari before anyone in the household is allowed to eat it.
festivals.who: Households across the western Odisha districts of Sambalpur, Bargarh, Jharsuguda, Bolangir, Kalahandi, Nuapada, and Sundargarh celebrate Nuakhai. For these communities, it works as the region's own version of a new year.
festivals.when: Nuakhai falls on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhadrapada, in August or September.
festivals.origin: Nuakhai is a regional harvest custom from western Odisha's rice growing districts, offered to Samaleswari as the presiding fertility goddess. Its timing is fixed to when the rice actually ripens, rather than to any wider calendar followed across all of India.
festivals.signifies: Nuakhai treats the new rice as something that belongs to the goddess first. It only belongs to the household after that offering has been properly made.
festivals.beliefs: Eating the new rice before the Nuakhai offering is considered a real breach of the proper order of things, not just a matter of bad manners.
festivals.celebrate: New rice is offered at the Samaleswari temple in Sambalpur and at local shrines elsewhere. Afterward, families share a meal built around the new rice. People exchange Nuakhai Juhar greetings with relatives and elders, and this is often the biggest family gathering of the whole year. Folk dance and music continue over the following days.
festivals.local: Nuakhai Juhar has become the occasion that western Odisha's diaspora treats as their must-attend homecoming, on a scale similar to how Durga Puja works for Bengalis. It is distinct from Odisha's own coastal festival calendar, and it sometimes even rivals it.
festivals.image: New rice offering at the Samaleswari temple, Sambalpur, Nuakhai morning

festivals.name: Bali Yatra
festivals.reach: Bali Yatra is held on the banks of the Mahanadi river in Cuttack, and it is one of Asia's largest open air trade fairs.
festivals.what: Bali Yatra is a riverside fair in Cuttack that remembers the old sea trade of Odia sailors, called sadhabas, to Southeast Asia. It is marked by the ritual of floating small boats on the Mahanadi river.
festivals.who: The whole city of Cuttack generally takes part, along with traders who set up stalls for the entire run of the fair.
festivals.when: The fair starts on the full moon day of the month of Kartik, in November, and continues for about a week and a half.
festivals.origin: The sadhabas' historic voyages to Bali, Java, Sumatra, and other Southeast Asian ports are believed to have begun around Kartik Purnima, the time when the monsoon eased up and the seas became safe to sail. The modern fair remembers that old trade rather than actually continuing it today.
festivals.signifies: Bali Yatra keeps alive Odisha's memory of itself as a seafaring, coastal state, through ritual and through this fair, long after the actual sea voyages themselves came to an end.
festivals.beliefs: Floating a small boat on the river is believed to honor the journeys the sadhabas once made, and it is also believed to carry along with it a wish for prosperity.
festivals.celebrate: In a ritual called Boita Bandana, women float small paper or sholapith boats carrying lit lamps on the Mahanadi river at dawn. A sprawling trade fair runs along the riverbank, selling everything from handicrafts to household goods, and cultural performances take place throughout the fair.
festivals.local: Bali Yatra's name comes from a specific historical claim, that Odia sailors actually reached the island of Bali itself. This link is still visible today, since modern Bali has place names and temple carvings that seem to point back to this connection.
festivals.image: Women floating lit paper boats on the Mahanadi at dawn, Bali Yatra, Cuttack

festivals.name: Eid al-Fitr
festivals.reach: Eid al-Fitr is concentrated in Cuttack, Balasore, and coastal areas with older Muslim trading settlements.
festivals.what: Eid al-Fitr marks the close of Ramadan. It is kept by a Muslim population concentrated in Cuttack's old town and in Balasore, both places that have historical ties to coastal and river trade.
festivals.who: Muslim communities settled through Cuttack, Balasore, and other coastal trading towns celebrate Eid. Overall, they make up a small share of the state's population.
festivals.when: Eid falls on the first day of the Islamic month of Shawwal, which moves earlier each year compared to the regular Gregorian calendar.
festivals.origin: Muslim traders and administrators settled in coastal Odisha starting in the medieval period. Their presence is tied to the region's port trade and to periods when the area was governed under Mughal and Bengal Sultanate rule.
festivals.signifies: Eid marks the end of the fast. It is celebrated at a fairly modest scale within Odisha's largely Hindu festival calendar.
festivals.beliefs: As elsewhere, zakat al-Fitr, a form of charity, is given before the Eid prayer.
festivals.celebrate: People gather for Eid prayers at Cuttack's older mosques and at open prayer grounds called Eidgahs elsewhere. At home, they eat sheer khurma, a sweet vermicelli dish, and biryani. They wear new clothes and spend the day visiting family and friends.
festivals.local: Cuttack's old town mosques sit within walking distance of the city's most famous Durga Puja pandals. Residents point to this closeness as evidence of how long the Muslim and Hindu communities have shared the very same streets.
festivals.image: Eid prayer at an old Cuttack mosque, morning crowd

festivals.name: Christmas
festivals.reach: Christmas is a minority observance kept across scattered congregations, with a notable concentration in tribal Kandhamal district.
festivals.what: Christmas in Odisha is kept by the state's small Christian population. This population is spread between older congregations along the coast and, more distinctively, tribal converts in interior districts like Kandhamal.
festivals.who: Catholic and Protestant congregations along the coast celebrate Christmas, along with Kandha and Pana Christian communities in Kandhamal and neighboring districts.
festivals.when: Christmas falls on December 25, with church services held throughout Advent.
festivals.origin: Coastal Christian congregations date back to missions from the era of European trade. Kandhamal's tribal Christian community grew through mission work among Kandha and Pana communities during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. This history has, at times, also been a source of local tension.
festivals.signifies: Christmas marks the nativity, the birth of Jesus. It is kept by a minority community whose presence in interior Odisha is more recent, and in some places more contested, than the older congregations along the coast.
festivals.beliefs: For most families who are able to reach a church, midnight mass remains the central service of the day.
festivals.celebrate: In the week before Christmas, there are carol services. There is a midnight mass, and on the day itself, people wear new clothes and share a family meal. Churches are decorated for the season, in both coastal parishes and interior villages in Kandhamal.
festivals.local: Kandhamal's Christian villages keep Christmas alongside their tribal Kandha customs, rather than replacing those customs with it. This pairing mirrors how tribal Christianity has taken root in other parts of central and eastern India as well.
festivals.image: Christmas carol service at a small church in Kandhamal, tribal congregation

name: Karnataka
tagline: Karnataka is a state with many different landscapes and cultures. It has a grand palace city called Mysuru, a northern region shaped by centuries of Deccan Muslim rulers, and a coast where villagers race buffaloes through muddy rice fields.

festivals.name: Ugadi
festivals.reach: Celebrated widely across the state.
festivals.what: Ugadi is the Kannada new year. People start the day by eating a special dish called Bevu Bella, made mainly from neem leaves and jaggery. Across the wider Deccan region, other communities eat a very similar six-taste dish on their own new year, just under different names.
festivals.who: Kannada-speaking families all across Karnataka celebrate Ugadi. Kannadiga communities living in Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, and other places far from home celebrate it too.
festivals.when: Ugadi falls on the first day of the Hindu month of Chaitra, based on a calendar that follows both the moon and the sun. This usually lands in late March or early April.
festivals.origin: Ugadi follows the same lunisolar calendar (a calendar based on both the moon and the sun) used across the whole southern Deccan region. Nobody can point to one single moment when the festival started. Instead, its traditions, including the Bevu Bella dish and the reading of the yearly almanac called the panchangam, grew and changed slowly over many centuries.
festivals.signifies: Ugadi starts the new year with the idea that bitter and sweet things in life come together at the same time, not one after the other.
festivals.beliefs: Many families treat the panchangam reading, done at temples and at home, as a real prediction of what the coming year will bring, not just a tradition to go through. Because of this, a lot of households wait to hear the reading before they make important plans.
festivals.celebrate: Families hang mango leaves in decorative strings called toranas above their doorways. They draw patterns called rangoli using rice flour at the entrance to their homes. They mix and eat Bevu Bella first thing in the morning, wear new clothes, and listen to the panchangam reading at temples throughout the morning.
festivals.local: Kannadiga families often argue about how much jaggery should go into the Bevu Bella mix. If a family makes theirs too sweet, people joke that the household is not being honest about facing the hard parts of the year ahead.
festivals.image: Bevu Bella being mixed in a steel bowl on a doorstep, mango leaf torana overhead

festivals.name: Sankranti
festivals.reach: Celebrated widely, strongest in the northern and central farming districts.
festivals.what: Sankranti is a harvest festival built around a tradition called Ellu Birodhu. Neighbors and relatives exchange a mix of sesame seeds, jaggery, groundnuts, and dried coconut. When people hand over the mix, they say the words "ellu bella thindu, olle maathu adu," which means "eat this and speak only good words."
festivals.who: Farming families across Karnataka celebrate Sankranti. The custom of exchanging the ellu mix is strongest among Kannadiga communities and communities influenced by Marathi culture in the north of the state.
festivals.when: Sankranti happens in mid-January, on the day the sun moves into the zodiac sign of Makara. This date is fixed by the solar calendar, so it falls on the same day each year.
festivals.origin: This festival is a solar and farming celebration that has been recorded across the Deccan region for centuries. The Ellu Birodhu exchange is a custom that belongs specifically to Kannada-speaking areas. It is not exactly the same as similar customs in neighboring Andhra Pradesh or Telangana, even though those regions also celebrate a harvest festival around this time.
festivals.signifies: Sankranti marks the sun beginning to move northward. It also stands for a deliberate effort to smooth over any arguments or bad feelings that built up between households during the year.
festivals.beliefs: The kind words people say while handing over the ellu mix are taken seriously and are expected to hold true for the whole year. If someone refuses to accept the mix, or refuses to say the phrase back, it is seen as a real insult.
festivals.celebrate: People hand out Ellu Birodhu packets of sesame and jaggery door to door. Homes are decorated with sugarcane and small haystacks. People fly kites in Bengaluru and towns in the north. In rural areas, farmers wash and parade their cattle in a ritual called Kichchu Haisodu.
festivals.local: In North Karnataka, households quietly keep track of whose ellu mix has the best balance of groundnuts to jaggery, and they are not shy about saying so out loud.
festivals.image: Ellu Birodhu packets of sesame and jaggery being handed over at a doorway

festivals.name: Mysuru Dasara
festivals.reach: Celebrated as the state festival, drawing visitors from across India.
festivals.what: Mysuru Dasara lasts ten nights and ends with a grand procession called the Jamboo Savari. During this procession, a statue of the goddess Chamundeshwari is carried through the city of Mysuru on the Golden Howdah, a gold-plated seat that weighs about eighty kilograms and sits on top of a lead elephant.
festivals.who: The city of Mysuru celebrates this festival, and because the state government sponsors it, the whole of Karnataka takes part in some way. The royal palace and the Wadiyar family, who used to rule Mysore, remain central to the ceremony.
festivals.when: Mysuru Dasara takes place over the ten nights of Sharad Navaratri, in September or October, and ends on the day called Vijayadashami.
festivals.origin: The Wadiyar kings of Mysore turned Dasara into an official royal state festival starting in the seventeenth century. The Golden Howdah itself, the special seat used in the procession, was finished during the reign of Krishnaraja Wadiyar IV in the early twentieth century.
festivals.signifies: The festival celebrates the goddess's victory over a demon named Mahishasura, and some say the city of Mysuru is even named after this demon. The festival also shows a monarchy's power and authority, made visible once a year through a public procession instead of through everyday rule.
festivals.beliefs: Until 1969, the reigning king from the Wadiyar family personally rode on the howdah during the procession. Since then, the howdah has carried only the goddess's statue. Locally, people accept this change as simply the correct way to do things now, not as something lesser than before.
festivals.celebrate: The Mysuru Palace is lit up with almost a hundred thousand light bulbs every night. There is a royal court gathering called durbar at the palace each day. The Jamboo Savari procession includes elephants, dance groups, and decorated floats on Vijayadashami, and the festival closes after dark with a torchlight parade called Panjina Kavayathu.
festivals.local: People in Mysuru can name the lead elephant of any given year the way people in other cities might name their mayor. If a different elephant is chosen to carry the howdah, it becomes local news for weeks before the festival even starts.
festivals.image: Mysuru palace illuminated at night during Dasara, golden howdah procession forming below

festivals.name: Bengaluru Karaga
festivals.reach: A Bengaluru city festival, drawn from and organised by the Thigala community.
festivals.what: The Bengaluru Karaga is a nine-night festival held at the Dharmaraya Swamy temple. During the festival, a priest dresses as a woman and carries a decorated pot called the karaga on his head. He walks through the old city at night while attendants carrying swords escort him.
festivals.who: The Thigala community organizes this festival because they are the temple's traditional caretakers. The wider neighborhoods of old Bengaluru that the procession passes through are also part of the celebration.
festivals.when: The festival lasts nine nights and ends on the full moon of the Hindu month of Chaitra, which falls in March or April, around the same time as Ugadi.
festivals.origin: State archaeologists believe the Dharmaraya Swamy temple, which is dedicated to the five Pandava brothers and to Draupadi from the epic Mahabharata, is roughly eight hundred years old. The Thigala community has kept the karaga tradition going as a duty passed down through generations at the temple.
festivals.signifies: According to belief, Draupadi promised to return every year to the warriors she is said to have created to protect her. The festival stands for her continued presence in the city.
festivals.beliefs: People believe the priest who carries the karaga becomes possessed by the goddess for the whole night. He keeps his eyes closed the entire time he walks the route through the city.
festivals.celebrate: The karaga is carried quickly through narrow lanes, surrounded by Veeragase dancers and people performing sword displays. Every year, the procession makes a stop at the tomb of an eighteenth-century Muslim saint. Finally, before dawn, the pot is immersed in water.
festivals.local: The stop at the Muslim saint's tomb, called a dargah, is not a recent addition just for show. In old Bengaluru, this pause is treated as one of the fixed and essential points along the route that cannot be skipped.
festivals.image: Karaga bearer carrying the flower-covered pot through a lit night lane, swordsmen alongside

festivals.name: Kambala
festivals.reach: Concentrated in coastal Karnataka, Dakshina Kannada and Udupi districts.
festivals.what: Kambala is a buffalo race held through flooded paddy fields. A handler stands on a wooden plank behind a pair of buffaloes and drives them down a muddy course. Judges time the race and score it based on speed and how well the handler and buffaloes perform.
festivals.who: Tuluva landowning families and village Kambala committees along the coast organize this event. Over forty races are run across a season, put on by roughly eighteen local associations.
festivals.when: The Kambala season runs from November to March, after the rice harvest is finished and the paddy fields used as race tracks are empty.
festivals.origin: Kambala is generally believed to be a tradition from the Tulunadu region going back several centuries. Historically, local landlords sponsored the races as a way to show off the wealth their harvest had brought, rather than any single temple organizing it.
festivals.signifies: Kambala represents a landowner's duty to publicly celebrate a good harvest, honoring the very animals that helped produce it.
festivals.beliefs: The buffaloes used in Kambala are not treated as ordinary farm animals just for the day. Well-regarded racing pairs are given names, fed special food, and their handlers can become locally famous, sometimes for longer than any single race is remembered.
festivals.celebrate: Pairs of buffaloes race down a muddy, waterlogged track at speeds that can reach fifty kilometres an hour. Part of the excitement comes from watching the handler keep his balance on the plank behind them. At the biggest events, crowds of several thousand people come to watch.
festivals.local: A serious Kambala fan watches the handler's footwork on the plank just as closely as the buffaloes' speed, because if the handler falls, the run does not count no matter how fast the buffaloes ran.
festivals.image: Handler balanced on a plank behind racing buffaloes through a muddy paddy track

festivals.name: Ganesha Chaturthi
festivals.reach: Celebrated widely across the state, in homes and neighbourhood pandals.
festivals.what: This festival is a two-day celebration. It begins with Gowri Habba, honoring the goddess Gowri, and continues the next day with Ganesha Chaturthi, when clay statues of her son, the god Ganesha, are set up in homes and in public tents called pandals.
festivals.who: Hindu families across the state celebrate this festival at home. In Bengaluru and Mangaluru, neighborhood associations organize larger public celebrations.
festivals.when: Ganesha Chaturthi falls on the fourth day of the bright half of the Hindu month of Bhadrapada, which is in August or September.
festivals.origin: Worshipping Ganesha at home on this day is a very old and widespread tradition across the Deccan region. The larger public pandal celebrations grew during the twentieth century, alongside similar big public festivals happening in Maharashtra at the same time.
festivals.signifies: The festival's order matters. The invitation to celebrate goes first to the mother, Gowri, and only the next day to her son, Ganesha. Kannadiga households are careful to keep this order correct.
festivals.beliefs: When the clay idol is immersed in water at the end, a ritual called Visarjana, people believe this sends the deity back home rather than simply throwing away an object. This is why even small statues kept at home are immersed with some ceremony and respect.
festivals.celebrate: Families buy clay statues of Gowri and Ganesha weeks ahead of time. They steam traditional foods called kadubu and modaka at home. They perform prayers, called puja, over one to three days, and the festival ends with processions that carry the idols to lakes and water tanks for immersion.
festivals.local: Bengaluru's lakes suffer real environmental damage every year from idol immersion. This creates a genuine tension between tradition and the health of the city's already struggling lakes, and people publicly argue about the issue every single year.
festivals.image: Household Ganesha idol on a decorated platform, kadubu offerings in front, oil lamps lit

festivals.name: Ramzan & Eid al-Fitr
festivals.season: Ninth month of the Hijri calendar
festivals.reach: Particularly significant in Kalaburagi, Bidar, Vijayapura and Bengaluru's older Muslim quarters.
festivals.what: This is a month of fasting from dawn to dusk, which ends with the celebration of Eid al-Fitr. It is observed with special importance in the old Deccan towns of Kalaburagi and Bidar, which were once the capitals of the Bahmani and Barid Shahi sultanates, and in Vijayapura, the former capital of the Adil Shahi rulers.
festivals.who: Karnataka's Muslim communities celebrate this festival. They are especially concentrated in the Kalyana-Karnataka region and in the older neighborhoods of Bengaluru and Mysuru.
festivals.when: This festival happens during the ninth month of the Islamic Hijri calendar. Because this calendar follows the moon, the dates shift about eleven days earlier each year compared to our regular calendar.
festivals.origin: The practice of fasting comes from the Qur'an, the Islamic holy book. The way it is celebrated in this region was shaped by the Bahmani, Barid Shahi, and Adil Shahi royal courts, whose old buildings and monuments still stand today in Bidar, Kalaburagi, and Vijayapura.
festivals.signifies: The festival stands for self-control and for the duty to give charity to those in need. In these towns, it also represents a connection to a Deccan Muslim political history that stretches back several centuries.
festivals.beliefs: People believe the last ten nights of the fasting month are the most important. During this time, they look for a special night called Laylat al-Qadr, considered the holiest night of the year.
festivals.celebrate: Before dawn, families eat a meal called sehri. At sunset, they break their fast with a meal called iftar, which includes dates and regional Deccani dishes. At night, people gather for special prayers called taraweeh. Before Eid, people give charity called Zakat and Fitra. On the morning of Eid, large crowds gather for prayers at the big outdoor prayer grounds, called Idgahs, in Bidar, Kalaburagi, and Bengaluru.
festivals.local: During Ramzan, Bidar's food stalls sell their own distinct collection of Deccani sweets, developed in the town's own royal kitchens from the sultanate era. These sweets are not the same as the sweets found in Hyderabad, even though both places share the general "Deccani" food label.
festivals.image: Iftar spread at sunset near a Bahmani-era mosque courtyard, Kalaburagi

festivals.name: Christmas
festivals.reach: Particularly significant among the Konkani Catholic community of coastal Karnataka.
festivals.what: Christmas along the coast of Karnataka centers on the old Konkani Catholic churches, called parishes, in Mangaluru. These churches were built before British rule began, and the community has its own history of migrating from Goa.
festivals.who: Konkani-speaking Catholic families in the districts of Dakshina Kannada and Udupi celebrate Christmas, along with smaller Protestant and Catholic groups in Bengaluru.
festivals.when: Christmas is celebrated on 25 December. Before that, there is an Advent season filled with carol singing and preparations for midnight church services.
festivals.origin: Konkani Catholic families settled in Mangaluru mostly starting in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, when they migrated from Goa to escape political and religious troubles under Portuguese rule there. Over time, this community built its own network of parish churches, separate from the churches that missionaries built later in other parts of the state.
festivals.signifies: Christmas celebrates the birth of Jesus. For Mangaluru's Konkani Catholics, it also marks a community whose roots in the region go back further than the city's colonial-era buildings might suggest.
festivals.beliefs: Midnight mass at Mangaluru's older basilicas and parish churches is seen as the most important event of the whole season. Even families who rarely attend church during the rest of the year usually come to this service.
festivals.celebrate: Parishes hold competitions for the best nativity scene, called a crib. Groups sing carols through Catholic neighborhoods. Families prepare kuswar at home, a Konkani Christmas sweet assortment made up of a dozen or more different treats. The season ends with midnight mass followed by a family meal.
festivals.local: People judge a Mangalorean Catholic family's kuswar box the same way a Bengali family might judge another family's Kali Puja sweets, by how many different kinds there are, not just how good they taste, and a short list of sweets is seen as a small failure of hospitality.
festivals.image: Kuswar sweets laid out on a table before Christmas, Mangaluru Konkani household

name: Tamil Nadu
tagline: Tamil Nadu is shaped by wide river deltas and old temple towns. The region still follows a calendar that is even older than the states around it.

festivals.name: Thai Pongal
festivals.reach: Celebrated across the state, in every community and district.
festivals.what: Thai Pongal is Tamil Nadu's main harvest festival, celebrated over four days. The first day, Bhogi, is for throwing away old things. The second day, Thai Pongal itself, honors the sun and the new rice harvest. The third day, Mattu Pongal, honors cattle. The fourth day, Kaanum Pongal, is for visiting family and friends.
festivals.who: Almost the entire state celebrates Thai Pongal, though it remains strongest as a farming tradition in the Kaveri river delta districts of Thanjavur and Tiruchirappalli.
festivals.when: Thai Pongal falls in mid-January, on the day the sun enters the Tamil month of Thai. This date is fixed by the solar calendar.
festivals.origin: This is a solar and farming festival that has been written about in Tamil literature for well over a thousand years. It is tied specifically to the rice-growing cycle of the Kaveri river delta.
festivals.signifies: The festival marks the end of the harvest season. It expresses thanks first to the sun, and then to the cattle that worked hard through the farming season.
festivals.beliefs: Families watch closely for the moment the milk boils over the new clay pot on Pongal morning. If it overflows generously, people take it as a sign of good fortune for the coming year.
festivals.celebrate: People light bonfires at dawn on Bhogi. They draw decorative patterns called kolam at their doorsteps. They cook sweet pongal outdoors in a new clay pot until the milk boils over. On Mattu Pongal, they wash and decorate their cattle. In some southern districts, people also take part in Jallikattu, a sport where participants try to tame a bull.
festivals.local: Many households treat the exact moment the pot boils over as a small sign about the future. People watch for it closely and talk about it afterward, rather than letting it happen unnoticed.
festivals.image: Sweet pongal boiling over a clay pot on an open fire, kolam at the threshold behind

festivals.name: Puthandu
festivals.reach: Celebrated across the state.
festivals.what: Puthandu is the Tamil solar new year. It begins with something called a kani, a tray filled with fruit, flowers, gold, and a mirror. Families arrange this tray the night before, so it is the very first thing they see when they wake up.
festivals.who: Tamil families across the state celebrate Puthandu, as do Tamil communities living in Sri Lanka, Malaysia, Singapore, and other places around the world.
festivals.when: Puthandu falls on the first day of the Tamil month of Chithirai, around 14 April. This is the same solar moment celebrated as Vishu in Kerala and Baisakhi in Punjab.
festivals.origin: This solar new year is celebrated, in one form or another, across South and Southeast Asia. Nobody knows exactly how old the Tamil version and the kani tray tradition are, but they have been part of regional practice for a very long time.
festivals.signifies: The tradition is based on the idea that the luck of the whole year depends on the very first thing a person sees, so it is worth arranging that first sight carefully.
festivals.beliefs: Parents often cover their children's eyes and lead them to the kani tray, so the arranged tray, rather than something random, is the first thing they see in the new year.
festivals.celebrate: The kani tray is set up in front of a mirror the night before. People wear new clothes, eat a sweet and sour dish called mangai pachadi, visit temples, and gather for family meals throughout the day.
festivals.local: If a Tamil family forgets to set up the kani tray overnight, people see it as truly messing up the start of the year, not just missing a small decoration.
festivals.image: Kani tray of fruit, flowers and a mirror arranged before dawn, Puthandu

festivals.name: Chithirai Thiruvizha
festivals.season: Tamil month of Chithirai, over two weeks
festivals.reach: A Madurai city festival drawing pilgrims from across Tamil Nadu.
festivals.what: This month-long festival at the Meenakshi Amman temple combines two stories that happen at the same time. One is the heavenly wedding of the goddess Meenakshi to the god Sundareswarar. The other is the journey of Kallazhagar, a form of the god Vishnu, who travels from Azhagar Kovil to bless his sister's wedding.
festivals.who: The whole city of Madurai takes part in this festival, which is organized jointly by the Meenakshi temple's Shaiva tradition, which worships Shiva, and the Vaishnava tradition, which worships Vishnu, of Azhagar Kovil.
festivals.when: This festival takes place during the Tamil month of Chithirai, which falls in April or May, and lasts roughly two weeks.
festivals.origin: The festival brings together two older temple traditions, one Shaiva and one Vaishnava, that were originally separate and are now celebrated as a single citywide event. Historians disagree about exactly when these two separate traditions were first combined into one shared festival.
festivals.signifies: The festival represents a kind of truce between two major traditions of Hindu worship, performed as public theater. It is treated as one big family celebration rather than a rivalry between the two groups.
festivals.beliefs: According to devotees, Kallazhagar is timed to arrive late for the wedding on purpose. As the festival's final act, he is believed to walk into the Vaigai river itself, dressed as Vishnu.
festivals.celebrate: Priests perform the full temple ceremony for Meenakshi's wedding. Kallazhagar is carried in procession from Azhagar Kovil into the city of Madurai. He then enters the Vaigai riverbed in front of large crowds, and several more days of processions and markets take place around the temple.
festivals.local: By April, the Vaigai river has often dried up completely, so most years Kallazhagar's river entry actually happens on dry sand rather than in water. The people of Madurai see this as completely normal, not as something disappointing.
festivals.image: Kallazhagar procession entering the dry Vaigai riverbed, Madurai, evening crowd

festivals.name: Karthigai Deepam
festivals.reach: Concentrated at Thiruvannamalai, though lamps are lit statewide on the same night.
festivals.what: Karthigai Deepam is a festival of lights. It ends with a giant flame called the Maha Deepam, lit on top of Arunachala hill in the town of Thiruvannamalai. This flame can be seen for miles across the surrounding plain.
festivals.who: Pilgrims travel to this festival from all across Tamil Nadu. The Arunachaleswarar temple, located at the base of the hill, is the center of the rituals.
festivals.when: The festival takes place on the full moon day of the Tamil month of Karthigai, usually in late November or December.
festivals.origin: Poems from the ancient Sangam era of Tamil literature, written roughly in the early centuries after the birth of Christ, already mention a festival of lights. This makes Karthigai Deepam one of the oldest Tamil festivals that has been continuously celebrated and recorded.
festivals.signifies: The festival represents the god Shiva appearing as an endless pillar of fire, called a Jyotirlingam. Locally, people see the hill itself as this very form of Shiva, and worship it directly.
festivals.beliefs: Many pilgrims believe that walking around the hill on foot, a practice called girivalam, brings special spiritual merit on this particular night, so large numbers of people walk it through the night.
festivals.celebrate: People light rows of oil lamps at homes and temples across the state on the evening of the full moon. At Thiruvannamalai itself, a huge cauldron filled with ghee and camphor is carried up to the hilltop and lit, where it burns through the entire night.
festivals.local: The whole point of the beacon, for local people, is that it can be seen from far away across the plain. Villages many kilometers from the hill watch closely for the exact moment the flame catches.
festivals.image: Maha Deepam beacon burning atop Arunachala hill at night, Thiruvannamalai

festivals.name: Thyagaraja Aradhana
festivals.reach: Particularly significant among Carnatic musicians and connoisseurs, drawing performers from across South India.
festivals.what: This is a five-day music festival held in the town of Thiruvaiyaru to honor Thyagaraja, a composer and saint. It takes place at the site of his tomb, called a samadhi, and combines religious worship with open concerts of Carnatic classical music.
festivals.who: Carnatic musicians and music lovers from across South India attend this festival, along with the local temple community of Thiruvaiyaru.
festivals.when: The festival lasts five days and ends on a day called Bahula Panchami in January, which is the anniversary of Thyagaraja's death.
festivals.origin: This festival has been held at Thyagaraja's tomb ever since he died in 1847. In 1908, two brothers named Narasimha Bhagavatar and Panchu Bhagavatar added the music concert format to the festival, building on decades of purely religious observance that came before.
festivals.signifies: The festival honors a saint through the very art form he practiced. Worship and musical performance are treated as one and the same thing here, not as two separate categories, one solemn and one not.
festivals.beliefs: The festival ends with hundreds of musicians singing together the Pancharatna Kritis, which means "five gem compositions," a special set of songs written by Thyagaraja. These are sung as a group, not performed by individual singers.
festivals.celebrate: Concerts and storytelling performances called harikathas run for all five days. There is also formal worship at Thyagaraja's tomb. The festival closes with visiting musicians sitting together to sing the Pancharatna Kritis as a group.
festivals.local: Within Carnatic music circles, a musician's first invitation to perform at Thiruvaiyaru is seen as a real professional achievement, not just a polite ceremonial gesture.
festivals.image: Massed Carnatic musicians seated for the Pancharatna Kritis at Thyagaraja's samadhi, Thiruvaiyaru

festivals.name: Deepavali
festivals.reach: Celebrated across the state.
festivals.what: In Tamil Nadu, Deepavali is celebrated a day earlier than in much of North India. Here, the festival's most important moment is an oil bath taken before dawn, rather than lighting lamps at night.
festivals.who: Hindu families across the state celebrate Deepavali. Many families who do not follow many other traditions on this day still make sure to keep the oil bath custom.
festivals.when: Tamil Deepavali falls on a day called Naraka Chaturdashi, which is the day before the main North Indian Diwali, during the Tamil month of Aippasi.
festivals.origin: Tamil Deepavali is connected to the story of the god Krishna defeating a demon named Narakasura. The specific tradition of bathing in oil before dawn is a regional custom, different from the evening-focused Lakshmi prayer ceremony celebrated in the north.
festivals.signifies: The festival represents light arriving before sunrise instead of after sunset. It also stands for cleansing oneself before celebrating, rather than doing both at the same time.
festivals.beliefs: People believe the oil bath must be taken specifically before sunrise. If someone bathes later in the day, it is considered to have missed the whole point of the tradition.
festivals.celebrate: Families take a ritual oil bath before dawn, then put on new clothes right afterward. In the days leading up to the festival, they prepare sweets and savory snacks like murukku and mysore pak. Firecrackers start going off before sunrise, and families visit each other throughout the day.
festivals.local: Tamil families quietly compete over how early their household woke up for the oil bath. If a family gets caught bathing after sunrise, people tease them about it for the rest of the year.
festivals.image: Pre-dawn oil bath preparations, new clothes laid out, Tamil household on Deepavali

festivals.name: Nagore Kanduri
festivals.aliases: Nagore Dargah Festival, Urs of Nagore Andavar
festivals.reach: Draws pilgrims from across Tamil Nadu and from Sri Lanka, Singapore and Malaysia.
festivals.what: This is a fourteen-day festival called an urs, held at the Nagore Dargah, a shrine built over the tomb of the Sufi saint Hazrat Syed Shahul Hamid. It marks the anniversary of his death with flag processions, music, and communal feeding of large crowds.
festivals.who: Muslim pilgrims from across Tamil Nadu and from Tamil communities living abroad attend this festival. There is also a long history of Hindu devotees visiting the shrine, which is well documented.
festivals.when: The festival lasts fourteen days during the Islamic month of Jamathul Aakhir. Because it follows the lunar calendar, the dates shift each year.
festivals.origin: The dargah shrine was built over the saint's tomb after he died in 1579. The festival, called the Kanduri, a word that comes from the Persian word for tablecloth, has been held every year since as an urs, or death anniversary celebration.
festivals.signifies: The festival represents the saint's continuing presence, made public through the sharing of a communal meal rather than through a private visit to his grave.
festivals.beliefs: Devotees believe that vows made at the dargah are heard and answered, no matter what religion the person making the vow follows. This belief is part of why the shrine has such a long history of attracting people from different faiths.
festivals.celebrate: The festival opens with a sacred flag being raised and carried through the streets by chariot. At night, people gather for qawwali, a form of devotional singing, that continues through the night. Pilgrims are fed as a community for the entire two weeks of the festival.
festivals.local: In the Nagapattinam area, there are documented Hindu families who have kept vows to the dargah for generations. This kind of shared Hindu-Muslim devotion is considered completely ordinary here, and it is recorded in other places along the Tamil coast as well.
festivals.image: Flag procession carried by chariot to Nagore Dargah, crowd along the street

festivals.name: Velankanni Feast
festivals.aliases: Our Lady of Good Health Festival, Annai Velankanni Feast
festivals.reach: Draws pilgrims of all faiths from across India and abroad.
festivals.what: This is an eleven-day religious feast at the Basilica of Our Lady of Good Health in the town of Velankanni. It opens with the raising of a flag and closes on the Feast of the Nativity of Mary. The festival draws pilgrims from far beyond just the Christian community.
festivals.who: Catholic pilgrims travel here from across Tamil Nadu and the rest of India. Large numbers of Hindu and Muslim visitors also come to fulfill vows they have made.
festivals.when: The festival runs for eleven days, starting on 29 August and ending on 8 September.
festivals.origin: Devotion to this shrine goes back to a set of events reported in the sixteenth century, including a vision, a healing, and the rescue of some Portuguese sailors. In 1962, Pope John XXIII officially raised the church's status to that of a minor basilica.
festivals.signifies: This is a healing shrine that has never belonged to just one religious community. On this stretch of coast, people of different faiths sharing the same holy site is a very old practice, not something new.
festivals.beliefs: Many pilgrims strongly believe that vows made here for healing are answered. Because of this, many walk long distances to reach the shrine, and some complete the last stretch of the journey barefoot as part of their vow.
festivals.celebrate: The feast opens with a flag-raising ceremony. There are daily church services and candlelight processions. A car procession carries a statue of Mary through the town, and the feast ends with a final Mass on 8 September attended by tens of thousands of people.
festivals.local: It is considered completely ordinary here, not remarkable at all, for pilgrims of every faith to arrive on foot from very far away, sometimes walking for days to reach the shrine.
festivals.image: Candlelight procession outside Velankanni basilica at night, crowd of pilgrims

name: Telangana
tagline: Telangana is a plateau region full of villages that depend on water tanks for farming, along with Hyderabad, a capital city once ruled by a Nizam. The state keeps a festival calendar that neighboring Andhra Pradesh never fully shared.

festivals.name: Bathukamma
festivals.season: Nine days through Durga Navaratri, closing on Durgashtami
festivals.reach: Celebrated as a state festival, kept especially by women across every district.
festivals.what: Bathukamma is a nine-day flower festival. Women build tall, pyramid-shaped stacks of seasonal flowers, called bathukammas, on brass plates. Each evening, they carry these stacks outside, sing and dance around them, and then immerse them in water.
festivals.who: Women and girls across Telangana are at the heart of this festival, in both villages and cities. Men mostly help by gathering flowers and taking part in the final immersion.
festivals.when: The festival lasts nine days, beginning on a day called Mahalaya Amavasya and ending on Durgashtami, which falls in September or October.
festivals.origin: This festival grew out of old traditions of worshipping the goddess Gauri in the Telangana countryside. Its history was passed down through spoken word and local practice rather than written down in one single text or tied to one temple. After Telangana became a separate state in 2014, the government officially adopted Bathukamma as a state festival.
festivals.signifies: The word "bathukamma" means roughly "mother goddess, come alive." The festival is essentially a wish made to the goddess Gauri for the wellbeing of women and their families.
festivals.beliefs: Each day of the festival uses a different combination of flowers, and people dance around the stack in a different pattern each day. If a family gets the pattern wrong on a particular day, people see it as a small mistake, not a serious problem.
festivals.celebrate: Fresh bathukammas are built each evening from seasonal flowers such as tangedu and gunuka. Women gather in circles to sing and dance around them. On the ninth day, called Saddula Bathukamma, the flower stacks are finally immersed in local tanks and lakes.
festivals.local: Since the government made it a state festival, Hyderabad now holds a massive Bathukamma celebration at Tank Bund with tens of thousands of participants. This is a much bigger scale than villages in Telangana used to have, but people have largely embraced it as their own.
festivals.image: Women dancing in a circle around lit bathukamma flower stacks, evening light

festivals.name: Bonalu
festivals.season: Ashada month, weekly across Hyderabad and Secunderabad
festivals.reach: Concentrated in Hyderabad and Secunderabad, with village versions across Telangana.
festivals.what: Bonalu is a monsoon-season festival for the goddess Mahakali. Women carry a pot called a bonam, filled with cooked rice, milk, and jaggery and topped with a lit lamp, on their heads as they walk in procession to her temples.
festivals.who: Women devotees are at the center of this festival. It is organized through neighborhood temple committees across Hyderabad and Secunderabad, as well as in rural Telangana.
festivals.when: Bonalu is celebrated on Sundays throughout the Hindu month of Ashada, which falls in July or August. Different temples in the city take their turn on different weeks.
festivals.origin: According to local tradition, the festival as it is celebrated today began after an outbreak of plague hit Hyderabad and Secunderabad around 1813. At that time, people prayed to the goddess for protection. The practice itself, however, builds on older Telangana traditions of worshipping goddesses that existed even before that outbreak.
festivals.signifies: The festival represents a direct, personal offering made by hand to a goddess who is believed to protect people from disease. Women carry the offering themselves rather than leaving it entirely to temple priests.
festivals.beliefs: Women carry the bonam pot balanced on their heads without using their hands to hold it. People believe that women carrying the pot can enter a state of possession, called Oggu, which shows itself through trembling or trance-like movements.
festivals.celebrate: Bonam pots are carried in procession to neighborhood Mahakali temples. The festival's citywide season officially begins at Golconda's Jagadamba Mahakali temple. The next morning, a woman believed to be possessed performs a ritual called Rangam to predict the future, and the festival closes with processions carrying sacred pots called ghatams.
festivals.local: Bonalu has grown much more prominent since 2014, when it was declared a state festival alongside Bathukamma. Older residents of Hyderabad describe this as a genuine change in scale that they have watched happen within their own lifetimes.
festivals.image: Woman carrying a decorated bonam pot with lit lamp, Golconda temple procession

festivals.name: Ugadi
festivals.reach: Celebrated widely across the state.
festivals.what: Ugadi is the Telugu new year. In Telangana, it is celebrated much like it is in Andhra Pradesh, but it fits into a wider festival calendar that continues on to Bathukamma and Bonalu later in the year, festivals that Andhra Pradesh does not celebrate in the same way.
festivals.who: Telugu-speaking families across Telangana celebrate Ugadi, both in the Hyderabad region and in the rural districts.
festivals.when: Ugadi falls on the first day of the Hindu month of Chaitra, usually in late March or early April.
festivals.origin: This lunisolar new year, based on both the sun and the moon, is celebrated across the whole Telugu-speaking Deccan region. Telangana's version of the festival has followed roughly the same traditions as Andhra Pradesh's, even though it sits within a different, distinct regional festival calendar overall.
festivals.signifies: Ugadi represents a fresh start for the new year, expressed through a special dish that combines six different tastes rather than just one.
festivals.beliefs: People take seriously the reading of the panchangam, the yearly almanac, at temples and at home, treating it as a genuine forecast for the year ahead.
festivals.celebrate: Families mix Ugadi pachadi from raw mango, neem flowers, jaggery, tamarind, salt, and chili. They hang mango-leaf decorations at their doorways, wear new clothes, and listen to the panchangam reading at temples.
festivals.local: In Telangana's Deccan towns, people make the exact same pachadi recipe as elsewhere, but conversations the next day usually turn quickly to the upcoming Bonalu season rather than staying focused on Ugadi itself.
festivals.image: Ugadi pachadi bowl on a kitchen counter, mango leaf torana in the background

festivals.name: Sammakka Saralamma Jatara
festivals.reach: The largest tribal gathering in Asia, drawing pilgrims from across South India.
festivals.what: This is a four-day tribal festival held every two years at Medaram, in Mulugu district, on the banks of a stream called the Jampanna Vagu. It honors a mother and daughter, Sammakka and Saralamma, who are worshipped as goddesses.
festivals.who: The Koya tribal community is at the heart of this festival, and it preserves their oral traditions. The festival now also draws Hindu pilgrims from many different communities across Telangana and neighboring states.
festivals.when: The festival lasts four days during the Hindu month of Magha, in January or February, and it only happens in even-numbered years.
festivals.origin: According to Koya oral tradition, Sammakka was found as a baby among tigers and was raised by a tribal chieftain. She and her daughter Saralamma led resistance against unfair taxes imposed by the Kakatiya rulers in the thirteenth century. After they died, they were worshipped as goddesses, and the festival has been held in roughly its current form ever since.
festivals.signifies: The festival honors two women who resisted an unjust ruling power. The Koya tribal community worships them on its own terms, rather than having their story absorbed into a mainstream temple tradition.
festivals.beliefs: Devotees carry offerings of jaggery equal to their own body weight, which they believe is a direct exchange for receiving the goddesses' blessing. They also bathe in the Jampanna Vagu stream as a way of purifying themselves.
festivals.celebrate: The festival includes Sammakka's symbolic arrival from the forest, carried in as a vermilion-covered casket, huge quantities of jaggery offered by the sackful, mass bathing in the stream, and a closing procession that symbolically sends the goddesses back into the forest.
festivals.local: The huge size of this festival is not exaggeration. Recent editions have drawn well over ten million pilgrims across the four days, making it one of the largest religious gatherings anywhere in India.
festivals.image: Pilgrims offering jaggery sacks at Medaram, forest clearing, dense crowd

festivals.name: Ramzan & Eid al-Fitr
festivals.season: Ninth month of the Hijri calendar
festivals.reach: Particularly significant in Hyderabad's Old City and across the state's Urdu-speaking communities.
festivals.what: This month of fasting from dawn to dusk ends with the celebration of Eid al-Fitr. It is observed with special intensity in Hyderabad's Old City, which was once the seat of the Nizam's kingdom and is home to its own distinct Deccani Muslim food and mosque traditions.
festivals.who: Telangana's Urdu-speaking Muslim communities celebrate this festival, especially around Charminar, Mecca Masjid, and the older neighborhoods of Hyderabad, and Muslim communities across the state's district towns celebrate it as well.
festivals.when: This festival takes place during the ninth month of the Islamic Hijri calendar, which shifts about eleven days earlier each year on our regular calendar.
festivals.origin: The practice of fasting comes from the Qur'an. Hyderabad's particular Ramzan traditions, including its food, its mosque schedule, and its local dialect called Dakhni Urdu, developed over roughly four centuries under the Qutb Shahi rulers and later the Nizam rulers.
festivals.signifies: The festival represents self-control and the duty to give charity. In Hyderabad, it also serves each year to reaffirm the Old City's own unique food culture and civic identity.
festivals.beliefs: People believe the last ten nights of the fasting month carry special weight, and they look for the holy night called Laylat al-Qadr during this time.
festivals.celebrate: Families eat sehri before dawn. At sunset, they break their fast with iftar, often built around haleem, a slow-cooked dish of meat and lentils sold at stalls across the city only during this season. People attend taraweeh prayers at night, give charity called Zakat and Fitra before Eid, and gather for Eid prayers at Mecca Masjid and other outdoor prayer grounds called Idgahs.
festivals.local: Haleem sold in Hyderabad during Ramzan carries an official Geographical Indication tag specific to the city, a formal government recognition given to a dish that otherwise only exists for one month out of the whole year.
festivals.image: Haleem stalls outside Mecca Masjid at dusk during Ramzan, Hyderabad Old City

festivals.name: Muharram & Bibi-ka-Alam
festivals.season: First month of the Hijri calendar
festivals.reach: Centred on Hyderabad's Old City, with village Peerla Panduga observance across rural Telangana.
festivals.what: Muharram mourning in Hyderabad centers on the Bibi-ka-Alam, a sacred standard that is said to contain a fragment of the wooden plank used to wash the body of Bibi Fatima, the daughter of the Prophet Muhammad. It is carried in procession from the neighborhood of Dabeerpura on the tenth day of Muharram.
festivals.who: Both Hyderabad's Shia and Sunni Muslim communities work together to maintain this procession. It also draws Hindu spectators, and in rural Telangana, Hindus even take part directly in village versions of the alam tradition.
festivals.when: The observance takes place over the first ten days of the Islamic month of Muharram, which shifts each year with the lunar calendar. The main procession happens on the tenth day, called Ashura.
festivals.origin: The alam, or sacred standard, was first set up at Golconda fort under Hayath Bakshi Begum, the wife of the fifth Qutb Shahi ruler, in the early seventeenth century. Later, the standard was moved to a specially built shrine in Dabeerpura, and its public procession grew larger under the later Asaf Jahi Nizam rulers.
