festivals.signifies: The festival mourns the death of Husain, the grandson of the Prophet Muhammad, at the Battle of Karbala. In Hyderabad specifically, it also represents a relic tradition that has continued without interruption since the Qutb Shahi period.
festivals.beliefs: People believe the alam carries the direct blessing of Bibi Fatima. Touching it or even approaching it closely during the procession is seen as an especially meaningful act of devotion.
festivals.celebrate: The alam is set up and visited throughout the first ten days. At night, people gather for mourning assemblies where poems called marsiya are recited. On Ashura, a large public procession travels from Dabeerpura through the Old City.
festivals.local: In many Telangana villages, a Hindu family holds the hereditary right to carry a particular alam during the local Peerla Panduga festival. This practice is documented across the wider Deccan region and is treated locally as completely ordinary.
festivals.image: Bibi-ka-Alam standard carried through Hyderabad's Old City on Ashura, crowd alongside

festivals.name: Christmas
festivals.reach: A minority observance, strongest among Secunderabad's older Christian and Anglo-Indian community.
festivals.what: Christmas in Telangana is smaller and more concentrated in one place compared to the coastal Andhra districts. It is mainly kept by Secunderabad's older Christian churches and its Anglo-Indian community, a legacy left over from the era when the British army was stationed there.
festivals.who: Catholic and Protestant church communities in Secunderabad and Hyderabad celebrate Christmas, along with a small but long-established Anglo-Indian community.
festivals.when: Christmas falls on 25 December, with Advent carol services held throughout December leading up to it.
festivals.origin: Secunderabad's Christian church communities grew out of the British military base, called a cantonment, that was established there in the late eighteenth century. This history is separate from the older missionary church networks found in coastal Andhra Pradesh.
festivals.signifies: Christmas celebrates the birth of Jesus. For Secunderabad's Anglo-Indian families, it also marks a community whose schools and churches date back to the era of the British military cantonment.
festivals.beliefs: Midnight mass at Secunderabad's older churches remains the most important service of the season for Christian families there.
festivals.celebrate: Carol services take place throughout December. Markets and bakeries around Secunderabad sell plum cake all season long. Families attend midnight mass and gather together on Christmas Day itself.
festivals.local: Several of Secunderabad's Christmas cake bakeries have roots going back to the British cantonment era, and they still do their busiest business of the whole year in the first weeks of December.
festivals.image: Plum cakes on display at an old Secunderabad bakery counter, December

name: Puducherry
tagline: Puducherry mixes French-style buildings with shutters over traditional Tamil courtyards. In this town, a sea-bathing festival and France's national day are both celebrated along the very same seaside promenade.

festivals.name: Thai Pongal
festivals.reach: Celebrated across the territory's Tamil-majority population.
festivals.what: The harvest festival is celebrated in Puducherry in exactly the same way as in the wider Tamil region surrounding it. Sweet pongal is boiled outdoors, and cattle are honored the following day.
festivals.who: The territory's Tamil Hindu majority celebrates this festival, both in Puducherry town and in the surrounding villages of the former French colonial territory.
festivals.when: Thai Pongal falls in mid-January, on the day the sun enters the Tamil month of Thai.
festivals.origin: This is a solar and farming festival celebrated across the Tamil region generally. Puducherry keeps it without any changes, even though the territory has a separate administrative and colonial history from the rest of Tamil Nadu.
festivals.signifies: The festival expresses thanks for the harvest, directed first at the sun and then, the following day, at the cattle that worked through the farming season.
festivals.beliefs: People watch the moment the milk boils over in the new clay pot as a small sign for what the coming year will bring.
festivals.celebrate: People light bonfires at dawn for Bhogi, draw kolam patterns at their doorsteps, cook sweet pongal in a new clay pot, and wash and decorate their cattle for Mattu Pongal.
festivals.local: Puducherry's Pongal celebration looks identical to Tamil Nadu's because the territory was originally carved out of the very same stretch of Tamil coastline. Locals often point this out when outsiders assume the French colonial period changed more about local culture than it actually did.
festivals.image: Sweet pongal boiling over in a clay pot, Puducherry village courtyard

festivals.name: Masi Magam
festivals.season: Tamil month of Masi, Magam nakshatra
festivals.reach: A major Puducherry town festival, drawing temples from across the region.
festivals.what: Masi Magam is a seaside festival in which deities from around fifty temples across Puducherry and neighboring parts of Tamil Nadu are carried in procession to the beach at Vaithikuppam. There, they receive a ritual bath in the sea.
festivals.who: The temple communities of Puducherry town and the surrounding villages take part together, rather than any single temple celebrating alone.
festivals.when: The festival happens during the Magam star period, or nakshatra, in the Tamil month of Masi, which falls in February or March.
festivals.origin: Masi Magam is celebrated all along the Tamil coast, based on the belief that heavenly deities come down to bathe in the sea on this day. Puducherry's version, which brings temples from across a wide region together into one shared seafront event, has grown to its current large scale gradually over time.
festivals.signifies: The festival represents a yearly act of purification. People believe that the deities' bath in the sea also purifies the devotees who bathe alongside them.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that taking a dip in the sea at the exact same time as the processed idols brings that day's blessing directly to them.
festivals.celebrate: Idols from dozens of temples are ceremonially bathed throughout the morning. In the evening, illuminated chariots carry the deities in procession to the shore, followed by mass bathing along the Vaithikuppam coastline.
festivals.local: The fact that temples with no shared calendar all join together for this one procession is seen locally as the festival's real achievement, something none of the individual temples could pull off on their own.
festivals.image: Illuminated temple chariots processing to the shore at dusk, Vaithikuppam beach, Puducherry

festivals.name: Bastille Day
festivals.reach: Observed by Puducherry's French citizens, French passport holders and the French Consulate, and watched as civic spectacle by the wider town.
festivals.what: Bastille Day is France's national day. In Puducherry, it is marked with a ceremony at the French War Memorial on Goubert Avenue, honoring soldiers from French India who died fighting for France.
festivals.who: Puducherry's French community celebrates this day. This is a group of French citizens and French passport holders left behind after France transferred the territory to India in 1954, along with the French Consulate.
festivals.when: Bastille Day is celebrated every year on 14 July.
festivals.origin: The war memorial was built in 1937, ordered by the Governor of French India at the time, to honor the roughly five hundred soldiers from French India who were sent to fight in the First World War. Names of soldiers from the Second World War, the Algerian War, and the war in Indochina were added to the memorial later.
festivals.signifies: The day represents a colonial-era military duty that is still remembered and honored, long after the political relationship that created that duty came to an end.
festivals.beliefs: People treat the ceremony as solemn first and celebratory second. It opens with tributes to the dead before moving on to the day's festivities.
festivals.celebrate: The day includes wreath-laying and tributes at the French War Memorial. The Indian and French national anthems are played together at the Consulate. The memorial is lit up at night, and the day ends with a parade and fireworks.
festivals.local: Puducherry is one of the very few places in India where the war dead of French India, rather than any Indian regiment, are the ones publicly mourned every year.
festivals.image: French War Memorial illuminated at night, Goubert Avenue, Puducherry, Bastille Day

festivals.name: Auroville Founding Day
festivals.reach: Centred on Auroville township, drawing residents and visitors from across the territory and abroad.
festivals.what: This day marks the anniversary of Auroville's founding in 1968. It is celebrated with a gathering at the Matrimandir, a large meditation structure, and in some years with a water ceremony that echoes the original founding ritual.
festivals.who: Auroville's international community of residents, who come from dozens of different countries, celebrates this day together with visitors from Puducherry and Tamil Nadu.
festivals.when: Auroville Founding Day takes place every year on 28 February.
festivals.origin: Auroville was officially opened on 28 February 1968, in a ceremony attended by around five thousand people. At that ceremony, representatives from over a hundred countries each placed a handful of soil from their home country into a central urn.
festivals.signifies: The day represents this deliberately international township's own story of how it began, built around soil and water rather than any single religious tradition.
festivals.beliefs: Residents treat the founding ceremony's rituals involving soil, and on anniversary years, water, as the community's own special origin story, separate from the religious calendars followed in the surrounding region.
festivals.celebrate: People gather at the Matrimandir for collective meditation. There are cultural performances and exhibits about Auroville's history. In milestone years, a water ceremony combines water from Auroville with water brought from other parts of India and other countries.
festivals.local: The founding urn, which still holds soil from over a hundred different countries, sits at the very center of the township. Each year's anniversary gathering is built around returning to that exact spot.
festivals.image: Collective meditation gathering at the Matrimandir, Auroville, Founding Day

festivals.name: Christmas & Immaculate Conception Feast
festivals.reach: Particularly significant among Puducherry's French-period Catholic community.
festivals.what: This December season centers on the Feast of the Immaculate Conception, celebrated at Puducherry's cathedral on 8 December, followed by Christmas itself. Both are celebrated by a Catholic community whose churches date back to the French colonial period and even earlier to the Portuguese period.
festivals.who: Tamil and French Catholic church communities at the Immaculate Conception Cathedral and Puducherry's other historic parish churches celebrate this season.
festivals.when: The Immaculate Conception feast falls on 8 December, and Christmas falls on 25 December. The season runs continuously between the two dates.
festivals.origin: Jesuit missionaries founded the cathedral, and construction began in 1699. The building was destroyed and rebuilt at the same site three separate times because of colonial conflicts, before finally reaching its current form in 1791.
festivals.signifies: The season represents a Catholic community's ability to keep going despite repeated destruction and rebuilding, caused by three different colonial powers fighting over control of the town.
festivals.beliefs: Special church services on both feast days are treated as essential attendance for the parish community, more so than on many other days of the year.
festivals.celebrate: There is a special Mass and processions on 8 December. Churches are decorated over the following weeks. People sing carols and attend midnight Mass on Christmas Eve. On Christmas Day itself, families eat a mix of French and Tamil food, including local bread and cake traditions alongside traditional Tamil festive dishes.
festivals.local: The cathedral's local nickname, Samba Kovil, is a Tamil version of the words "Saint Paul's church." This nickname is itself a small reminder of how French and Tamil words and traditions sit layered on top of each other in Puducherry's Catholic community.
festivals.image: Immaculate Conception Cathedral lit for Christmas, Puducherry, evening crowd outside

festivals.name: Deepavali
festivals.reach: Celebrated across the territory's Tamil Hindu population.
festivals.what: Deepavali in Puducherry follows the same pattern as the rest of Tamil Nadu. It is marked with an oil bath before dawn, rather than being celebrated purely as an evening festival of lamps.
festivals.who: The territory's Tamil Hindu households celebrate Deepavali, along with Telugu and Malayalam-speaking minority communities who keep their own regional versions of the festival.
festivals.when: Deepavali falls on a day called Naraka Chaturdashi, the day before the main North Indian Diwali, during the Tamil month of Aippasi.
festivals.origin: This festival is tied to the story of the god Krishna defeating the demon Narakasura. Puducherry keeps the same pre-dawn oil-bath tradition found throughout the surrounding Tamil region.
festivals.signifies: The festival represents light and cleansing that happen before sunrise, rather than after sunset.
festivals.beliefs: People believe the oil bath is only effective if it is taken before sunrise, a rule that most households treat as something you simply cannot skip.
festivals.celebrate: Families take a pre-dawn oil bath, wear new clothes, prepare sweets in the days beforehand, and set off firecrackers from before sunrise through the morning.
festivals.local: Because Puducherry has such a mixed population, the very same morning can include a Tamil family's oil bath, a Telugu family's own Deepavali customs, and a French Catholic neighbor going about an ordinary working day, all happening on the same street.
festivals.image: Firecrackers and lit lamps at dawn on a Puducherry street, Deepavali morning

name: Lakshadweep
tagline: Lakshadweep is a scattered group of coral islands where the Islamic calendar is, in practical terms, the only calendar that really matters for daily life.

festivals.name: Eid al-Fitr
festivals.reach: Kept across every inhabited island.
festivals.what: This festival marks the close of a month of dawn-to-dusk fasting. It is kept across Lakshadweep's islands, where over ninety-six percent of the population is Muslim, most of them following the Shafi'i school of Sunni Islam.
festivals.who: Almost the entire population of the inhabited islands celebrates this festival, including Kavaratti, Agatti, Amini, Andrott, Kadmat, Kalpeni, Kiltan, Chetlat, Bitra, and Minicoy.
festivals.when: The festival falls on the first day of the Islamic month of Shawwal, which moves each year with the lunar Hijri calendar.
festivals.origin: Islam reached Lakshadweep by sea from the Malabar and Arabian coasts centuries ago, and the islands' Shafi'i tradition follows the same maritime, trade-linked pattern of transmission that has been documented along the Malabar coast opposite the islands.
festivals.signifies: The festival marks the end of the fast. On islands this small, it is also a day when practically the entire community is doing the same thing at the same time.
festivals.beliefs: People settle a charitable payment called Zakat al-Fitr before the Eid prayer. Everyone on every island follows closely the sighting of the moon that fixes the exact date.
festivals.celebrate: People attend Eid prayer at the island's mosque, wear new clothes, visit each other's households, and share festive meals built around fish, coconut, and rice, the staple foods of the island kitchen.
festivals.local: On an island of just a few thousand people, Eid morning genuinely empties every household onto the same stretch of path leading to the mosque, a scale of shared participation that comes as much from the island's small size as from religious devotion.
festivals.image: Crowd walking to the island mosque for Eid prayer, Lakshadweep coastline behind

festivals.name: Eid al-Adha
festivals.reach: Kept across every inhabited island.
festivals.what: This is the festival of sacrifice, marking the close of the Hajj pilgrimage season. It is kept on islands where livestock is scarce, so the way the sacrifice is carried out is shaped by what a small coral island can actually supply.
festivals.who: The Muslim population of every inhabited island celebrates this festival.
festivals.when: The festival falls on the tenth day of the Islamic month of Dhu al-Hijjah, which moves each year with the Hijri calendar.
festivals.origin: This observance remembers the Prophet Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice his son on God's command, as recorded in the Qur'an. In Lakshadweep, it is practiced following the same Shafi'i school of Islamic law used across the wider Malabar-linked Islamic tradition of the islands.
festivals.signifies: The festival represents submission and obedience, tested and then relieved. It is marked each year through an act of sacrifice and by sharing the meat from it.
festivals.beliefs: People believe the meat from the sacrifice should be divided into fixed portions between family, relatives, and the poor. On islands where charitable giving is highly visible within such a small community, this obligation is taken very seriously.
festivals.celebrate: People attend Eid prayer at the mosque. Because livestock is limited locally, the sacrifice is arranged communally, and the meat is then distributed among family, neighbors, and those in need.
festivals.local: Because livestock has to be brought in or carefully managed on a small coral island, the Bakrid sacrifice here is organized more as a community effort than it is in mainland towns. This is a practical adjustment to real scarcity, not a difference in belief.
festivals.image: Communal Eid al-Adha meal preparation on an island courtyard, Lakshadweep

festivals.name: Milad un-Nabi
festivals.reach: Kept across every inhabited island.
festivals.what: This festival observes the birth of the Prophet Muhammad. It is marked at island mosques with the recitation of devotional poems called maulood and with communal feasting, rather than with any public procession.
festivals.who: The Muslim population of every inhabited island celebrates this festival, organized through the local mosque committee.
festivals.when: The festival falls on the twelfth day of the Islamic month of Rabi al-Awwal, which moves each year with the Hijri calendar.
festivals.origin: Mawlid, the celebration of the Prophet's birth, is observed across much of the Muslim world. Its form in Lakshadweep follows the same devotional pattern found along the Malabar coast, where maulood texts are recited at the mosque.
festivals.signifies: The festival marks the Prophet's birth through recitation and shared food, rather than through public spectacle.
festivals.beliefs: People believe the maulood recitation brings blessing on the household or mosque that hosts it, so hosting one is treated as a genuine act of devotion.
festivals.celebrate: Mosques hold maulood recitations, which sometimes extend into private homes, followed by communal feasts prepared and shared among everyone who attends.
festivals.local: On several islands, this observance also includes a remembered respect for local religious teachers and preceptors who are credited with establishing island mosque life generations ago, alongside the mawlid celebration itself.
festivals.image: Maulood recitation gathering inside an island mosque, Lakshadweep

festivals.name: Muharram
festivals.season: First month of the Hijri calendar
festivals.reach: Kept quietly across the islands, without the large processions seen on the mainland.
festivals.what: Muharram in Lakshadweep is kept as a period of quiet reflection and prayer, rather than as a procession-based mourning festival, since the island's Muslim population is overwhelmingly Sunni Shafi'i rather than Shia.
festivals.who: The Muslim population of the islands generally observes Muharram, through prayer centered at the mosque.
festivals.when: The observance covers the first ten days of the Islamic month of Muharram, which moves each year with the Hijri calendar, with particular observance on the tenth day, called Ashura.
festivals.origin: Muharram is marked across the Muslim world in memory of the events at Karbala. Its low-key, prayer-centered form in Lakshadweep reflects the islands' predominantly Sunni Shafi'i character, rather than the Shia-influenced procession traditions found in parts of the Deccan mainland.
festivals.signifies: The month is treated with solemnity and extra prayer, rather than as an occasion for public mourning displays.
festivals.beliefs: Many people keep a voluntary fast on Ashura, following a practice recorded across Sunni tradition generally.
festivals.celebrate: The day includes additional prayers at the mosque, voluntary fasting on Ashura by those who choose to observe it, and a generally quiet, reflective tone rather than public procession.
festivals.local: Visitors who expect the alam processions seen during mainland Deccan Muharram find nothing similar on the islands. Islanders explain this plainly as a result of the islands' Shafi'i Sunni character, not as any lesser regard for the occasion.
festivals.image: Quiet evening prayers at an island mosque during Muharram, Lakshadweep

name: Assam
tagline: Assam is a state in the Brahmaputra river valley, and its farmers follow three separate Bihu festivals spread across the farming year, one for planting, one for the main harvest, and one for the lean season in between. The state is also home to the Kamakhya temple, where every year the goddess is honored during a very private and unusual week tied to her own body.

festivals.name: Rongali Bihu
festivals.season: Bohag, first month of the Assamese year
festivals.reach: Rongali Bihu is celebrated across the whole state by Assamese speakers from every community.
festivals.what: Rongali Bihu is the Assamese new year and the most important festival in the state. It begins with a special day set aside just for taking care of cattle, and only after that do the celebrations for people begin.
festivals.who: Assamese-speaking families across the Brahmaputra valley celebrate Rongali Bihu, and so do Assamese communities who now live in other parts of India and in other countries.
festivals.when: Rongali Bihu falls in mid-April, on the same solar new year date that other parts of India celebrate as Baisakhi, Puthandu, and Vishu. The main celebration lasts seven days, but people keep celebrating all through the month of Bohag.
festivals.origin: Bihu began long ago as a farming new year tied to spring planting on the fertile floodplain of the Brahmaputra river. Language experts still disagree about exactly where the word Bihu comes from, and no one knows for certain how or when the festival first began.
festivals.signifies: Rongali Bihu marks the start of a fresh farming year. It is also a season when young men and women sing and dance together openly as a kind of courtship, something that is usually done much more quietly and carefully during the rest of the year.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that cattle must be washed and blessed before the human new year can properly begin. That is why Goru Bihu, the day for cattle, always comes before Manuh Bihu, the day for people.
festivals.celebrate: On Goru Bihu, people bathe their cattle in local ponds and feed them turmeric and lentils. On Manuh Bihu, people wear new clothes, get blessings from their elders, and share family feasts. Groups called Husori troupes go from house to house singing blessings, and young men and women perform the Bihu dance wearing traditional clothing, mekhela sador for women and dhoti for men.
festivals.local: When a Husori troupe shows up at a house, even without warning, that family is expected to welcome them and offer something on the spot. If a family has nothing ready to give, people see it as a real embarrassment, not just a small slip.
festivals.image: Bihu dancers in a Guwahati field, dhol drums, monsoon-green paddy behind

festivals.name: Magh Bihu
festivals.reach: Magh Bihu is celebrated widely across the state, and it is strongest in rural districts.
festivals.what: Magh Bihu is Assam's harvest festival. It is built around a night of communal feasting called Uruka, followed by a bonfire lit at dawn.
festivals.who: Farming households celebrate Magh Bihu the most, but really the whole state joins in, in villages and cities alike.
festivals.when: Magh Bihu happens in mid-January, at the same time as Makar Sankranti is celebrated elsewhere in India, and it marks the end of the paddy rice harvest.
festivals.origin: Magh Bihu is a farming festival tied to the sun's yearly cycle and to the rice-growing calendar of the Brahmaputra valley. Its name comes from the word bhog, which means feasting, celebrating the time once the granaries are full of grain.
festivals.signifies: Magh Bihu celebrates the abundance that a whole season of hard work has earned. The bonfire that is lit is meant to carry away the tiredness and troubles of the old year along with it.
festivals.beliefs: People build a tall structure of hay and bamboo called the meji and burn it at dawn as an offering to the fire god. They believe the ash left behind makes the soil more fertile when it is scattered on the fields for the next season.
festivals.celebrate: The night before, people build temporary bamboo huts called bhelaghar and sleep in them. They share a big Uruka feast that lasts until sunrise, and at first light they light the meji bonfire. In some villages, people also play traditional games such as buffalo fights and egg fights, though both of these are increasingly being challenged and questioned.
festivals.local: Sleeping overnight in the bhelaghar, instead of just showing up for the bonfire the next morning, is what separates a household that celebrates Uruka properly from one that treats Magh Bihu as a single-day event.
festivals.image: Meji bonfire at dawn in a village courtyard, bamboo bhelaghar nearby

festivals.name: Kati Bihu
festivals.reach: Kati Bihu is kept quietly across rural Assam, without the big crowds that gather for the other two Bihus.
festivals.what: Kati Bihu is the plainest and most serious of the three Bihus. It falls during the period when the rice crop is still growing and the granaries from the last harvest are almost empty.
festivals.who: Farming households across the Brahmaputra valley observe Kati Bihu, but they keep it as a quiet family event rather than a public celebration.
festivals.when: Kati Bihu falls on a fixed date in the lunar month of Kati, in mid to late October.
festivals.origin: Kati Bihu marks the gap between planting the rice and harvesting it. Unlike Assam's other two Bihus, it has no dance and no big feast attached to it at all.
festivals.signifies: Kati Bihu is about patience during a lean, difficult month. It focuses on taking care of a crop that is still growing, rather than celebrating one that has already been brought in.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that small earthen lamps called sakis, lit near the tulsi plant, help keep the household steady through the hard weeks. They also believe that akash banti lamps, raised on tall bamboo poles in the paddy fields, guide the family's ancestors home and help keep pests away from the crop.
festivals.celebrate: People light earthen lamps at the tulsi plant and at the doorway of the house. They raise akash banti, or sky lamps, on tall bamboo poles at the edges of the paddy fields. They also say a quiet prayer to the goddess Lakshmi at home, asking for a good harvest to come.
festivals.local: In many villages, the only visible sign of the festival is a farmer walking alone along the field paths at dusk, lighting akash banti lamp poles one by one. There is no music and no crowd expected, and that quietness is exactly the point.
festivals.image: Rows of small earthen lamps along a paddy field bund at dusk

festivals.name: Ambubachi Mela
festivals.reach: Ambubachi Mela draws pilgrims, sadhus, and tantric practitioners from across eastern India and beyond.
festivals.what: Ambubachi Mela is the yearly festival of the Kamakhya temple on Nilachal Hill. It is built around the belief that the goddess goes through her menstrual cycle during these days, so the inner sanctum is closed for three days and then reopened.
festivals.who: Shakta and tantric pilgrims, Assamese Hindu devotees, and sadhus from across India take part, many of them camping on the hill for the whole festival.
festivals.when: Ambubachi Mela lasts four days around the summer solstice, usually in mid-June. The temple stays closed for the middle three days and reopens on the fourth.
festivals.origin: Kamakhya has long been known as a seat of the goddess's power to create life, and this idea is written about in old Shakta and tantric texts from medieval times. However, nobody can say exactly how far back the specific belief about the goddess's menstrual cycle and the temple closing goes in its present form.
festivals.signifies: Ambubachi Mela treats fertility and creation as something to be honored openly through the body, instead of being treated as something impure that should be hidden away.
festivals.beliefs: People believe the temple doors are shut because the goddess is going through her monthly cycle. When the temple reopens, red cloth is handed out, and people treasure it as prasad, a blessed gift, that carries this fertility forward.
festivals.celebrate: Large numbers of sadhus and ascetics camp on Nilachal Hill during the closure. Chanting and rituals continue through the nights. On the fourth day, the temple reopens and red angabastra cloth is given out as prasad. A big fair with many stalls also fills the approach to the temple.
festivals.local: The line that forms outside Kamakhya on the morning the temple reopens is mainly there for the red cloth, not just to see the goddess. Regular visitors plan their whole trip around getting a piece of it.
festivals.image: Pilgrims and sadhus camped on Nilachal Hill outside Kamakhya temple, monsoon cloud

festivals.name: Durga Puja
festivals.reach: Durga Puja is celebrated widely in Guwahati and in district towns, alongside Assam's older tradition of household Durga worship.
festivals.what: Durga Puja is five days of worshipping the goddess Durga. In Guwahati especially, it has taken on the large pandal, or decorated stage, culture that is more commonly linked to neighboring Bengal, and this sits on top of Assam's own older Shakta worship tradition.
festivals.who: Assamese and Bengali Hindu households celebrate Durga Puja, and because of the public pandals, much of Guwahati joins in no matter what their background is.
festivals.when: Durga Puja takes place during the bright half of the lunar month of Ashwin, from the sixth day, called Shashthi, through the tenth day, called Dashami.
festivals.origin: Assam already had its own long-standing Durga worship, connected to its Shakta temple tradition centered on Kamakhya. The large public pandal style of celebration grew through the twentieth century as Guwahati grew bigger and welcomed more Bengali migration and influence.
festivals.signifies: Durga Puja marks the goddess's visit to earth and her later departure. Here, this story sits alongside a state that already follows its own Shakta religious calendar closely all year, especially at Kamakhya.
festivals.beliefs: At the end of the five days, people carry the clay images of the goddess to the Brahmaputra river and place them in the water. This returns the clay material to the river instead of keeping it.
festivals.celebrate: People go pandal-hopping through Guwahati's neighborhoods to see the different decorated stages. Sandhi Puja is held at the exact meeting point of the eighth and ninth days. Sindoor Khela, where married women smear each other with red vermillion powder, takes place on the tenth day. Immersion processions then head to the city's Brahmaputra ghats, the steps leading down to the river.
festivals.local: On immersion evening, most of Guwahati heads down to the very same stretch of riverbank at the same time. The ghats were never built to handle that many people, but somehow they manage it every single year.
festivals.image: Durga idol immersion procession at a Brahmaputra ghat, Guwahati, evening

festivals.name: Eid al-Fitr
festivals.reach: Eid al-Fitr is a major festival across Assam, which has one of the largest Muslim populations of any Indian state by share of people.
festivals.what: Eid al-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan. It is celebrated by Assamese-speaking Muslim communities in Lower Assam and by Bengali-speaking Muslim communities in the Barak Valley.
festivals.who: Asomiya Muslim communities live mostly in Dhubri, Barpeta, Goalpara, and other districts of Lower Assam, and Bengali-speaking Muslim communities live in the Barak Valley to the south.
festivals.when: Eid al-Fitr falls on the first day of the Islamic month of Shawwal, which moves about eleven days earlier each year compared to the regular calendar.
festivals.origin: Islam first came to the Brahmaputra valley through trade and through the eastward spread of the Delhi Sultanate, followed by centuries of Bengali-speaking people moving into the valley. The Assamese Muslim community's language and identity are old and rooted in the region, not something recently brought in.
festivals.signifies: Eid al-Fitr marks the end of the fast. In river-island villages, the shared meal that follows is arranged around the Brahmaputra river's own changing moods and seasons.
festivals.beliefs: Before the Eid prayer, people give zakat al-fitr, a required charity payment, and the exact date of Eid is only confirmed the night before, once the new moon has actually been sighted, just as it is in Muslim communities elsewhere.
festivals.celebrate: People gather for Eid prayers at large eidgahs, open prayer grounds, and at smaller village grounds. At home, families eat sewai and other sweets, wear new clothes, and spend the afternoon visiting friends and relatives.
festivals.local: In Lower Assam's char villages, which are built on shifting river islands, the eidgah can be the only patch of ground that is not underwater for half the year. Because of this, where the prayer is actually held can change almost as often as the river itself does.
festivals.image: Eid prayer congregation at a riverside eidgah, Lower Assam char village

festivals.name: Bwisagu
festivals.season: Start of Bohag, the Bodo new year
festivals.reach: Bwisagu is kept across Bodo-majority areas of the Bodoland Territorial Region and in other Bodo settlements throughout Assam.
festivals.what: Bwisagu is the Bodo new year. It falls at the same solar turning point as Bihu, but it is celebrated as its own separate festival, with its own order of days.
festivals.who: Bodo households celebrate Bwisagu. The Bodo are the largest indigenous community living in the plains of Assam.
festivals.when: Bwisagu begins with the mid-April solar turning point, called Sankranti, and lasts about a week. This is the same solar moment celebrated elsewhere as Bihu and Baisakhi.
festivals.origin: Bwisagu is an old Bodo farming new year, timed to the same solar calendar as Assam's Bihu, but it is kept under Bodo customs with its own order of ceremonies: cattle first, then people, then the gods.
festivals.signifies: Bwisagu marks a fresh start. It is deliberately arranged so that the animals that worked the land all year are thanked before the human celebrations begin.
festivals.beliefs: Households that follow Bathouism, the traditional Bodo faith centered on the sijou plant kept at a household altar, treat the new year ceremonies as simply a continuation of the worship they already do at home all year round, not as a separate event.
festivals.celebrate: On the first day, called Makhau, people bathe their cattle in the river and feed them rice beer and vegetables. On the day called Mansi, households worship at their altar and share a feast. Throughout the week, people play the sifung flute and the serja fiddle, and women perform the Bagurumba dance wearing traditional dokhona clothing.
festivals.local: The sijou plant, a type of Euphorbia kept in a fixed corner of the courtyard, is the one household marker that stays in place all year round, not just during the festival. Whether a family has one or not tells you what faith they follow before anyone says a single word.
festivals.image: Bwisagu dancers with sifung flutes in a Bodoland village courtyard

festivals.name: Christmas
festivals.reach: Christmas is an important festival among Assam's smaller Christian population, which is concentrated in the hills and in the tea garden areas.
festivals.what: Christmas is celebrated among Assam's Karbi and Dimasa Christian communities in the hills, and among Adivasi tea garden communities whose ancestors converted to Christianity over generations of working on tea plantations.
festivals.who: Karbi and Dimasa Christians from Karbi Anglong and Dima Hasao celebrate Christmas, along with tea garden communities of Adivasi descent and older Assamese Christian congregations that trace back to nineteenth-century missionary work.
festivals.when: Christmas falls on 25 December, and church services run from Advent all the way into the new year.
festivals.origin: American Baptist and other Christian missions reached the Assam hills in the nineteenth century, as part of the same wave of missionary work that shaped Christianity in neighboring Nagaland and Meghalaya. The conversions among tea garden communities happened later and separately, tied to the migrant labor communities that the tea plantations had brought in.
festivals.signifies: Christmas celebrates the birth of Jesus. For tea garden Christians, it is also a marker of a community history that is distinct from the surrounding Hindu and Muslim communities of the plains.
festivals.beliefs: Congregations in the hills generally keep their Christmas observance plain and centered on church services, which fits with the Baptist missions that first built these churches.
festivals.celebrate: People sing carols, attend church services on Christmas Eve and Christmas morning, share community feasts, and give gifts in Karbi and Dimasa households.
festivals.local: Tea garden Christmas services are often held partly in Sadri, the common language of Assam's Adivasi plantation communities, alongside Assamese. This detail shows the festival's roots in migrant labor history just as clearly as anything else about it.
festivals.image: Christmas eve service at a small church in the Karbi hills, lanterns outside

name: Meghalaya
tagline: Meghalaya is a hill state in northeastern India, and most of its people are Christian. Even so, two older traditions still shape daily life there: families pass down property and belonging through mothers rather than fathers, a system called matrilineal inheritance, and many people still follow the old Khasi and Garo festival calendars alongside their Christian faith.

festivals.name: Wangala
festivals.reach: Wangala is celebrated most strongly in the Garo Hills around Tura, and Garo communities keep it across Meghalaya.
festivals.what: Wangala is the Garo people's thanksgiving festival held after the harvest. Its biggest version is a gathering with a hundred drums at Chibragre near Tura, though individual villages also hold their own smaller wangala celebrations at slightly different times during the season.
festivals.who: The Garo people, who are also called the A'chik, celebrate Wangala.
festivals.when: The main hundred-drum event happens in the second week of November, but village-level celebrations take place from October through November as each community finishes its own harvest.
festivals.origin: Wangala began as a thanksgiving to Misi Saljong, the sun god of fertility, marking the end of the jhum farming cycle and settled farming for the year. Bringing everyone together for one big hundred-drum event at a single location is a twentieth-century change. Originally, these were separate rituals held village by village.
festivals.signifies: Wangala expresses gratitude to Misi Saljong for the harvest, given before the community allows itself to freely eat and enjoy what has been grown.
festivals.beliefs: Households that follow Songsarek, the traditional Garo faith, begin the season with the Ragula ceremony. Rice beer is offered and prayers are spoken quietly inside the Nokma's house before the wider public dancing starts.
festivals.celebrate: Long, oval wooden drums called dama are played together in large groups. Dancers wear feathered headgear and traditional dress. The community shares a feast, and craft and produce stalls come in from across the Garo Hills.
festivals.local: The rhythms played on the dama drums are matched to specific moments in the ceremony, and older Nokmas, or village chiefs, can name exactly which rhythm belongs to which moment. This detail tends to get lost when the massed public performance at Chibragre blends everything into one continuous sound.
festivals.image: Massed dama drummers in feathered headgear at Wangala, near Tura

festivals.name: Shad Suk Mynsiem
festivals.aliases: Dance of the Joyful Hearts, Ka Shad Suk Mynsiem
festivals.reach: Shad Suk Mynsiem is centered on Shillong, and Khasi communities across the state celebrate it.
festivals.what: Shad Suk Mynsiem is a three-day Khasi thanksgiving dance held once the spring planting is finished. It thanks the gods for the season that has passed and asks for their blessing on the season ahead.
festivals.who: Khasi households who follow Niam Khasi, the indigenous Khasi faith, celebrate Shad Suk Mynsiem.
festivals.when: Shad Suk Mynsiem lasts three days in April, right after the spring planting season.
festivals.origin: Shad Suk Mynsiem is an old Khasi thanksgiving dance connected to the farming calendar. Its current public form, held at Shillong's Ward's Lake grounds, took shape over the later colonial period and after India's independence.
festivals.signifies: Shad Suk Mynsiem expresses gratitude for the season and a hope for peace and prosperity ahead, expressed through dance rather than through words.
festivals.beliefs: In the dance, unmarried women move slowly at the center while men circle around them holding swords and whisks made of yak hair. Locally, people read this as a symbol of harmony between men and women, rather than as men protecting the women.
festivals.celebrate: The dance runs for three days at Ward's Lake. Women wear jainsem silk clothing and a headdress called a dumper, while men wear a traditional turban and carry a sword and a whisk. Musicians play the tangmuri, a wind instrument, along with drums and the duitara, a stringed instrument.
festivals.local: The women dance almost perfectly still, keeping their eyes lowered, while the men circling them move faster and faster as the piece goes on. When Khasi people talk about the dance, they almost always focus on this contrast rather than on the music itself.
festivals.image: Khasi dancers at Shad Suk Mynsiem, Ward's Lake grounds, Shillong

festivals.name: Behdienkhlam
festivals.reach: Behdienkhlam is centered on Jowai, and the Pnar people of the Jaintia Hills keep it.
festivals.what: Behdienkhlam is a four-day Pnar monsoon ritual meant to drive away disease, historically understood to mean cholera, and to protect the season's crops.
festivals.who: The Pnar people, also called the Jaintia, celebrate Behdienkhlam, and they follow the Niamtre faith.
festivals.when: Behdienkhlam lasts four days in July, timed to the end of the planting season.
festivals.origin: The name Behdienkhlam comes from Pnar words meaning to drive away plague using sticks. Its current four-day form, centered on Jowai, has been recorded throughout both the colonial period and the years since India's independence.
festivals.signifies: Behdienkhlam is a communal effort to clean out illness and misfortune, driven away by force, so the crops can then grow undisturbed.
festivals.beliefs: Food offered to the ancestors is prepared and handled by women, who by custom do not join in the dancing itself. This division of roles is treated as a fixed rule rather than something incidental.
festivals.celebrate: People beat wooden rats, which represent the plague, through the streets with sticks. Teams of men haul tall wooden poles called Khnong through mud pits. At the end, people play Dad Lawakor, a ritual form of football.
festivals.local: Hauling the Khnong pole through the mud pit is genuinely dangerous, and everyone knows it. Injuries are expected rather than seen as unusual, and how well the pole performs is part of how people judge the whole year's festival.
festivals.image: Khnong pole hauled through a mud pit at Behdienkhlam, Jowai

festivals.name: Nongkrem Dance
festivals.reach: Nongkrem Dance is centered on Smit, the traditional seat of the Hima Khyrim near Shillong.
festivals.what: Nongkrem Dance is a five-day religious festival of the Hima Khyrim, a Khasi kingdom. It thanks the goddess Ka Blei Synshar for the harvest, and through the same ceremony, it renews the standing of the Syiem, the traditional ruler.
festivals.who: The Khasi Hima Khyrim kingdom, its Syiem or ruler, priestly households, and Khasi people more broadly all take part in the Nongkrem Dance.
festivals.when: Nongkrem Dance lasts five days in November, with the exact dates set by the Hima's own calendar.
festivals.origin: Nongkrem Dance is a thanksgiving tied to the Khyrim kingdom's own worship of its guardian deity and its ruling family's ancestor rituals. It is distinct from, though related to, the other harvest festivals of the Khasi Hills.
festivals.signifies: Nongkrem Dance ties together thanks for the harvest with the ongoing legitimacy of the Syiem's rule, and the whole Hima, or kingdom, prays together for this.
festivals.beliefs: Goats are ceremonially sacrificed, called Pomblang, before the dancing begins. The Hima Khyrim considers this offering necessary both for giving thanks for the harvest and for honoring the ruling family's ancestors.
festivals.celebrate: The festival includes the Pomblang sacrifice, and Ka Shad Mastieh, in which men dance holding swords and yak-hair whisks. Unmarried women dance at the center wearing silver ornaments that have been passed down through their families for generations. Days of feasting follow at Smit.
festivals.local: The silver ornaments worn by the dancing women are heirloom pieces that belong to specific families. Because of this, which family's jewelry appears each year is itself a small event that people watch closely.
festivals.image: Khasi dancers at Ka Pomblang Nongkrem, Smit, silver ornaments and swords

festivals.name: Seng Kut Snem
festivals.reach: Seng Kut Snem is kept by Khasi communities around Shillong and in other Khasi-populated areas of Meghalaya.
festivals.what: Seng Kut Snem is the foundation day of the Seng Khasi, an organization set up to give Niam Khasi, the traditional Khasi faith, an organized standing against the growth of Christian missionary activity in the nineteenth century.
festivals.who: The Seng Khasi organization and Khasi families who mark the day through it celebrate Seng Kut Snem.
festivals.when: Seng Kut Snem falls on 23 November every year.
festivals.origin: The Seng Khasi organization was founded in 1899 as a direct response to the growth of Christian missionary work in the Khasi Hills. It was meant to give the indigenous faith and its institutions, such as schools and public presence, the same organized footing that the missions already had.
festivals.signifies: Seng Kut Snem represents the ongoing continuity of Khasi custom and language on its own terms, kept separate from both the Christian missions and the government.
festivals.beliefs: Members believe that the founding of the Seng Khasi gave Niam Khasi the standing needed to be practiced openly and taught formally, rather than treating the faith as something that could only be quietly preserved in private, unchanged.
festivals.celebrate: The day includes processions in traditional Khasi dress, folk dance and song competitions, a fair with handicraft and produce stalls, and formal speeches marking the organization's founding.
festivals.local: People treat this date less like a folk festival and more like an institutional anniversary, closer in feeling to a foundation day than to a harvest celebration. In fact, Seng Khasi members themselves describe it in exactly those terms.
festivals.image: Seng Kut Snem procession in traditional Khasi dress, Shillong

festivals.name: Christmas
festivals.reach: Christmas is the single largest festival in Meghalaya, a state where roughly three out of every four people are Christian.
festivals.what: Christmas is Meghalaya's central annual holiday. Meghalaya is one of only three states in India where most people are Christian.
festivals.who: Presbyterian, Catholic, and Baptist congregations, the three largest Christian groups among Khasi and Garo people, celebrate Christmas, along with smaller Anglican and other Protestant communities.
festivals.when: Christmas falls on 25 December, and markets and church services run from early December through the new year.
festivals.origin: Welsh Presbyterian missionaries first reached the Khasi Hills in 1841. American Baptists began working in the Garo Hills in the 1860s and 1870s, and Catholic missionaries arrived starting in the 1890s. Within a few generations, conversion across both hill peoples was mostly complete.
festivals.signifies: For most people in the state, Christmas is simply the year's biggest holiday, not a small observance layered onto a different religious majority.
festivals.beliefs: Most congregations here consider Easter more important than Christmas in terms of religious meaning, but Christmas remains by far the bigger public and family celebration.
festivals.celebrate: Shillong's Police Bazar and Laitumkhrah neighborhoods are lit up and crowded throughout December. Carol services are sung in Khasi and Garo hymns. Families gather for feasts and give gifts, and star-shaped lanterns hang outside homes and churches.
festivals.local: Shillong's Christmas lights and busy markets feel like a citywide event rather than something limited to church calendars, more similar to how a Hindu-majority Indian city treats Diwali than to how Christmas is usually celebrated elsewhere in the country.
festivals.image: Police Bazar Christmas lights and crowds, Shillong, December evening

festivals.name: Easter
festivals.reach: Easter is kept across Meghalaya's Christian congregations, among both Khasi and Garo communities.
festivals.what: Easter is the most important event of the Christian religious year in Meghalaya. Most congregations consider it more important than Christmas in religious terms, even though Christmas draws the bigger public crowd.
festivals.who: Presbyterian, Catholic, and Baptist congregations across the state celebrate Easter.
festivals.when: Easter falls on the Sunday after the first full moon following the spring equinox, so it lands in either March or April.
festivals.origin: Easter follows the general Christian dating and traditions brought by nineteenth-century missionaries, and it is celebrated in Khasi and Garo hymns alongside English ones.
festivals.signifies: Easter celebrates the resurrection of Jesus. Most denominations here treat it as the true religious center of the year, rather than just a lead-up to Christmas.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that Good Friday's solemn, often fasting-filled mood cannot be separated from the celebration on Easter Sunday. One is considered incomplete without the other.
festivals.celebrate: Churches hold solemn Good Friday services and joyful Easter Sunday services with singing in Khasi and Garo. Families gather afterward for meals together.
festivals.local: Presbyterian churches, the oldest mission institution in the hills, generally keep the plainest Holy Week services. This is different from the more elaborate Catholic parish processions found in the very same towns.
festivals.image: Easter Sunday congregation outside a Presbyterian church, Khasi Hills

name: Tripura
tagline: Tripura used to be its own kingdom ruled by a king before it joined India. Since then, large numbers of Bengali refugees have settled there and now make up most of the population, but nineteen different indigenous tribal communities still live there too, each keeping its own gods and traditions.

festivals.name: Kharchi Puja
festivals.aliases: Puja of Fourteen Gods, Chaturdasha Devata Puja
festivals.season: Eighth day of the waning moon
festivals.reach: Kharchi Puja is the state's largest single religious festival. It is centered on Agartala but observed all across the state.
festivals.what: Kharchi Puja is a week-long worship of the Chaturdasha Devata, a group of fourteen deities that blend the old Tripuri royal family's own gods with the wider Hindu pantheon. It is held at their temple in Old Agartala.
festivals.who: Bengali Hindu and Tripuri communities worship together at the Chaturdasha Devata temple during Kharchi Puja.
festivals.when: Kharchi Puja lasts a week, beginning on the eighth day of the waning moon, usually in July.
festivals.origin: The Chaturdasha Devata temple was built in 1761 under King Krishna Manikya, though the fourteen deities themselves are older. They came together from a blending of Tripuri royal worship with the wider Hindu pantheon over an earlier period that is less precisely documented.
festivals.signifies: Kharchi Puja is about purification. The word Kharchi roughly means cleaning away sin, and this cleansing is done together as a community, on behalf of the whole kingdom, rather than privately at home.
festivals.beliefs: People believe the fourteen deities need a ritual bath in the nearby river before the year's worship can properly begin, so each year they are carried there for exactly that purpose.
festivals.celebrate: The fourteen deities are carried to the river for a ceremonial bath. A week of worship follows at the temple, along with a large fair where tribal and Bengali stalls sit side by side, and folk and classical performances continue throughout the week.
festivals.local: The temple does not keep a human-shaped image for several of the fourteen deities. Instead, it worships them as symbolic wooden or metal objects, which sets Kharchi Puja apart from most Bengali temple worship nearby.
festivals.image: Fourteen deities carried for their ritual river bath, Old Agartala

festivals.name: Ker Puja
festivals.reach: Ker Puja is centered on the old royal palace area in Agartala.
festivals.what: Ker Puja is a two-and-a-half-day ritual held around the old royal palace. It worships Ker, the guardian deity of boundaries, asking for the protection of the whole state.
festivals.who: The palace priesthood and the residents living within the marked boundary take part in Ker Puja, acting on behalf of the whole state.
festivals.when: Ker Puja lasts two and a half days, roughly two weeks after Kharchi Puja.
festivals.origin: Ker Puja is a royal-era Tripuri ritual going back to the Manikya dynasty's worship of Ker, protector against disaster and guardian of a defined boundary.
festivals.signifies: Ker Puja represents a boundary that is drawn and defended, with protection sought for the state as a whole rather than for individual households.
festivals.beliefs: No one is allowed to cross the bamboo boundary marking Ker's protected ground while the puja is happening. This rule is still followed by tradition around the palace area.
festivals.celebrate: People build a large, bent bamboo structure to represent Ker. The head priest, called the chantai, takes on the ceremonial role of a king for the duration of the festival, and offerings are made for the well-being of every community and tribe in the state.
festivals.local: The puja is still partly funded by the state government, which continues an obligation from the days of the kingdom. This is one of the few such traditions in Tripura that was never fully broken after the monarchy ended.
festivals.image: Bamboo Ker structure at the old royal palace precinct, Agartala

festivals.name: Garia Puja
festivals.season: Seven days from the first of Boishakh
festivals.reach: Garia Puja is kept across Tripuri, Reang, Jamatia, and Noatia communities throughout the state.
festivals.what: Garia Puja is a seven-day tribal harvest ritual honoring Baba Garia, the deity of livestock, crops, and household prosperity.
festivals.who: Kokborok-speaking communities celebrate Garia Puja, most prominently the Tripuri, Reang, Jamatia, and Noatia households.
festivals.when: Garia Puja lasts seven days, beginning on the first day of the month of Boishakh, in mid-April.
festivals.origin: Garia Puja is an old farming ritual honoring a deity that belongs specifically to Tripura's Kokborok-speaking tribes. It runs alongside the state's Bengali Hindu festival calendar rather than coming from it.
festivals.signifies: Garia Puja asks for prosperity and protection for the coming farming year from a deity that belongs specifically to these communities.
festivals.beliefs: People worship a bamboo pole, dressed up and decorated with garlands, directly as the deity itself, rather than using any separate image or statue.
festivals.celebrate: People raise the bamboo pole and worship it with flowers. The community dances and sings across all seven days, and a shared feast closes the celebration.
festivals.local: The week that ends Garia Puja leads directly into the festival of Buisu, so in Tripuri villages, the two festivals feel like one continuous April season rather than two separate events.
festivals.image: Bamboo Garia pole garlanded and worshipped, Tripuri village

festivals.name: Buisu
festivals.aliases: Baisuk, shared with Chakma Biju and Marma Sangrai
festivals.reach: Buisu is kept across Tripuri, Chakma, Marma, Tangchangya, and other indigenous communities of Tripura.
festivals.what: Buisu is a three-day spring new year celebration kept under different names by different communities on the very same days: it is called Baisuk by the Tripuri, Biju by the Chakma, and Sangrai by the Marma.
festivals.who: Tripuri, Chakma, Marma, and Tangchangya households each celebrate their own version of the same three days.
festivals.when: Buisu lasts three days, from around 12 to 15 April. This is the same solar new year shared with Bihu, Baisakhi, and several related festivals across the borderlands of Southeast Asia.
festivals.origin: Buisu is a shared regional new year tradition celebrated by several communities across Tripura, Bangladesh, and Myanmar's borderlands. Nobody has documented its exact common root, though the shared mid-April timing itself is very old.
festivals.signifies: Buisu represents the old year being cleaned out, both literally and ritually, before the new year is allowed to come in.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that flowers offered to the river on the first day carry away the old year's bad luck along with the current.
festivals.celebrate: On Phul Biju, people make floral offerings to the river and to household deities. Mul Biju is the central day, filled with feasting, singing, and the Bizu dance. On the closing day, people visit their elders for a shared meal.
festivals.local: On Mul Biju, households try to cook an unusually large number of different vegetable dishes. Locally, people see this as a wish for variety and plenty in the coming year, not simply as ordinary feasting.
festivals.image: Floral offerings laid at a riverbank on Phul Biju morning, Tripura

festivals.name: Durga Puja
festivals.reach: Durga Puja is celebrated across the state, especially in Agartala and in Bengali-majority districts.
festivals.what: Durga Puja is five days of goddess worship centered around large decorated stages called pandals. It became widely practiced in Tripura's public life through the Bengali Hindu population, which came to make up most of the state's people over the twentieth century.
festivals.who: Tripura's Bengali Hindu majority celebrates Durga Puja, and this majority was built up substantially through refugees moving in from East Pakistan and later Bangladesh.
festivals.when: Durga Puja takes place during the bright half of the lunar month of Ashwin, from Shashthi to Dashami.
festivals.origin: Durga Puja was brought into Tripura's public life by the waves of Bengali settlement that reshaped the state's population after 1947 and 1971. It was added on top of an already-existing royal-era Hindu festival calendar that included Durga worship at the palace.
festivals.signifies: Durga Puja marks the same story of the goddess's homecoming and farewell told across Bengali Durga Puja generally. Here it also carries the added weight of a displaced population's festival calendar taking root in a new home.
festivals.beliefs: At the close of the festival, the clay images are placed into the Haora or Gomati river, returning the material to the river rather than keeping it, following the same practice as in Bengal.
festivals.celebrate: Pandals go up across Agartala and the district towns. Immersion processions head to the Haora and Gomati rivers, Sindoor Khela is celebrated, and community feasting continues through all five days.
festivals.local: Agartala's puja organizing committees compete over theme and design much like Kolkata's do, though with smaller budgets. They still share the same appetite for building a pandal worth waiting in line to see.
festivals.image: Pandal-lined street in Agartala during Durga Puja, evening crowd

festivals.name: Kali Puja
festivals.reach: Kali Puja is celebrated widely across Bengali Hindu households throughout the state.
festivals.what: Kali Puja is a night festival honoring the goddess Kali, held on the same new-moon night that is celebrated elsewhere in India as Diwali. This follows Bengal's own preference for honoring the fiercer goddess Kali on this particular night.
festivals.who: Bengali Hindu households across Tripura celebrate Kali Puja.
festivals.when: Kali Puja falls on Kartik Amavasya, the new-moon night of the month of Kartik, in October or November.
festivals.origin: Kali Puja was brought into Tripura along with the wider Bengali Hindu festival calendar, carrying Bengal's particular devotion to Shakta and tantric worship on this night, rather than the Lakshmi-focused Diwali celebrated across most of India.
festivals.signifies: Kali Puja gives this night over to the fiercer form of the goddess, rather than focusing only on household prosperity.
festivals.beliefs: Worship takes place at midnight, and lamps are lit for ancestors the evening before, as a practice kept separate from the puja itself.
festivals.celebrate: People hold midnight puja ceremonies with hibiscus flower offerings, set off fireworks, and light lamps along streets and homes. Community pandals are also built, on a smaller scale than for Durga Puja but following the same style.
festivals.local: Agartala's Kali Puja pandals cluster in the older Bengali neighborhoods near the palace. They draw a much smaller crowd than Durga Puja does, but people still bring the same love for a striking, memorable image.
festivals.image: Midnight Kali Puja lamps and fireworks, Agartala neighbourhood

festivals.name: Eid al-Fitr
festivals.reach: Eid al-Fitr is an important festival among Tripura's Bengali Muslim minority, who are concentrated in the border districts near Bangladesh.
festivals.what: Eid al-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan. It is celebrated by a Bengali-speaking Muslim community that has long-standing family and trade ties across the nearby Bangladesh border.
festivals.who: Bengali-speaking Muslim communities celebrate Eid al-Fitr, making up roughly a tenth of the state's population.
festivals.when: Eid al-Fitr falls on the first day of the Islamic month of Shawwal, moving each year according to the Hijri lunar calendar.
festivals.origin: Islam's presence in Tripura is closely tied to the wider settlement of Bengali Muslims that shaped the whole region, and it was reinforced by the state's long, historically easy-to-cross border with what is now Bangladesh.
festivals.signifies: Eid al-Fitr marks the end of the fast. Locally, it is also a day that draws heavily on family ties that stretch across the border, just as much as it draws on the religious calendar.
festivals.beliefs: People give zakat al-fitr, a required charity payment, before the Eid prayer, and the exact date is only confirmed once the new moon is sighted the night before.
festivals.celebrate: People attend Eid prayers at Agartala's mosques and at district eidgahs. At home, they eat sewai and biryani, wear new clothes, and spend the afternoon visiting others.
festivals.local: Families in the border districts often exchange visits and small gifts with relatives across the frontier in the days around Eid, a rhythm shaped as much by the easy-to-cross border as by the religious calendar itself.
festivals.image: Eid prayer congregation outside a mosque in Agartala

festivals.name: Christmas
festivals.reach: Christmas is an important festival among Tripura's Christian tribal minority, and it is strongest among the Kuki and Halam communities.
festivals.what: Christmas is celebrated among Tripura's tribal Christian minority, but how many people celebrate it varies sharply from community to community. It is celebrated by nearly everyone in Kuki households, by roughly half of Halam households, and by smaller numbers of Tripuri and Reang households.
festivals.who: Kuki communities, where conversion to Christianity is now nearly complete, celebrate Christmas, along with roughly half of Halam communities and smaller shares of Tripuri and Reang households.
festivals.when: Christmas falls on 25 December.
festivals.origin: Christian missions, mostly Baptist, worked in the Tripura hills throughout the twentieth century, following lines similar to the neighboring Lushai and Naga Hills. Conversion was concentrated in specific tribes rather than spread evenly across the state's nineteen recognized tribal communities.
festivals.signifies: For these communities, Christmas is the year's most important Christian holiday. In a Hindu-majority state, it is also a marker of a distinct tribal and religious identity.
festivals.beliefs: Baptist congregations here generally keep the focus on the church service and sermon rather than on elaborate ritual, a style that can be traced directly back to the original missions.
festivals.celebrate: People attend church services, sing carols, share community feasts in tribal Christian villages, and give gifts.
festivals.local: The sharp difference in conversion rates between neighboring tribes, nearly complete in Kuki villages and much lower in Tripuri villages right next door, is easy to see just by looking at which villages put up a lit-up church at Christmas and which do not.
festivals.image: A lit church in a Kuki village in the Tripura hills, Christmas Eve

name: Manipur
tagline: Manipur's central valley is home to the Meitei people, who mostly follow Vaishnava Hinduism. The valley is surrounded by hills where Naga and Kuki-Zo communities live, and most of those hill communities follow their own, mostly Christian, calendar of festivals instead.

festivals.name: Sajibu Cheiraoba
festivals.aliases: Sajibu Nongma Panba, Meitei New Year
festivals.reach: Sajibu Cheiraoba is celebrated across the Imphal valley by Meitei households.
festivals.what: Sajibu Cheiraoba is the Meitei new year. It begins with a thorough cleaning of the whole house and a family feast that is first offered at the household shrine.
festivals.who: Meitei households celebrate Sajibu Cheiraoba. They follow Sanamahism, the indigenous Meitei faith, often alongside Vaishnava Hindu practice.
festivals.when: Sajibu Cheiraoba falls on the first day of the lunar month of Sajibu, usually in late March or early April.
festivals.origin: Sajibu Cheiraoba is an old Meitei new year tied to the indigenous Sanamahi calendar. It was celebrated separately from, and existed before, the Vaishnava Hindu practices that spread through the valley starting in the eighteenth century.
festivals.signifies: Sajibu Cheiraoba treats a clean household and a clean year as one and the same undertaking.
festivals.beliefs: People offer seasonal fruits and vegetables to the deity Lainingthou Sanamahi at the household altar before the family eats, giving the deity the very first taste of the year.
festivals.celebrate: Houses and courtyards are cleaned thoroughly the day before. A family feast is offered first at the household shrine. In some households, family members climb a nearby hill on the day itself to look out over the valley.
festivals.local: The custom of climbing a nearby hill to look over the valley on New Year's morning is treated locally as much as a way of reading omens for the year ahead as it is simply an outing.
festivals.image: A Meitei family's New Year offering at a household Sanamahi altar, Imphal valley

festivals.name: Yaoshang
festivals.reach: Yaoshang is the valley's largest festival, and it is celebrated across Meitei Imphal for five days.
festivals.what: Yaoshang is a five-day spring festival that combines a Holika-style bonfire and color-throwing play with Thabal Chongba, a moonlit courtship dance that is its most famous feature.
festivals.who: Meitei households celebrate Yaoshang, and young people in particular take part through Thabal Chongba.
festivals.when: Yaoshang lasts five days starting from the full moon of the month of Lamta, in February or March.
festivals.origin: Yaoshang was layered onto an older Meitei spring ritual after Vaishnava Hinduism took hold in the valley starting in the eighteenth century. This is why a Holika bonfire and color play linked to the god Krishna now sit on top of what was already a seasonal festival.
festivals.signifies: Yaoshang celebrates renewal, and through Thabal Chongba, it allows courtship to happen openly and publicly in a way that is not normally allowed the rest of the year.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that burning the Yaoshang hut on the first night burns away the old year's bad luck along with it.
festivals.celebrate: A thatched hut called the Yaoshang hut is built and then burned at dawn on the first day. Gulal, colored powder, is thrown through the following days. Thabal Chongba circle dancing, once done strictly by moonlight, is now often held under electric lights on most nights of the festival. Traditional sports, including thouri and wrestling, are also played.
festivals.local: The shift of Thabal Chongba from moonlight to fluorescent-lit grounds on most nights of the festival is a change that older Meitei residents discuss openly, naming exactly what they feel has been lost and what has been gained because of it.
festivals.image: Thabal Chongba circle dance under lights, Imphal, Yaoshang night

festivals.name: Lai Haraoba
festivals.season: Varies by shrine, spring to early summer
festivals.reach: Lai Haraoba is kept at Umang Lai shrines across the Imphal valley, and each shrine follows its own local calendar.
festivals.what: Lai Haraoba is a ritual dance that re-enacts the Meitei creation myth. It is led by Maibi priestesses at shrines dedicated to the Umang Lai, the forest deities of the valley.
festivals.who: Meitei communities who follow Sanamahism take part in Lai Haraoba, organized around specific local deities and their own shrines.
festivals.when: Lai Haraoba has no single fixed date. Each of several hundred Umang Lai shrines sets its own days, most commonly sometime between February and June, with April and May being the busiest months.
festivals.origin: Lai Haraoba is one of the oldest continuously performed Meitei rituals. Locally, it is understood as a re-enactment of the creation of the world by Sanamahi and the other main deities. Its present-day choreography has been shaped over centuries by the Maibi priestesses who carry the tradition forward.
festivals.signifies: Lai Haraoba shows the gods enjoying themselves, and by extension, the community enjoying itself along with them. It is presented as an origin myth rather than as a request or plea to the gods.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that the Maibi priestesses actually channel the deities during key parts of the dance, rather than simply acting out a role that was written for them.
festivals.celebrate: The festival includes days of ritual dance re-enacting creation myths, led by Maibi priestesses, along with music played on the pena, a traditional stringed instrument. At some shrines there are also boat-race sequences, and offerings are made at the Umang Lai grove.
festivals.local: Because each shrine keeps its own calendar, some version of Lai Haraoba is happening somewhere in the valley during most weeks of the spring season, rather than on one single shared date the way most Indian festivals work.
festivals.image: Maibi priestesses dancing at an Umang Lai shrine, Lai Haraoba

festivals.name: Ningol Chakkouba
festivals.reach: Ningol Chakkouba is kept by Meitei households in the valley and by Meitei communities living in Assam, Bangladesh, and Myanmar.
festivals.what: Ningol Chakkouba is a family reunion day. On this day, married women, called ningol, are invited back to their parents' home for a hosted feast.
festivals.who: Meitei families celebrate Ningol Chakkouba, and it specifically involves married women and the families they were born into.
festivals.when: Ningol Chakkouba falls on the second day of the lunar month of Hiyangei, in October or November.
festivals.origin: Ningol Chakkouba is an old Meitei family custom that formally recognizes a married woman's continuing tie to the family she was born into. Nobody has recorded exactly how old the custom is, though locally people treat it as long-standing rather than as something recently invented.
festivals.signifies: Ningol Chakkouba represents a married daughter's ongoing claim on her parents' home, renewed once every year no matter how far away she has moved.
festivals.beliefs: People treat sending the invitation as a matter of honor for the parents' side of the family. If a married daughter is not invited for Ningol Chakkouba, people locally understand this as a sign that something has gone wrong within the family.
festivals.celebrate: Married women and their children travel, sometimes long distances, to their parents' home. A hosted feast follows, along with gifts and cash given by parents or brothers, and an afternoon spent visiting.
festivals.local: Women who cannot travel are increasingly sent gifts and called on the phone instead. Families and festival organizers now openly discuss this change as more and more Meitei people move away from the valley.
festivals.image: A Ningol Chakkouba family feast, Imphal household

festivals.name: Kut Festival
festivals.reach: Kut Festival is celebrated across the Kuki-Chin-Zomi hill communities of Manipur, and it is a declared state holiday.
festivals.what: Kut Festival is a harvest thanksgiving celebrated by the Kuki-Chin-Zomi hill communities. It has been brought together in its current form into one shared, statewide date.
festivals.who: Kuki, Zomi, and related Chin-Kuki-Mizo tribal communities of the hill districts celebrate Kut Festival.
festivals.when: Kut Festival falls on 1 November every year, a fixed date rather than one based on the lunar calendar.
festivals.origin: Separate village and clan harvest festivals, held under related names, were brought together into a single common date called Chavang Kut in the late twentieth century. This was a deliberate way of marking a shared Kuki-Zomi identity across many different clans.
festivals.signifies: Kut Festival gives thanks for the harvest, and in its unified modern form, it also represents a shared identity that holds together clans that otherwise keep quite different customs.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that rice beer, called ju, offered by the village priest must come before any private feasting, as an offering of thanks that is part of the harvest ritual itself, not something separate from it.
festivals.celebrate: A village priest offers ju after the harvest rituals are finished. The day also includes folk dance and singing competitions, traditional games and sports, and community feasting.
festivals.local: The fact that this day is now a state holiday, with offices and businesses closed across all of Manipur regardless of community, is still a fairly recent piece of recognition for the hill districts, and people openly note this.
festivals.image: Kut Festival dancers in traditional dress, Churachandpur

festivals.name: Sangai Festival
festivals.reach: Sangai Festival is a tourism festival organized by the state government and held across Manipur, centered on Imphal and Moirang.
festivals.what: Sangai Festival is a ten-day state tourism showcase named after the Sangai, an endangered deer with branching antlers that is found only in Manipur. It brings together crafts, sports, and performances from across the state.
festivals.who: Manipur's government tourism department organizes Sangai Festival, with performers and vendors coming from Meitei, Naga, and Kuki-Zo communities across the state.
festivals.when: Sangai Festival runs for ten days, from 21 to 30 November.
festivals.origin: Sangai Festival was launched in 2010 as a deliberate showcase built to attract visitors from outside the state, rather than growing out of an older local tradition. It is named after a deer that is found nowhere else in the world.
festivals.signifies: Sangai Festival is an official effort to present Manipur's full range of communities on one shared platform, even though the state's actual social divisions are considerable.
festivals.beliefs: There is no religious belief attached to the festival itself. Its organizers describe it plainly as a promotional event rather than a ritual, which makes it different from every other festival on this list.
festivals.celebrate: The festival includes handicraft and food stalls from across the state, demonstrations of indigenous sports and martial arts, music and dance performed by Meitei, Naga, and Kuki-Zo performers, and adventure sports on Loktak Lake.
festivals.local: Moirang, one of the two host towns, is also the place where the Indian National Army is believed to have raised its flag in 1944. The festival's program touches on this history alongside its crafts and music.
festivals.image: Craft stalls and performers at the Sangai Festival, Imphal

festivals.name: Christmas
festivals.reach: Christmas is the central festival across Manipur's Naga and Kuki-Zo hill districts, though it has a much smaller presence in the Meitei valley.
festivals.what: Christmas is celebrated in Manipur's hill districts, which are overwhelmingly Christian, in contrast to the largely Hindu Meitei valley below.
