festivals.who: Naga and Kuki-Zo Christian communities of the hill districts celebrate Christmas, most of them Baptist, along with smaller Catholic and other Protestant congregations.
festivals.when: Christmas falls on 25 December.
festivals.origin: American Baptist missions worked in the Naga and Kuki-Zo hills of Manipur through the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries, part of the same missionary wave that shaped neighboring Nagaland and Mizoram. Conversion in these communities is now nearly complete.
festivals.signifies: Christmas is the year's central holiday for a large share of the state's population, and it also marks a religious line that roughly follows the divide between the hills and the valley.
festivals.beliefs: For most of these congregations, Baptist practice keeps the focus on the church service and sermon rather than on elaborate ritual, a style that traces directly back to the original American Baptist missions.
festivals.celebrate: Church services and carol singing take place across hill towns such as Churachandpur, Ukhrul, and Senapati. Communities share feasts, decorate their town centers, and give gifts.
festivals.local: Lit-up crosses and church spires on the hillsides are a distinctive sight on the drive between Imphal and any of the surrounding hill towns in December. Locally, this visual marker of the divide between valley and hills needs no explanation.
festivals.image: A decorated church in a Kuki hill town, Manipur, Christmas Eve

festivals.name: Eid al-Fitr
festivals.reach: Eid al-Fitr is an important festival among the Meitei Pangal, Manipur's Meitei-speaking Muslim community, who are concentrated in the valley.
festivals.what: Eid al-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan. It is celebrated by the Meitei Pangal, a Sunni Muslim community that speaks Meiteilon and is the second-largest community in the Imphal valley after the Hindu Meitei.
festivals.who: The Meitei Pangal celebrate Eid al-Fitr. They speak Meiteilon as their mother tongue and share much of the valley's everyday customs with their Hindu Meitei neighbors.
festivals.when: Eid al-Fitr falls on the first day of the Islamic month of Shawwal, moving each year according to the Hijri calendar.
festivals.origin: The Meitei Pangal settled in the valley during the reign of King Khagemba in the early seventeenth century, an event recorded in the Manipuri royal chronicles. This makes them one of the older Muslim communities in Northeast India.
festivals.signifies: Eid al-Fitr marks the end of the fast, celebrated by a community that shares much of its language and daily customs with its Hindu Meitei neighbors, even though their religion is different.
festivals.beliefs: People give zakat al-fitr, a required charity payment, before the Eid prayer, just as in Sunni Muslim communities elsewhere.
festivals.celebrate: People attend Eid prayers at mosques across the valley, eat sewai and Manipuri-style biryani, wear new clothes, and visit both Pangal and Meitei neighbors.
festivals.local: Imphal's Muslim neighborhoods hold their own Eid market and food stalls in the days before the festival. These markets are smaller than the city's main bazaars, but just as busy that week.
festivals.image: Eid prayer congregation at a Pangal mosque, Imphal valley

name: Nagaland
languages: English (official), various Naga languages (Ao, Angami, Sumi, Konyak, Lotha and others), Nagamese as a lingua franca
tagline: Nagaland is home to sixteen major tribes, and each one keeps its own festival calendar. Even so, almost every tribe's community life centers around a church, because most people in Nagaland are Christian.

festivals.name: Hornbill Festival
festivals.reach: The state government organizes this festival, and it draws all the major Naga tribes together along with visitors from across India and other countries.
festivals.what: The Hornbill Festival is a ten-day showcase held at Kisama Heritage Village, just outside Kohima. Each of Nagaland's recognized tribes sets up its own morung, which is a traditional tribal house, and performs its own dances, songs, and rituals there. Normally each tribe would celebrate on its own separate calendar, but during this festival they all perform together on one shared calendar.
festivals.who: All of the state's major tribes take part, including the Angami, Ao, Sumi, Konyak, Lotha, Chakhesang, and others. Each tribe has its own morung to represent it, and large crowds of visitors come to watch as well.
festivals.when: It happens every year from December 1st to December 10th at Kisama, which is about twelve kilometers from Kohima.
festivals.origin: The state government started the festival in the year 2000. Its goal was to bring all the different tribal festivals, which normally happen on different dates throughout the year, together into one shared event. The festival is named after the hornbill, a bird that appears often in Naga folklore and is used to decorate traditional Naga headgear.
festivals.signifies: The festival is an attempt to bring together sixteen very different tribal identities into one state-level event, without pretending they are all part of one single Naga culture. In other words, it celebrates the tribes together while still keeping each one's identity separate and clear.
festivals.beliefs: The Hornbill Festival is a civic event organized by the government, not a religious one. Each individual tribe still keeps its own older, traditional festivals in its own way at other times of the year.
festivals.celebrate: People celebrate with war dances, performances on log drums, and traditional local games. There is also a contest where people compete to eat the extremely spicy Naga king chilli, along with motor vehicle rallies. In recent years, rock and metal music concerts have become part of the festival too, and they now attract their own crowd of fans.
festivals.local: Visitors usually notice the log drums first. These are made from hollowed out tree trunks, and they are large enough for several drummers to sit on at once. In the past, villages used these drums to send messages to each other over long distances. Today, they are mainly used to keep the beat for dancers.
festivals.image: Naga tribal dancers at Kisama Heritage Village, morungs and log drums, December dusk

festivals.name: Christmas
festivals.reach: Christmas is the single biggest festival of the year across the whole state.
festivals.what: Most people in Nagaland are Christian, and most of them belong to the Baptist church. Because of this, Christmas is treated as the most important event of the year, even more important than other festivals on the calendar, including the Hornbill Festival.
festivals.who: Almost the entire population of Nagaland takes part. Village Baptist churches, along with Catholic churches and other Christian groups, work together to organize the celebrations for the season.
festivals.when: Christmas Day is on December 25th, but carol singing services happen throughout December, and the celebrations often continue on into the new year.
festivals.origin: American Baptist missionaries began working among the Naga tribes in the 1800s. Over the course of the 1900s, more and more Naga people converted to Christianity. Today, Nagaland is one of the most heavily Baptist regions found anywhere in the world.
festivals.signifies: Christmas celebrates the birth of Jesus, which Christians call the nativity. It is also the one date that almost every Naga village and family celebrates together, even though the different tribes usually keep their own separate festivals on different days throughout the year.
festivals.beliefs: Nearly everyone in Nagaland goes to church on Christmas Eve and Christmas morning. Village choirs spend weeks practicing their singing before the big day arrives.
festivals.celebrate: People celebrate by singing carols as they go from house to house, and churches are decorated for the season. Villages hold community feasts that can last for several days. People also wear new clothes and give gifts to their neighbors and extended family.
festivals.local: In many villages, the Christmas feast is not just a meal for one household. Instead, it is a meal for the whole community, and every family brings food to share at a common table.
festivals.image: Village Baptist church decorated for Christmas, Naga congregation gathered outside, evening

festivals.name: Sekrenyi
festivals.reach: Angami villages keep this festival, and it is celebrated most strongly in and around Kohima district.
festivals.what: Sekrenyi is a ten-day purification festival celebrated by the Angami tribe. It marks the end of the old year's rituals and includes a ritual cleansing before the farming cycle starts again.
festivals.who: Angami Naga villages celebrate this festival, especially those in and around Kohima district.
festivals.when: It falls on the 25th day of the Angami month called Kezei, which usually lands in late February.
festivals.origin: Sekrenyi is an old Angami farming and purification tradition. The Angami tribe keeps track of its date using their own lunar calendar rather than the regular Gregorian calendar that most of the world uses.
festivals.signifies: The festival stands for cleansing before the year's work begins. This cleansing is thought of as happening both to the body and to the relationships that hold the village together.
festivals.beliefs: The most important ritual is called Kizie. During Kizie, a person takes a ritual bath at a chosen water source, and this bath is believed to purify them for the year ahead.
festivals.celebrate: People celebrate with a ceremonial bath at dawn, followed by feasting. Households share rice beer with each other, and people play traditional games and sing songs that tell the story of the community's history.
festivals.local: Each year, it is the young men who are formally initiated through the bathing ritual. Older Angami residents still think of this as marking which age group, or age-set, a young man belongs to.
festivals.image: Angami villagers at a ceremonial water source for Sekrenyi bathing rite, early morning

festivals.name: Aoling
festivals.reach: Konyak villages keep this festival, mostly in Mon district.
festivals.what: Aoling is the Konyak tribe's spring festival. It marks the end of the sowing season and the start of a new year, and it is celebrated over several days in Mon district, in the far north of the state.
festivals.who: Konyak Naga communities of Mon district celebrate this festival. The Konyak are historically known for their tradition of tattooed warriors and for having a system of chiefs that is different from other Naga tribes.
festivals.when: It runs from April 1st to April 6th.
festivals.origin: Aoling is an older Konyak farming new-year tradition, tied to the schedule for sowing crops in the hill fields.
festivals.signifies: It marks the turning point of the farming year, and it gives villages a chance to strengthen their ties to each other through feasting and dancing.
festivals.beliefs: Traditionally, this festival marked the start of a season of relative rest before the next round of farm work began.
festivals.celebrate: People celebrate with war dances performed in traditional Konyak clothing, along with feasting and rice beer. The festival also features displays of the region's distinctive headgear and body decorations.
festivals.local: The older generation in Mon district still carries facial tattoos that were once given to warriors. The festival is one of the few settings where this older tradition is actually worn by people, rather than just shown in a museum or display.
festivals.image: Konyak dancers in traditional dress and headgear, Mon district, daylight

festivals.name: Moatsu
festivals.reach: Ao villages keep this festival, mostly in Mokokchung district.
festivals.what: Moatsu is the Ao tribe's festival held after the sowing season. It gives villages a break before the long wait for the harvest to come in.
festivals.who: Ao Naga communities of Mokokchung district celebrate this festival.
festivals.when: It usually runs from May 1st to May 3rd, though some villages extend it to a full week.
festivals.origin: Moatsu is an older Ao farming tradition, timed to fall in the gap between sowing the crops and waiting for them to grow. The Ao tribe keeps track of the date using its own customary calendar.
festivals.signifies: It stands for rest that has been earned after the hard physical work of sowing is finished, before the labor of harvesting begins.
festivals.beliefs: The festival traditionally included something called the Sangpangtu, which is a shared fire and feast meant to strengthen unity among the young men of a village.
festivals.celebrate: People celebrate with communal feasting, folk songs, and dances, and households share rice beer with each other. In Ao villages that still keep the tradition, the Sangpangtu bonfire remains a central part of the celebration.
festivals.local: Older Ao residents describe Moatsu as the one clear pause in a farming year that otherwise never stops. This is part of the reason why the feasting at Moatsu tends to run longer than it does at other tribal festivals.
festivals.image: Ao villagers gathered around a Sangpangtu bonfire at night, Mokokchung

festivals.name: Tuluni
festivals.reach: Sumi villages keep this festival, mostly in Zunheboto district.
festivals.what: Tuluni is the Sumi tribe's most important festival. It is held when the crops in the fields reach a critical stage of growth, and it is named after tuluni, a rice beer that is specially prepared for the occasion.
festivals.who: Sumi Naga communities, also called Sema, of Zunheboto district celebrate this festival.
festivals.when: It falls on July 8th every year.
festivals.origin: Tuluni is an older Sumi farming festival tied to the growing season, rather than to the harvest itself.
festivals.signifies: It represents a request for a good crop, made at a point in the season when nobody yet knows how the harvest will turn out.
festivals.beliefs: Tuluni, the rice beer brewed specially for this day, is treated as central to the festival's blessing. It is not just a drink people happen to have on the side.
festivals.celebrate: People celebrate by brewing and sharing tuluni, feasting together, singing folk songs, and playing traditional games between neighboring villages.
festivals.local: Households judge the quality of a tuluni brew just as carefully as other Naga communities judge their own festival foods, and everyone notices if a batch turns out poorly.
festivals.image: Sumi villagers sharing rice beer at a Tuluni gathering, Zunheboto district

festivals.name: Tokhu Emong
festivals.reach: Lotha villages keep this festival, mostly in Wokha district.
festivals.what: Tokhu Emong is the Lotha tribe's post-harvest festival. Once the year's crop has been brought in, it becomes nine days of visiting, feasting, and making peace with others.
festivals.who: Lotha Naga communities of Wokha district celebrate this festival.
festivals.when: It begins on November 7th and lasts for nine days. Lotha elders set this fixed date in the twentieth century so that all villages, which had drifted onto slightly different local calendars over time, could celebrate the festival together on the same days.
festivals.origin: Tokhu Emong is an older Lotha tradition marking the close of the harvest. The community itself later agreed on a fixed common date for it, rather than having any outside authority set the date for them.
festivals.signifies: It stands for gratitude for the harvest, and it is deliberately set aside as a season for repairing quarrels before the year ends.
festivals.beliefs: The festival is built specifically around the idea of forgiveness. During Tokhu Emong, families and neighbors are expected to set aside any grudges they have been holding against each other.
festivals.celebrate: People celebrate by visiting each other's houses, sharing feasts, and performing community songs and dances. Friends and neighbors extend open invitations to each other for the entire nine days.
festivals.local: For Lotha families, the visiting itself is the whole point of the festival. If a household does not receive any visitors during Tokhu Emong, people understand this to mean the household has some kind of problem that is worth asking about.
festivals.image: Lotha villagers feasting together during Tokhu Emong, Wokha district

name: Mizoram
tagline: Mizoram is a hill state that shapes its year around three harvest festivals called kuts. It also spends a long stretch of the year preparing for and celebrating Christmas, which Mizos call Advent.

festivals.name: Christmas
festivals.reach: Christmas is the largest festival of the year across the whole state.
festivals.what: Most people in Mizoram are Christian, mostly belonging to the Presbyterian or Baptist churches. Christmas is the most important event of the year there, marked by church services that run for several days and feasts organized for the whole community to share.
festivals.who: Almost the entire population takes part, through the Presbyterian Church of Mizoram, which is the largest denomination, along with the Baptist Church and other congregations.
festivals.when: Christmas Day is December 25th, and celebrations often continue for several more days afterward.
festivals.origin: Welsh Presbyterian and British Baptist missionaries began working among the Mizo people in the late 1800s. Within just a few generations, nearly the entire Mizo population had converted to Christianity, and this reshaped the whole festival calendar around the Christian year.
festivals.signifies: Christmas celebrates the nativity, the birth of Jesus, and it is the one date that all of Mizo society observes together.
festivals.beliefs: Zaikhawm, which is congregational singing held on Christmas Eve, is treated as a central part of the celebration. In a single church service, hundreds of voices can be heard singing together.
festivals.celebrate: People celebrate with Zaikhawm singing on Christmas Eve, followed by midnight and Christmas morning church services. Churches or neighborhoods organize community feasts on the days that follow, and groups go around singing carols through Aizawl and the villages.
festivals.local: The community feast is often held on the second day of Christmas rather than on Christmas Day itself. This timing means that organizing the church services and preparing all the food do not have to compete for the same day.
festivals.image: Congregation singing at a lit Presbyterian church in Aizawl, Christmas Eve

festivals.name: Chapchar Kut
festivals.reach: It is celebrated widely across the state as a public cultural festival.
festivals.what: Chapchar Kut is Mizoram's largest cultural festival. It is held after bamboo and forest that has been cut down from hill slopes, as part of a farming method called jhum or shifting cultivation, has been left out to dry before it gets burned.
festivals.who: Mizo communities across the whole state take part. Today, it is organized just as much as a public cultural event as it is a village ritual.
festivals.when: It is held in March, during the gap of time between clearing the jhum fields and burning them.
festivals.origin: The festival is tied to a specific stage of the traditional jhum farming cycle. Originally, people kept it to give thanks and to mark having safely gotten through the dangerous work of clearing forest on the hillsides.
festivals.signifies: It stands for relief and thankfulness for having gotten through the clearing season without anyone getting hurt. It is also a pause before the harder work of the farming year continues.
festivals.beliefs: The festival used to have more religious content, thanking spirits connected to the land and to the work of farming. Since the Mizo people became Christian, this older religious meaning has mostly been replaced by a focus on culture and community instead.
festivals.celebrate: People celebrate with Cheraw, the bamboo dance, in which dancers form long lines and step in and out between bamboo poles that are clapped together in rhythm. The festival also includes traditional dress, folk songs, and public performances in Aizawl and other district towns.
festivals.local: Cheraw is the signature image of the festival, and it is now performed at cultural events far outside Mizoram too. However, Mizo dancers will point out that timing your steps between the clapping bamboo poles is much harder than it looks when you watch it on stage.
festivals.image: Cheraw bamboo dance in traditional Mizo dress, Aizawl festival ground

festivals.name: Mim Kut
festivals.aliases: Mim Kût, Festival of the Dead
festivals.reach: Mizo communities across the state keep this festival, though it is celebrated on a smaller public scale than Chapchar Kut.
festivals.what: Mim Kut is a harvest festival tied to the maize crop, which is called mim in Mizo. Traditionally, it is also a time to remember people who have died. It is one of the three main kuts, or festivals, of the Mizo farming year.
festivals.who: Mizo communities across the state celebrate this festival.
festivals.when: It happens in August or September, right after the maize harvest comes in.
festivals.origin: Mim Kut is an older Mizo farming tradition that combines giving thanks for the maize crop with rituals to remember anyone who had died since the last Mim Kut.
festivals.signifies: It stands for the harvest itself, celebrated alongside the memory of family members who have died and are no longer there to share in it.
festivals.beliefs: Traditionally, people believed that family members who had died were, in some sense, still present during the festival to receive the food that was offered in their memory.
festivals.celebrate: People celebrate by setting aside food and rice beer in memory of those who have died, feasting on the new maize crop, and gathering together as families.
festivals.local: Of the three kuts, Mim Kut has kept the most of its older, quieter character. It feels closer to a family observance than to a big public festival.
festivals.image: Mizo family gathering with maize harvest offerings, village home

festivals.name: Pawl Kut
festivals.season: After the rice and other crops are fully in
festivals.reach: Mizo communities across the state keep this festival, and in some areas it stretches into January.
festivals.what: Pawl Kut is the last of the three main kuts. It is a thanksgiving festival held once every crop for the year has been brought in, not just the rice.
festivals.who: Mizo communities across the state celebrate this festival.
festivals.when: It is held in December, or in some communities it continues into January, once the entire harvest is fully complete.
festivals.origin: Pawl Kut is an older Mizo farming tradition marking the close of the farming year. The name is generally understood as combining pawl, which means straw, and kut, which means festival.
festivals.signifies: It stands for thankfulness for a completed harvest and a full granary of stored food, celebrated just before the year turns over.
festivals.beliefs: Historically, this festival was treated as an occasion for households to show off and share the abundance of a harvest that had just been finished.
festivals.celebrate: People celebrate with feasting, rice beer, traditional games and songs, and visiting family and neighbors once all the fieldwork is done for the year.
festivals.local: Because Pawl Kut falls so close to Christmas, many villages now celebrate it on a smaller scale than they once did. It has essentially been folded into the same season as the church calendar.
festivals.image: Mizo village granary and harvest feast, Pawl Kut, December

festivals.name: Easter
festivals.reach: Easter is widely observed across the state's churches.
festivals.what: Easter is the second most important date on Mizoram's Christian calendar after Christmas. It is marked with services held across Presbyterian, Baptist, and other church denominations.
festivals.who: Mizo Christian congregations across the state celebrate Easter.
festivals.when: It falls in March or April, on the date set by the Christian liturgical calendar.
festivals.origin: Easter was brought to Mizoram by the same Welsh Presbyterian and Baptist missionaries who established Christianity in the Mizo hills starting in the late 1800s.
festivals.signifies: Easter marks the resurrection of Jesus. It involves less public feasting than Christmas does, but church attendance is about the same.
festivals.beliefs: Good Friday services, held in the days before Easter, are widely attended, along with the Easter Sunday service itself.
festivals.celebrate: People celebrate with church services throughout Holy Week, congregational singing, and family gatherings after the Easter Sunday service.
festivals.local: Aizawl's churches are at their fullest on Easter Sunday, just as they are at Christmas, in a state where regular Sunday church attendance is already high to begin with.
festivals.image: Easter Sunday service inside an Aizawl church, congregation seated

name: Arunachal Pradesh
languages: English (official), many distinct tribal languages (Nyishi, Adi, Apatani, Monpa (མོན་པ) and many others)
tagline: Arunachal Pradesh is home to twenty-six major tribes and more than a hundred smaller sub-tribes. Because there are so many different communities, there is no single festival that represents all of them together.

festivals.name: Losar
festivals.season: First day of the Tibetan lunar calendar
festivals.reach: The Monpa people and other Buddhist communities keep this festival, and it is celebrated most strongly in Tawang and West Kameng.
festivals.what: Losar is the Tibetan Buddhist new year. It is kept by the Monpa people of Tawang and West Kameng districts, whose religious life centers around Tawang Monastery.
festivals.who: Monpa communities celebrate Losar, along with other Buddhist groups in the western districts who practice Tibetan Buddhism.
festivals.when: It falls on the first day of the Tibetan lunar calendar, which usually lands in February or March.
festivals.origin: Losar is the shared new year celebrated by Tibetan Buddhist populations across the whole Himalayan region. The way the Monpa people observe it is closely tied to Tawang Monastery, which belongs to the Gelug school of Tibetan Buddhism and has centuries of history behind it.
festivals.signifies: Losar represents a ritual clearing away of the old year's obstacles and problems before the new year begins.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that the prayers and rituals performed in the days before Losar remove bad luck that has built up over the past year.
festivals.celebrate: People celebrate by putting up new prayer flags and bringing butter sculptures and offerings to the monastery. Monks perform Cham, which are masked dances, and families gather together and visit each other's homes.
festivals.local: The Cham dances at Tawang are performed in a set sequence over specific days. The local community does not just watch these dances, they also read meaning into them, since every mask and gesture stands for something. Visitors, however, are rarely given an explanation of what each part means.
festivals.image: Cham masked dance at Tawang Monastery, monks performing, prayer flags

festivals.name: Nyokum
festivals.reach: Nyishi communities across central Arunachal Pradesh keep this festival.
festivals.what: Nyokum is the main festival of the Nyishi, the largest tribe in the state. It is dedicated to Nyokum Yullo, a deity that people call upon for the community's prosperity and protection.
festivals.who: Nyishi communities celebrate this festival across Papum Pare, Kurung Kumey, Lower Subansiri, and other districts where the tribe has settled.
festivals.when: It falls on February 26th every year. The Nyishi Elders' Council set this fixed date so that villages, which had previously kept the festival on different local schedules, could celebrate it together.
festivals.origin: Nyokum is an older Nyishi ritual of calling upon the gods and giving thanks to the indigenous Donyi-Polo group of deities. It was later given one common fixed date so that the whole tribe could celebrate together with more unity.
festivals.signifies: It represents an appeal for the well-being and prosperity of the whole community, rather than just a single household or village.
festivals.beliefs: People call upon Nyokum Yullo as a deity of prosperity. They believe that the rituals performed by the priest secure the community's welfare for the coming year.
festivals.celebrate: The celebration includes rituals led by a priest, along with folk songs and dances performed by women and men in traditional dress. There is also feasting and community gatherings that bring Nyishi families back to their ancestral villages.
festivals.local: The festival has become a marker of Nyishi identity that goes beyond just the ritual itself. Nyishi families who work elsewhere in India increasingly plan their visits home to line up with this festival.
festivals.image: Nyishi community gathering in traditional dress for Nyokum rites, central Arunachal

festivals.name: Solung
festivals.reach: Adi communities of East Siang, Upper Siang, and neighboring districts keep this festival.
festivals.what: Solung is the Adi tribe's major farming festival. It is a five-day observance built around protecting the year's crop and giving thanks for it.
festivals.who: Adi communities across East Siang, Upper Siang, Siang, and neighboring districts celebrate this festival.
festivals.when: It lasts five days in early September.
festivals.origin: Solung is an older Adi farming ritual tied to the crop cycle. It combines protective rituals for the crop while it is still standing in the field with thanksgiving once the harvest is safely brought in.
festivals.signifies: It stands for protecting the crop against bad luck, and for gratitude once the harvest is safely secured.
festivals.beliefs: The rituals performed during Solung are meant to guard the harvest against disease and disaster. This concern is reflected in the animal sacrifices that traditionally go along with the festival.
festivals.celebrate: People celebrate with Ponung, a group dance performed by women while a male singer narrates stories from Adi oral tradition. There is also feasting, rice beer, and community gatherings across Adi villages.
festivals.local: The Ponung dance is also a way that the Adi people keep their oral history alive. The songs that go along with the dance tell stories, and villages treat these songs as a kind of historical record, not just as entertainment.
festivals.image: Adi women performing the Ponung dance during Solung, Siang valley

festivals.name: Mopin
festivals.reach: Galo communities of West Siang and neighboring districts keep this festival.
festivals.what: Mopin is the Galo tribe's spring festival. It is meant to drive away bad luck and invite a good harvest, and it centers around a distinctive dance performed by women.
festivals.who: Galo communities of West Siang, Lower Siang, and neighboring districts celebrate this festival.
festivals.when: It runs from April 5th to April 7th every year.
festivals.origin: Mopin is an older Galo ritual of purification and calling upon the gods before the growing season begins. It is related to festivals of the neighboring Adi tribe, but the Galo keep it as their own distinct tradition.
festivals.signifies: It stands for clearing away bad luck before planting begins, and for an appeal for abundance in the year ahead.
festivals.beliefs: People believe that the rituals performed by priests during Mopin drive out evil influence from the community before the farming season truly begins.
festivals.celebrate: People celebrate with Popir, a synchronized dance performed by women wearing white traditional dress. There is also rice beer, feasting, and community gatherings across Galo villages.
festivals.local: Popir is danced in long, coordinated lines, and the dancers are expected to move with great precision. This precision is a point of local pride that stands apart from the festival's religious meaning.
festivals.image: Galo women in white performing the Popir dance during Mopin, West Siang

festivals.name: Reh
festivals.reach: Idu Mishmi communities of Lower Dibang Valley and Dibang Valley districts keep this festival.
festivals.what: Reh is the main festival of the Idu Mishmi people. It is a six-day observance of thanksgiving and community feasting.
festivals.who: Idu Mishmi communities of Lower Dibang Valley and Dibang Valley districts celebrate this festival.
festivals.when: It is held in February, over six days.
festivals.origin: Reh is an older Idu Mishmi ritual of thanksgiving. It is kept within its own religious framework, which is distinct from the Donyi-Polo practices of neighboring tribes.
festivals.signifies: It stands for thanks for the community's well-being, and an appeal for abundance to continue.
festivals.beliefs: The rituals during Reh are conducted by an Igu, who is a priest and ritual specialist. The Igu's role in Idu Mishmi religious life extends far beyond just this one festival.
festivals.celebrate: People celebrate with rituals led by the priest, traditional dances and songs, feasting, and community gatherings across Idu Mishmi villages.
festivals.local: Because the Idu Mishmi population is fairly small and concentrated in the Dibang valley, Reh works almost as much as a way of counting who is still part of the community as it does as a religious occasion.
festivals.image: Idu Mishmi community gathering for Reh festival, Dibang Valley

festivals.name: Christmas
festivals.reach: Christmas is becoming increasingly significant, especially among the Nyishi, Nocte, Tangsa, Adi, and Tagin communities.
festivals.what: Christianity has grown very quickly in Arunachal Pradesh over the past fifty years, and it is now one of the state's largest religious groups, alongside Hinduism, the indigenous Donyi-Polo faith, and Buddhism. Christmas is celebrated on a real, large scale in the districts where the most people have converted to Christianity.
festivals.who: Christian congregations across many different tribes celebrate Christmas. Particularly high rates of conversion have been recorded among the Nyishi, Nocte, Tangsa, and Tagin, and a substantial minority of the Adi and Apatani have converted as well.
festivals.when: Christmas Day is December 25th, and church services and community gatherings take place throughout the weeks leading up to it.
festivals.origin: Christian missions, both from foreign countries and from within India, expanded across Arunachal Pradesh starting in the mid 1900s. Growth became especially rapid after the state's 2011 census, which showed that in several districts, the number of Christians had more than doubled over the previous ten years.
festivals.signifies: Christmas celebrates the nativity, the birth of Jesus. In this state, it now exists alongside indigenous festivals in many households, rather than replacing them.
festivals.beliefs: How often people attend church varies a lot depending on the district and the denomination. In many families, celebrating Christmas is added on top of their tribal festival calendar, rather than replacing it.
festivals.celebrate: People celebrate with church services, carol singing, community feasts, and family gatherings. The style of celebration varies locally depending on which tribe and which church denomination is involved.
festivals.local: How Christmas is celebrated differs enormously from one Arunachal district to the next, in a state where festival traditions were never the same everywhere to begin with.
festivals.image: Church congregation gathered for Christmas service, Arunachal hill town

name: Andaman and Nicobar Islands
tagline: The Andaman and Nicobar Islands are home to many settler communities who moved there from mainland India, and they keep celebrating their mainland festivals right by the sea. At the same time, there are remote islands in this archipelago that these mainland festivals rarely reach.

festivals.name: Island Tourism Festival
festivals.reach: The Island Tourism Festival is the territory's largest organized public festival, and it is centered on Port Blair.
festivals.what: This is a government-organized cultural festival held at Port Blair. It brings together the dance, food, and craft traditions of the territory's many settler communities into one shared program.
festivals.who: The territory administration organizes the festival, and performers and stallholders come from the islands' Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Malayali, Hindi-speaking, and other settler communities.
festivals.when: It is held in January, over roughly ten to twelve days, at the ITF Ground on VIP Road in Port Blair.
festivals.origin: The territory administration established this festival in 1988, and it was renamed the Island Tourism Festival in 1994. It was designed specifically to represent the islands' mixed population of mainland settlers, rather than to represent any single community.
festivals.signifies: It represents the patchwork of regional identities found among the settler population, presented as one shared civic event rather than as a bunch of separate community festivals.
festivals.beliefs: The festival has no religious content of its own. It is a secular event focused on civic pride and tourism.
festivals.celebrate: People celebrate with folk dance performances from each settler community, food stalls representing different regional cuisines, handicraft exhibitions, and water sports competitions.
festivals.local: In a single evening, the lineup of dances, Bengali, then Tamil, then Telugu, then Malayali, one after another on the same stage, gives a fair snapshot of who actually lives in Port Blair.
festivals.image: Folk dance performance at Island Tourism Festival ground, Port Blair, evening

festivals.name: Christmas
festivals.reach: Christmas is a major festival among Nicobarese communities and settler Christians, but it is largely absent from the life of the indigenous Andamanese people.
festivals.what: Christmas is kept in two quite different ways in this territory. In Port Blair and the Andaman islands, it is a festival kept by settler Christians. Among the Nicobarese people of the Nicobar group, however, Christianity is the dominant faith, since most Nicobarese are Christian, so Christmas is their main festival too.
festivals.who: The Nicobarese people of Car Nicobar and the wider Nicobar group celebrate Christmas, along with Christian settler communities such as the Anglo-Indian, Goan, Malayali, and others, who are mostly concentrated around Port Blair.
festivals.when: Christmas Day is December 25th.
festivals.origin: Christianity reached the Nicobarese through Anglican missionary work that was sponsored by the British administration starting in the 1800s. It kept expanding through the 1900s under Nicobarese church leadership, and today the community is among the most thoroughly Christian communities anywhere in India.
festivals.signifies: For the Nicobarese, Christmas represents a faith that has become almost universal within living memory. For settler communities, it represents a mainland church festival that has been transplanted to the islands.
festivals.beliefs: Church services on Car Nicobar draw close to the entire village population. This scale of attendance is uncommon even among strongly Christian communities on the mainland.
festivals.celebrate: People celebrate with church services, carol singing, and community feasting. In Nicobarese villages, these gatherings draw in most of the whole settlement, not just the households that regularly go to church.
festivals.local: Car Nicobar's Christmas is a village-wide event, but this is easy to miss if you are only looking from Port Blair, where the same date mostly registers as a settler holiday and an administrative day off.
festivals.image: Church service on Car Nicobar, Nicobarese congregation, Christmas morning

festivals.name: Pongal
festivals.reach: The territory's Tamil settler community keeps this festival, concentrated in parts of South Andaman and in pockets of the Nicobar islands.
festivals.what: Pongal is the Tamil harvest festival. Tamil settler families keep it here much the same way it is kept on the mainland, with the boiling over of the pongal pot as its central ritual.
festivals.who: Tamil-speaking settler households celebrate Pongal. Many of them are descended from laborers and settlers who were brought to the islands starting in the mid 1900s, including into parts of the Nicobar group.
festivals.when: It falls in mid-January, lining up with the festival of Makara Sankranti.
festivals.origin: Pongal was brought to the islands by Tamil settlers rather than developing there on its own. The festival is kept in essentially the same form as it is on the mainland.
festivals.signifies: It stands for thanks for the harvest and for the sun beginning to turn northward. On the islands, it is observed without the farmland that originally gave the festival its meaning.
festivals.beliefs: People treat the boiling over of milk and rice in the pongal pot as a sign, or omen, of how abundant the coming year will be, exactly as they do on the mainland.
festivals.celebrate: People celebrate by boiling the pongal pot outdoors, tying sugarcane and turmeric plants to their doorframes, drawing a kolam design at the threshold of the home, and gathering as families.
festivals.local: Tamil settler families in the islands keep the festival with noticeably little change from how it is done back on the mainland. It feels like a transplanted piece of Tamil Nadu, rather than a tradition that grew up on the islands themselves.
festivals.image: Pongal pot boiling over outdoors, kolam at the threshold, Tamil settler household

festivals.name: Durga Puja
festivals.reach: The territory's Bengali settler community keeps this festival, concentrated in parts of South and Middle Andaman.
festivals.what: Durga Puja is the central festival of the Bengali settler community. It is kept over several days, with community pandals, which are temporary decorated structures, set up in Bengali-majority settlements that trace back to resettlement after the Partition of India.
festivals.who: Bengali-speaking settler households celebrate Durga Puja. Many of them are descended from East Bengali refugees who were resettled on the islands starting in the 1950s.
festivals.when: It falls during the bright fortnight of the month of Ashwin, in September or October.
festivals.origin: Durga Puja was brought to the islands along with the organized resettlement of Bengali refugee families after Partition, when these families were given land across South and Middle Andaman. The festival was kept as a direct continuation of the way it had been practiced in the districts they had left behind.
festivals.signifies: It represents a piece of Bengali community identity that people have held onto, in settlements that were originally built out of displacement.
festivals.beliefs: At the close of the festival, people immerse the clay image of the goddess in water, just as they do on the mainland. On the islands, though, this happens in the sea instead of in a river.
festivals.celebrate: People celebrate by building pandals and clay images of the goddess, holding community worship over several days, putting on cultural programs, and holding immersion processions that end at the coast.
festivals.local: Immersing the goddess in the sea instead of a river is the one clearly local difference that Bengali settler families point to when asked how their Puja differs from the one they, or their parents, left behind on the mainland.
festivals.image: Durga Puja pandal in a Bengali settlement, South Andaman, immersion procession to the sea

festivals.name: Onam
festivals.reach: The territory's Malayali settler community keeps this festival, concentrated in Port Blair and parts of the Nicobar islands.
festivals.what: Onam is the Malayali settler community's harvest festival. It is kept with a sadya feast and community gatherings, though on a smaller scale than the equivalent Bengali or Tamil festivals.
festivals.who: Malayali-speaking settler households celebrate Onam, including communities in parts of the Nicobar Islands where a noticeable number of Malayalis have settled.
festivals.when: It falls in the month of Chingam, which is in August or September.
festivals.origin: Onam was brought to the islands through Malayali settlement and through government job postings, rather than developing there on its own.
festivals.signifies: It represents a piece of Kerala identity that people have held onto, kept alive by a settler community that is spread across a small number of islands rather than living together in one connected district.
festivals.beliefs: The festival carries the same legend of King Mahabali and the same way of observing it as it does in Kerala, without any local changes.
festivals.celebrate: People celebrate with Pookalam, which are flower carpets, an Onasadya feast served on a banana leaf, and community cultural programs put on by Malayali associations.
festivals.local: Malayali associations in Port Blair organize a shared community Onasadya specifically because individual households are often too scattered across the islands to hold their own feast on their own.
festivals.image: Onasadya feast on banana leaf at a Malayali community hall, Port Blair
